Some first translations were fiercely literal, produced by scholars who cared more about accuracy than about readers, and some of the most domesticating versions came decades later, written for mass-market series that wanted the classics to read like contemporary novels. A twentieth-century retranslation of an ancient epic into brisk modern prose is hardly a step closer to the source than a stiff Victorian version that preserved every repeated epithet.

What the record suggests instead is that retranslations answer to their own moment. Publishers commission new versions when copyrights expire, when a new readership appears, when a school curriculum changes, or when a rival house wants a product of its own. Translators, for their part, often define their work against a predecessor, so that a new version may be literal because the last one was loose, or loose because the last one was literal. The sequence looks less like progress than like a conversation, with each speaker responding to the one before.

Seeing retranslation this way does not make every version equally good. It does, however, free us from judging a translation by its place in a line. The useful question is not whether a version is later and therefore more faithful, but what it was trying to do, for whom, and against what.

qs.q: As the passage describes it, the retranslation hypothesis holds that:
o: first translations are usually the most literal versions
Paragraph 1 says the hypothesis treats first translations as domesticating, not literal.
later translations tend to be more faithful to the source than first ones
Correct: Paragraph 1 summarizes the hypothesis as a march toward fidelity.
classics are retranslated mainly when their copyrights expire
Copyright is one of the author’s own explanations in paragraph 3, not the hypothesis.
domesticating translations best serve readers new to a work
The hypothesis explains why first versions domesticate; it does not rank them as best.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 summarizes the retranslation hypothesis: first translations domesticate, later ones restore the original's strangeness, so retranslation is a march toward fidelity. Keep the hypothesis separate from the author's alternative in paragraph 3, which is where copyright and market reasons appear. Mixing up a reported view with the author's own view is a common CARS trap.

qs.q: The example of an ancient epic retranslated into brisk modern prose serves mainly to show that:
o: Victorian translators had no interest in their readers
Paragraph 2 calls the Victorian version stiff but makes no claim about indifference to readers.
modern prose cannot convey the meaning of ancient poetry
The author questions the prose version’s fidelity, not whether prose can ever convey meaning.
a later version can be more domesticating than an earlier one
Correct: Paragraph 2 uses it to show the sequence need not move toward fidelity.
mass-market publishers have improved access to the classics
Paragraph 2 cites mass-market series as a source of domestication, not of improved access.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 uses the brisk modern prose epic as a counterexample: a later version that is less faithful than a stiff Victorian one. Its job is to show that the sequence of translations does not always move toward fidelity. The choice about prose being unable to convey poetry overreaches, since the author only compares two versions and makes no general claim about prose.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT cited in the passage as a reason that publishers commission new translations?
o: Expiration of the copyright on an earlier version
Paragraph 3 lists expiring copyrights as a reason.
A change in what schools assign
Paragraph 3 lists curriculum changes as a reason.
A competing publisher’s wish for its own edition
Paragraph 3 lists a rival house wanting its own product.
Discovery of errors in an earlier translation
Correct: Paragraph 3 never mentions correcting errors as a reason.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 lists four reasons publishers commission new versions: expiring copyrights, a new readership, curriculum changes and a rival house wanting its own product. Correcting errors in an earlier translation is never mentioned. For NOT/EXCEPT questions, check each choice against the text and pick the one with no support.

qs.q: The author’s description of the sequence of translations as “a conversation” most strongly implies that:
o: each version is shaped partly by reaction to earlier ones rather than by steady approach to an ideal
Correct: Paragraph 3 says translators define their work against a predecessor, literal or loose in turn.
translators of the same work usually consult with each other directly
The metaphor is about responding to prior versions, not literal collaboration.
all versions of a classic are equally valuable
Paragraph 4 explicitly says not every version is equally good.
readers should compare every version before choosing one
The passage recommends asking what a version aimed to do, not reading them all.
qs.x: A conversation is a series of replies, so the metaphor means each version answers the one before it. Paragraph 3 makes this concrete: a new version may be literal because the last was loose, or loose because the last was literal. This replaces the image of steady progress toward an ideal. The 'equally valuable' choice is ruled out by paragraph 4.

qs.q: Which finding would most strongly support the author’s position over the retranslation hypothesis?
o: Successive translations of a novel over a century alternate between literal and free approaches.
Correct: Alternation fits paragraph 3’s reaction-to-predecessor model, not a steady march to fidelity.
Each successive translation of a play preserves more of its wordplay.
Steadily rising fidelity is exactly what the hypothesis in paragraph 1 predicts.
Most first translations of classics were made by scholars.
Paragraph 2 says only that some were; this alone does not decide between the views.
Readers usually prefer the most recent translation available.
Reader preference says nothing about whether versions grow more faithful.
qs.x: The two views predict different patterns: the hypothesis predicts fidelity rising over time, while the author predicts reactions to predecessors, which could swing back and forth. Alternating literal and free versions fit only the author's model in paragraph 3. Steadily rising fidelity in the play choice is exactly what the hypothesis predicts, so it supports the opposing view.

passages.title: Behind the Glass
text: The glass case is so familiar a feature of museums that visitors rarely notice it, yet it embodies a theory of what objects are for. Placed behind glass, a bowl ceases to be something one might drink from and becomes something one looks at. The case protects the object from dust, theft and the oils of human hands, but it also teaches a posture: stand back, keep still, use only your eyes.

This posture is historically recent. Early collectors often allowed, even expected, guests to handle their treasures; diarists of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries describe lifting antique vases, weighing coins in the palm and sniffing botanical specimens. As collections moved from private cabinets into public institutions, handling came to seem both dangerous and vulgar. The public was large and anonymous, conservators were learning how fragile many materials were, and a new ideal of disinterested contemplation held that the highest response to an object was visual and detached.

The conservators’ concerns were real, and many objects would not have survived a century of public fingering. But the triumph of the glass case also impoverished our relationship to things that were made to be used. A cooking pot is partly a matter of its weight, its balance, the way its handle fits the hand; a musical instrument is partly a sound. To present such objects as pure surfaces is to display them in a condition their makers never intended and their first users never knew. The case does not simply preserve the object; it translates it into the vocabulary of fine art.

Some museums now keep handling collections: replicas or sturdy duplicates that visitors may pick up, sometimes beside the originals in their cases. These programs are often treated as a concession to children. They might better be understood as a correction, a way of restoring senses the modern museum taught us to set aside.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Glass cases should be removed so visitors can handle every object.
Paragraph 3 accepts that many objects would not survive handling; the author wants correction, not removal.
Early collectors cared more about their objects than museums do.
Paragraph 2 describes handling, not greater care; conservators’ concerns are called real.
Handling collections are mainly useful for teaching children.
Paragraph 4 rejects treating them as a concession to children.
Glass cases protect objects but also impose a narrowly visual way of knowing them.
Correct: Paragraphs 1 and 3 grant protection but argue the case teaches look-only contemplation.
qs.x: The passage grants that cases protect objects (paragraphs 1 and 3) but argues they teach a look-only posture that impoverishes our relation to things made for use. A good main-idea choice includes both the concession and the criticism. The 'remove all cases' choice overstates the author, who accepts that many objects would not survive handling.

qs.q: Paragraph 2 cites each of the following as making handling seem inappropriate EXCEPT:
o: the size and anonymity of the new museum public
Paragraph 2 says the public was large and anonymous.
growing awareness of how fragile many materials were
Paragraph 2 says conservators were learning about fragility.
an ideal of detached, visual contemplation
Paragraph 2 names the ideal of disinterested contemplation.
a sharp drop in the number of objects held in collections
Correct: Paragraph 2 never mentions shrinking collections.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 gives three reasons handling came to seem dangerous and vulgar: a large anonymous public, conservators learning about fragility, and an ideal of detached visual contemplation. A drop in the size of collections never appears. In EXCEPT questions, the correct answer is the one the passage does not mention, even if it sounds plausible.

qs.q: The author’s attitude toward the conservators’ concerns is best described as:
o: dismissing them as a pretext for elitism
Paragraph 3 explicitly says the concerns were real.
treating them as decisive against any handling
Paragraph 4 endorses handling collections, so the concerns are not decisive.
regarding them as irrelevant to the argument
The author addresses them directly in paragraph 3 as a real consideration.
accepting them as legitimate while arguing they carried a cost
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the concerns real, then says the case impoverished our relation to used objects.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 begins by calling the conservators' concerns real, then turns with 'But' to the cost: objects made to be used became pure surfaces. That pattern is a qualified acceptance. The 'decisive' choice fails because paragraph 4 endorses handling collections, so the author does not think conservation concerns rule out all handling.

qs.q: In saying the case “translates” an object “into the vocabulary of fine art,” the author most likely means that the case:
o: leads viewers to treat a made-to-be-used object chiefly as something to look at
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the case presents used objects as pure surfaces for viewing.
causes curators to label objects with art-historical terms
The claim concerns how objects are experienced, not the wording of labels.
shows that museums value paintings above everyday artifacts
The author does not rank kinds of objects; the point is about mode of perception.
physically alters how an object’s colors appear
Translation here is a metaphor for changed meaning, not optical distortion.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a pot is partly its weight and an instrument partly its sound, and that the case shows such things as pure surfaces. 'Translating into the vocabulary of fine art' is a metaphor for that shift from use to viewing. Choices about labels or optical effects read the metaphor too literally.

qs.q: Which museum practice would the author most likely endorse?
o: Taking every fragile object out of its case for handling
Paragraph 3 concedes many objects would not survive handling.
Letting visitors hear recordings of displayed instruments being played
Correct: Paragraph 3 says an instrument is partly a sound, a sense the case removes.
Restricting handling collections to school groups
Paragraph 4 objects to treating handling as merely a concession to children.
Adding brighter lighting to sculpture galleries
Better lighting only intensifies the visual mode the author thinks is too narrow.
qs.x: The author wants to restore senses beyond sight for objects made to be used, and paragraph 3 says an instrument is partly a sound. Letting visitors hear instruments played does that without endangering the originals. Taking every fragile object out of its case contradicts the concession in paragraph 3, and brighter lighting only strengthens the visual mode the author criticizes.

qs.q: Which discovery would most challenge the historical claim made in paragraph 2?
o: Inventories show most early collectors kept prized items in locked cabinets guests could only view.
Correct: This contradicts paragraph 2’s claim that early guests were allowed or expected to handle objects.
Eighteenth-century diarists describe viewing paintings without touching them.
Paintings were never meant to be handled; this fits the passage’s focus on used objects.
Visitors spend more time in museums that offer handling collections.
Modern visitor behavior says nothing about early collecting practices.
Nineteenth-century conservators underestimated the fragility of textiles.
This concerns conservation knowledge, not whether early collectors allowed handling.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 claims early collectors let guests handle their treasures and even expected them to. Inventories showing items kept in locked, view-only cabinets would directly contradict that historical claim. The painting choice is consistent with the passage, because paintings were never objects meant for handling.

passages.title: The Workshop in the Kitchen
text: The standard image of industrialization is the factory: a tall brick building, a steam engine, rows of machines and a bell that calls workers in at dawn. Labor history grew up around this image. Its classic subjects were the mill hand, the strike, the union hall and the long fight over the length of the working day, and its sources were the records that factories and unions kept.

Yet across much of the nineteenth century, a large share of manufacturing never entered a factory at all. Shirts, matchboxes, artificial flowers, gloves and cigars were often finished in tenement rooms by women and children paid by the piece. Contractors delivered materials and collected finished goods; the work fit around cooking, nursing and other household tasks, and it often stretched late into the night. Because such labor left few payroll records and was rarely organized, it is thin in the archives that historians first consulted, and it long remained thin in the histories they wrote.

The omission was not merely a gap to be filled. It shaped the conclusions historians drew. If the factory is the model of industrial work, then industrialization looks like a process that pulled labor out of the home and drew a sharp line between paid work and domestic life. Homework suggests the opposite: for many families, industrial capitalism pushed wage labor into the home and made the line between the two more porous than ever. The struggle for a shorter working day, so central to the factory narrative, meant little to a woman whose pay depended on how many pieces she could finish before morning.

Recovering homework requires different sources: the reports of reformers and inspectors, court cases, and the recollections of the workers’ children. These sources have biases of their own, since reformers often described tenement workers as pitiable or dangerous. But they reveal an industrial world in which the factory was one site among several, and not always the most typical.

qs.q: According to the passage, home-based piecework long remained underrepresented in labor history because it:
o: left few payroll records and was rarely organized
Correct: Paragraph 2 says this is why homework is thin in the archives historians first used.
was illegal in most nineteenth-century cities
The passage never says homework was illegal.
employed only a small share of industrial workers
Paragraph 2 says a large share of manufacturing happened outside factories.
was dismissed by historians as unskilled labor
The passage blames missing sources, not a judgment about skill.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 explains the gap: homework left few payroll records and was rarely organized, so it was thin in the factory and union archives historians first used. The author's explanation is about sources, not about how much homework there was. The 'small share' choice contradicts paragraph 2, which says a large share of manufacturing happened outside factories.

qs.q: The primary purpose of paragraph 3 is to:
o: argue that neglecting homework distorted the broader account of industrialization
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the omission shaped historians’ conclusions about home and paid work.
describe the daily routine of tenement workers
Daily routine appears in paragraph 2; paragraph 3 is about historical interpretation.
show that factory work declined in the nineteenth century
The passage does not claim factory work declined.
explain why reformers opposed homework
Reformers appear in paragraph 4 as sources, not in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 opens by saying the omission was not merely a gap but shaped historians' conclusions. It then shows how the factory model made industrialization look like it separated home and paid work, while homework shows the reverse. Purpose questions ask what a paragraph does in the argument; the daily-routine details belong to paragraph 2.

qs.q: The author’s reference to the struggle for a shorter working day most likely suggests that:
o: a central issue of factory-based labor history did not match homeworkers’ conditions
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the issue meant little to a worker paid per piece finished by morning.
homeworkers opposed limits on the length of the workday
The author says the issue meant little to them, not that they opposed it.
the campaign for shorter hours ultimately failed
The passage says nothing about the campaign’s outcome.
piece rates paid more than factory wages did
No wage comparison is made; the point is about how pay was structured.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the shorter-day struggle meant little to a woman paid by the piece. The point is that a central issue of factory-based history did not fit homeworkers' conditions, which supports the claim that the factory model distorted the story. 'Meant little to' is not the same as opposing, so the opposition choice overreads the text.

qs.q: The author’s view of reformers’ and inspectors’ reports is that they are:
o: too biased to tell us anything reliable about homework
Paragraph 4 says they still reveal an industrial world beyond the factory.
more objective than the records factories kept
The author never ranks their objectivity above factory records.
valuable sources that must be read with attention to their biases
Correct: Paragraph 4 says these sources have biases yet reveal a world beyond the factory.
useful mainly for studying the reformers themselves
The author uses them to recover homework, not mainly to study reformers.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 admits reformers' reports carry biases, since reformers often described tenement workers as pitiable or dangerous, yet says these sources still reveal a world beyond the factory. That is a balanced view: useful evidence, read critically. The 'too biased' choice ignores the paragraph's 'But' clause.

qs.q: Which finding would most strongly support the passage’s argument?
o: Factory employment grew faster than homework late in the century.
This does not show homework was overlooked or that the home and work line blurred.
Unions successfully organized most homeworkers by 1880.
Paragraph 2 says homework was rarely organized, so this conflicts with the passage.
Most piecework was done by men in small workshops.
Paragraph 2 describes piecework by women and children in tenement rooms.
Surviving contractors’ ledgers show paid sewing by many married women whom a census listed as having no occupation.
Correct: This shows home wage labor hidden in standard records, as paragraphs 2 and 3 claim.
qs.x: The argument has two parts: standard records hid home wage labor, and that labor blurred the line between home and paid work. Ledgers showing paid sewing by married women whom the census listed as having no occupation support both parts at once. The union choice contradicts paragraph 2, which says homework was rarely organized.

passages.title: Ruins Made to Order
text: In the eighteenth century, wealthy English landowners began commissioning ruins. Architects designed crumbling abbeys, broken columns and roofless towers to stand at the end of garden vistas, and builders took care to make new stone look old, leaving gaps in walls and sometimes planting ivy to finish the effect. Two verdicts on these follies have dominated. Critics found them ridiculous, proof of a decadent taste that preferred the counterfeit to the genuine; admirers have defended them as pure scenery, built to frame a pleasing melancholy. Both verdicts treat the folly as a question of taste. I think it is better read as a claim about property.

Consider who built them. Some of the great estates had been assembled from land that changed hands under pressure, through the seizure of monastic property in the sixteenth century or the enclosure of common fields in the eighteenth. Some owners were recent arrivals whose fortunes came from trade, finance or overseas plantations. For such families, a ruined abbey at the end of the lawn did useful work. It lent the estate an antiquity its owners lacked, implied a continuity between the medieval past and the present household, and turned the traces of dispossession into ornament.

The sham ruin, in other words, was a kind of pedigree in stone. An old family could point to an old house; a new one could build a past and place it where every guest would see it. The ivy was not only picturesque. It was a signature of time, applied by hand to a title that time had not yet granted.

None of this means the follies were not also beautiful, or that their owners felt nothing before them. Motives are rarely single. But a reading that stops at mood takes the landowners' own presentation at face value. To ask what a ruin was for is to notice that the past, in these gardens, was not merely contemplated. It was owned.

qs.q: The author’s main argument is that eighteenth-century artificial ruins are best understood as:
o: evidence of a decadent preference for the counterfeit
This is the critics’ verdict, which paragraph 1 says treats the folly merely as a question of taste.
assertions of social standing and a claim to own the past
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the folly is better read as a claim about property, and paragraph 3 calls it a pedigree in stone.
scenery designed purely to frame a pleasing melancholy
This is the admirers’ verdict; paragraph 4 says stopping at mood takes owners at face value.
faithful copies of particular medieval abbeys
The passage never says follies copied specific real buildings.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 lays out two verdicts, critics’ mockery and admirers’ praise of mood, and rejects both as treating the folly only as taste. The author’s own claim is that the folly asserted property and pedigree, as paragraphs 2 and 3 develop. The melancholy choice is tempting because paragraph 4 grants the follies were beautiful, but it says a reading that stops at mood misses their purpose.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, builders made new follies look old by:
o: reusing stones taken from real medieval abbeys
The passage never mentions reusing old stone.
staining the stone with soot and tar
No such technique is described in paragraph 1.
leaving gaps in walls and sometimes planting ivy
Correct: Paragraph 1 names both techniques.
burying parts of the structure in earth
Paragraph 1 does not mention burial.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says builders made new stone look old by leaving gaps in walls and sometimes planting ivy to finish the effect. Detail questions are answered by locating the exact sentence. Reusing abbey stone sounds plausible given paragraph 2’s mention of monastic land, but the passage never says it happened.

qs.q: The author mentions that some owners’ fortunes came from trade, finance or overseas plantations primarily in order to:
o: condemn the moral basis of colonial wealth
The passage notes the sources of wealth without passing moral judgment on them.
show that follies were too costly for older families
Cost is never discussed in the passage.
explain why such owners would want to display an antiquity they lacked
Correct: Paragraph 2 says the ruin lent the estate an antiquity its owners lacked.
suggest that new families had worse taste than old ones
The author sets aside judgments of taste in paragraph 1.
qs.x: The newcomer detail supplies a motive: families without old lineage had reason to manufacture the look of one. Paragraph 2 then says the ruin lent the estate an antiquity its owners lacked, and paragraph 3 calls it a pedigree in stone. The taste choice fails because paragraph 1 explicitly moves the discussion away from taste.

qs.q: In describing ivy as “applied by hand to a title that time had not yet granted,” the author most likely means that:
o: ivy grew too slowly, so builders transplanted mature plants
This reads the metaphor literally; the passage is about meaning, not gardening.
the look of age lent owners’ claims a legitimacy usually earned only by long possession
Correct: Paragraph 3 casts the ruin as a pedigree, faking the standing that time confers.
the owners lacked legal title to their estates
The passage questions social legitimacy, not the legality of ownership.
the follies were built before the estates were purchased
Nothing in the passage concerns the order of building and purchase.
qs.x: In paragraph 3, 'title' plays on two senses: a claim to the land and the standing of an old family. Time normally grants that standing through generations of possession; the ivy fakes the marks of those generations. The legal-title choice is tempting but too literal, since the author never says the owners did not legally own their estates.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author’s argument?
o: Many visitors described feeling melancholy before follies.
Paragraph 4 already grants that follies had aesthetic and emotional effects.
Follies were built mostly by long-established families, rarely by newcomers or owners of former monastic land.
Correct: Paragraph 2 rests the property reading on newcomers and contested land.
Some follies were modeled loosely on real ruined abbeys.
This fits the author’s account of building a borrowed past.
Critics mocked follies as early as the 1760s.
When critics objected says nothing about why owners built follies.
qs.x: The author infers the follies’ purpose from who built them: newcomers and holders of seized or enclosed land had a reason to fake antiquity, per paragraph 2. If builders were mostly old families on long-held land, that motive disappears and the property reading loses its main support. Reports of melancholy do not weaken it, because paragraph 4 concedes the follies also moved people.

qs.q: Which of the following is most analogous to the folly as the author interprets it?
o: A museum displays genuine artifacts with careful labels.
Genuine, labeled objects are evidence, not a manufactured past.
A novelist sets a story in a ruined abbey to create a gloomy mood.
This is the mood-centered reading the author finds incomplete.
A city restores a damaged cathedral to its original form.
Restoring a real building is not inventing a past to claim status.
A newly rich family commissions a coat of arms and portraits of invented ancestors.
Correct: Like the folly in paragraph 3, this builds a visible pedigree to claim standing.
qs.x: On the author’s reading, the folly’s function is social: a newly risen family manufactures visible signs of age to claim standing it has not inherited (paragraphs 2 and 3). A commissioned coat of arms and invented ancestral portraits do the same work. The novelist choice uses a ruin too, but for mood, the reading paragraph 4 says takes the owners’ presentation at face value.

passages.title: The Tale Without an Original
text: When nineteenth-century collectors went into the countryside to record folktales, they believed they were rescuing something old and fragile: the authentic voice of the people, preserved by oral tradition and threatened by literacy and the city. Their published volumes presented the tales as found objects, faithfully transcribed. We now know that many collectors polished what they heard, merging versions from different tellers, cutting coarse episodes, adding moral reflections and, in some cases, relying on informants who were themselves well-read members of the middle class.

It is tempting to respond to these revelations with disillusionment, to conclude that the collections are forgeries and that the true folktale lies somewhere behind them, uncontaminated. But this response repeats the collectors’ own error. It assumes that there was once a pure, original version of each tale, and that every later telling is a degradation of it. Oral tradition does not work that way. A tale exists only in its performances, and each teller adapts it to an audience, a season and a purpose. There is no first telling to recover, only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale itself.

Seen in this light, the collector who edited a story was not stepping outside tradition but taking part in it. He was one more teller, adapting the material for a new audience, the reading public, as village storytellers had adapted it for the hearth. His version differs from theirs in its medium and its reach, not in its basic relationship to some lost source.

This does not excuse the collectors’ claims of fidelity, which misled readers about what they were getting. The problem was not that they changed the tales; it was that they denied changing them. The honest folklorist today records the variants, names the tellers, and admits her own hand in shaping the record.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the discovery that collectors edited the tales they published?
o: The collections are forgeries that hide the true folktales.
Paragraph 2 rejects this disillusioned response as repeating the collectors’ error.
The editing was harmless because readers knew the tales had been changed.
Paragraph 4 says the claims of fidelity misled readers.
Scholars should reconstruct each tale’s original version.
Paragraph 2 says there is no first telling to recover.
The claims of fidelity were wrong, but the editing itself continued oral tradition.
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the editor one more teller; paragraph 4 faults only the denial of changes.
qs.x: The author splits the verdict: paragraph 4 faults the collectors for claiming fidelity, while paragraph 3 says editing a tale was itself part of oral tradition. Watch for answers that capture only half a two-part position. The 'forgeries' choice is the disillusioned reaction paragraph 2 rejects, because it assumes a pure original that never existed.

qs.q: The phrase “a cloud of variants” in paragraph 2 primarily emphasizes that:
o: no single version of a tale is privileged as the original
Correct: Paragraph 2 says no variant has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale.
the tales were vague and hard to transcribe
The image concerns many equal versions, not vagueness of content.
the oldest versions have been lost forever
The author denies there was a single first version to lose.
collectors confused tales from different regions
The phrase describes oral tradition itself, not collectors’ mistakes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a tale exists only in its performances, so there is 'only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others.' The image stresses many equal versions with no privileged original. The 'lost oldest version' choice is tempting but backwards, since the author denies there was ever a single first telling to lose.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, which practice did some collectors engage in?
o: Recording tellers with early sound equipment
The passage never mentions sound recording.
Merging versions told by different storytellers
Correct: Paragraph 1 lists merging versions from different tellers.
Paying storytellers to invent new tales
Paragraph 1 describes polishing tales, not commissioning inventions.
Translating foreign tales and passing them off as local
No such practice is described in paragraph 1.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 lists what some collectors did: polished tales, merged versions from different tellers, cut coarse episodes, added morals and used well-read middle-class informants. Merging versions is named directly. The other choices sound like plausible editorial abuses, but none appears in the passage.

qs.q: The author would most likely criticize a modern folklorist who:
o: publishes several variants of a tale with tellers named
Paragraph 4 describes this as the honest folklorist’s practice.
adapts a tale for children and notes the changes made
Paragraph 3 treats adapting as tradition; noting changes meets paragraph 4’s honesty standard.
publishes one composite tale as a single teller’s exact words
Correct: Paragraph 4 faults denying changes, which this does by hiding the merging.
describes her own role in shaping the record
Paragraph 4 says the honest folklorist admits her own hand.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 locates the collectors’ fault in denying their changes, not in making them. A folklorist who presents a composite tale as one teller’s exact words repeats that denial. The children’s-adaptation choice is a trap: adapting is acceptable on paragraph 3’s view, and noting the changes meets paragraph 4’s standard of honesty.

qs.q: Which approach is most consistent with the author’s view of oral tales?
o: An editor restores a novel to the text of the author’s original manuscript.
This assumes an authoritative original, the model paragraph 2 says oral tradition lacks.
A scholar seeks the earliest written version of a tale to identify its true form.
Paragraph 2 rejects the idea of a pure first version.
A curator removes later additions from a medieval song collection.
This treats later changes as contamination, the error the author identifies.
A musicologist treats each recorded performance of a traditional ballad as an equally legitimate form of the song.
Correct: This mirrors paragraph 2: the work exists only in performances, none privileged.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 holds that an oral tale has no authoritative original and exists only in performances, none privileged over the others. A musicologist treating every ballad performance as an equally legitimate form of the song applies that view directly. The other three choices all assume an original or earlier form against which later versions count as departures or contamination.

passages.title: Where the Mind Stops
text: Where does a mind end? The natural answer is at the skull, or perhaps the skin. But a well-known argument in philosophy challenges that boundary. Imagine a man with failing memory who records everything he needs in a notebook he always carries. When he wants to visit a museum, he consults the notebook for the address, just as another person would consult biological memory. If the two processes play the same role in guiding behavior, the argument runs, then we should count the notebook as part of the man’s memory, and so part of his mind. To insist otherwise is to privilege the inside of the head for no principled reason.

The argument is ingenious, and its defenders have been careful. They do not claim that every tool we touch becomes mental. The notebook counts only because it is reliably available, routinely consulted and automatically trusted, conditions that a library book or a stranger’s advice would fail. Still, I think the conclusion moves too quickly.

Consider what happens when the notebook is wrong. If someone secretly alters an entry, the man will go to the wrong street with complete confidence. Biological memory errs too, of course, but its errors are his own in a way the notebook’s are not: they arise from processes that are bound up with his other beliefs and that he can, in principle, question from within. The tampered notebook is a case not of misremembering but of being deceived. That we describe the two failures so differently suggests that our concept of the mind tracks something besides functional role, something like ownership, a sense in which certain processes answer to the person and others are merely relied upon.

None of this shows that tools do not matter to thinking; plainly they do, and much human intelligence lies in the skillful use of external aids. But a mind that depends deeply on its tools is not thereby a mind that contains them.

qs.q: The argument described in paragraph 1 concludes that the notebook is part of the man’s mind because:
o: it plays the same role in guiding his behavior as biological memory would
Correct: Paragraph 1 rests the conclusion on the two processes playing the same role.
he wrote every entry in it himself
Authorship is never offered as the reason in paragraph 1.
it stores more information than his biological memory
The argument is about equal role, not greater capacity.
his biological memory no longer functions at all
Paragraph 1 says his memory is failing, and the argument does not depend on total loss.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 rests the extended-mind conclusion on functional role: the notebook guides behavior just as biological memory would, so it counts as memory. The argument depends on equal function, not on authorship or greater capacity. The 'total memory loss' choice overstates the case, since paragraph 1 describes memory as failing, not gone.

qs.q: Which condition is NOT among those the argument’s defenders require for a tool to count as part of the mind?
o: The tool must be reliably available.
Paragraph 2 lists reliable availability.
The person must have created the tool himself.
Correct: Paragraph 2 lists availability, routine use and automatic trust, not creation.
The tool must be routinely consulted.
Paragraph 2 lists routine consultation.
The tool’s contents must be automatically trusted.
Paragraph 2 lists automatic trust.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists three conditions: reliable availability, routine consultation and automatic trust. These rule out casual tools such as a library book. The passage never requires that the person made the tool himself; the man does write in his notebook, which makes the creation choice tempting, but authorship is never given as a condition.

qs.q: The author introduces the case of the altered notebook in order to:
o: prove that notebooks are less reliable than biological memory
Paragraph 3 grants that biological memory errs too; reliability is not the point.
argue that the man should stop relying on his notebook
Paragraph 4 praises skillful use of external aids.
illustrate the conditions the argument’s defenders impose
Those conditions appear in paragraph 2; the tampering case is the author’s objection.
show that notebook errors are described as deception, suggesting mind involves more than functional role
Correct: Paragraph 3 says we call it being deceived, not misremembering, which points to ownership.
qs.x: The tampering case is the author’s objection. Paragraph 3 notes that we call an altered entry being deceived, not misremembering, and infers that our concept of mind tracks ownership as well as function. The reliability choice misreads the point, because the author grants that biological memory errs too.

qs.q: The reasoning in paragraph 3 depends most heavily on which assumption?
o: Biological memory is never influenced by other people.
The author says only that its errors are the person’s own, not that others never affect it.
Functional role has no bearing at all on what counts as mental.
The author says the concept tracks something besides functional role, not instead of it.
Notebooks are usually tampered with by others.
The case is hypothetical; nothing assumes tampering is common.
How we ordinarily describe failures reveals something about our concept of mind.
Correct: Paragraph 3 infers what the concept tracks from the different ways we describe two failures.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 moves from how we describe two failures (misremembering versus being deceived) to a conclusion about what our concept of mind tracks. That step only works if ordinary descriptions reveal something about the concept. The 'functional role has no bearing' choice overstates the claim: the author says the concept tracks something besides functional role, not instead of it.

qs.q: Which reply by a defender of the notebook argument would most directly counter paragraph 3?
o: Notebooks are often more reliable than human memory.
Paragraph 3 does not turn on reliability, so this misses the objection.
Many people now store information on their phones.
How common the practice is does not address the ownership argument.
Others can also reshape biological memory, as with misleading questions, yet we still call the result misremembering.
Correct: This attacks paragraph 3’s asymmetry between deception from outside and misremembering from within.
A library book fails the condition of reliable availability.
This restates paragraph 2 and leaves the tampering argument untouched.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 depends on an asymmetry: errors from inside the head are one’s own, while altered notebook entries count as outside deception. If others can reshape biological memory through misleading questions and we still call it misremembering, the asymmetry weakens. Replies about reliability or how common phones are leave the ownership argument untouched.

qs.q: The author would most likely describe a driver who relies entirely on a navigation app as:
o: having a mind that extends into the app
This is the view the author rejects in paragraph 4.
showing a failure of intelligence
Paragraph 4 says skillful use of external aids is part of human intelligence.
using an external aid intelligently without the app becoming part of her mind
Correct: Paragraph 4 says tools matter and reflect intelligence, but a mind that depends on tools does not contain them.
being deceived whenever she follows the app
Deception arises only when contents are altered, per paragraph 3, not from reliance itself.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 holds two things together: skillful use of external aids is part of intelligence, but depending on a tool does not make the tool part of the mind. A driver relying on a navigation app fits both. The 'mind extends into the app' choice is the extended-mind conclusion the author rejects.

passages.title: When the House Lights Went Down
text: For most of theatrical history, audiences sat in the light. In the public playhouses of Shakespeare’s London, performances took place in the afternoon under an open sky; in the indoor theaters of the following centuries, candles and later oil lamps lit the auditorium as well as the stage, and they stayed lit throughout the performance. Spectators could see one another as clearly as they saw the actors, and they behaved accordingly. They talked, ate, flirted, called out to the performers and demanded encores in the middle of scenes. Going to the theater was a social event in which the play was one attraction among several.

The darkened auditorium arrived only in the nineteenth century, made practical by gas lighting that could be dimmed from a central control and promoted by reformers and composers who wanted undivided attention. Wagner’s festival theater at Bayreuth, which plunged its audience into darkness and hid the orchestra from view, became the emblem of the new regime. Within a few decades, silence in the dark had come to seem not one convention among others but simply what serious theatergoing meant.

We usually tell this story as one of refinement: the rowdy crowd was tamed, and the artwork at last received the concentration it deserved. But something was lost too. In the dark, each spectator is alone with the stage. The audience ceases to be a public that can see itself and becomes a collection of private viewers, each absorbed in an experience that is, in effect, delivered to them. The lit house made the audience a participant whose responses the actors had to reckon with; the dark house made it a recipient.

It is telling that many of the twentieth century’s most adventurous directors tried to break the darkness, turning up the house lights, sending actors into the aisles or seating spectators on the stage. They were not inventing a new relation between stage and audience. They were trying to recover an old one.

qs.q: According to the passage, what made the darkened auditorium practical?
o: Gas lighting that could be dimmed from a central control
Correct: Paragraph 2 credits dimmable, centrally controlled gas lighting.
Electric lighting introduced at Bayreuth
Paragraph 2 mentions gas, not electric, lighting.
Candles placed only around the stage
Paragraph 1 says candles lit the auditorium too and stayed lit.
Shifting performances from afternoon to evening
The passage does not attribute darkening to performance times.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the darkened auditorium was made practical by gas lighting that could be dimmed from a central control. Detail questions reward the specific technology named. The electric-lighting choice is a trap built from outside knowledge; the passage mentions only gas, and it describes Bayreuth by its darkness and hidden orchestra, not its lighting system.

qs.q: The author’s attitude toward the story of “refinement” is best described as:
o: fully endorsing it as an account of progress
Paragraph 3 says something was lost, so the endorsement is not complete.
rejecting it as a myth with no basis
The author does not deny that crowds were tamed or attention gained.
indifferent, since it is irrelevant to the argument
The refinement story is the view the author’s argument is built against.
accepting part of it while insisting it leaves out a real loss
Correct: Paragraph 3 grants the taming story, then says, “But something was lost too.”
qs.x: Paragraph 3 grants the refinement story (the crowd was tamed and the artwork got concentration) and then says, 'But something was lost too.' That is partial acceptance with a stated cost. The 'myth with no basis' choice is too strong, since the author never denies that attention increased.

qs.q: In calling the lit-house audience a “participant,” the author most likely means that:
o: spectators were regularly invited to act in the play
Paragraph 3 refers to responses like calling out, not acting roles.
spectators’ visible responses were something the actors had to take into account
Correct: Paragraph 3 says actors had to reckon with the lit audience’s responses.
spectators paid to help produce the performances
Nothing in the passage concerns financing.
spectators were quieter and more attentive than later audiences
Paragraph 1 describes lit-house audiences as talkative and rowdy.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 contrasts a lit-house audience the actors had to reckon with against a dark-house audience that simply receives the performance. 'Participant' therefore means that spectators’ visible, audible responses shaped the performance. The literal reading, that spectators acted in the play, confuses taking part in the event with being cast in it.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author’s account of why audience behavior changed?
o: Gas lighting was more expensive to run than candles.
Cost does not bear on whether darkness changed behavior.
Bayreuth hid its orchestra from the audience’s view.
Paragraph 2 already states this; it is consistent with the account.
Audiences had already become quiet and attentive decades before auditoriums were darkened.
Correct: Paragraphs 2 and 3 tie silent, private viewing to darkness; earlier quiet would undercut that link.
Some modern theaters keep a dim light in the auditorium.
Partial modern lighting does not address the nineteenth-century change.
qs.x: The author ties the move to silent, private viewing to the darkened house (paragraphs 2 and 3). If audiences had grown quiet decades before the lights went down, darkness could not be the cause, so the account would be undercut. The Bayreuth orchestra choice repeats a detail the passage already states, so it cannot challenge the account.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely see a comedy club where performers respond to a visible, vocal crowd as:
o: an example of the refined attention Wagner promoted
Paragraph 2 links Wagner to silence in the dark, the opposite of this.
proof that darkened theaters create private viewers
A visible, vocal crowd is the contrast to private viewing, not proof of it.
closer to the older theater, with the audience as participant
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the lit house made the audience a participant the performers reckoned with.
a wholly new relation between stage and audience
Paragraph 4 says such relations recover an old one rather than invent a new one.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the lit house made the audience a participant whose responses performers had to reckon with. A comedy club where performers work off a visible, vocal crowd fits that older relation. The 'wholly new relation' choice contradicts paragraph 4, which says efforts to break the darkness recover an old relation rather than invent a new one.

passages.title: A Pattern, Not a Law
text: Few ideas in the social sciences have been as influential as the demographic transition. In its classic form, the model describes a sequence through which every society passes as it modernizes: first, high birth and death rates; then falling death rates, as food supply and sanitation improve, while births remain high and population grows rapidly; finally, falling birth rates, as urban life, schooling and industrial wages make large families costly. The model is elegant, and it describes the broad arc of many countries’ histories reasonably well.

The difficulty arises when the description is treated as an explanation. Historical demographers who mapped the decline of fertility across nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century Europe found that it did not follow economic development as closely as the model implies. France, still largely rural, saw marital fertility begin to fall around the time of the Revolution, generations before more industrialized England. Within countries, the timing of decline often tracked boundaries of language and religion more closely than levels of urbanization or income: neighboring districts with similar economies limited births at very different dates if they spoke different languages.

These findings point to something the classic model left out: the spread of ideas. Deliberately limiting births within marriage requires not only an economic motive but also the conviction that family size is a matter of choice rather than fate, and that conviction appears to have traveled along networks of communication and shared culture. Once it took hold in a community, it could spread whether or not the local economy had changed much.

None of this means that economic conditions are irrelevant; incomes, schooling and child mortality clearly matter. But the transition is better understood as a historical pattern produced by many interacting causes than as a law that modernization automatically sets in motion. Policymakers who expect development alone to lower birth rates on a fixed schedule are relying on a regularity that was never as regular as it looked.

qs.q: According to the classic model described in paragraph 1, what happens in the middle stage of the transition?
o: Birth rates fall while death rates stay high, so population shrinks.
This reverses the order given in paragraph 1.
Birth and death rates both fall, so population stabilizes.
Paragraph 1 places falling births in the final stage.
Death rates fall while birth rates stay high, so population grows quickly.
Correct: Paragraph 1 describes falling deaths with high births and rapid growth.
Birth and death rates both stay high, so population is steady.
Paragraph 1 describes this as the first stage.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 gives three stages: high birth and death rates, then falling death rates with births still high and rapid growth, then falling birth rates. The middle stage is the gap between falling deaths and still-high births, which is why population surges. The 'both fall' choice describes the final stage, not the middle.

qs.q: The author mentions France primarily to show that:
o: the French Revolution caused fertility to decline
The Revolution is a time marker; no causal claim is made.
fertility decline could begin without extensive industrialization
Correct: Paragraph 2 notes rural France limited births generations before industrial England.
England’s fertility never fell to French levels
The passage says nothing about England’s later fertility levels.
rural societies always limit births earlier than urban ones
One case cannot establish “always,” and the author does not claim it.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes that France, still largely rural, began limiting marital fertility generations before industrial England. That example separates fertility decline from industrialization, against the classic model. The Revolution is only a time marker, so reading it as a cause is unsupported.

qs.q: The author’s main criticism of the demographic transition model is that it:
o: fails to describe any country’s history accurately
Paragraph 1 says it describes many countries’ broad arc reasonably well.
is often treated as a causal law driven by economic development rather than as a description
Correct: Paragraph 2 says the difficulty arises when the description is treated as explanation.
ignores the role of falling death rates
Falling death rates are part of the model as paragraph 1 describes it.
overstates the importance of language and religion
The author says the model left out such cultural factors.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 places the problem precisely: the difficulty arises when the description is treated as an explanation. The author grants in paragraph 1 that the model describes many countries’ broad arc reasonably well, so the 'fails to describe any history' choice is too strong. The objection is to reading the pattern as an economic law.

qs.q: The evidence about language boundaries supports the author’s emphasis on ideas because it shows that:
o: districts speaking different languages had different income levels
Paragraph 2 stresses the districts had similar economies.
urbanization spread along linguistic boundaries
The passage contrasts language boundaries with urbanization.
districts with similar economies but different languages limited births at different times
Correct: Paragraph 2 notes this; holding economy constant points to cultural networks as in paragraph 3.
religious districts resisted all forms of birth limitation
The passage claims only that timing tracked religion, not total resistance.
qs.x: The language-boundary evidence works like a natural experiment: neighboring districts with similar economies limited births at different dates when they spoke different languages. Holding the economy roughly constant points to culture and communication, the networks paragraph 3 credits with spreading ideas about family size. The income choice contradicts paragraph 2, which stresses that the economies were similar.

qs.q: Which policy would the author most likely support for a country seeking lower birth rates?
o: Considering how ideas about family size spread, not only promoting economic growth
Correct: Paragraphs 3 and 4 stress ideas and many interacting causes, not development alone.
Relying on industrialization to lower fertility on a known schedule
Paragraph 4 warns against expecting development alone to work on a fixed schedule.
Ignoring income and schooling as irrelevant to fertility
Paragraph 4 says incomes and schooling clearly matter.
Lowering child mortality first, since births must fall in fixed order
This assumes the fixed sequence that the author doubts.
qs.x: Paragraphs 3 and 4 say fertility decline came from many interacting causes, including the spread of ideas, while economics still matters. A policy that looks at how ideas about family size spread, not only at growth, follows that view. The 'ignore income' choice overcorrects, since paragraph 4 says income and schooling clearly matter.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author’s explanation of the language-boundary evidence?
o: England’s fertility later fell to levels like France’s.
Later convergence does not explain why timing tracked language.
Some rural Italian districts limited births unusually early.
Early rural decline fits the author’s doubts about economic timing.
Urbanization rose rapidly across Europe in the nineteenth century.
This general trend does not account for differences between neighboring districts.
Districts with different languages also differed in child mortality, which fell first where births fell first.
Correct: A mortality difference could explain the timing without the idea diffusion of paragraph 3.
qs.x: The author explains the language-boundary pattern by idea diffusion. A good weakener offers a rival cause that varies along the same boundary: if child mortality also differed and fell first where births fell first, mortality could explain the timing without ideas. Later convergence or general urbanization does not explain differences between neighboring districts.

passages.title: Geometry as Offering
text: During Japan’s Edo period, from the early seventeenth to the mid-nineteenth century, people of many backgrounds hung wooden tablets bearing geometry problems in Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples. These sangaku typically displayed a brightly colored figure, perhaps circles nested inside a triangle or spheres packed inside a cylinder, along with a statement of the problem and, often, only the answer. Samurai, merchants, farmers and occasionally women and children made them. Some offered thanks for a discovery; others challenged visitors to find a solution.

Historians of mathematics long treated sangaku, and the Japanese mathematics called wasan of which they were a part, as a curiosity. Measured against the European tradition, wasan seemed to lack what mattered most: general theorems, rigorous proofs and application to physics. Many of its problems were intricate puzzles about tangent circles that led nowhere in particular. The verdict was that Japan had produced ingenious calculators but not mathematics in the full sense.

This verdict says more about the historians than about wasan. It assumes that mathematics is a single enterprise with a single goal, the accumulation of general truths, and grades every culture by its progress toward that goal. But the sangaku suggest that mathematics in Edo Japan served other purposes. A tablet in a shrine was at once a gift to the gods, a public display of skill, a beautiful object and an invitation to a community of solvers that crossed lines of class. Omitting the proof was not a failure of rigor; it was the point, because the tablet existed to provoke others to work the problem themselves.

To recognize this is not to deny that wasan and European mathematics differ, or to pretend that Edo mathematicians anticipated every European result. It is to accept that the question “Was this real mathematics?” is less illuminating than the question “What was mathematics for, here?” Asked of our own tradition, the second question might yield some surprising answers too.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, a typical sangaku included:
o: a colored figure, a problem statement and often only the answer
Correct: Paragraph 1 lists these three features.
a full written proof signed by a temple priest
Paragraph 1 says tablets often gave only the answer, and priests are not mentioned.
a list of solvers ranked by social class
The passage says solvers crossed class lines; no rankings are described.
a prayer asking the gods to reveal a solution
Some tablets gave thanks, but none is described as asking for a solution.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 describes a typical sangaku: a brightly colored figure, a statement of the problem and often only the answer. Detail questions are answered by the passage’s own list. The full-proof choice is the opposite of what the passage says, and priests are never mentioned.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
o: Wasan was mathematically superior to European mathematics.
Paragraph 4 declines to claim this and admits real differences.
Judging wasan only by European standards hides the purposes mathematics served in Edo Japan.
Correct: Paragraphs 3 and 4 argue that asking what mathematics was for is more illuminating.
Sangaku were mainly religious objects with little mathematical content.
The author treats them as both offerings and real mathematics.
Historians were right that wasan lacked rigorous proofs.
The author recasts the missing proofs as deliberate, not as a confirmed deficiency.
qs.x: The author argues that grading wasan only against European standards (general theorems, proofs, physics) hides what mathematics did in Edo Japan, and proposes asking what mathematics was for (paragraphs 3 and 4). The superiority choice is a trap: paragraph 4 explicitly declines to claim wasan outdid or anticipated European work.

qs.q: The author interprets the frequent omission of proofs on sangaku as:
o: a deliberate feature meant to invite viewers to solve the problems
Correct: Paragraph 3 says omitting the proof was the point, provoking others to work the problem.
evidence that wasan mathematicians could not construct proofs
Paragraph 3 says the omission was not a failure of rigor.
a result of limited space on wooden tablets
Physical space is never offered as the explanation.
a way to protect solutions from rival schools
Secrecy is not mentioned; the author stresses public invitation.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says omitting the proof was not a failure of rigor but the point, because the tablet existed to provoke others to work the problem. The author reinterprets a supposed defect as a purpose. The 'could not construct proofs' choice is the older historians’ verdict, which the author rejects.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage most strongly suggests that:
o: European mathematics is less rigorous than historians claim
The sentence concerns purposes, not rigor.
wasan anticipated many later European discoveries
Paragraph 4 explicitly refuses to claim this.
historians should stop studying European mathematics
The author proposes a new question, not an end to such study.
European-derived mathematics may also serve purposes beyond accumulating general truths
Correct: Paragraph 4 applies the question “What was mathematics for?” back to our own tradition.
qs.x: The last sentence turns the question 'What was mathematics for, here?' back on the European tradition and predicts surprising answers. That implies European mathematics may also serve purposes beyond accumulating general truths. It does not say European mathematics lacks rigor, so the rigor choice misreads a claim about purpose as a claim about quality.

qs.q: Which discovery would most support the author’s interpretation of the omitted proofs?
o: A few sangaku included complete proofs.
This does not show that omission served to invite solvers.
Wasan schools guarded their methods as trade secrets.
This suggests a rival reason for omitting proofs, weakening the author’s reading.
Sangaku pigments were costly to obtain.
Paint cost says nothing about why proofs were omitted.
Shrine records show visitors posting their own solutions to problems on earlier tablets.
Correct: This confirms paragraph 3’s claim that tablets existed to provoke others to solve them.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims sangaku omitted proofs to invite others to solve the problems. Shrine records of visitors posting their own solutions to earlier tablets would confirm that invitation actually worked. The trade-secret choice offers a rival reason for leaving out proofs, so it weakens rather than supports the author’s reading.

qs.q: Which approach to the history of science would the author most likely endorse?
o: Ranking ancient cultures by how close they came to modern physics
Paragraph 3 criticizes grading cultures by progress toward one goal.
Treating all scientific traditions as essentially the same
Paragraph 4 says it does not deny that traditions differ.
Studying medieval astronomy by the calendar and ritual needs it met, not only its accuracy
Correct: This asks what the practice was for, as paragraph 4 recommends.
Studying only the most original individual discoverers
The passage stresses communal practice across class lines, not lone geniuses.
qs.x: The author’s method is to ask what a practice was for in its own setting rather than grade it by progress toward a single modern goal (paragraphs 3 and 4). Studying medieval astronomy by the calendar and ritual needs it served applies that method. Ranking cultures by closeness to modern physics is exactly the grading paragraph 3 criticizes.

passages.title: The Tyranny of the Station Clock
text: Historians often tell the story of standard time as a triumph of coordination. Before the railways, every town kept its own noon, set by the sun crossing the meridian, and the resulting patchwork of local times made timetables nearly unreadable. When railway companies imposed a single reference time, and governments later ratified it, chaos supposedly yielded to rational order. This account is not false, but it is incomplete in a way that matters. It treats local time as a defect awaiting correction rather than as a different relationship between people and the day.

Solar time was not merely inaccurate; it was answerable to something everyone could see. A farmer who glanced at the shadow of a church spire and a clerk who consulted the town clock were reading, in principle, the same source. Authority over the hour was distributed across the landscape itself. Standard time relocated that authority to observatories and telegraph offices, distant institutions whose signals had to be taken on trust. The clock in the station did not tell people when the sun was overhead; it told them when a company in the capital said it was noon.

Resistance to the change is usually remembered as quaint. Some towns kept two sets of hands on their public clocks for years, and a few clergy refused to ring bells by 'railway time.' Yet these holdouts grasped something the triumphal narrative misses: that adopting a common hour meant accepting a common master. The gain in coordination was real, but it was purchased with a loss of local self-description, and the people paying that price were rarely consulted.

None of this is an argument for returning to sundials. It is an argument for writing the history honestly. Standardization did not simply remove confusion; it redistributed power over a basic dimension of daily life. Seeing it that way allows us to ask better questions about later reforms, from daylight saving schemes to the precisely synchronized clocks of financial markets, each of which likewise decides whose convenience the hour will serve.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Standard time was a mistake, and communities should restore solar time.
Paragraph 4 explicitly says the argument is not for 'returning to sundials.'
Local solar time was more accurate than the railway time that replaced it.
Paragraph 2 says solar time was 'not merely inaccurate,' conceding its inaccuracy rather than praising its precision.
Standard time is best understood as a transfer of authority over the hour, not merely a cure for confusion.
Correct: paragraph 4 says standardization 'redistributed power over a basic dimension of daily life.'
Railway companies adopted standard time mainly to defeat rural resistance.
The passage says railways sought coordination; resistance is a response, not the motive (paragraphs 1 and 3).
qs.x: Main-point questions want the claim the whole passage builds toward. Paragraph 1 calls the triumph story 'incomplete,' and paragraph 4 says standardization 'redistributed power,' so the thesis is about a shift of authority. The tempting 'restore solar time' answer is extreme: paragraph 4 explicitly rules out 'returning to sundials.'

qs.q: The author mentions towns that kept two sets of hands on their public clocks primarily to:
o: suggest that resisters understood that a common hour implied a common authority.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the holdouts 'grasped' that a common hour meant 'accepting a common master.'
show that most people found standard time too confusing to use.
Paragraph 3 presents the clocks as principled resistance, not as evidence of confusion.
illustrate how quaint and backward the opponents of reform were.
The author reports that resistance 'is usually remembered as quaint' in order to challenge that view.
prove that standard time was adopted without any legal basis.
Paragraph 1 says governments 'ratified' standard time; the clocks say nothing about legality.
qs.x: Ask why the author includes a detail. Paragraph 3 says the holdouts with two sets of hands 'grasped' that a common hour meant 'accepting a common master,' so the example credits their insight. The 'quaint and backward' choice is a trap: the author mentions that the resistance is remembered as quaint only to overturn that view.

qs.q: According to the passage, under solar time authority over the hour was:
o: held by the clergy who rang the church bells.
Clergy appear in paragraph 3 only as resisters; paragraph 2 locates authority in the visible sun and shadows.
concentrated in observatories and telegraph offices.
Paragraph 2 says this describes standard time, which 'relocated' authority to those institutions.
divided between farmers and town clerks.
Paragraph 2 uses the farmer and clerk to show both read 'the same source,' not that they shared authority.
spread across a landscape anyone could observe directly.
Correct: paragraph 2 says this authority 'was distributed across the landscape itself.'
qs.x: Paragraph 2 contrasts two locations of authority. Under solar time it 'was distributed across the landscape itself,' since anyone could read the sun or a shadow. Observatories and telegraph offices are where standard time moved that authority, so choosing them confuses the before and after of the shift the author describes.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's claim that the people who bore the cost of standard time were rarely consulted?
o: Evidence that railway timetables were far easier to read after standardization
This supports the gain in coordination the author already concedes in paragraph 3; it says nothing about consultation.
Records showing many towns adopted railway time only after public meetings and local votes
Correct: broad local deliberation would contradict paragraph 3's claim that those paying the price 'were rarely consulted.'
Letters showing clergy disliked railway time for religious rather than civic reasons
The motives of a few clergy do not show that ordinary residents were consulted.
Data showing solar noon varied by many minutes between neighboring towns
This confirms the patchwork described in paragraph 1 but does not address who was consulted.
qs.x: To weaken a claim, find evidence that directly contradicts it. Paragraph 3 says those who paid the price of standard time 'were rarely consulted'; records of public meetings and local votes show the opposite. Easier timetables is tempting but only confirms the coordination gain the author already concedes, leaving the consultation claim untouched.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the 'triumphal narrative' of standard time is best described as:
o: qualified criticism: its facts are accepted but its framing is faulted.
Correct: paragraph 1 calls the account 'not false' but 'incomplete in a way that matters.'
complete rejection of its factual claims.
Paragraph 1 states the account is 'not false,' so its facts are not rejected.
enthusiastic endorsement of its conclusions.
The author says it 'misses' what the holdouts grasped (paragraph 3), which is not endorsement.
neutral indifference toward how the history is told.
Paragraph 4 urges 'writing the history honestly,' showing the author cares about framing.
qs.x: Tone questions reward precise wording. Paragraph 1 says the triumphal account 'is not false, but it is incomplete in a way that matters,' which accepts its facts while faulting its framing. 'Complete rejection' overshoots because the author explicitly grants the story's truth; the criticism concerns what it leaves out.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the shift from solar time to standard time as the author describes it?
o: A town adds a second clock tower so that more residents can see the time
This widens access to the same visible source; paragraph 2 describes authority moving away from it.
A town lets each household choose its own working hours
This spreads authority further, the reverse of the centralization described in paragraph 2.
A town replaces a public notice board anyone can read with a central app whose data residents cannot check
Correct: like paragraph 2's shift, a shared visible source gives way to a distant authority taken on trust.
A town repairs its old sundial so it shows solar noon more precisely
This improves solar time itself rather than relocating authority to distant institutions.
qs.x: An analogy must match the structure of the original. In paragraph 2, a source anyone could check (the sun) is replaced by a distant institution whose signals 'had to be taken on trust.' Swapping a public board for an unverifiable central app has that same shape. A second clock tower only widens access to the same visible source, so no authority moves.

passages.title: Borrowed Knowledge
text: Most of what any of us knows we did not discover. I believe that the Earth orbits the Sun, that my great-grandmother was born in a village I have never visited, and that the medicine in my cabinet will not poison me, yet I have checked none of these claims myself. Philosophers have long debated what entitles us to such beliefs. One tradition, often called reductionism, holds that testimony justifies belief only when the hearer has independent reasons, drawn from her own experience, to think the speaker reliable. The rival view, anti-reductionism, holds that we are entitled to accept what we are told unless we have positive reason for doubt.

Reductionism has the appeal of intellectual self-respect. It refuses to let anyone's knowledge rest on mere credulity. But taken seriously, it cannot be satisfied. The track record by which I would judge a speaker's reliability is itself known largely through testimony: I learned which encyclopedias are trustworthy from teachers, and which teachers are trustworthy from other people. A child, who must accept the meanings of words from adults before she can evaluate anything, would on this view know almost nothing at all.

Anti-reductionism avoids this regress, yet it seems to license gullibility. If default acceptance is permitted, what distinguishes the knowledgeable listener from the dupe? The answer, I suggest, lies less in the individual hearer than in the community. Testimony works because speakers are embedded in practices that punish lying and reward accuracy, and because claims circulate among many listeners, some of whom are positioned to catch errors. The individual is entitled to trust not because she has personally audited the speaker but because she belongs to a network that does a good deal of auditing on her behalf.

This shifts the question of testimonial knowledge from psychology to institutions. When the networks that check claims erode, as when sources multiply faster than any community can assess them, default trust becomes less defensible, not because individuals have grown more foolish but because the scaffolding beneath their trust has weakened.

qs.q: As the passage describes it, reductionism requires that a hearer:
o: accept testimony unless she has a positive reason for doubt.
Paragraph 1 attributes this default-acceptance view to anti-reductionism.
have reasons from her own experience to think the speaker reliable.
Correct: paragraph 1 says reductionism requires 'independent reasons, drawn from her own experience.'
personally verify every claim before believing it.
Reductionism checks the speaker's reliability, not each claim itself (paragraph 1).
rely on her community to audit speakers on her behalf.
Paragraph 3 presents this as the author's own proposal, not reductionism.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 defines reductionism: testimony justifies belief only when the hearer has 'independent reasons, drawn from her own experience,' to think the speaker reliable. The trap is 'verify every claim'; reductionism asks for evidence about the speaker's reliability, not personal checking of each claim, and default acceptance belongs to the rival view.

qs.q: The example of the child in paragraph 2 is used to:
o: argue that children are more gullible than adults.
The child's dependence is presented as unavoidable, not as gullibility (paragraph 2).
support the claim that meanings of words are arbitrary.
Paragraph 2 says the child must learn word meanings from adults; arbitrariness is not discussed.
illustrate how communities punish lying.
Punishing lying is discussed in paragraph 3, not in the child example.
show that reductionism implies people know implausibly little.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the child 'would on this view know almost nothing at all.'
qs.x: The child example is a reductio. Paragraph 2 argues that a child must accept word meanings before she can evaluate anything, so under reductionism she 'would on this view know almost nothing at all,' an implausible result. It is not about gullibility; the author presents her dependence as unavoidable, which is exactly why it embarrasses reductionism.

qs.q: The author's own view locates the justification for trusting testimony mainly in:
o: social practices and networks that check claims.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the hearer belongs to 'a network that does a good deal of auditing on her behalf.'
each hearer's personal record of past verification.
Paragraph 2 argues this reductionist basis 'cannot be satisfied.'
the sincerity and good intentions of speakers.
The author stresses practices that sanction lying, not speakers' intentions (paragraph 3).
a natural psychological tendency to believe others.
Paragraph 4 moves the question 'from psychology to institutions.'
qs.x: The author's own proposal appears in paragraph 3: trust is justified because the hearer 'belongs to a network that does a good deal of auditing on her behalf,' with practices that punish lying.
