A personal verification record is the reductionist basis paragraph 2 rejects, and paragraph 4 moves the question 'from psychology to institutions,' ruling out a psychological tendency.

qs.q: In which setting would the author most likely judge default trust LEAST defensible?
o: A small village where everyone knows who spread past rumors
Shared knowledge of past rumors is a form of the community auditing praised in paragraph 3.
A scientific journal whose articles are reviewed and often criticized after publication
Review and criticism are the error-catching practices paragraph 3 says justify trust.
An anonymous forum where false posts are rarely corrected and errors carry no consequences
Correct: paragraph 3 ties trust to practices that punish lying and catch errors, and this forum has neither.
A classroom where a teacher explains facts the students cannot yet check
Paragraph 2 treats such reliance as unavoidable, and schools sit within checking institutions.
qs.x: Apply the author's criterion: per paragraph 3, default trust is defensible when practices punish lying and some listeners are positioned to catch errors. An anonymous forum where false posts go uncorrected and carry no consequences lacks both, so trust there is least defensible. The classroom is tempting, but paragraph 2 treats such reliance as unavoidable, and teachers sit within checking institutions.

qs.q: The conclusion in paragraph 4 depends on which assumption?
o: Individuals today are less careful reasoners than people in the past.
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that individuals have 'grown more foolish.'
Reductionism is correct for adults but not for children.
The author rejects reductionism generally in paragraph 2, not only for children.
Having more sources always makes beliefs more reliable.
Paragraph 4 suggests that sources multiplying faster than they can be checked weakens trust.
How well a community checks claims can change even if individual hearers do not.
Correct: paragraph 4 says trust weakens 'not because individuals have grown more foolish' but because the scaffolding erodes.
qs.x: An assumption is what must hold for the conclusion to follow. Paragraph 4 says default trust can weaken 'not because individuals have grown more foolish' but because the scaffolding of checking erodes, which requires that a community's checking can change while individual hearers stay the same. The 'less careful reasoners' choice is the very explanation the author denies.

passages.title: The Picturesque Disguise
text: The eighteenth-century English landscape garden is often praised as a liberation. Where the formal gardens of the previous century had marched hedges in straight lines and clipped yews into cones, the new style offered winding lakes, scattered clumps of trees, and lawns that seemed to roll unbroken to the horizon. Its champions described it as nature freed from geometry, and later admirers have tended to accept their description.

Yet the landscape garden was among the most labor-intensive artifacts of its age. Hills were raised and lowered, streams dammed into lakes, and whole villages occasionally demolished and rebuilt out of sight because they spoiled a view. The ha-ha, a sunken wall that kept livestock off the lawn while remaining invisible from the house, captures the genre perfectly: it concealed a boundary in order to make the owner's land appear limitless. The formal garden announced human control openly; the landscape garden disguised it.

This disguise was not incidental. A landowner whose prospect seemed to merge seamlessly with the countryside was making a claim about his relation to that countryside, presenting his estate not as one property among many but as the natural order itself. The laborers who built the scene, and the tenants whose cottages were moved, vanished from the picture along with the fences. What looks like humility before nature was, on this reading, a more sophisticated assertion of possession.

I do not mean that the landscape garden is unlovely, or that pleasure in it is naive. But the habit of calling one design 'natural' and another 'artificial' obscures what all gardens share: each is a deliberate arrangement that encodes its maker's ideas about order, ownership, and who belongs in the view. The more effortless a garden appears, the more carefully we should ask what effort has been hidden.

qs.q: The central claim of the passage is that the English landscape garden:
o: presented a constructed appearance of nature that concealed control and ownership.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 argue the style 'disguised' control as 'a more sophisticated assertion of possession.'
was a genuine liberation of nature from human design.
Paragraph 1 reports this view only so that paragraphs 2 and 3 can dispute it.
was less beautiful than the formal garden it replaced.
Paragraph 4 says the author does not consider it 'unlovely.'
required less labor than the formal gardens before it.
Paragraph 2 calls it 'among the most labor-intensive artifacts of its age.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states the received view (the garden as liberation) only so paragraphs 2 and 3 can overturn it: the style 'disguised' human control and was 'a more sophisticated assertion of possession.' Choosing 'genuine liberation' mistakes the view the author reports for the one the author holds; paragraph 4 also rules out any claim that the garden was less beautiful.

qs.q: Within the argument, the ha-ha serves as:
o: evidence that landowners cared mainly about protecting livestock.
Keeping livestock out is its practical role; paragraph 2 stresses what its invisibility signified.
an example of the geometric style of earlier formal gardens.
The ha-ha belongs to the landscape style, which paragraph 1 contrasts with geometric design.
an emblem of hiding a boundary to make ownership seem limitless.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it 'concealed a boundary in order to make the owner's land appear limitless.'
proof that the landscape garden was open to the public.
Paragraph 2 presents the ha-ha as a hidden barrier, which points the other way.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 calls the ha-ha a feature that 'captures the genre perfectly' because it 'concealed a boundary in order to make the owner's land appear limitless.' It is an emblem of disguised ownership. Keeping out livestock is its literal function, but the author cares about what its invisibility signified, so the livestock choice stops at the surface.

qs.q: According to the author, the formal garden differs from the landscape garden in that the formal garden:
o: encoded no ideas about order or ownership.
Paragraph 4 says every garden 'encodes its maker's ideas about order, ownership.'
displayed human control openly instead of hiding it.
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'the formal garden announced human control openly.'
required villages to be moved out of sight.
Paragraph 2 links moving villages to the landscape garden, not the formal one.
was praised as nature freed from geometry.
Paragraph 1 applies that praise to the landscape garden.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 sums up the contrast: 'The formal garden announced human control openly; the landscape garden disguised it.' The distinction concerns openness versus concealment of control. Saying the formal garden encoded no ideas contradicts paragraph 4, which says every garden 'encodes its maker's ideas about order, ownership.'

qs.q: The author would most likely agree with which statement?
o: Enjoying landscape gardens is a sign of naive taste.
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that 'pleasure in it is naive.'
Formal gardens were more honest and therefore more beautiful.
The author contrasts openness and disguise but never ranks the styles' beauty.
Gardens should be judged on appearance alone, not on their history.
Paragraph 4 urges asking what the appearance hides, rejecting appearance-only judgment.
One can enjoy a landscape garden while recognizing what it was designed to conceal.
Correct: paragraph 4 says pleasure in it is not 'naive' even as we ask 'what effort has been hidden.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 holds two ideas together: the author does not find the garden 'unlovely' or pleasure in it 'naive,' yet urges asking 'what effort has been hidden.' So enjoyment and critical awareness can coexist. Calling formal gardens 'more honest and therefore more beautiful' is tempting, but the author never ranks the styles' beauty.

qs.q: Which modern design would the author most likely see as similar to the landscape garden?
o: A city plaza laid out in a strict grid with clearly marked gates
Open, visible geometry matches the formal garden, which 'announced human control openly.'
A private corporate campus that uses hidden fences and planted mounds to look like a public park
Correct: like the ha-ha in paragraph 2, hidden barriers make controlled property look open and natural.
A wild meadow left untended on abandoned farmland
An untended meadow involves no hidden effort or disguised ownership, the core of paragraphs 2 and 3.
A botanical garden that labels every plant with its origin
Labeling reveals the work of arrangement rather than hiding it.
qs.x: The key feature of the landscape garden is controlled property disguised as open nature, as with the ha-ha in paragraph 2. A corporate campus using hidden fences and planted mounds to look like a public park repeats that disguise. The untended meadow is tempting because it looks natural, but it involves no hidden effort or concealed ownership.

qs.q: Suppose records showed that many landscape-garden owners let local villagers walk freely through their parks. This would most directly weaken the claim that:
o: tenants and laborers were removed from the garden's scene.
Correct: villagers using the parks would challenge paragraph 3's claim that such people 'vanished from the picture.'
the gardens required great effort to build.
Public access says nothing about the labor described in paragraph 2.
formal gardens displayed control openly.
That claim concerns the earlier style and is untouched by evidence about landscape parks.
every garden encodes its maker's ideas.
Paragraph 4's general claim would still hold; open access is itself an idea about who belongs.
qs.x: Match the new evidence to the specific claim it touches. Paragraph 3 says tenants and laborers 'vanished from the picture'; villagers walking freely through the parks would put such people back in the scene. The general claim that every garden encodes ideas survives untouched, and the labor and formal-garden claims are unrelated to who walked in the park.

passages.title: Ninety Minutes of Nation
text: Commentators tend to treat sporting nationalism in one of two ways. To some it is harmless theater, a safe outlet for tribal feeling that would otherwise find uglier expression. To others it is a rehearsal for the real thing, a training ground for chauvinism in which flags and anthems prepare citizens to see neighbors as enemies. Both views assume that national feeling exists before the match, and that sport merely releases or amplifies it.

I think the relation runs partly the other way. A nation of millions is an abstraction no one can perceive directly. A national team, by contrast, is eleven visible people who win or lose on a given afternoon. In the stadium and in the crowded bars where the match is watched, strangers sing the same songs and groan at the same moment, experiencing a unity that ordinary life rarely provides. Sport does not simply express a community that already exists; it is one of the few occasions on which that community becomes something people can feel.

If this is right, then the political character of sporting nationalism is not fixed in advance. It depends on what the team is taken to represent. When a squad drawn largely from immigrant neighborhoods wins a tournament and is celebrated as the face of the country, the match can widen the circle of who counts as national. When the same players are cheered in victory but blamed for their origins in defeat, the ritual narrows that circle. The ninety minutes are the same; the stories told about them differ.

This means that critics who want to abolish sporting patriotism and enthusiasts who want to leave it alone share an error. Neither notices that the meaning of the ritual is continually fought over by journalists, fans, players, and politicians. The most important question is not whether people should feel national pride at a match, but what version of the nation that pride is being attached to.

qs.q: According to the passage, the two common views of sporting nationalism share the assumption that:
o: sport is a dangerous rehearsal for war.
Paragraph 1 attributes this to only one of the two views.
sporting nationalism should be abolished.
Paragraph 4 attributes abolition to critics only, not to both views.
the meaning of a match is contested by many groups.
Paragraph 4 says this is what both sides fail to notice.
national feeling exists before the match and sport only releases or amplifies it.
Correct: paragraph 1 states that 'both views assume that national feeling exists before the match.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 lays out the two views (harmless theater and rehearsal for chauvinism) and then names what they share: 'Both views assume that national feeling exists before the match.' The author's own argument in paragraph 2 challenges that shared premise. 'Rehearsal for war' is tempting but describes only one of the two views.

qs.q: The example of the squad drawn from immigrant neighborhoods mainly illustrates that:
o: immigrant players perform better in international tournaments.
Paragraph 3 says nothing about relative performance; it concerns how players are framed.
the stories told about a team shape whether national identity widens or narrows.
Correct: paragraph 3 concludes 'the ninety minutes are the same; the stories told about them differ.'
winning always makes a nation more inclusive.
Paragraph 3 shows the same players can be 'blamed for their origins in defeat,' so victory alone settles nothing.
sporting nationalism is harmless theater.
That is one of the views paragraph 1 sets up to dispute.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 shows the same immigrant squad can widen the national circle when celebrated in victory or narrow it when blamed for its origins in defeat. Its conclusion, 'the ninety minutes are the same; the stories told about them differ,' means framing, not results, decides the effect. 'Winning always makes a nation more inclusive' ignores that the narrowing story can follow a win just as easily.

qs.q: Which finding would most support the author's claim in paragraph 2?
o: Data showing that sports fans vote at the same rates as other citizens
Voting rates do not bear on whether sport makes national community felt.
Studies finding that most fans watch matches alone at home
This would undercut the shared-experience scenes in paragraph 2 rather than support them.
Surveys showing people feel the strongest sense of national belonging during international tournaments
Correct: this supports paragraph 2's claim that sport makes the community 'something people can feel.'
Reports that national teams rarely win major tournaments
How often teams win is irrelevant to the felt unity that paragraph 2 describes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 claims sport is one of the few occasions when the national community 'becomes something people can feel.' Surveys showing national belonging peaks during tournaments directly support that. The 'fans watch alone' finding is a trap: it would undercut the shared-experience scenes of stadiums and bars that paragraph 2 relies on.

qs.q: The claim that critics and enthusiasts 'share an error' relies most on which assumption?
o: How a team is portrayed can affect who is regarded as belonging to the nation.
Correct: paragraph 4's charge holds only if contested framing changes the 'version of the nation' at stake.
National pride at sporting events is always harmful.
The author treats its effect as open, depending on the story told (paragraph 3).
Journalists have more influence than fans or players.
Paragraph 4 lists journalists, fans, players and politicians without ranking them.
Sport should be kept separate from politics.
The passage treats sport as inherently political ground, the opposite assumption.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says critics and enthusiasts err because neither notices that the ritual's meaning is fought over, and what matters is 'what version of the nation' pride attaches to. That charge only matters if portrayal can change who counts as national, as paragraph 3 illustrates. 'Pride is always harmful' contradicts the author's view that the effect depends on the story told.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely advise a journalist covering a national team to:
o: avoid mentioning national pride in match reports.
The author does not want pride avoided; paragraph 4 asks what it is attached to.
focus strictly on tactics and results.
Paragraph 3 holds that the stories around results matter as much as the results.
pay attention to how coverage frames which players and fans belong to the nation.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the key question is 'what version of the nation that pride is being attached to.'
encourage readers to stop caring about international sport.
This is the abolitionist view that paragraph 4 calls mistaken.
qs.x: Turn the passage's thesis into advice. Paragraph 4 says the key question is 'what version of the nation that pride is being attached to,' and lists journalists among those who fight over that meaning. So a journalist should watch how coverage frames who belongs. 'Focus strictly on tactics' fails because paragraph 3 shows the stories around results shape their meaning.

passages.title: What the Tape Remembers
text: Oral history entered the academy under suspicion. Historians trained on archives worried that memories recorded decades after the fact were contaminated by hindsight, nostalgia, and the stories communities tell about themselves. A narrator might misdate a strike, merge two floods into one, or place herself at an event she only heard about. Early practitioners responded defensively, cross-checking interviews against documents and discarding whatever failed the test.

That defensive posture conceded too much. Consider a former mill worker who insists that a fatal accident at her factory happened in the same year the union was broken, when the records show the two events were five years apart. Treated as testimony about dates, her account is simply wrong. Treated as testimony about meaning, it is revealing: in her memory the death and the defeat belong together, two parts of one story about what the company cost its workers. The error is not noise obscuring the evidence; it is evidence of how the past has been organized by those who lived it.

This insight has sometimes been stretched into the claim that factual accuracy does not matter in oral history at all, that every memory is equally valid as a 'truth' of its own kind. That claim is a mistake, and an unkind one. We can recognize the mill worker's merging of events as meaningful only because we know, from other sources, that the events were in fact separate. Without the documentary record, her interpretation would be invisible, mistaken for a simple report.

The interviewer's task, then, is double. She must listen for the shape a narrator gives to the past, including the shape carried by mistakes, while keeping hold of the independent evidence against which that shape becomes legible. Oral history at its best neither defers to memory nor polices it, but reads memory and record against each other.

qs.q: According to the passage, early oral historians responded to suspicion by:
o: treating every memory as a valid truth of its own kind.
Paragraph 3 describes this as a later overextension, not the early response.
refusing to use written archives at all.
Paragraph 1 says they relied on documents to test interviews.
interviewing narrators soon after events occurred.
Paragraph 1 refers to memories 'recorded decades after the fact' and mentions no such remedy.
checking interviews against documents and discarding what failed.
Correct: paragraph 1 says they were 'cross-checking interviews against documents and discarding whatever failed the test.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 describes the early defensive response: practitioners were 'cross-checking interviews against documents and discarding whatever failed the test.' Treating every memory as its own truth is the opposite extreme, which paragraph 3 presents as a later overextension of the author's insight, not the original response.

qs.q: The mill worker example is used chiefly to show that:
o: a factual error in testimony can reveal how a narrator understands the past.
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'the error is not noise' but evidence of how the past 'has been organized.'
factory records are generally unreliable.
Paragraph 2 relies on the records being right; they are what reveal her error.
narrators deliberately distort events for political ends.
Paragraph 2 presents the merging as a feature of memory, not a deliberate lie.
union defeats caused fatal accidents.
The passage says the events were five years apart and makes no causal claim.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 reads the mill worker's merged dates two ways: as a report of dates it is wrong, but as testimony about meaning it shows the death and the union defeat belong to one story. 'The error is not noise' but evidence of how the past was organized. Saying factory records are unreliable reverses the logic, since the records are what expose her error.

qs.q: Why does the author reject the claim that every memory is equally valid as its own kind of truth?
o: Memories are usually too inaccurate to be useful to historians.
The author values memory, even its errors, as evidence (paragraph 2).
Seeing an error as meaningful depends on knowing the facts from other sources.
Correct: paragraph 3 says we see the merging as meaningful 'only because we know, from other sources' the events were separate.
Documents are always more truthful than people.
The author treats documents as a needed counterpart, not as superior in every respect (paragraph 4).
Narrators usually object when their errors are pointed out.
Paragraph 3 says nothing about narrators' reactions; the argument is about how meaning becomes visible.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that the merging of events is visible as meaningful 'only because we know, from other sources, that the events were in fact separate.' Without the documentary record her interpretation would look like a simple report. The 'memories are too inaccurate' choice is tempting but contradicts the author, who treats even errors as valuable evidence.

qs.q: The author regards the 'defensive posture' of early practitioners as:
o: a fully adequate method that later historians abandoned.
Paragraph 2 says it 'conceded too much,' so the author did not find it adequate.
a reckless refusal to check facts.
The posture involved heavy fact-checking (paragraph 1), not a refusal.
conceding too much by treating memory only as a report of facts.
Correct: paragraph 2 opens 'That defensive posture conceded too much' and shows what reading for facts alone misses.
an unkind dismissal of narrators' emotions.
Paragraph 3 calls a different claim, 'every memory is equally valid,' unkind.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 begins 'That defensive posture conceded too much,' then shows that reading the mill worker only for dates misses what her error reveals. So the posture's flaw was treating memory merely as a factual report to be confirmed or discarded. It was not a refusal to check facts; it involved heavy fact-checking, so 'reckless' gets it backwards.

qs.q: A narrator recalls fleeing her city on a freezing winter night, but records show the evacuation happened in summer. The author would most likely recommend that the interviewer:
o: delete the memory from the transcript as unreliable.
This repeats the discarding that paragraph 2 says 'conceded too much.'
accept the winter date and correct the records.
Paragraph 4 says good practice does not simply 'defer to memory.'
avoid mentioning the records so the narrator's truth stands alone.
Paragraph 3 says that without the record her interpretation 'would be invisible.'
note the discrepancy and explore what the winter setting means in her account.
Correct: paragraph 4 asks the interviewer to read 'memory and record against each other.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 gives the method: 'read memory and record against each other,' listening for the shape a narrator gives the past, including its mistakes. Here the winter detail conflicts with the records, so the interviewer should note the discrepancy and ask what it means. Deleting the memory repeats the discarding that 'conceded too much,' and accepting the winter date defers to memory.

qs.q: Which project would the author consider most at odds with good oral history practice?
o: Comparing a narrator's account with newspaper archives from the period
Reading memory against the record is what paragraph 4 recommends.
Publishing interviews as self-validating truths with no documentary context
Correct: paragraph 3 calls the view that accuracy does not matter 'a mistake, and an unkind one.'
Asking a narrator why she connects two separate events
Exploring the shape she gives the past fits paragraph 4's 'double' task.
Interviewing several workers about the same strike
Gathering multiple accounts is compatible with the passage and criticized nowhere.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls the claim that accuracy does not matter 'a mistake, and an unkind one,' because without the record a narrator's interpretation 'would be invisible.' Publishing interviews as self-validating truths with no documentary context does exactly that. Asking a narrator why she links two events is tempting to reject, but it is the meaning-seeking half of paragraph 4's double task.

passages.title: The Person in the Frame
text: Arguments about the ethics of documentary photography usually circle two figures. One is the photographer: did she exploit her subject, or bear witness on his behalf? The other is the viewer: does the image of a starving child move us to act, or merely invite us to consume another's misery from a comfortable distance? Each side of the debate has eloquent defenders, and each has a point.

What both conversations neglect is the person in the frame. A photograph of a flood survivor taken in the worst hour of her life does not stay in that hour. It is reprinted in textbooks, cropped into appeals for charities she never heard of, and retrieved by search engines when her grandchildren type her name. The photographer's intentions were formed once; the viewer's response lasts minutes. The subject lives with the image indefinitely.

Recognizing this changes what consent should mean. Many photographers now ask permission before taking a picture, and that is an improvement over the older habit of simply shooting. But a signature obtained in a relief camp, from someone who may fear that refusal will cost her aid, is a thin kind of agreement. Even freely given consent covers only the uses the subject could foresee at that moment, not the uses that decades of circulation will invent.

I do not conclude that such pictures should never be taken. Some images of suffering have changed policy and saved lives, and a rule against them would protect the comfortable more than the afflicted. The conclusion is narrower: the ethical life of a photograph lasts as long as the photograph does. Archives, publishers, and the photographers who license their work owe subjects something like a continuing relationship, including the possibility of withdrawing an image whose original purpose has long since been served.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's main argument?
o: Photographs of suffering should no longer be taken.
Paragraph 4 says 'I do not conclude that such pictures should never be taken.'
The ethics of a documentary photograph must account for the subject's ongoing stake in it.
Correct: paragraph 4 says 'the ethical life of a photograph lasts as long as the photograph does.'
The photographer's intentions settle whether an image is ethical.
Paragraph 2 says intentions 'were formed once' while the subject lives with the image indefinitely.
Viewers who look at images of suffering are usually indifferent.
Paragraph 1 notes this worry but says each side 'has a point'; it is not the thesis.
qs.x: The thesis comes in paragraph 4: 'the ethical life of a photograph lasts as long as the photograph does,' because, as paragraph 2 argues, the subject 'lives with the image indefinitely.' The banning choice is extreme and directly denied: 'I do not conclude that such pictures should never be taken.'

qs.q: The reference to a signature obtained in a relief camp mainly serves to show that:
o: relief workers routinely force subjects to be photographed.
Paragraph 3 describes the subject's fear, not coercion by relief workers.
asking permission is worse than not asking at all.
Paragraph 3 calls asking permission 'an improvement' over simply shooting.
written consent is legally required for publication.
The passage discusses ethics, not legal requirements.
consent given under pressure of dependence may be weak.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it 'a thin kind of agreement' when refusal might seem to 'cost her aid.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a signature from someone who 'may fear that refusal will cost her aid' is 'a thin kind of agreement,' so consent given under dependence is weak. The tempting 'asking is worse than not asking' choice reverses the author's view, since paragraph 3 calls asking permission 'an improvement' over simply shooting.

qs.q: The author declines to support a ban on images of suffering because such a ban would:
o: give up real benefits and mainly protect the comfortable.
Correct: paragraph 4 says such images 'have changed policy and saved lives' and a ban 'would protect the comfortable.'
violate the photographer's freedom of expression.
Paragraph 4 gives no free-expression argument.
be impossible to enforce in the age of search engines.
Search engines appear in paragraph 2 to show circulation, not enforcement problems.
make viewers less likely to donate to charity.
Charities appear in paragraph 2 only as places where images are reused.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 gives two reasons against a ban: some images of suffering 'have changed policy and saved lives,' and a ban 'would protect the comfortable more than the afflicted.' The other choices import reasons the author never gives; free expression and enforcement problems are plausible-sounding arguments but are absent from the passage.

qs.q: Which policy would best put the author's recommendation into practice?
o: A newspaper bans all photographs taken in disaster zones
Paragraph 4 rejects a general ban on such images.
A magazine requires a signed release before any photo is taken
Paragraph 3 says one-time consent covers only foreseeable uses, so it falls short.
An archive lets subjects or their families ask to withdraw decades-old images from licensing
Correct: paragraph 4 calls for 'the possibility of withdrawing an image' through a 'continuing relationship.'
A photographer donates her fees to the charities that use her images
This addresses money, not the subject's continuing say over the image (paragraph 4).
qs.x: Paragraph 4 calls for 'something like a continuing relationship' with subjects, 'including the possibility of withdrawing an image' whose purpose has been served. An archive letting subjects or families withdraw old images fits exactly. A signed release before shooting is tempting, but paragraph 3 says one-time consent covers only uses the subject could foresee at that moment.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the reasoning in paragraph 2?
o: Many photographers feel guilty about their work.
Photographers' feelings do not affect the claim about how images circulate.
Viewers remember striking images for years.
Longer viewer memory leaves the subject's indefinite stake intact.
Some subjects are proud of their photographs.
Pride does not show that the image stops circulating or that the subject loses a stake in it.
Images of disaster survivors are rarely republished after their first appearance.
Correct: paragraph 2 rests on the claim that such a photo 'does not stay in that hour' but keeps circulating.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 rests on the premise that a disaster photo 'does not stay in that hour' but is reprinted, cropped and retrieved for decades. If such images were rarely republished, the subject's indefinite stake would shrink and the argument would lose its basis. Subjects' pride is tempting but does not deny ongoing circulation or the subject's stake in it.

passages.title: Brothers Within the Walls
text: To many economic historians, the medieval craft guild is a textbook cartel. By limiting the number of masters, fixing prices, and forbidding outsiders to sell within the town walls, guilds enriched their members at the expense of consumers and slowed innovation for centuries. The verdict has the clarity of a model, and much evidence supports it.

But the cartel story describes what guilds restricted without explaining what their members believed they were doing. Guild ordinances spend remarkable energy on matters that brought no obvious profit: the inspection of cloth for hidden flaws, the punishment of bakers who sold underweight loaves, the payment of funeral costs for poor brothers, the support of widows. A guild was also a religious brotherhood with its own altar and feast day, and in many towns a unit of the militia and a seat on the council. Membership defined a man's standing in the community, not just his trade.

Seen this way, guild rules expressed an ideal of the 'just price,' one that let an honest craftsman support his household without enriching himself at his neighbors' expense. Competition, in this moral economy, was not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers. Restrictions that look like rent-seeking to a modern economist could look like integrity to a fifteenth-century weaver.

It would be sentimental to stop there. The brotherhood that supported widows also excluded Jews, foreigners, and, increasingly, women who had once practiced trades in their own right; the solidarity inside the walls was built partly on hostility toward those outside them. The point is not that guilds were benign rather than self-serving, but that the two descriptions cannot be pulled apart. Protection of members and exclusion of others were, for the guilds, the same act seen from different sides.

qs.q: According to the cartel view described in paragraph 1, guilds:
o: mainly provided welfare for widows and poor members.
Paragraph 2 raises welfare to show what the cartel story leaves out.
encouraged innovation by protecting skilled craftsmen.
Paragraph 1 says the cartel view holds that guilds 'slowed innovation.'
enriched their members by restricting competition at consumers' expense.
Correct: paragraph 1 says guilds 'enriched their members at the expense of consumers.'
expressed a sincere ideal of the just price.
Paragraph 3 offers this as the author's alternative reading.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 sums up the cartel view: by limiting masters, fixing prices and excluding outsiders, guilds 'enriched their members at the expense of consumers.' The just-price ideal and welfare for widows are the author's additions in paragraphs 2 and 3, offered to complicate the cartel story, so they are not part of that view.

qs.q: The author mentions cloth inspection and funeral payments primarily to:
o: show that guilds pursued aims the profit motive does not explain.
Correct: paragraph 2 calls these 'matters that brought no obvious profit.'
prove that guilds were not cartels at all.
Paragraph 1 concedes 'much evidence supports' the cartel view; the examples supplement that view rather than refute it.
illustrate how guilds excluded outsiders.
Exclusion is the subject of paragraph 4; these examples concern members' welfare and quality.
explain why guilds eventually disappeared.
The passage never discusses the decline of guilds.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists cloth inspection, underweight loaves, funeral costs and support of widows as 'matters that brought no obvious profit,' showing that the cartel story misses part of what guilds did. The tempting 'prove guilds were not cartels' goes too far: paragraph 1 grants that 'much evidence supports' the cartel view, so the examples supplement it rather than refute it.

qs.q: In the moral economy described in paragraph 3, competition was regarded as:
o: a neutral way of discovering the value of goods.
Paragraph 3 says competition was 'not a neutral mechanism for discovering value.'
a temptation to dishonest practices and underselling.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it 'a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.'
a religious duty owed to the brotherhood.
Religious ties appear in paragraph 2 but are not linked to competition.
the main source of the just price.
The just price was protected by restrictions, not by competition (paragraph 3).
qs.x: In paragraph 3's moral economy, competition was 'not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.' The 'neutral mechanism' choice is the modern economist's view that the passage explicitly contrasts with the guild outlook, so it is the reverse of what was asked.

qs.q: What is the main function of the final paragraph?
o: To abandon the moral-economy reading in favor of the cartel model
Paragraph 4 says the two descriptions 'cannot be pulled apart,' so neither replaces the other.
To argue that guilds were mainly benign institutions
Paragraph 4 denies that guilds were 'benign rather than self-serving.'
To introduce new evidence about guild pricing
Paragraph 4 concerns membership and exclusion, not prices.
To qualify the sympathetic account by arguing that protection and exclusion were inseparable
Correct: paragraph 4 says 'it would be sentimental to stop there' and calls the two 'the same act seen from different sides.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens 'It would be sentimental to stop there,' then adds that guild solidarity rested on excluding Jews, foreigners and women, and that protection and exclusion were 'the same act seen from different sides.' It qualifies the sympathetic reading without abandoning it, which rules out the choice that the author returns to the cartel model.

qs.q: Which modern institution most closely resembles the guild as the author portrays it?
o: A licensing board that enforces ethical standards and also limits entry into a profession
Correct: like the guild in paragraphs 2 to 4, it combines care for standards with restricted membership.
An open online community that anyone may join and leave freely
Open entry lacks the exclusion that paragraph 4 makes central.
A commodity exchange where prices are set purely by bidding
Pure price competition is what the guild moral economy opposed (paragraph 3).
A charity that gives aid to anyone in need
Universal aid lacks the insider-outsider line drawn in paragraph 4.
qs.x: The author's guild combines a real commitment to standards and members' welfare (paragraphs 2 and 3) with restricted entry and exclusion of outsiders (paragraph 4). A licensing board that enforces ethics while limiting entry joins both features. A charity aiding anyone is tempting for its welfare role, but it lacks the insider-outsider line that paragraph 4 makes central.

qs.q: Suppose records showed that a guild loosened its quality inspections whenever it could raise prices without penalty. This would most weaken the claim that:
o: guilds limited the number of masters.
Limiting masters is a cartel feature this finding leaves untouched.
guilds excluded Jews, foreigners and women.
The finding concerns quality and prices, not membership.
guild rules reflected members' sincere commitment to honest work.
Correct: putting profit ahead of standards undercuts paragraph 3's claim that the rules could express 'integrity.'
guilds served religious and civic roles.
Altars, feasts and militia roles (paragraph 2) are unaffected by inspection practices.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 suggests guild restrictions could reflect 'integrity,' a sincere commitment to honest work and the just price. If a guild relaxed quality inspections whenever it could raise prices safely, profit would be driving its standards, which undercuts that sincerity. Limiting the number of masters is a cartel feature that this finding leaves untouched, even reinforces.

passages.title: Words at Work
text: For much of the history of philosophy, the meaning of a word was thought to be the thing it stood for. 'Apple' meant apples; 'justice' meant some more elusive object that philosophers were charged with locating. The later Wittgenstein proposed a different picture. Words, he suggested, are less like labels than like tools, and their meanings are found in the uses to which they are put within particular activities, which he called language-games. A builder who calls out 'Slab!' to an assistant is not naming an object for contemplation but giving an instruction within a shared task.

Critics have often heard this as a recipe for relativism. If meaning is simply use, and different communities use words differently, then it seems no use can be wrong and no claim can be criticized from outside its own game. This reading, though common, misunderstands the analogy. Games have rules, and a move can be mistaken: one can castle illegally in chess or call a strike when the pitch was wide. To say that meaning lies in use is to say that it lies in a practice with standards of correctness, not in whatever a speaker happens to intend.

The more interesting consequence of the view is not relativism but a diagnosis of confusion. Many apparent disagreements arise when a word migrates from one game to another while carrying the expectations of its first home. When an economist and a theologian argue about whether a gift can ever be truly 'free,' they may not be disputing a fact at all, but talking past each other with a single word that does different work in each of their practices.

The lesson is not that every dispute dissolves under analysis. Some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out. But before we argue, it is worth asking whether we are playing the same game, and whether the word at the center of the quarrel means for our opponent what it means for us.

qs.q: According to the passage, the traditional view held that a word's meaning is:
o: the use it is put to within an activity.
Paragraph 1 attributes this to the later Wittgenstein, as an alternative.
whatever the speaker happens to intend.
Paragraph 2 rejects this as a reading of use-based meaning; it is not the traditional view.
a rule within a shared game.
Rules and games belong to Wittgenstein's picture (paragraphs 1 and 2).
the thing the word stands for.
Correct: paragraph 1 says meaning 'was thought to be the thing it stood for.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 opens with the traditional view: a word's meaning 'was thought to be the thing it stood for,' as 'apple' means apples. Meaning as use within an activity is Wittgenstein's alternative, introduced as a contrast. 'Whatever the speaker intends' is a trap from paragraph 2, where the author rejects it as a misreading of the use view.

qs.q: The examples of illegal castling and a mistaken strike call are offered to show that:
o: games are a poor analogy for language.
The author uses the examples to defend the analogy, saying critics 'misunderstand' it.
meaning grounded in use still allows for mistakes.
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'games have rules, and a move can be mistaken.'
different communities play games differently.
Paragraph 2 uses the examples to show standards of correctness, not variation.
umpires and referees decide what words mean.
The examples show that rules exist, not that officials set meanings.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 answers the relativism charge by noting that 'games have rules, and a move can be mistaken,' like illegal castling or a wrong strike call. So meaning grounded in use still has standards of correctness. The choice that games are a poor analogy reverses the author's purpose; the examples defend the analogy against critics who 'misunderstand' it.

qs.q: The author's reply to the charge of relativism would be most weakened if it were shown that:
o: many disputes arise when words move between practices.
This is the author's own claim in paragraph 3, so it would not weaken the reply.
some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out.
Paragraph 4 already grants this point.
language-games lack any shared standards by which a move can be judged wrong.
Correct: paragraph 2's defense rests on use being 'a practice with standards of correctness.'
builders rarely shout single-word commands.
The builder is only an illustration; its frequency is beside the point (paragraph 1).
qs.x: The author's reply in paragraph 2 depends on use being 'a practice with standards of correctness.' If language-games had no shared standards for judging a move wrong, the reply would collapse and relativism would return. The other choices restate points the author already grants (paragraphs 3 and 4) or attack a mere illustration, so they cannot weaken the argument.

qs.q: Which scenario best illustrates the kind of confusion described in paragraph 3?
o: A doctor calls an illness 'chronic' to mean long-lasting, while the patient hears it as 'severe'
Correct: one word does different work in two practices, so the two talk past each other (paragraph 3).
Two chess players disagree about whether a move broke the rules
This is a dispute within a single game with shared standards, as in paragraph 2.
Two historians disagree about the date of a battle
Both use 'date' the same way; this is a genuine factual dispute.
A child learns the word 'apple' by being shown an apple
This matches the labeling picture in paragraph 1, not a word moving between practices.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 describes confusion that arises when one word does different work in two practices, so speakers talk past each other, as with 'free' for the economist and the theologian. A doctor's 'chronic' (long-lasting) heard by a patient as 'severe' fits this exactly. Two chess players arguing over a rule is a dispute inside one game with shared standards, which is genuine rather than confused.

qs.q: What does the author ultimately recommend?
o: Treat every disagreement as a misunderstanding about words.
Paragraph 4 says 'not that every dispute dissolves under analysis.'
Before arguing, check whether both sides use the key word the same way.
Correct: paragraph 4 urges asking 'whether we are playing the same game.'
Return to defining words by the objects they name.
The author favors use over the labeling view of paragraph 1.
Avoid disputes between different academic fields.
The author asks for clarity about terms, not avoidance of dispute.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 concludes that 'before we argue,' we should ask 'whether we are playing the same game' and whether the key word means the same to both sides. Treating every disagreement as verbal is the overreach the author rules out by saying not 'every dispute dissolves under analysis' and that some disagreements are genuine.

passages.title: The Grammar of a Meal
text: Why do people eat what they eat, and refuse what they refuse? One influential answer in anthropology is materialist. On this view, food rules that look arbitrary turn out, on inspection, to serve practical ends: a ban on eating a particular animal preserves a beast more valuable alive as a source of labor or milk, and a preference for certain grains reflects what local soils can reliably produce. Culture, in this account, is ecology in ceremonial dress.

The rival answer treats food as a language. A meal is not merely a quantity of calories but a structured sequence, with rules about what may be combined, what must come first, and what is fit for guests rather than family. A household that serves soup, then meat, then something sweet is following a grammar as surely as a speaker who places the subject before the verb. Departures from the pattern carry meaning: breakfast foods at dinner signal informality or play, and a feast differs from an everyday supper not only in quantity but in structure.

Each approach is often presented as a refutation of the other, but each fails precisely where the other succeeds. The materialist can explain why a staple grain became central to a diet but has little to say about why it must be served in a particular dish on a particular holiday. The symbolic analyst can trace the elegant contrasts of a festive menu but cannot explain why the menu changed when a famine made its central ingredient scarce.

The more productive question is how material conditions and systems of meaning act on each other. Scarcity can make an ingredient precious and therefore ceremonial; abundance can drain a once-festive food of its significance until it becomes merely ordinary. A grammar of food is written with the ingredients history provides, and the ingredients, once written into the grammar, acquire a value no calorie count can measure.

qs.q: According to the materialist view, food rules that look arbitrary:
o: usually serve practical or ecological purposes.
Correct: paragraph 1 says such rules 'serve practical ends.'
form a grammar like that of a language.
Paragraph 2 attributes this to the rival, symbolic view.
are best explained by religious belief.
The materialist view in paragraph 1 explains rules by ecology, not belief.
change only when their meaning is forgotten.
Paragraph 1 makes no claim about how food rules change.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states that under the materialist view, rules that look arbitrary 'serve practical ends,' such as sparing an animal more useful alive; 'culture is ecology in ceremonial dress.' The grammar idea belongs to the rival symbolic view in paragraph 2, a common mix-up when two theories are presented in sequence.

qs.q: The author mentions breakfast foods served at dinner in order to illustrate that:
o: meal order is determined by nutritional needs.
Paragraph 2 treats meal order as grammar, not nutrition.
materialist explanations work best for everyday meals.
The example supports the symbolic view, not the materialist one.
departures from a meal's usual structure carry meaning.
Correct: paragraph 2 says 'departures from the pattern carry meaning,' such as 'informality or play.'
families no longer follow traditional meal patterns.
Paragraph 2 makes no claim about decline; a departure presupposes the pattern.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that meals follow a grammar and that 'departures from the pattern carry meaning'; breakfast at dinner signals 'informality or play.' The example supports the symbolic view, not nutrition. The 'families no longer follow patterns' choice misses that a departure carries meaning only because the pattern still exists.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, the symbolic approach cannot explain:
o: why a dish must appear on a particular holiday.
Paragraph 3 names this as something the materialist cannot explain.
the contrasts that structure a festive menu.
Paragraph 3 says the symbolic analyst 'can trace' these contrasts.
why a feast differs from an everyday supper.
Paragraph 2 offers this as something the symbolic view does explain.
changes to a menu caused by a shortage of its central ingredient.
Correct: paragraph 3 says it 'cannot explain why the menu changed when a famine made its central ingredient scarce.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 pairs each approach with its blind spot: the symbolic analyst 'cannot explain why the menu changed when a famine made its central ingredient scarce.' The holiday-dish choice is a reversal trap, since paragraph 3 assigns that failure to the materialist, while the festive-menu contrasts are something the symbolic analyst 'can trace.'

qs.q: Which statement best describes the author's position on the two approaches?
o: The materialist approach is correct and the symbolic one is mistaken.
Paragraph 3 says the materialist 'has little to say' about holiday dishes.
Each covers the other's blind spot, so their interaction should be studied.
Correct: paragraph 3 says each 'fails precisely where the other succeeds,' and paragraph 4 asks how they 'act on each other.'
The symbolic approach makes the materialist one unnecessary.
Paragraph 3 says the symbolic view cannot explain famine-driven change.
Neither approach tells us anything useful about food.
The author credits each with real successes in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says each approach 'fails precisely where the other succeeds,' and paragraph 4 proposes studying 'how material conditions and systems of meaning act on each other.' So the author credits both and asks how they interact. Picking one approach as correct ignores that the author lists a real failure for each.

qs.q: A spice once rare and served only at weddings becomes cheap after new trade routes open, and it is now used daily. The author would most likely see this as:
o: proof that the spice never had symbolic value.
Paragraph 4 says the food lost a significance it once had, so it did have value.
evidence that materialist explanations are always wrong.
Here a material cause explains the change, which fits paragraph 3's credit to materialism.
a case that only the symbolic approach can explain.
Paragraph 3 says the symbolic view alone cannot explain supply-driven change.
abundance draining a festive food of significance, showing material change acting on meaning.
Correct: paragraph 4 says abundance 'can drain a once-festive food of its significance.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says 'abundance can drain a once-festive food of its significance until it becomes merely ordinary.' A wedding spice made cheap by trade and now used daily is exactly this: material change acting on meaning. 'Proof the spice never had symbolic value' fails because the spice lost a significance it once had, which presupposes that it had one.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's claim that scarcity can make an ingredient ceremonial?
o: Across many cultures, ingredients that became scarce were dropped from rituals rather than elevated in them.
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 4's claim that scarcity can make an ingredient 'precious and therefore ceremonial.'
Many festive dishes use the same staple grains as everyday meals.
This is compatible with paragraph 4; it does not show scarcity failing to raise status.
Some food bans protect animals more valuable alive.
This supports the materialist view in paragraph 1 and does not address scarcity and ritual.
Meal order differs widely between societies.
Varied grammars fit paragraph 2 and say nothing about scarcity.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 claims 'scarcity can make an ingredient precious and therefore ceremonial.' A broad finding that scarce ingredients were dropped from rituals rather than elevated contradicts that causal link directly. Festive dishes sharing everyday grains is tempting, but it does not show that scarcity fails to raise status, so it leaves the claim standing.

passages.title: The Open Stacks
text: The history of libraries is commonly told as a march toward openness. Medieval books were chained to their desks; early modern collections admitted only scholars bearing letters of introduction; nineteenth-century reformers founded free public libraries; and twentieth-century librarians at last let readers wander the stacks and pull down volumes for themselves. Each step, in this telling, removed a barrier between people and books.

The story is true as far as it goes, but it obscures a change in what a library was for. The chained book was not a symbol of hostility toward readers. In an age when a single volume might cost as much as a farm, a library was a treasury, and its first duty was to ensure that what it held would survive. The open-stacks library, by contrast, is a service whose success is measured by circulation. These are not more and less enlightened versions of one institution so much as two institutions with different goods in view.

The difference becomes visible when shelves fill. A treasury keeps everything; a service must make room. Modern libraries routinely 'weed' their collections, discarding books that have not been borrowed for some years, and the logic is sound for an institution judged by use. But low circulation is a poor guide to future value. Pamphlets and popular novels that no one checked out for decades have become, for later historians, irreplaceable windows onto the ordinary life of their time, and many survive only because some library failed to discard them.

I am not urging a return to chains. The aim is to see that preservation and access are rival goods that no library can fully reconcile, and that each generation's choice between them shapes what the next will be able to know. A history that sees only the triumph of access forgets the books that access quietly sacrificed.

qs.q: According to the author, books were chained in medieval libraries chiefly because:
o: librarians were hostile toward readers.
Paragraph 2 says the chained book 'was not a symbol of hostility toward readers.'
only scholars were permitted to read.
Restricted admission is an early modern step in paragraph 1, not the reason for chains.
books were so costly that preserving them was the library's first duty.
Correct: paragraph 2 says a volume 'might cost as much as a farm' and the library's duty was that holdings 'would survive.'
circulation was the measure of a library's success.
Paragraph 2 ties circulation to the modern open-stacks library.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 reinterprets the chained book: it 'was not a symbol of hostility toward readers.' When a volume 'might cost as much as a farm,' the library was a treasury whose first duty was survival of its holdings. Reader hostility is the tempting popular assumption the author explicitly rejects, and circulation as a measure belongs to modern libraries.

qs.q: The author mentions pamphlets and popular novels in order to show that:
o: historians prefer popular works to scholarly ones.
Paragraph 3 says these works are valuable windows onto ordinary life, not that historians prefer them.
low circulation poorly predicts a book's later value.
Correct: paragraph 3 says 'low circulation is a poor guide to future value' and cites these works.
libraries should stop collecting popular fiction.
The point of paragraph 3 is that such works deserve keeping.
weeding is never justified for any library.
Paragraph 3 calls the logic of weeding 'sound for an institution judged by use.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says 'low circulation is a poor guide to future value,' then gives pamphlets and popular novels that went unborrowed for decades yet became 'irreplaceable windows' for historians. The 'weeding is never justified' choice overshoots: the author calls weeding 'sound for an institution judged by use' and only questions its cost.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's criticism of the 'march toward openness' narrative?
o: It treats two institutions with different goals as stages in the improvement of one.
Correct: paragraph 2 says they are 'not more and less enlightened versions of one institution' but 'two institutions with different goods.'
It gets the order of historical events wrong.
Paragraph 2 says the story 'is true as far as it goes,' so its sequence is not disputed.
It exaggerates how expensive medieval books were.
The author accepts and stresses their great expense (paragraph 2).
It overstates how open modern libraries are.
The author does not dispute modern openness; the concern is what openness sacrificed.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 grants that the openness story 'is true as far as it goes' but says treasury and service libraries are 'not more and less enlightened versions of one institution' but 'two institutions with different goods in view.' So the critique concerns framing, not facts; 'gets the order of events wrong' fails because the sequence is accepted.

qs.q: A digital archive automatically deletes files that no one has opened in five years in order to save storage costs. The author would most likely view this policy as:
o: a sensible end to the old conflict between access and preservation.
Paragraph 4 says these are 'rival goods that no library can fully reconcile.'
a return to the treasury model of medieval libraries.
A treasury 'keeps everything' (paragraph 3), the opposite of deleting files.
irrelevant, because digital files are not books.
The reasoning of paragraph 3 concerns judging value by use, which applies to any medium.
repeating the service logic of weeding, at the risk of losing materials later found valuable.
Correct: paragraph 3 warns that discarding by low use sacrifices works that later become 'irreplaceable.'
qs.x: Deleting files no one has opened in five years applies the service logic of weeding from paragraph 3: judging value by use. The author warns this sacrifices works later found 'irreplaceable,' and paragraph 4 says preservation and access are rival goods no library can fully reconcile. Calling it a return to the treasury model is backwards, since a treasury 'keeps everything.'

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the claim in paragraph 3?
o: Public libraries lend more books today than ever before.
Higher lending supports the service model's success but not paragraph 3's warning.
Medieval libraries held far fewer books than modern ones.
Collection size does not bear on whether low use predicts future value.
Many sources historians cite survive in only one library that kept them despite years of no use.
Correct: this confirms that many works survive 'only because some library failed to discard them.'
Most readers prefer open stacks to closed ones.
Reader preference is beside the point of paragraph 3's argument about discarding.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims low use poorly predicts future value and that many works survive 'only because some library failed to discard them.' Finding that many sources historians cite survive in a single library that kept them despite years of no use confirms this directly. Record lending figures support the service model's success but say nothing about what weeding loses.

passages.title: The Grammar of Scent
text: The standard story of perfume is a story of concealment. Before sewers and daily baths, the account runs, Europeans drenched themselves in musk and civet to cover the stench of unwashed bodies, and as hygiene improved, the heavy animal scents gave way to the delicate florals we know today. The story is tidy, and it flatters us, since it makes our own fragrances a luxury rather than a necessity. It is also, I think, mostly wrong.

Consider the timing. The great retreat from animal notes in France began in the 1760s and 1770s, decades before bathing became a regular habit among even the wealthy. Courtiers who still washed rarely were already abandoning musk, which physicians had begun to describe as a scent that inflamed the passions and disordered the nerves. If perfume had been chiefly a mask, the switch to fainter waters of rose and violet would have made little sense: one does not hide a strong odor with a weaker one.

What changed was not the body but the meaning of the self it carried. Musk announced a person from across a room; it filled space and claimed it. The new floral waters, by contrast, could be detected only at close quarters, by someone already admitted to intimacy. A scent that whispered rather than proclaimed suited a culture that had begun to prize sensibility, the private and refined inner life cultivated by novel readers and letter writers. To wear violet was to suggest that one's depths were worth leaning in to discover.

None of this means that smell was unimportant to people living amid the odors of the early modern city. But treating perfume as a deodorant reduces a language to a tool. Fragrance was a grammar of distance, telling others how near they might come, and its history tracks changing ideas of who deserved to come near. The animal notes did not vanish because noses grew more sensitive. They vanished because a certain way of being seen had gone out of fashion.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: The decline of musk shows that perfume became a luxury once bathing made it unnecessary.
This is the concealment story that paragraph 1 introduces and the author calls mostly wrong.
Changes in perfume reflected shifting ideas about the self and social distance, not mainly hygiene.
Correct: paragraphs 3 and 4 tie scent to the meaning of the self and a grammar of distance.
Eighteenth-century physicians drove fashion away from animal scents through medical warnings.
Paragraph 2 mentions physicians as a detail; the thesis concerns the changing meaning of the self.
Perfume mattered little to early modern people because urban odors were overwhelming.
Paragraph 4 says smell did matter; the author denies only that perfume was chiefly a deodorant.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 sets up the concealment story only to call it mostly wrong, and paragraphs 3 and 4 replace it with the claim that scent signaled the self and social distance. Main-idea answers must cover the whole argument. The physicians are one supporting detail in paragraph 2, too narrow to be the thesis.

qs.q: The author's main evidence against the claim that perfume was chiefly a mask for body odor is that:
o: floral waters were more expensive than musk and civet.
The passage never compares the prices of different scents.
novel readers preferred violet to rose.
Paragraph 3 links florals to readers generally but never ranks violet against rose.
physicians recommended floral scents as healthful.
Paragraph 2 says physicians criticized musk, not that they recommended florals.
the move away from musk began well before regular bathing did.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the retreat began in the 1760s, decades before bathing became habitual.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues from timing: courtiers abandoned musk in the 1760s and 1770s, decades before regular bathing. If hygiene had driven the change, the change should have followed bathing, not preceded it. The physicians are mentioned only as critics of musk; the passage never says they praised florals.

qs.q: The remark that 'one does not hide a strong odor with a weaker one' is used to suggest that:
o: the shift to faint florals is hard to explain if perfume's purpose was concealment.
Correct: paragraph 2 argues weaker scents make no sense as masks, undercutting the deodorant story.
eighteenth-century bodies smelled less strongly than earlier ones.
Paragraph 2 says bathing was still rare, so the author does not claim bodies smelled less.
floral perfumes proved ineffective and were soon abandoned.
Paragraph 3 says florals flourished as signs of a new ideal of the self.
musk was preferred by those who bathed most rarely.
Paragraph 2 says even courtiers who rarely washed were abandoning musk.
qs.x: The quoted remark is a reductio: if perfume existed to mask odor, switching to fainter scents while people still rarely washed would defeat the purpose. The point is about the logic of the mask theory, not about bodies smelling better, since paragraph 2 stresses bathing was still rare.

qs.q: According to the passage, eighteenth-century physicians described musk as a scent that:
o: masked disease-causing vapors.
Paragraph 2 says nothing about vapors; it reports a claim about passions and nerves.
was too faint to be useful.
Paragraph 3 describes musk as strong enough to fill a room.
inflamed the passions and disordered the nerves.
Correct: paragraph 2 reports exactly this medical description of musk.
should be reserved for royalty.
No such restriction appears; paragraph 2 notes that courtiers were abandoning musk.
qs.x: This is a retrieval question: paragraph 2 says physicians described musk as a scent that inflamed the passions and disordered the nerves. Wrong choices borrow plausible period ideas (miasmas, royal privilege) that the passage never mentions. On detail questions, match the passage's own wording.

qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Letters from the 1770s describe violet water as suited to intimate company.
This would support paragraph 3's claim that florals signaled closeness.
Medical texts of the 1760s criticized several scents besides musk.
Broader medical criticism leaves the timing argument of paragraph 2 intact.
A few wealthy households bathed regularly before 1760.
Scattered early bathers would not overturn the general timing pattern in paragraph 2.
Sales of musk in France fell sharply only after daily washing became common among the wealthy.
Correct: this reverses the timing paragraph 2 relies on and revives the hygiene explanation.
qs.x: The author's case against the hygiene story rests on timing: the musk retreat came before bathing. Evidence that musk sales fell only after washing became common would reverse that sequence and revive the hygiene explanation. A few early bathers would not, since the author's claim concerns the general pattern.

qs.q: The author would most likely interpret a modern revival of heavy, room-filling fragrances as a sign that:
o: cultural ideals of self-presentation had shifted toward open display.
Correct: paragraph 4 treats scent choices as tracking changing ways people wish to be seen.
standards of personal hygiene had declined.
The author rejects hygiene as the explanation for scent choices in paragraphs 2 and 4.
people's sense of smell had grown less sensitive.
Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that changes in noses explain shifts in scent.
perfumers had found cheaper ways to make musk.
The author explains scent change through meaning, not production costs.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says scent choices track how people wish to be seen, and that musk vanished because a way of being seen went out of fashion. A return of room-filling scents would therefore signal renewed taste for open display. The author explicitly rejects hygiene and nose sensitivity as explanations.

passages.title: The Ark and the Window
text: Modern zoos have learned to speak the language of rescue. Signs beside the enclosures mention breeding programs and threatened habitats, and the institutions describe themselves less as menageries than as arks, carrying vulnerable species through a flood of extinction. The image is powerful, and in a handful of cases it is accurate: some species survive today only because captive populations were bred and later returned to the wild.

Yet the ark is a poor description of the typical zoo. Most animals on display belong to species that are not threatened, and of those that are, only a small fraction take part in programs that ever release animals back into their habitats. Many of the creatures that draw the largest crowds, the elephants, great apes, and big cats, are also those whose needs for range, social complexity, or both are hardest to meet behind walls. The ark, in other words, carries mostly passengers who were never in danger of drowning, and it carries the most demanding of them in the most cramped quarters.

Defenders often fall back on education: children who see a living tiger, they argue, will grow into adults who care about tigers. Perhaps. But the evidence that a zoo visit changes behavior, as opposed to producing a pleasant afternoon, is thin, and the lesson a caged animal teaches is ambiguous. It may teach reverence; it may equally teach that wild things exist for our viewing.

I do not conclude that zoos should be abolished. Abolition would strand the animals already held, and it would end the genuine conservation work that some institutions perform. The better conclusion is that the conservation argument licenses far less than zoos claim for it. A zoo that took its own rhetoric seriously would hold fewer species, favor those that are both endangered and able to flourish in captivity, and phase out exhibits whose main justification is that visitors enjoy them. It would, that is, become less of a window and more of an ark.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose is to argue that:
o: zoos should be abolished because captivity harms animals.
Paragraph 4 explicitly rejects abolition.
zoos' educational benefits outweigh their conservation failures.
Paragraph 3 doubts the educational case rather than ranking it above conservation.
the conservation rationale justifies a much narrower role than zoos claim.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the argument licenses far less and sketches a smaller, ark-like zoo.
captive breeding has failed to save any species.
Paragraph 1 grants that some species survive only because of captive breeding.
qs.x: The author grants some conservation successes but argues that the ark rationale justifies far less than zoos claim, recommending fewer, carefully chosen species. Abolition is a tempting extreme, but paragraph 4 explicitly rejects it because it would strand animals and end real conservation work.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the description of the ark as carrying 'passengers who were never in danger of drowning' implies that:
o: zoo animals are well protected from physical harm.
The metaphor concerns extinction risk, not physical safety inside zoos.
most animals held in zoos belong to species that are not threatened.
Correct: paragraph 2 states that most displayed species are not threatened.
endangered animals are rarely shown to the public.
The point is that unthreatened species dominate, not that endangered ones are hidden.
release programs are too risky for most species.
Paragraph 2 notes that few programs release animals but gives no reason of risk.
qs.x: The ark metaphor casts extinction as a flood; passengers never in danger of drowning are animals whose species are not threatened. Paragraph 2 states this plainly. Reading drowning as physical harm inside the zoo misses that the metaphor is about extinction risk.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the claim that zoo visits make children care about wildlife is best described as:
o: enthusiastic agreement.
Paragraph 3 calls the supporting evidence thin, which rules out enthusiasm.
complete dismissal.
The author's 'Perhaps' and 'it may teach reverence' leave the claim open.
indifference to the question.
The author engages the claim directly and weighs its evidence in paragraph 3.
guarded skepticism.
Correct: paragraph 3 grants the claim is possible but finds the evidence thin and the lesson ambiguous.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 answers the education argument with 'Perhaps,' then calls the evidence thin and the lesson ambiguous. That combination is doubt without outright rejection. Complete dismissal is too strong because the author concedes a caged animal may teach reverence.

qs.q: Which zoo policy would the author most likely endorse?
o: Phasing out an elephant exhibit while expanding breeding of an endangered frog that thrives in small enclosures
Correct: paragraph 4 favors endangered species that flourish in captivity and fewer demanding exhibits.
Adding a great ape exhibit to boost attendance and fund education programs
Paragraph 2 says apes are hard to house, and paragraph 4 opposes exhibits justified by enjoyment.
Closing the zoo and releasing all of its animals into nearby forests
Paragraph 4 rejects abolition because it would strand the animals already held.
Doubling the number of common species so visitors see more diversity
Paragraph 4 recommends holding fewer species, chosen for endangerment.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 sets out criteria: hold fewer species, favor those both endangered and able to thrive in captivity, and drop exhibits justified only by enjoyment. Retiring a demanding elephant exhibit while breeding a frog that thrives in small spaces meets every criterion. Closing the zoo is ruled out by the rejection of abolition.

qs.q: The author rejects abolishing zoos chiefly because abolition would:
o: deprive children of a valuable education.
Paragraph 3 doubts the educational benefit, and paragraph 4 does not cite it.
reduce public interest in wild habitats.
Paragraph 4 cites stranded animals and lost conservation work, not public interest.
strand captive animals and end genuine conservation work.
Correct: paragraph 4 gives exactly these two reasons.
violate legal duties that zoos owe to donors.
The passage never mentions legal duties or donors.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 gives two reasons for rejecting abolition: it would strand the animals already held and end the genuine conservation work some zoos do. Education is a tempting distractor, but the author doubts that benefit in paragraph 3 and never uses it to oppose abolition.

passages.title: The Quarrel Over Images
text: Historians have long been tempted to treat Byzantine iconoclasm, the eighth- and ninth-century campaign against religious images, as theology in costume. On this view, the emperors who ordered icons removed were really pursuing something else: imitating the military success of image-free Islam, seizing the wealth of monasteries that profited from icons, or asserting imperial authority over a church grown too independent. The doctrinal treatises, by this reading, were the ornament on a struggle about power.

There is something to each of these explanations, but together they share a condescension toward the people they describe. They assume that arguments about images could not have mattered for their own sake. Yet the arguments were neither shallow nor easily dismissed. Opponents of icons posed a genuine dilemma: an image of Christ either depicts only his human nature, splitting him in two, or it claims to depict his divine nature as well, which would mean confining the infinite within paint and wood. Either way, they argued, the icon falls into error.

The defenders of images answered with an argument just as subtle. Because God had become flesh, they said, the invisible had made itself visible, and to refuse to depict Christ was in effect to doubt that the incarnation had really occurred. Moreover, an icon did not contain what it showed; it pointed beyond itself, so that honor given to the image passed through it to its subject. The distinction between the veneration owed to images and the worship owed to God alone was not a quibble but the hinge of the whole position.

To reduce such a debate to a pretext is to miss what made it fierce. People were exiled and blinded over these questions because they believed that the meaning of the incarnation was at stake, and that a mistake about pictures was a mistake about salvation. We need not share their beliefs to recognize that they were asking a question we have never fully settled: what is the relationship between a representation and the thing it represents?

qs.q: The central claim of the passage is that Byzantine iconoclasm:
o: involved substantive theological arguments that participants took seriously for their own sake.
Correct: paragraphs 2 through 4 argue the debate was real rather than a pretext.
was chiefly an imperial effort to seize monastic wealth.
Paragraph 1 presents this as one view that the author finds partial and condescending.
resulted mainly from imitation of Islamic military success.
Paragraph 2 grants such explanations only some truth; this is not the thesis.
has been correctly understood by most historians.
The author challenges the long-standing historical tendency described in paragraph 1.
qs.x: The author presents the power-politics reading of iconoclasm, calls it condescending, and spends paragraphs 2 through 4 showing the theology was subtle and sincerely held. Monastic wealth and Islamic influence are explanations the author grants only partial truth, so they cannot be the central claim.
