qs.q: According to the passage, opponents of icons argued that an image of Christ:
o: honored the image rather than its subject.
Paragraph 3 presents honor passing to the subject as the defenders' argument, not the critics'.
was permissible only inside churches.
No such limit appears; paragraph 2 describes a dilemma about any depiction.
would weaken the empire's armies.
Military motives belong to the political explanations in paragraph 1, not the theology.
either divided his natures or tried to confine the divine.
Correct: paragraph 2 lays out this two-horned dilemma.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 gives the opponents' dilemma: an image shows only Christ's human nature, splitting him, or claims to show the divine, confining the infinite. Either way the icon errs. The idea that honor passes through an image to its subject belongs to the defenders in paragraph 3, a common mix-up.

qs.q: The author's view of the political and economic explanations described in paragraph 1 is that they:
o: are entirely without foundation.
Paragraph 2 says 'there is something to each of these explanations.'
contain some truth but wrongly treat the doctrinal dispute as mere ornament.
Correct: paragraph 2 grants them partial truth but faults their condescension.
are more convincing than the theological explanations.
The author argues the reverse, defending the weight of theology in paragraph 4.
apply to the defenders of icons but not to their opponents.
The passage draws no such division between the two parties.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 opens by conceding 'there is something to each of these explanations,' then faults them for assuming the arguments could not matter for their own sake. That is partial agreement plus a criticism. 'Entirely without foundation' ignores the concession.

qs.q: Within the defenders' position, the distinction between veneration and worship mattered mainly because it:
o: allowed emperors to tax icons separately from churches.
Taxation is never connected to this distinction in the passage.
proved that icons contained the divine nature.
Paragraph 3 says an icon did not contain what it showed.
let them honor images without giving them the worship owed to God alone.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it the hinge, since honor passed through the image to its subject.
conceded the iconoclasts' charge that images divide Christ.
Paragraph 3 shows defenders answering the dilemma, not conceding it.
qs.x: The defenders had to show that honoring icons was not idolatry. Distinguishing veneration of images from worship owed to God alone let them honor icons while reserving worship for God, which is why paragraph 3 calls it the hinge. The passage says icons did not contain what they showed, ruling out the claim they held the divine.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the defenders' claim that honor paid to an icon passes to its subject?
o: A collector prizes a painting for the fame of its artist.
This values the object and its maker, not a subject the image points toward.
A museum displays a statue for its fine craftsmanship.
Admiring craft treats the image as an end, unlike the pointing-beyond of paragraph 3.
A tourist photographs a monument to show friends where she traveled.
The photo records a visit; it directs no honor to the monument's subject.
A citizen saluting a flag says she honors the nation, not the cloth.
Correct: like the icon in paragraph 3, the flag directs honor beyond itself to what it represents.
qs.x: The defenders held that an icon points beyond itself, so honor given to it passes to its subject. A citizen who salutes a flag while honoring the nation, not the cloth, has the same structure. Admiring craftsmanship or an artist's fame treats the object itself as the end.

qs.q: Which discovery would most challenge the author's argument?
o: Evidence that some monasteries grew rich from selling icons
Paragraph 2 already grants such factors some truth; the theology could still matter.
Letters in which leading iconoclast theologians privately dismissed their own arguments as written to order
Correct: this would suggest doctrine really was a costume for power, as paragraph 1's view holds.
Records showing that defenders of icons were exiled more often than opponents
Who suffered more does not bear on whether the arguments were sincerely held.
Sermons showing that ordinary believers were stirred by debates over images
This would support paragraph 4's claim that people believed salvation was at stake.
qs.x: The author's thesis is that iconoclast theology was sincere, not a cover for power. Private letters in which iconoclast theologians admit their arguments were written to order would directly show the doctrine was a costume. Monastic wealth does not challenge the thesis, since the author already grants such factors some role.

passages.title: What the Laugh Knows
text: Philosophers who write about humor usually sort their predecessors into three camps. Superiority theorists, following Hobbes, hold that we laugh at the misfortunes and failings of others because they let us feel elevated. Relief theorists, following Freud, treat laughter as the discharge of nervous energy that social prohibition has bottled up. Incongruity theorists, the largest camp today, locate the comic in a mismatch between what we expect and what we encounter.

The incongruity theory has won its dominance honestly. It explains puns, absurdities, and the sudden twist at the end of a joke far better than either rival, and it accounts for the fact that much of what amuses us involves no victim and no forbidden impulse at all. But as usually stated, it proves too much. Incongruity is everywhere, and most of it is not funny. A stranger in a hospital gown standing in the middle of a highway is incongruous; so is an unexpected lump discovered in the shower. The first produces alarm and the second dread. If mismatch alone made us laugh, we would laugh at our own diagnoses.

What is missing is the frame within which the mismatch is met. We laugh at incongruity when we can afford not to resolve it, when nothing practical hangs on the gap between expectation and outcome. The joke-teller's preamble, the clown's makeup, the friend's raised eyebrow all announce that we are in a space where violations of sense can be savored rather than repaired. Humor, on this account, is a kind of play with our own expectations, conducted in conditions of safety.

This amendment explains something the bare theory cannot: why the same event can be terrifying in the moment and hilarious in the retelling. The incongruity has not changed. What has changed is that the danger has passed, and the mind is free to enjoy the absurdity it was once too busy to notice.

qs.q: According to the author, the chief weakness of the incongruity theory as usually stated is that it:
o: cannot explain puns or absurd twists.
Paragraph 2 says it explains these better than either rival theory.
depends on Freud's notion of bottled-up energy.
That idea belongs to the relief theory, a separate camp in paragraph 1.
does not explain why most incongruities are not funny.
Correct: paragraph 2 says incongruity is everywhere and mostly unfunny, so the theory proves too much.
assumes that every joke needs a victim.
That fits the superiority theory; paragraph 2 says much humor has no victim.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 praises incongruity theory for explaining puns and twists, then says it proves too much: mismatch is everywhere and mostly not funny. That overreach is its chief flaw. Saying it cannot explain puns reverses the passage, which names puns as a strength.

qs.q: The examples of the stranger in a hospital gown and the lump found in the shower serve primarily to:
o: show that incongruity can produce alarm or dread rather than laughter.
Correct: paragraph 2 uses them as incongruities that are plainly not funny.
illustrate the superiority theory's view of misfortune.
In paragraph 2 they target the incongruity theory, not superiority.
suggest that medical settings suppress humor.
The setting is incidental; the point is that mismatch alone is not funny.
show that frightening events can never become funny.
Paragraph 4 says frightening events can become hilarious in the retelling.
qs.x: A stranger in a hospital gown on a highway and a lump found in the shower are both incongruous, yet they cause alarm and dread. Paragraph 2 uses them as counterexamples showing mismatch alone does not produce laughter. They do not show frightening events can never become funny, which paragraph 4 contradicts.

qs.q: The author would most likely say that a clown's makeup contributes to humor by:
o: creating an incongruity between face and expectation.
Paragraph 3 lists makeup as a signal of the frame, not as the incongruity itself.
letting the audience feel superior to the clown.
The author's account rests on safe play, not on superiority.
releasing tension built up by social rules.
That is the relief theory's mechanism from paragraph 1.
signaling a safe space where violations of sense can be enjoyed.
Correct: paragraph 3 says such cues announce a space where violations are savored, not repaired.
qs.x: In paragraph 3, the joke-teller's preamble, the clown's makeup, and the raised eyebrow are cues that frame a situation as safe play. The makeup matters as a signal, not as the incongruity itself. Choices built on superiority or relief borrow mechanisms from rival theories the author does not adopt.

qs.q: Which observation would most strongly support the author's amendment to the incongruity theory?
o: Adults laugh more at jokes about rival groups than about their own group.
This fits the superiority theory rather than the frame-of-safety account.
Infants laugh at peekaboo from a parent but cry when a stranger plays the same game.
Correct: the incongruity is identical but the sense of safety differs, as paragraph 3 predicts.
Puns are rated funnier when the double meaning is more surprising.
This supports bare incongruity, not the frame the author adds.
People laugh more readily after drinking alcohol.
This concerns disinhibition generally, not the safety frame the author adds.
qs.x: The amendment holds that incongruity is funny only within a frame of safety. Peekaboo is ideal evidence: the same game makes an infant laugh with a trusted parent and cry with a stranger, so only safety varies. Surprise ratings for puns support bare incongruity theory, not the added safety frame.

qs.q: Faced with a superiority theorist who cites laughter at slapstick falls, the author would most likely reply that such laughter:
o: proves that humor requires a victim.
Paragraph 2 says much of what amuses us involves no victim.
is nervous relief after witnessing danger.
That is the relief theory's account, not the author's play-frame view.
depends on the fall being harmless, which the safety frame explains.
Correct: paragraph 3 says we laugh when nothing practical hangs on the mismatch.
is not genuine humor at all.
The author never denies that such laughter is real humor.
qs.x: The author would reinterpret slapstick through the safety frame: we laugh at a fall when nothing practical hangs on it, meaning no one is really hurt. That explains the laughter without needing a victim's misfortune. The author also notes that much humor has no victim, so a victim is not required.

passages.title: Water and Dominion
text: The canal occupies an honored place in the story of progress. Where the road bends to the land, the canal bends the land to its purpose, and the great waterways of history are usually remembered as triumphs of engineering that knit regions together and opened them to trade. This account is not false, but it leaves out the question of whom a canal serves. A channel of water runs in a direction, and the direction it runs tells us a great deal about who commanded its digging.

China's Grand Canal, extended and linked under the Sui dynasty around the year 600, is often praised for uniting the rice-growing south with the political north. Yet its central function for centuries was to carry grain levied from southern farmers to feed the capital and its armies. The canal did not distribute abundance so much as gather it. Its route was the map of a tax.

The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, tells a similar story in a modern key. Its early years of excavation relied heavily on forced Egyptian labor, and its construction contributed to the debts that led Egypt's ruler to sell his shares in the canal company to Britain in 1875. Within a few years British troops occupied the country. A project advertised as connecting the world had the effect of placing one of its crossroads under foreign control.

I do not mean that canals were simply crimes dressed as achievements. Trade did flow along them, and many people far from any palace benefited from cheaper goods. But the language of connection conceals the asymmetry built into such works. They were dug by many and directed by few, and the wealth they moved tended to flow toward the center that had ordered them. To admire a canal properly, we must ask not only what it joined but what it drained.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the passage's central argument?
o: Canals were crimes disguised as achievements.
Paragraph 4 explicitly rejects this characterization.
Canals mainly lowered the cost of goods for ordinary people.
Paragraph 4 grants this benefit as a concession, not as the thesis.
Engineering advances made canals obsolete after 1869.
The passage makes no claim that canals became obsolete.
Canals often drew wealth and power toward those who ordered them, a fact the progress story omits.
Correct: paragraphs 1 and 4 stress whom canals served and what they drained.
qs.x: The author grants that canals brought trade but argues the progress story hides whom they served: wealth tended to flow toward the center that ordered them. 'Crimes disguised as achievements' is tempting but too strong, since paragraph 4 explicitly rejects that characterization.

qs.q: The statement that the Grand Canal's 'route was the map of a tax' most nearly means that the canal:
o: followed the path by which levied grain moved to the capital.
Correct: paragraph 2 says its central function was carrying southern grain levies north.
was financed by a special tax on boatmen.
Paragraph 2 says nothing about how the canal was financed.
was planned using tax records as maps.
This reads the metaphor literally; paragraph 2 describes the flow of tribute.
exempted southern farmers from taxation.
Paragraph 2 says grain was levied from southern farmers.
qs.x: The metaphor means the canal's path traced the flow of tribute: southern grain levied as tax and shipped north to feed the capital and armies. Taking 'map' literally, as tax records used for planning, misses the figurative sense. Paragraph 2 never discusses financing.

qs.q: According to the passage, the 1875 sale of Egypt's canal shares to Britain was connected to:
o: the canal's failure to attract shipping.
Paragraph 3 never claims the canal lacked traffic.
debts to which the canal's construction had contributed.
Correct: paragraph 3 links construction to the debts behind the sale.
a British military occupation already underway.
Paragraph 3 says the occupation came within a few years after the sale.
the end of forced labor on the project.
Paragraph 3 mentions forced labor but does not tie the sale to its end.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says construction contributed to the debts that led Egypt's ruler to sell his canal shares to Britain in 1875. The British occupation came afterward, within a few years, so it cannot be a cause of the sale. Watch the order of events in detail questions.

qs.q: The concession in paragraph 4 that trade flowed along canals and benefited many people functions to:
o: abandon the critique developed in paragraphs 2 and 3.
The author keeps the critique, saying the language of connection conceals asymmetry.
prove that canals were primarily commercial projects.
The author still emphasizes control and the direction of wealth.
grant real benefits while maintaining that canals were asymmetric in whom they served.
Correct: paragraph 4 grants benefits, then says canals were dug by many and directed by few.
show that the Grand Canal was more beneficial than Suez.
Paragraph 4 makes no comparison between the two canals.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 opens with a concession (trade flowed, many benefited) and then reasserts the thesis that canals were dug by many and directed by few. Concessions like this strengthen an argument by acknowledging counterpoints without giving up the main claim, so it does not abandon the critique.

qs.q: Which new example would best fit the author's argument?
o: A village digs a small channel so farmers can irrigate shared fields.
A local shared project lacks the center-ward flow of wealth the author highlights.
A colonial railway runs from inland mines straight to a port, with no lines linking local towns.
Correct: like the canal in paragraph 2, its route maps extraction toward a commanding center.
Two neighboring cities jointly build a bridge to ease commuting.
This connects equals; the author's point concerns asymmetric flows.
A highway is built mainly for tourists visiting a national park.
Tourist access is not the gathering of wealth toward the center that ordered it.
qs.x: The author's pattern is infrastructure whose route traces extraction toward a commanding center rather than mutual connection. A colonial railway running from mines straight to a port, skipping local towns, fits exactly. A village irrigation channel is a canal but lacks the asymmetric flow toward a distant center.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's account of the Grand Canal?
o: Building the canal required very large numbers of laborers.
This fits the author's claim that canals were dug by many.
The capital's armies depended on grain shipped from the south.
This supports paragraph 2's account of grain feeding the capital.
Later dynasties repaired and extended the canal.
Repairs do not change what the canal chiefly carried.
Most of the canal's cargo was private goods traded among southern towns, with tribute grain a minor share.
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that its central function was moving levied grain.
qs.x: The author's Grand Canal claim is that its central function was moving levied grain to the capital. Evidence that most cargo was private trade among southern towns, with tribute minor, would contradict that directly. Large labor forces or armies fed by southern grain would support, not weaken, the account.

passages.title: The Instructed Child
text: Histories of children's literature tend to follow a plot of liberation. In the beginning, we are told, were the improving tracts of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, in which disobedient children fell into ponds and pious ones died serenely, and in which every story ended in a lesson. Then came Lewis Carroll, whose Alice tumbled into a world of nonsense where the morals were mocked, and children's books were set free to delight rather than instruct.

The plot has its truth. Carroll did parody the moral verses that Victorian children memorized, and the books that followed him gave imagination a standing it had seldom enjoyed. But the liberation narrative mistakes a change in what children's books teach for a change in whether they teach. Walk through the picture-book section of any modern bookstore and you will find books about sharing, about naming one's feelings, about welcoming the new child in class, about the dignity of every kind of family. These books are no less earnest than the tracts they supposedly replaced. They have simply exchanged obedience and piety for empathy and self-acceptance.

This is not a complaint. Adults who write for children are, almost unavoidably, telling them what kind of people to become, and it would be strange to wish otherwise. The trouble with the liberation story is that it lets each generation imagine that its own lessons are not lessons at all but simply the truth, while the moralizing belongs only to the past. The Victorian author who warned against vanity believed he was describing reality, not imposing a value. So, very often, do we.

A more honest history would read the didactic tract and the contemporary picture book side by side, as documents of what different societies hoped their children would be. It would also ask why the books children love most, from Carroll's to the present, so often seem to slip free of whatever lesson the adults intended.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the liberation narrative is that it:
o: exaggerates the harshness of early moral tracts.
The author does not dispute paragraph 1's depiction of the tracts.
gives Lewis Carroll too little credit.
Paragraph 2 affirms Carroll's role; the problem lies elsewhere.
mistakes a change in what children's books teach for an end to teaching.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it confuses a change in what books teach with whether they teach.
ignores the commercial pressures on publishers.
Commercial pressures are never discussed in the passage.
qs.x: The author accepts that Carroll changed children's books but says the liberation story confuses a change in what books teach with an end to teaching. Modern picture books still instruct, just about empathy instead of piety. The author does not dispute the description of the old tracts.

qs.q: The author's remark about the Victorian author who warned against vanity, followed by 'So, very often, do we,' suggests that:
o: modern writers also tend to mistake their own values for plain truth.
Correct: paragraph 3 says each generation treats its own lessons as simply the truth.
modern writers warn against vanity more than Victorians did.
The parallel concerns self-perception, not the topic of vanity.
Victorian authors knowingly imposed their values.
Paragraph 3 says the Victorian believed he was describing reality.
readers today reject moral lessons in children's books.
The author describes writers' assumptions, not readers' rejection of lessons.
qs.x: The Victorian thought he was describing reality, not imposing a value; 'So, very often, do we' says moderns make the same mistake about their own lessons. The parallel concerns self-perception, not vanity. It cannot mean Victorians knowingly imposed values, since the passage says the opposite.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward instruction in children's books is best described as:
o: disapproving, since lessons stifle imagination.
Paragraph 3 opens by saying 'This is not a complaint.'
nostalgic for the moral clarity of earlier tracts.
The author shows no preference for the older lessons.
indifferent, since children ignore lessons anyway.
The author treats the lessons as revealing and worth studying, not ignorable.
accepting of it as nearly unavoidable while urging awareness of it.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls instruction almost unavoidable and faults only self-deception about it.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says 'This is not a complaint' and calls instruction almost unavoidable; the author's objection is only to each generation's blindness to its own lessons. So the attitude is acceptance plus a call for awareness. Disapproval is ruled out by the author's explicit disclaimer.

qs.q: Which research project would the author most likely recommend?
o: Measuring whether modern picture books raise children's empathy scores
The author's interest is in what books reveal about societies, not their measured effects.
Comparing a Victorian moral tract with a recent picture book as evidence of each era's ideals
Correct: paragraph 4 calls for reading them side by side as documents of each society's hopes.
Cataloging which moral verses Carroll parodied in his books
This narrows to Carroll and misses the comparative aim of paragraph 4.
Surveying parents on which lessons they want books to teach
Paragraph 4 proposes a historical reading of texts, not an opinion survey.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 proposes reading the didactic tract and the modern picture book side by side as documents of what each society hoped its children would be. A comparative historical study of both matches that directly. Measuring empathy effects shifts the focus to outcomes, which the author never asks about.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage most strongly implies that the books children love most:
o: contain no moral content at all.
The sentence says they slip free of intended lessons, not that they lack morals.
were written without any adult intention.
Paragraph 4 says adults intended lessons; the books simply exceed them.
owe part of their appeal to what escapes their authors' intended lessons.
Correct: paragraph 4 notes that favorites seem to slip free of the lessons adults intended.
are mostly nonsense books in Carroll's tradition.
The sentence spans Carroll to the present without limiting itself to nonsense.
qs.x: The final sentence notes that the most loved books seem to slip free of the lessons adults intended, implying their appeal partly lies in what exceeds those lessons. It does not say they lack morals or adult intention; slipping free of an intended lesson presupposes one existed.

passages.title: The Patient Copy
text: We usually picture the medieval scriptorium in one of two ways. In the first, monks are heroic custodians, carrying the learning of antiquity across centuries of darkness by copying it word by word. In the second, less flattering image, they are human photocopiers, dutifully reproducing texts they barely understood, their labor made obsolete the moment movable type arrived. Both pictures share an assumption: that the point of copying was the copy.

For many monastic scribes, the point was also the copying. Monastic rules treated the work of the pen as a form of prayer and discipline, a way of keeping the hands busy and the mind fixed on sacred words. Some writers compared each letter to a wound inflicted on the devil. The scribe who spent months on a single book was not merely producing an object; he was submitting himself to a text at the pace of the hand, letter by letter, in a way no silent reader skimming a page ever would.

Nor was copying as mechanical as the photocopier image implies. Scribes compared exemplars, corrected what they took to be errors, added glosses in the margins, and sometimes left notes of their own, complaints about the cold, the poor light, the ache in the back. A manuscript bears the traces of its makers in a way a printed edition rarely does. Every copy was, in a small sense, a new edition, shaped by the judgment and the fatigue of a particular person.

When printing arrived, then, it did not simply do the scribe's job faster. It changed what a book was. Texts became more uniform and more abundant, and the reader's relation to them grew more private and more rapid. These were real gains. But something was lost along with the slowness: the sense that to reproduce a text was to inhabit it, and that the labor of transmission was itself a way of understanding.

qs.q: According to the author, the two common pictures of the scriptorium share the assumption that:
o: monks understood little of what they copied.
Paragraph 1 attributes this only to the second, photocopier picture.
the value of copying lay in the finished copy.
Correct: paragraph 1 says both assume the point of copying was the copy.
printing improved the accuracy of texts.
Paragraph 1 does not attribute this view to either picture.
monks were heroic custodians of learning.
Only the first picture holds this view, per paragraph 1.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states the shared assumption directly: in both pictures, the point of copying was the copy. The author then argues the act of copying also mattered. The other choices each describe only one of the two pictures, not what they share.

qs.q: According to the passage, monastic rules treated the work of copying as:
o: a form of prayer and discipline.
Correct: paragraph 2 says rules treated the pen's work as prayer and discipline.
a punishment for disobedient monks.
Paragraph 2 uses discipline in a devotional sense, not as punishment.
a source of income for the monastery.
Income is never mentioned in paragraph 2.
a task best left to hired lay craftsmen.
The passage describes monks themselves as the scribes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says monastic rules treated the work of the pen as prayer and discipline. Here discipline means devotional self-training, not punishment. Reading discipline as penalty is a common trap that ignores the passage's context of prayer and focus on sacred words.

qs.q: The author mentions scribes' notes complaining about the cold, poor light, and back pain primarily to show that:
o: monastic conditions were harsher than commonly believed.
Hardship is incidental; paragraph 3 uses the notes to show individual traces.
scribes resented the work of copying.
Paragraph 2 presents copying as devotion, not resented labor.
printed books were produced in better conditions.
Printing conditions are never discussed.
manuscripts bear personal traces of the individuals who made them.
Correct: paragraph 3 says a manuscript bears its makers' traces in a way print rarely does.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 lists corrections, glosses, and complaints about cold, light, and back pain as evidence that a manuscript bears traces of its makers. The complaints show individual presence, not resentment of the work. The author frames copying as devotion in paragraph 2, so resentment misreads them.

qs.q: The claim that 'every copy was, in a small sense, a new edition' most nearly means that each manuscript:
o: was deliberately revised to update its content.
Paragraph 3 describes corrections and glosses, not systematic revision.
was more accurate than the exemplar it copied.
The passage claims no gain in accuracy, only the scribe's shaping hand.
reflected the judgment and conditions of the particular scribe who made it.
Correct: paragraph 3 says each copy was shaped by one person's judgment and fatigue.
was intended for a different audience.
Audiences are not discussed in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Each copy was a new edition in a small sense because it carried the corrections, glosses, and fatigue of one scribe. The author means personal shaping, not systematic revision. 'In a small sense' signals a modest claim, which rules out deliberate updating of content.

qs.q: Which modern practice is most analogous to copying as the author says monks understood it?
o: A clerk scanning documents to create digital backups
This values the copy alone, like the views paragraph 1 critiques.
A student retyping messy notes to get a clean version
The aim is a better product, not the act of copying itself.
A print shop producing identical posters for an event
Uniform mass production matches print, not the scribe's practice.
A calligraphy student copying a poem by hand as a meditation
Correct: as for paragraph 2's scribes, the act of copying is itself the point.
qs.x: For monastic scribes the act of copying was itself valuable as prayer and discipline. A calligraphy student copying a poem as meditation values the process the same way. Retyping notes to get a clean version is tempting, but its aim is a better product, which is the copy-centered view the author critiques.

qs.q: The author would most likely regard the claim that printing merely made book production more efficient as:
o: accurate, since printing did the scribe's job faster.
Paragraph 4 says printing did not simply do the scribe's job faster.
incomplete, since printing also changed readers' relation to texts.
Correct: paragraph 4 says it changed what a book was and how readers related to it.
false, since printing made texts less uniform.
Paragraph 4 says texts became more uniform.
exaggerated, since early printing was slower than copying.
The author makes no such speed claim and grants printing's real gains.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says printing did not simply do the scribe's job faster; it changed what a book was and made reading more private and rapid. So the efficiency claim is true as far as it goes but leaves things out. It is not false, because the author grants printing's real gains.

passages.title: The Ladder and the Swarm
text: In 1904 the sociologist Georg Simmel proposed that fashion is driven by two opposing human needs: the wish to belong and the wish to stand apart. Elites adopt a new style to distinguish themselves; those beneath them imitate it to share in their prestige; and once imitation makes the style common, the elites abandon it for something new. The cycle, in this account, never ends because its fuel, the desire to be both like others and unlike them, never runs out.

Critics have long pointed out that Simmel's model no longer fits the way styles actually move. Denim, sneakers, and the hooded sweatshirt did not descend from aristocrats; they rose from laborers, athletes, and teenagers, and only later appeared on runways at extravagant prices. Today trends often seem to spread sideways, through networks of peers who copy one another without any clear apex. The neat ladder of trickle-down has become something more like a swarm.

Yet it is a mistake to conclude that Simmel was simply wrong. What has collapsed is the ladder, not the engine. His real insight was not that styles flow from rich to poor but that fashion lives on the tension between imitation and distinction, and that tension is visible everywhere in the swarm. The teenager who discovers an obscure band's merchandise prizes it precisely because few others wear it, and loses interest when it shows up at the mall. The status being sought may come from subcultural knowledge rather than wealth, but the rhythm is the one Simmel described.

If anything, the speed of contemporary trends confirms his model rather than refuting it. When imitation can happen overnight, distinction must be renewed just as quickly, and the cycle accelerates. A theory that seemed to describe the slow drift of styles through a stratified society turns out to describe, more vividly than ever, the restlessness of a connected one.

qs.q: The author's main claim about Simmel's theory is that:
o: it was mistaken from the start.
Paragraph 3 says it is a mistake to conclude Simmel was simply wrong.
its account of class hierarchy remains fully accurate.
Paragraph 2 concedes that the trickle-down ladder no longer fits.
it applies only to luxury goods.
The author applies it to sneakers and band merchandise as well.
its core mechanism survives even though its class ladder does not.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the ladder has collapsed but the engine remains.
qs.x: The author concedes that Simmel's trickle-down ladder no longer fits but argues his core engine, the tension between imitation and distinction, still drives fashion. Paragraph 4 even says faster trends confirm it. 'Mistaken from the start' contradicts the author's statement that Simmel was not simply wrong.

qs.q: In the statement 'What has collapsed is the ladder, not the engine,' the author distinguishes between:
o: the direction in which styles travel and the motive that drives them.
Correct: the ladder is top-down flow; the engine is the tension between imitation and distinction.
elite fashion and working-class fashion.
Paragraph 3 places both kinds of fashion under the same engine.
fashion in 1904 and fashion in the future.
The contrast is between mechanisms, not between time periods.
the need to imitate and the need for distinction.
These two needs together form the engine; they are not the terms being contrasted.
qs.x: The ladder is the top-down route styles once took from elites to others; the engine is the motive behind fashion, the pull between imitation and distinction. So the contrast is direction of travel versus driving force. Imitation and distinction are tempting, but together they make up the engine rather than being contrasted.

qs.q: The example of the teenager and the obscure band's merchandise is used to illustrate that:
o: young people are indifferent to status.
Paragraph 3 says the teenager seeks status through rarity.
trends still begin among the wealthy.
Paragraph 3 says this status comes from subcultural knowledge, not wealth.
distinction can rest on subcultural knowledge rather than wealth.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the status may come from knowledge, yet the rhythm is Simmel's.
shopping malls are the main source of new trends.
The mall marks where the item loses its distinction, not where trends start.
qs.x: The teenager values obscure band merchandise because few others wear it and drops it once it reaches the mall. That is distinction based on subcultural knowledge rather than wealth, yet it follows Simmel's rhythm. It does not show indifference to status, since the teenager is seeking status through rarity.

qs.q: Which finding would most seriously challenge the author's position?
o: Many trends now originate on social media rather than runways.
Paragraph 2 already accepts that trends spread sideways through peers.
Most people adopt styles for comfort and price and keep them no matter how common they become.
Correct: this denies the imitation-distinction tension the author says survives.
Luxury brands now copy streetwear designs.
This fits paragraph 2's account of styles rising to the runway.
Fashion cycles have grown shorter in recent decades.
Paragraph 4 predicts exactly this acceleration.
qs.x: The author's position depends on people seeking distinction and abandoning styles once they become common. If most people chose clothes for comfort and price and kept them however common they got, that engine would be absent. Sideways spread and faster cycles are features the author already accepts or predicts.

qs.q: Based on paragraph 4, which prediction would the author most likely make?
o: As styles spread faster online, early adopters will abandon them sooner.
Correct: paragraph 4 says faster imitation forces faster renewal of distinction.
As styles spread faster, fashion will become more uniform and stable.
Paragraph 4 predicts acceleration, not stability.
Elites will regain control of fashion as trends speed up.
The author does not predict a return of the trickle-down ladder.
Faster trends will eventually end the desire for distinction.
Paragraph 4 says distinction is renewed more quickly, not abandoned.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says that when imitation happens overnight, distinction must be renewed just as fast, so the cycle accelerates. That implies early adopters will drop styles sooner as they spread faster. Predicting stability or uniformity reverses the author's logic, which links speed to restlessness.

passages.title: The Inner Citadel Reconsidered
text: Stoicism is enjoying a revival, mostly in the form of advice. Its popular modern versions promise resilience: distinguish what you can control from what you cannot, stop worrying about the latter, and you will meet setbacks with calm. Executives and athletes quote Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius as they might quote a coach. There is nothing wrong with taking comfort from ancient writers, but this Stoicism of the stiff upper lip resembles its source less than its admirers suppose.

To begin with, the Stoics did not counsel suppressing emotion. They argued something more radical: that the passions, such as fear, grief, and craving, are themselves judgments, and mistaken ones. To fear losing one's wealth is to judge that wealth is a genuine good whose loss is a genuine harm. Since the Stoics held that virtue alone is truly good, such judgments were simply false, and the cure was not to clench one's jaw against fear but to see clearly that there was nothing to fear. The goal was not a feeling held down but a feeling that never arose, because its premise had been corrected.

Second, and more important, the ancient Stoic was not a solitary figure retreating into an inner citadel. Stoic thinkers described human concern as a series of widening circles, from oneself to family to city to all of humanity, and urged that the outer circles be drawn ever inward. The famous division between what is and is not up to us was meant to free a person for duty, not from it. Marcus Aurelius wrote his reflections between campaigns, reminding himself that he had been born to work with others as the hands work with the feet.

A Stoicism reduced to stress management keeps the technique and discards the ethics. It teaches people to be untroubled without asking what they ought to be troubled about, and so risks making them comfortable with the very things a Stoic would have called vice.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose is to:
o: argue that popular Stoicism omits the ancient school's account of judgment and social duty.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 name these omissions, and paragraph 4 states their cost.
recommend Stoic techniques for managing workplace stress.
The author criticizes reducing Stoicism to stress management.
show that Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius disagreed about ethics.
No disagreement between them is described.
argue that ancient philosophy has no modern relevance.
Paragraph 1 says there is nothing wrong with taking comfort from ancient writers.
qs.x: The author contrasts popular stress-management Stoicism with the ancient school, showing it drops the theory that passions are false judgments and the emphasis on social duty. Recommending Stoic techniques for stress is tempting, but paragraph 4 criticizes exactly that reduction.

qs.q: According to the passage, the Stoics regarded fear of losing one's wealth as:
o: a natural feeling to be endured calmly.
Paragraph 2 says the goal was a feeling that never arose, not one endured.
a prudent concern for one's family.
Paragraph 2 calls it a false judgment about what is good.
resting on the false judgment that wealth is truly good.
Correct: paragraph 2 says such fear judges wealth a genuine good, which the Stoics denied.
an emotion best suppressed through willpower.
Paragraph 2 says the Stoics did not counsel suppressing emotion.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says passions are judgments: fearing loss of wealth means judging wealth a real good. Since Stoics held virtue alone is good, the judgment is false, and correcting it removes the fear. Suppression through willpower is the modern stiff-upper-lip version the author says the Stoics did not counsel.

qs.q: The reference to Marcus Aurelius writing his reflections between military campaigns serves mainly to:
o: show that Stoicism was popular among soldiers.
The detail concerns Marcus's own practice, not soldiers' tastes.
illustrate that Stoic reflection was tied to active duty among others.
Correct: paragraph 3 uses it to show the Stoic was no solitary retreater.
suggest that warfare is compatible with virtue.
The author draws no conclusion about the morality of war.
explain why his writings were unsystematic.
The form of his writings is never discussed.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues the Stoic was not a solitary figure in an inner citadel. Marcus Aurelius writing between campaigns, reminding himself he was born to work with others, shows reflection joined to active duty. The detail concerns his own practice, not soldiers' tastes or the ethics of war.

qs.q: The author suggests popular Stoicism risks making people 'comfortable with the very things a Stoic would have called vice' because it:
o: teaches people to suppress their emotions.
The concern in paragraph 4 is lost ethics, not suppression as such.
encourages excessive concern for others.
The author says it lacks attention to duty, not that it has too much.
relies on misquotations of ancient authors.
The author never alleges misquotation.
cultivates calm without asking what one ought to be troubled about.
Correct: paragraph 4 says it teaches being untroubled without asking what should trouble us.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says reduced Stoicism keeps the technique but discards the ethics, teaching calm without asking what ought to trouble us. So people may grow calm about injustice a Stoic would call vice. Suppression is not the issue here, since the risk comes from missing ethics, not from technique.

qs.q: Which person best exemplifies the Stoic ideal as the author describes it?
o: An investor who meditates daily so market losses no longer upset him
This is calm as technique, which paragraph 4 says omits the ethics.
A hermit who withdraws from society to protect his peace of mind
Paragraph 3 says the Stoic was not a solitary figure in an inner citadel.
A judge who, untroubled by threats to her career, rules justly in an unpopular case
Correct: she pairs freedom from false fears with active duty, per paragraphs 2 and 3.
An athlete who forcibly suppresses his fear before every match
Paragraph 2 says the Stoics did not counsel suppressing emotion.
qs.x: The author's Stoic both corrects false judgments, so fear does not arise, and acts on duty to others. A judge unmoved by career threats who rules justly does both. The meditating investor has calm but no ethical purpose, and the hermit retreats, which paragraph 3 rejects.

qs.q: A modern Stoicism coach says that since we cannot control politics, we should stop caring about public affairs. The author would most likely respond that this:
o: applies the dichotomy of control correctly.
Paragraph 3 says the division was meant to free people for duty.
turns a principle meant to free people for duty into an excuse to avoid it.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the division freed a person for duty, not from it.
is right about politics but wrong about family life.
Paragraph 3's widening circles include city and humanity, not just family.
confuses the passion of fear with that of grief.
The difference between passions is irrelevant to the coach's error.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the division between what is and is not up to us was meant to free a person for duty, not from it, and Stoic concern widened to city and humanity. A coach who uses that division to excuse indifference to public affairs inverts its purpose. That is a misapplication, not a correct use of the principle.

passages.title: Forty Days
text: The word quarantine preserves a number. It comes from the Venetian quaranta giorni, the forty days that ships arriving from plague-stricken ports were made to wait before their crews and cargo could come ashore. The practice is older than the word: in 1377 the Adriatic port of Ragusa ordered travelers from infected areas to spend thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Venice later built permanent island stations where suspect travelers and goods were held.

Because these measures predate germ theory by nearly five centuries, it is tempting to treat them as lucky superstition, the right action for the wrong reasons. Contemporary physicians explained plague through corrupted air and the alignment of planets, and the choice of forty days may well owe more to biblical resonance than to any measured interval. But the officials who imposed quarantine were not reasoning from cosmology. They were reasoning from experience. They had watched disease arrive with ships and travelers, and had noticed that separating the newly arrived for a time seemed to keep it out. One need not know what a bacterium is to observe that sickness travels with people.

If quarantine was more rational than its reputation, it was also more political. Deciding which ports counted as infected, which travelers were suspect, and how long they must wait were never purely medical judgments. Cities used quarantine to harass commercial rivals and to mark foreigners, the poor, and religious minorities as carriers of danger. The same measure that protected a population also defined who stood outside it.

Both lessons remain worth keeping. Quarantine has always been a way of acting under uncertainty, before the cause of a disease is understood, and its early history suggests that such action can be sound. But its history also suggests that the line drawn around the sick has a way of following lines already drawn around the distrusted. A public that wishes to keep the first should watch closely for the second.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Quarantine was a superstition that happened to work.
Paragraph 2 rejects this reading, stressing that officials reasoned from experience.
Quarantine was purely a tool for persecuting outsiders.
Paragraph 4 says its protective value is worth keeping.
Quarantine began only after the rise of germ theory.
Paragraph 2 says it predated germ theory by nearly five centuries.
Early quarantine was grounded in experience but also shaped by politics.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 make these two points, and paragraph 4 keeps both lessons.
qs.x: The author argues that early quarantine was rational because officials reasoned from experience, and also political because it was used against rivals and outsiders; paragraph 4 keeps both lessons. 'Purely a tool for persecuting outsiders' is one-sided and ignores the protective value the author defends.

qs.q: According to the passage, the choice of forty days for quarantine:
o: was based on measured incubation periods.
Paragraph 2 says it may owe more to biblical resonance than to measurement.
may reflect biblical associations more than any measured interval.
Correct: paragraph 2 says this directly.
was first adopted by Ragusa in 1377.
Paragraph 1 says Ragusa required thirty days, not forty.
was set by physicians who studied planetary alignment.
Paragraph 2 says officials reasoned from experience, not cosmology.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the forty-day figure may owe more to biblical resonance than to any measured interval. Ragusa is a trap: paragraph 1 says its 1377 rule required thirty days, and the forty-day term came from Venetian practice. Measured incubation periods are never claimed.

qs.q: The statement that 'one need not know what a bacterium is to observe that sickness travels with people' supports the claim that:
o: medieval physicians correctly understood plague.
Paragraph 2 says physicians blamed corrupted air and the planets.
germ theory was unnecessary for modern medicine.
The point concerns early officials, not modern medicine.
quarantine officials reasoned soundly from observation despite lacking the correct theory.
Correct: paragraph 2 says they reasoned from experience rather than cosmology.
travelers deliberately spread disease to rival cities.
The passage suggests no intent on the part of travelers.
qs.x: The sentence means people can see that disease arrives with travelers without knowing its microbial cause. It supports paragraph 2's claim that officials reasoned soundly from observation even without germ theory. It does not say physicians understood plague; they blamed bad air and planets.

qs.q: In the final sentence of the passage, the author urges the public to:
o: abandon quarantine until the causes of disease are understood.
Paragraph 4 says acting under uncertainty can be sound.
trust officials to decide which travelers are suspect.
The author warns that such decisions can follow existing lines of distrust.
rely on medical experts rather than political leaders.
The passage never contrasts experts with political leaders.
keep quarantine's protective value while guarding against its use against distrusted groups.
Correct: 'the first' is sound action under uncertainty; 'the second' is its drift toward prejudice.
qs.x: In the final sentence, 'the first' is quarantine's protective value as sound action under uncertainty, and 'the second' is the tendency for lines around the sick to follow lines around the distrusted. The author urges keeping one while watching for the other. Trusting officials to choose suspects ignores that warning.

qs.q: Which modern case best illustrates the political dimension of quarantine described in paragraph 3?
o: A nation isolates arrivals only from a rival state, though its allies have similar infection rates.
Correct: like paragraph 3's cities, it uses quarantine to target rivals rather than actual risk.
A hospital isolates a patient with a confirmed contagious infection.
This is a medically grounded case, not the politically driven use of paragraph 3.
A city closes all schools during a severe influenza outbreak.
This applies to everyone equally and marks no group as suspect.
Officials lengthen isolation after learning a disease has a long incubation period.
This is a medical adjustment to evidence, not a political one.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's political dimension is the use of quarantine to target rivals or distrusted groups rather than actual risk. Isolating arrivals only from a rival when allies have similar infection rates fits exactly. Isolating a confirmed patient or extending isolation for a long incubation are medically grounded choices.

passages.title: The Room Was the Point
text: When the first boxes and floor-bound bricks appeared in galleries in the 1960s, critics complained that there was nothing to look at. The complaint was accurate in a narrow sense and mistaken in every other. The minimalist object refused the things viewers had been trained to seek: a handmade surface, a hidden narrative, a composition whose parts answered one another. What remained was a plain thing in a room, and the room, it turned out, was the point.

A painting asks to be entered; it offers a window and invites the viewer to forget the wall around it. A row of identical steel units offers no window. Instead it returns viewers to their own bodies: the distance at which they stand, the angle from which the row seems to shorten, the way light from a doorway alters one end. The work does not withhold experience so much as relocate it, from the object to the encounter. Those who found minimalism cold were often registering, without naming it, the discomfort of being made responsible for what they saw.

This is why I resist the common claim that minimalism is an art of subtraction. Subtraction implies that something valuable has been removed and that the remainder is a diminished version of a fuller work. But the minimalists did not pare down a richer original; they built a different kind of occasion, one in which attention itself becomes the material. The emptiness is structural, like the silence that lets a listener hear the hum of a building.

The irony is that the word has since migrated into a vocabulary of consumption. The minimalist apartment, the minimalist wardrobe and the minimalist phone are sold as relief from attention: fewer things to notice, fewer demands on the eye. The gallery work asked viewers to notice more by being given less; the lifestyle product promises that they can notice less. The two share a look, but their ambitions run in opposite directions, and to confuse them is to mistake a discipline for an anesthetic.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim about minimalist art?
o: It removes valuable elements to reveal a purer version of a fuller work.
Paragraph 3 explicitly rejects the idea that minimalism is an art of subtraction.
It abandons the gallery in favor of everyday domestic settings.
The passage places minimalist works in galleries; domestic minimalism is the later lifestyle trend it criticizes.
It shares its basic aims with today's minimalist consumer products.
Paragraph 4 says the two share a look but have ambitions running in opposite directions.
It shifts experience from the object itself to the viewer's encounter with it.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the work relocates experience 'from the object to the encounter.'
qs.x: Paragraph 2 states the thesis directly: the work relocates experience 'from the object to the encounter,' and paragraphs 3 and 4 defend that view against rivals. The subtraction reading is tempting because the objects look stripped down, but paragraph 3 rejects it, saying nothing richer was pared away and that attention itself becomes the material.

qs.q: The author compares minimalist emptiness to 'the silence that lets a listener hear the hum of a building' mainly to suggest that:
o: minimalist works are best experienced in quiet, empty galleries.
The analogy concerns how emptiness functions, not the acoustic conditions of display.
minimalism borrowed its methods from experimental music.
The passage draws an analogy, not a claim of historical influence.
an absence can make perceptible what usually goes unnoticed.
Correct: like silence revealing a hum, the bare work makes the room and the viewer's attention noticeable (paragraph 3).
viewers should ignore the object and attend only to the room.
Paragraph 2 says viewers attend to their relation to the object, not that the object is ignored.
qs.x: An analogy's job is to explain how something works. Silence lets a hidden hum become audible, just as the bare work in paragraph 3 lets the room and the viewer's own attention become perceptible. The tempting reading that viewers should ignore the object overshoots: paragraph 2 says the work returns viewers to their bodies in relation to the object, not that the object drops out.

qs.q: According to the author, critics who found minimalism 'cold' were most likely reacting to:
o: the industrial materials used, such as steel and brick.
The passage mentions these materials but does not tie the coldness charge to them.
the unease of being made responsible for their own perception.
Correct: paragraph 2 says they registered 'the discomfort of being made responsible for what they saw.'
the lack of any hidden narrative inside the objects.
Lack of narrative is listed in paragraph 1, but paragraph 2 explains coldness as discomfort with responsibility.
the high prices commanded by minimalist works.
The passage never discusses the market value of gallery works.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 explains the coldness charge itself: critics were registering, without naming it, 'the discomfort of being made responsible for what they saw.' Missing narrative appears in paragraph 1 as something the work refused, but the author ties the reaction of coldness specifically to the burden of responsibility for one's own perception.

qs.q: A new installation consists of a single mirror-polished cube that reflects visitors as they circle it. How does this work relate to the author's argument?
o: It fits the argument, since it directs attention to the viewer's position and movement.
Correct: paragraph 2 says minimalism returns viewers to their bodies and stance, which the reflecting cube makes literal.
It undermines the argument, since reflected images give the cube pictorial content.
The reflections show the viewer's own encounter, which paragraph 2 treats as the work's real subject.
It illustrates the lifestyle minimalism criticized in paragraph 4.
Paragraph 4 faults products that reduce attention; the cube heightens it.
It is irrelevant, since the author discusses only rows of identical units.
Rows of units are one example; the argument concerns minimalist works generally.
qs.x: To apply a passage to a new case, match the case to the author's key mechanism. The author says minimalism returns viewers to their own bodies, stance and movement (paragraph 2); a mirror cube does exactly that. The reflections may look like pictorial content, but what they show is the viewer's encounter, the very thing the author calls the work's real subject.

qs.q: The contrast between 'a discipline' and 'an anesthetic' in the final sentence implies that lifestyle minimalism:
o: trains people to perceive their surroundings more keenly.
That describes the gallery work, the 'discipline,' not the lifestyle product.
is a medical treatment for stress and overstimulation.
'Anesthetic' is metaphorical here; the author makes no medical claim.
is more authentic than the original gallery movement.
The author treats the lifestyle trend as a confusion of the movement, not a truer form.
aims to dull the demands placed on attention.
Correct: paragraph 4 says such products promise 'relief from attention' and that buyers 'can notice less.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 contrasts the gallery work, which asked viewers to notice more by being given less, with products that promise they can notice less. A discipline sharpens attention; an anesthetic dulls feeling. 'Anesthetic' is a metaphor for that dulling, not a medical claim, and the sharpening role belongs to the gallery art, not the lifestyle product.

qs.q: Which finding would most directly challenge the author's characterization of minimalist consumer products?
o: Minimalist apartments are typically more expensive than cluttered ones.
Price says nothing about whether the products promise less noticing.
Ads for such products mostly promise sharper awareness of one's surroundings.
Correct: paragraph 4 claims these products are sold as relief from attention; ads promising heightened attention would contradict that.
Many gallery minimalists also designed furniture for sale.
Shared makers do not show the products' ambitions match the art's.
Minimalist phones sell fewer units than standard smartphones.
Sales volume is irrelevant to what the products promise buyers.
qs.x: To challenge a claim, find evidence that directly contradicts its content. Paragraph 4 says minimalist products are sold as 'relief from attention.' Ads promising sharper awareness would contradict that description head-on. Price, sales volume or shared designers might seem relevant, but none of them bears on what the products promise buyers, which is the author's actual claim.

passages.title: Stories Told From the Center
text: Every society that has pushed against an edge has told stories about the edge. In the United States the most famous version was given scholarly form in 1893, when a young historian argued that the availability of open land had shaped the national character, producing individualism, practical ingenuity and a democratic suspicion of inherited rank. The thesis was elegant, and it arrived just as the census office had announced that a continuous line of settlement could no longer be drawn on the map.

That timing deserves more attention than the thesis itself. A myth of the frontier is rarely composed on the frontier. It is composed afterward, in cities, by people who feel the loss of something they never personally possessed. The settlers whose diaries survive wrote mostly about debt, weather, illness and the price of seed. The grand narrative of self-reliance belongs to their grandchildren, who needed an origin story capable of reassuring an industrial and increasingly crowded nation that its virtues had been forged somewhere wider than a factory floor.

Read this way, frontier myths are documents of the center rather than of the margin. They record what a settled society fears it lacks. Where the city feels hemmed in, the myth supplies space; where the corporation dissolves individual achievement, the myth supplies the lone homesteader; where politics feels corrupt, the myth supplies a simpler justice. The people already living on the supposedly open land appear in such stories chiefly as obstacles or as scenery, a revealing absence that tells us whose needs the story serves.

None of this means the myths are merely false. They have real effects, shaping policy, advertising and the private ambitions of people who will never see a prairie. But their truth is the truth of a symptom. To ask whether the frontier really produced self-reliant democrats is to ask the wrong question. The better question is why a nation, at a particular moment, needed so badly to believe that it had.

qs.q: The author's main point is that frontier myths are best understood as:
o: evidence about the anxieties of the settled society that tells them.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls them 'documents of the center' that record what a settled society fears it lacks.
accurate accounts of how open land shaped national character.
Paragraph 4 says asking whether the frontier really did this is 'the wrong question.'
harmless fictions with little effect on public life.
Paragraph 4 says the myths shape policy, advertising and private ambitions.
records written by settlers about their daily hardships.
Paragraph 2 contrasts the settlers' diaries with the later myth composed in cities.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: frontier myths are 'documents of the center rather than of the margin,' recording what a settled society fears it lacks. The tempting choice, that they accurately show how open land shaped character, is the 1893 thesis the author sets aside in paragraph 4 as 'the wrong question.'

qs.q: The author mentions settlers' diaries about debt, weather and seed prices primarily in order to:
o: show that settlers were more self-reliant than historians believed.
The diaries are used to show ordinary worries, not to confirm the myth.
argue that diaries are the most reliable historical sources.
The author uses the diaries as a contrast, not to rank source types.
contrast settlers' actual concerns with the later myth of self-reliance.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the grand narrative 'belongs to their grandchildren,' not the settlers themselves.
explain why the frontier thesis appeared in 1893.
The 1893 timing is tied to the closing of settlement in paragraph 1, not to the diaries.
qs.x: Ask what work a detail does in the argument. The diaries' worries about debt, weather and seed prices show that settlers did not write the grand narrative; paragraph 2 says it 'belongs to their grandchildren' in the cities. The detail is a contrast between lived concerns and later myth, not evidence for settler self-reliance or a ranking of sources.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, people already living on the 'supposedly open land' appear in frontier myths mainly as:
o: heroic models of self-reliance.
Paragraph 3 assigns that role to the lone homesteader, not to existing inhabitants.
the main authors of the stories.
Paragraph 2 says the myths were composed in cities by later generations.
obstacles or scenery.
Correct: paragraph 3 says they appear 'chiefly as obstacles or as scenery.'
victims whose losses the myths mourn.
The passage says their near-absence reveals whose needs the story serves, not that it mourns them.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says existing inhabitants appear 'chiefly as obstacles or as scenery,' and calls this a revealing absence that shows whose needs the story serves. The heroic role goes to the lone homesteader, and the passage never says the myths mourn the inhabitants; their marginal place is evidence that the stories serve the center.

qs.q: In saying that the myths possess 'the truth of a symptom,' the author most likely means that they:
o: reveal real underlying needs even when they misdescribe the past.
Correct: paragraph 4 treats the myths as signs of what a nation 'needed so badly to believe.'
are true only for the generation that first experienced the frontier.
Paragraph 2 says the myths were composed by later generations, not frontier settlers.
describe a disease that weakened the national character.
'Symptom' is a metaphor for what the myth indicates, not a literal claim of illness.
were proven accurate by later historical research.
The author sets aside whether the myth is accurate as 'the wrong question.'
qs.x: A symptom is a real sign of an underlying condition, even if it is not the condition itself. Paragraph 4 says the myths are not merely false and that the better question is why a nation 'needed so badly to believe' them. So their truth lies in what they reveal about present needs, not in accuracy about the past; 'symptom' is a metaphor, not a claim of disease.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Most frontier novels were written by people who had lived on homesteads.
That would cut against paragraph 2's claim that the myth is composed afterward, in cities.
Frontier novels sold best among city readers in eras of rapid corporate growth.
Correct: paragraph 3 links the myth to urban anxieties such as crowding and corporations dissolving individual achievement.
Settlers' diaries frequently praised individualism and self-reliance.
That would weaken paragraph 2's contrast between diaries and the later myth.
Frontier myths had little influence on later government land policy.
That contradicts paragraph 4, which says the myths shaped policy.
qs.x: The author argues that frontier myths answer urban anxieties such as crowding and corporations dissolving individual achievement (paragraph 3). City readers buying frontier novels most during corporate growth fits that link directly. Novels written by homesteaders would do the opposite, undercutting paragraph 2's claim that the myth is composed afterward, in cities.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's account of frontier myths?
o: Farmers keep careful ledgers of rainfall and crop prices each season.
This matches the settlers' diaries, not the later myth the author analyzes.
A historian corrects errors in an earlier account of a famous battle.
The author is not concerned with factual correction but with why a myth was needed.
A village records its own festivals in a locally kept chronicle.
Myths in the passage come from the center about the margin, not from the margin itself.
Films romanticizing village life thrive in fast-growing cities during housing shortages.
Correct: like frontier myths, they supply an urban audience with what it fears it lacks (paragraph 3).
qs.x: The core structure is that a settled center produces a romantic story about a margin to supply what it feels it lacks (paragraph 3). City audiences embracing romantic village films during housing shortages share that structure. A village's own chronicle is tempting because it involves village life, but it comes from the margin itself, the opposite of the author's model.

passages.title: The Uneasy Gift
text: Histories of surgery often tell the arrival of anesthesia as a story with only one possible ending. Before the 1840s, operations were performed on conscious patients held down by assistants; after the first public demonstrations of ether, pain could be suspended, and a grateful world embraced the gift. The story is true in its broad outline, but its tidiness hides how unsettling the new power first seemed to many who encountered it.

For one thing, an anesthetized patient was not merely spared pain; the patient was absent. Contemporary observers wrote with unease about bodies that breathed but did not answer, and about the trust required to hand one's unconscious self to a stranger. Reports of patients who spoke wildly or behaved strangely under the vapors fed a suspicion that the drugs loosened moral restraint. Some physicians, moreover, valued pain as a clinical signal and worried that a silent patient deprived the surgeon of information.

Objections also drew on older ideas about suffering. A few writers argued that pain, especially in childbirth, had a purpose ordained by nature or by scripture, though historians now suspect such objections were rarer than later legend claims. More common was a practical fear: early deaths under chloroform were widely publicized, and newspapers that celebrated painless surgery one month reported fatal cases the next.

What eventually settled the matter was less a refutation of these worries than a change in who seemed to bear them. When a reigning monarch accepted chloroform during childbirth in 1853, the act answered no theological argument; it simply made the choice respectable. Anesthesia became normal not because doubters were convinced point by point but because the people whose behavior defined propriety had adopted it. The episode suggests that new medical powers are often accepted socially before they are justified intellectually, and that the order matters for what kinds of questions later generations think to ask.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: complicate a tidy account of anesthesia's acceptance by recovering early doubts.
Correct: paragraph 1 says the tidy story 'hides how unsettling the new power first seemed,' and later paragraphs detail those doubts.
argue that anesthesia was adopted too quickly and caused needless deaths.
The passage mentions publicized deaths but does not argue adoption was a mistake.
explain the chemical differences between ether and chloroform.
The passage discusses reception, not chemistry.
prove that religious opposition delayed anesthesia for decades.
Paragraph 3 says such objections were probably rarer than legend claims.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 sets up a tidy story and says it 'hides how unsettling the new power first seemed'; paragraphs 2 to 4 recover those doubts and explain how they faded. The passage mentions publicized deaths, but it never argues that adopting anesthesia was a mistake, so a choice claiming it was adopted too quickly overstates the author's aim.

qs.q: Which concern about early anesthesia is NOT described in the passage?
o: That the drugs might loosen patients' moral restraint.
Paragraph 2 mentions this suspicion, fed by reports of strange behavior.
That surgeons would lose pain as a source of clinical information.
Paragraph 2 says some physicians valued pain as a clinical signal.
That patients might die under the influence of chloroform.
Paragraph 3 says early chloroform deaths were widely publicized.
That the drugs were too costly for most hospitals to afford.
Correct: cost is never mentioned; the other concerns appear in paragraphs 2 and 3.
qs.x: For NOT questions, check each choice against the text and eliminate the ones that appear. Moral restraint and lost clinical signals are in paragraph 2, and chloroform deaths are in paragraph 3. Cost is never mentioned, so it is the only concern the passage does not describe.

qs.q: The author's remark that religious objections were 'rarer than later legend claims' serves mainly to:
o: show that religious leaders strongly supported anesthesia.
The author says objections were rare, not that clergy actively endorsed anesthesia.
suggest that historians' research on the topic is unreliable.
The author relies on historians' judgment rather than dismissing it.
qualify a commonly repeated account without denying such objections existed.
Correct: paragraph 3 grants that 'a few writers' objected but cautions that legend exaggerates them.
prove that fear of death was the only real obstacle.
Paragraph 2 lists several other worries, so 'only' overstates the claim.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 grants that 'a few writers' raised religious objections, then adds that historians suspect these were rarer than later legend claims. That is a qualification: it corrects an exaggerated story without denying the objections existed. It does not show clergy supported anesthesia, and the author relies on historians rather than doubting them.

qs.q: The author's account of the 1853 royal childbirth implies that anesthesia gained acceptance chiefly because:
o: the monarch's physicians refuted each theological objection.
Paragraph 4 says doubters were not 'convinced point by point.'
its adoption by socially authoritative figures made it respectable.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the act 'answered no theological argument; it simply made the choice respectable.'
chloroform proved safer than ether in the royal case.
No comparison of the two drugs' safety is made in paragraph 4.
newspapers stopped reporting deaths after 1853.
The passage never says press coverage of deaths ended.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the monarch's act 'answered no theological argument; it simply made the choice respectable,' and that doubters were not convinced point by point. Acceptance came from social prestige, not from refutation. The tempting idea that physicians answered each objection is exactly what the author denies.

qs.q: Which modern situation best parallels the pattern the author describes in paragraph 4?
o: A drug is approved only after years of controlled clinical trials.
This is intellectual justification preceding acceptance, the reverse of the pattern.
Physicians abandon a procedure after a study shows it does not work.
This is rejection driven by evidence, not acceptance driven by prestige.
A religious group publishes arguments against a medical practice.
This resembles the objections in paragraph 3, not how they were overcome.
A new device becomes common after celebrities use it, though its risks are still debated.
Correct: like chloroform, it is accepted socially, via prestigious adopters, before being justified intellectually.
qs.x: The pattern in paragraph 4 is social acceptance before intellectual justification, driven by prestigious adopters. A device that spreads after celebrity use while its risks are still debated matches that order. Approval after clinical trials reverses it: there, justification comes first, which is the opposite of what the author describes.

qs.q: Suppose archives showed that newspapers of the 1840s and 1850s almost never reported deaths under anesthesia. This would most weaken the claim that:
o: patients' unconsciousness unsettled contemporary observers.
That claim in paragraph 2 rests on observers' writings, not newspaper death reports.
some physicians valued pain as a clinical signal.
This physician concern in paragraph 2 is independent of press reporting.
the public had practical fears fueled by press coverage of fatal cases.
Correct: paragraph 3 says deaths were 'widely publicized' and that papers reported fatal cases.
royal use of chloroform made anesthesia respectable.
The 1853 claim in paragraph 4 does not depend on how deaths were reported.
qs.x: A new finding weakens the claim that depends on it. Only paragraph 3's practical fear rests on deaths being 'widely publicized' in newspapers, so archives showing almost no such reports would undercut it. The other claims rest on observers' writings, physicians' views or a royal act, none of which depends on press coverage of deaths.

passages.title: Changing the Game
text: During the Cold War, a branch of mathematics developed to analyze poker and parlor games found itself advising governments on nuclear strategy. Game theory offered something diplomats had long lacked: a precise language for situations in which each party's best move depends on what it expects the others to do. Concepts such as credible threats, mutual deterrence and the prisoner's dilemma gave shape to intuitions that had previously been expressed only in proverbs.

The clarity was real, and so was the danger. A model is useful because it simplifies, and the simplifications of classic game theory are severe. Players are assumed to be single, coherent actors with stable preferences, and the payoffs of each outcome are treated as given before the game begins. A state, however, is a coalition of ministries, factions and publics, and its preferences shift in response to the very interactions the model holds fixed. When analysts forgot this, they could produce strategies that were logically impeccable and politically blind.

Consider the prisoner's dilemma, in which each of two parties gains by betraying the other, yet both do worse when both betray than when both cooperate. The lesson usually drawn is pessimistic: rational actors will defect. But diplomats rarely accept the payoffs as written. They link issues, so that betrayal on arms control jeopardizes a trade agreement; they create inspection regimes that make betrayal detectable; they arrange repeated meetings so that today's defection can be punished tomorrow. In effect, skilled diplomacy is the art of transforming one game into another.

This is why I think game theory serves diplomacy best as a diagnostic rather than a prescription. It can reveal why a negotiation is stuck, by showing which incentives make cooperation irrational for one side or both. It cannot by itself say what should be done, because the most important diplomatic move is usually one the model does not contain: changing the rules, the players or what the players want.
