qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the author's view of game theory in diplomacy?
o: It should be abandoned because its assumptions are false.
The author calls its clarity 'real' and assigns it a diagnostic role, not abandonment.
It helps diagnose stalemates but cannot by itself prescribe what to do.
Correct: paragraph 4 says game theory serves 'best as a diagnostic rather than a prescription.'
It proves that rational states will always betray one another.
Paragraph 3 argues diplomats change the payoffs so defection need not follow.
It is most useful for predicting the outcome of military conflicts.
The passage discusses negotiation and diplomacy, not battlefield prediction.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 gives the thesis: game theory serves diplomacy 'best as a diagnostic rather than a prescription.' It can show why talks are stuck but cannot say what to do. The author criticizes its assumptions in paragraph 2, yet calls its clarity 'real,' so abandoning it goes further than the author does.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, a key limitation of classic game theory is that it:
o: treats states as unified actors whose preferences stay fixed.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it assumes 'single, coherent actors with stable preferences.'
requires calculations too complex for diplomats to perform.
The passage never says the math is too hard for diplomats.
ignores the possibility of mutual deterrence.
Paragraph 1 lists mutual deterrence as one of game theory's concepts.
was designed only for nuclear strategy.
Paragraph 1 says it was developed for poker and parlor games.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 names the simplification: players are 'single, coherent actors with stable preferences,' and payoffs are fixed in advance. Real states are coalitions whose preferences shift. Mutual deterrence is a tempting distractor, but paragraph 1 lists it as one of game theory's own concepts, so the theory does not ignore it.

qs.q: The examples of issue linkage, inspection regimes and repeated meetings are offered mainly to show that diplomats:
o: reliably choose to defect when the payoffs favor it.
The examples show ways to make cooperation rational, not defection.
depend on mathematical models to choose their strategies.
These moves are presented as diplomatic craft that goes beyond the model.
prefer one-time agreements to ongoing relationships.
Repeated meetings are cited precisely because ongoing relationships allow punishment of defection.
alter the structure and payoffs of the situation they face.
Correct: paragraph 3 says diplomats 'rarely accept the payoffs as written' and transform 'one game into another.'
qs.x: Each example in paragraph 3 changes the game itself: linkage raises the cost of betrayal, inspection makes it detectable, and repeated meetings allow later punishment. Together they show diplomats 'rarely accept the payoffs as written' and transform 'one game into another.' The examples make cooperation rational, so reading them as proof that diplomats defect gets the point backward.

qs.q: Which scenario best exemplifies what the author calls 'transforming one game into another'?
o: Two rivals calculate that each gains most by overfishing the shared sea.
This only describes the original dilemma without changing it.
Two fishing rivals agree on shared satellite monitoring and tie catch limits to tariff cuts.
Correct: this adds detection and issue linkage, two moves paragraph 3 describes as changing the game.
One country secretly exceeds its catch limit and is never caught.
This is defection within the existing game, not a transformation of it.
An analyst publishes a model predicting that both rivals will overfish.
This is the diagnostic use of game theory, not a diplomatic transformation.
qs.x: Transforming a game means changing its payoffs or rules, not playing within them. Monitoring makes cheating detectable and tying catch limits to tariffs links issues, two moves paragraph 3 names. Publishing a model that predicts overfishing is tempting because it involves analysis, but that is the diagnostic use of game theory, not a change to the game.

qs.q: Suppose newer game-theoretic models routinely include repeated play, issue linkage and monitoring. How would this affect the author's argument?
o: It would weaken the claim that the moves in paragraph 3 lie outside the model.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the key diplomatic moves are ones 'the model does not contain'; models including them would undercut this.
It would strengthen the claim that classic models are politically blind.
Better models would not show anything new about the blindness of classic ones.
It would confirm that rational actors must always defect.
Repeated play and linkage generally make cooperation more rational, not less.
It would have no bearing, since the author discusses only nuclear strategy.
The author discusses diplomacy broadly, including arms control and trade linkage.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 argues that game theory cannot prescribe because the key diplomatic move is one 'the model does not contain.' If models routinely included repeated play, linkage and monitoring, those moves would be inside the model, weakening that claim. Such models say nothing new about classic models' blindness, so they would not strengthen that point.

passages.title: A Conversation, Not a Miracle
text: Audiences who hear a saxophonist spin a long, unrepeatable solo often imagine they are witnessing creation out of nothing. The romance of jazz improvisation depends on this image: the musician as a channel for pure spontaneity, freed from the score that binds the orchestral player. Musicians themselves tend to describe something quite different, and their account is more interesting.

An improviser arrives on the bandstand carrying thousands of hours of preparation. She has memorized the harmonic structure of the tune, practiced patterns over each chord in every key, and absorbed the phrasing of predecessors by transcribing their recordings note for note. Much of what sounds invented is retrieved, recombined from a vocabulary built so thoroughly that it can be summoned faster than conscious deliberation. To call this spontaneous is not exactly wrong, but it is like calling fluent conversation spontaneous: true of the sentences, false of the language.

Some critics conclude from such facts that improvisation is a kind of illusion, a performance of freedom that conceals routine. This conclusion seems to me as mistaken as the romance it replaces. What preparation makes possible is not repetition but responsiveness. The drummer shifts an accent; the pianist voices a chord unexpectedly; a phrase from the bassist suggests a rhythm worth answering. The improviser's vocabulary is what allows her to answer in real time, as a large vocabulary allows a speaker to reply to an unexpected remark rather than recite a prepared speech.

The freedom of jazz, then, is located not in the absence of constraint but in the moment-to-moment negotiation among players who share an idiom deeply enough to surprise one another. A solo practiced alone against a recording would draw on the same vocabulary yet lose something essential, because no one could answer. Improvisation is less an individual feat than a conversation, and its unrepeatability comes from the conversation, not from the speaker.

qs.q: The author's main argument is that jazz improvisation:
o: is pure creation that owes nothing to prior practice.
Paragraph 2 stresses thousands of hours of preparation.
is an illusion that conceals rehearsed routines.
Paragraph 3 calls this critics' view 'as mistaken as the romance it replaces.'
finds its freedom in prepared, real-time responsiveness among players.
Correct: paragraph 4 locates jazz's freedom in 'moment-to-moment negotiation among players.'
is chiefly an individual achievement of the soloist.
Paragraph 4 says it is 'less an individual feat than a conversation.'
qs.x: Paragraph 4 locates jazz's freedom in 'moment-to-moment negotiation among players' who share an idiom. The author rejects two views: the romance of pure creation (paragraph 1) and the critics' claim that improvisation is an illusion hiding routine (paragraph 3). The right answer keeps both preparation and real-time response.

qs.q: The comparison to fluent conversation in paragraph 2 suggests that an improvised solo:
o: is memorized in advance like a prepared speech.
Paragraph 3 contrasts real-time reply with reciting a prepared speech.
is less valuable than a composed piece of music.
The analogy explains how improvisation works, not its relative value.
can contain new phrases while relying on a deeply learned system.
Correct: spontaneity is 'true of the sentences, false of the language,' i.e., new utterances from a learned vocabulary.
requires no knowledge of harmony to perform well.
Paragraph 2 says the improviser has memorized the tune's harmonic structure.
qs.x: The analogy says spontaneity is 'true of the sentences, false of the language.' A speaker forms new sentences from a deeply learned language, and an improviser forms new phrases from a deeply learned musical vocabulary. Memorizing a prepared speech is the opposite case, and paragraph 3 uses it as the contrast to real-time reply.

qs.q: How does the author respond to critics who call improvisation 'a performance of freedom that conceals routine'?
o: By denying that improvisers prepare extensively before performing.
The author affirms extensive preparation in paragraph 2.
By agreeing with them and defending the romantic image instead.
The author rejects both the critics' view and the romance.
By claiming that orchestral music is equally routine.
Orchestral players are mentioned only in paragraph 1 and not used to answer the critics.
By arguing that preparation makes responsiveness possible rather than mere repetition.
Correct: paragraph 3 says 'what preparation makes possible is not repetition but responsiveness.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 grants the critics' facts about preparation but rejects their conclusion: 'what preparation makes possible is not repetition but responsiveness.' Vocabulary lets players answer one another in real time. The author does not deny preparation, which paragraph 2 affirms, and rejects the romantic view as firmly as the critics' view.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely predict that two skilled musicians from unrelated traditions, sharing no common idiom, would improvise together:
o: with greater freedom, since neither is bound by a shared idiom.
The author locates freedom within shared constraint, not in its absence.
with more difficulty surprising each other in ways the other can answer.
Correct: paragraph 4 ties freedom to players who 'share an idiom deeply enough to surprise one another.'
exactly as well as players from the same tradition.
Paragraph 4 makes a shared idiom central to the conversation.
by abandoning their prepared vocabularies entirely.
Nothing suggests they would drop their training; the issue is mutual intelligibility.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says freedom arises among players who 'share an idiom deeply enough to surprise one another.' Without a shared idiom, surprises are harder to recognize and answer, so the conversation suffers. The tempting idea that no shared constraint means more freedom is the romantic view the author rejects; freedom here depends on shared constraint.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's claim about improvisation?
o: Soloists' phrases change measurably in response to accompanists' choices mid-performance.
Correct: this supports paragraph 3's claim that preparation enables real-time answers to bandmates.
Soloists' phrases are nearly identical across performances regardless of the band.
This supports the critics' view of concealed routine, not responsiveness.
Audiences rate solos as more original when told they were unplanned.
This concerns audience belief, the romance in paragraph 1, not how improvisation works.
Most jazz musicians learned by transcribing recordings.
This confirms preparation but not that preparation serves responsiveness.
qs.x: The author claims preparation serves responsiveness to bandmates (paragraphs 3 and 4). Evidence that soloists' phrases change in response to accompanists' choices confirms that link directly. Learning by transcription is tempting because the passage mentions it, but it shows only preparation, which both the author and the critics accept.

passages.title: The Uninvited Guest
text: The biographer is a peculiar kind of guest. She enters a life uninvited, reads letters never addressed to her, and leaves with whatever she finds most telling. The subject, usually dead, cannot object, and that silence is often taken as permission. Yet the inability to protest is not the same as the absence of anything to protest. Most of us care about how we will be remembered, and it is odd to suppose that such concerns lose all weight the moment the person who held them can no longer press them.

Two familiar ethics of biography answer this problem badly. The first is the ethic of reverence, in which the biographer acts as custodian of a reputation, smoothing over cruelty and failure out of loyalty to the subject or deference to the family. The second is the ethic of exposure, which treats every secret as a debt owed to readers and measures a biography's courage by the intimacy of what it reveals. The first sacrifices truth to comfort; the second mistakes disclosure for understanding.

A better standard asks what a private fact explains. That a novelist kept a lover may be mere gossip, or it may illuminate the triangles that recur in her fiction; that a statesman suffered from depression may be idle detail, or it may clarify decisions he made in office. The same fact can be justified in one book and gratuitous in another, depending on the work it does. Relevance, not secrecy, is the test, and it cuts in both directions: it forbids the biographer to suppress what explains and to display what merely titillates.

This standard will not settle every case, and applying it requires judgment that reasonable biographers will exercise differently. But it relocates the question usefully. Instead of asking whether the dead have forfeited their privacy, or whether readers are entitled to everything, it asks what the biography is for. A life is written to be understood, and understanding, not appetite, sets the limit of what a biographer may take.

qs.q: According to the author, a biographer is justified in including a private fact when it:
o: was carefully hidden by the subject during life.
Paragraph 3 says 'relevance, not secrecy, is the test.'
helps explain the subject's work or public conduct.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the test is 'what a private fact explains.'
is approved by the subject's surviving family.
Deference to family is part of the ethic of reverence that paragraph 2 rejects.
would interest the largest number of readers.
Paragraph 4 says understanding, 'not appetite,' sets the limit.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 sets the test: what a private fact explains, so 'relevance, not secrecy' decides inclusion. Hidden facts are not automatically justified, family approval belongs to the rejected ethic of reverence, and reader interest is the 'appetite' paragraph 4 says must not set the limit.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the 'ethic of exposure' is that it:
o: sacrifices truth for the comfort of the subject's family.
That is the author's objection to the ethic of reverence, not exposure.
relies too heavily on letters rather than interviews.
The passage never compares types of sources.
confuses revealing secrets with achieving understanding.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it 'mistakes disclosure for understanding.'
is forbidden by the legal rights of the dead.
The author makes an ethical argument, not a legal one.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the ethic of exposure 'mistakes disclosure for understanding,' treating each revealed secret as a gain. The tempting choice about sacrificing truth for comfort is the author's charge against the other ethic, reverence. Keep the two criticisms paired with the right ethic.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the author suggests that a dead subject's inability to object:
o: does not show that the subject has no interests that could be wronged.
Correct: paragraph 1 says inability to protest 'is not the same as the absence of anything to protest.'
grants the biographer permission to publish anything.
The author raises this common assumption in order to challenge it.
means the family must speak on the subject's behalf.
The author never assigns this role to the family and criticizes deference to it.
makes biography of the dead ethically simpler than of the living.
The paragraph argues that the dead's concerns still carry weight, complicating the matter.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 argues that 'the inability to protest is not the same as the absence of anything to protest.' People care how they will be remembered, and those concerns do not lose all weight at death. The idea that silence grants permission is the common assumption the author raises in order to challenge it.

qs.q: A biographer learns that a composer's gambling debts forced him to accept commissions that shaped his late style. By the author's standard, the biographer should:
o: omit the debts, because they would embarrass the composer's family.
Protecting reputation at the cost of explanation is the ethic of reverence, rejected in paragraph 2.
omit the debts, because financial matters are always private.
The author rejects fixed categories; a fact's justification depends on 'the work it does.'
include the debts, because every secret is owed to readers.
That reasoning is the ethic of exposure; the right answer depends on relevance.
include the debts, because they explain features of the work.
Correct: paragraph 3 forbids suppressing 'what explains,' and the debts explain the late style.
qs.x: Apply the relevance test from paragraph 3: a private fact belongs in the book if it explains something. Here the debts explain the commissions that shaped the late style, so they should be included. Choosing to include them 'because every secret is owed to readers' reaches the right action for the wrong reason, the ethic of exposure.

qs.q: The author's acknowledgment that the standard 'will not settle every case' functions mainly to:
o: withdraw the standard in favor of the ethic of reverence.
The author continues to defend the standard and never returns to reverence.
suggest that biographers should avoid private facts entirely.
Paragraph 3 says relevant private facts must not be suppressed.
concede a limitation while maintaining that the standard frames the question better.
Correct: paragraph 4 admits judgment will vary 'but it relocates the question usefully.'
argue that no ethical standard for biography is possible.
The author proposes a standard and claims it is better than the alternatives.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 admits the standard 'will not settle every case' and that judgment will vary, then adds 'but it relocates the question usefully.' This is a concession that keeps the main claim: the standard frames the issue better than its rivals. It does not abandon the standard or claim that no standard is possible.

qs.q: Which choice would the author most clearly regard as a failure to meet the proposed standard?
o: Including a childhood illness that inspired a doctor's later research.
The illness explains the subject's work, so the standard justifies including it.
Omitting a politician's brief affair that had no bearing on his career.
Leaving out a fact that explains nothing is consistent with the standard.
Including a painter's depression that shaped the mood of her late work.
The depression illuminates the work, as in the paragraph 3 examples.
Omitting a scientist's fraud in the experiment that made her famous, to spare her family.
Correct: this suppresses 'what explains,' which paragraph 3 forbids.
qs.x: The relevance test forbids both suppressing what explains and displaying what merely titillates (paragraph 3). Hiding fraud in the experiment that made a scientist famous suppresses the very fact that explains her career, and doing it to spare the family is the ethic of reverence. Omitting an affair that explains nothing is consistent with the standard.

passages.title: Not a Warehouse
text: A common story about medieval Islamic astronomy casts it as a storehouse. Greek learning, so the story goes, was translated into Arabic in Baghdad, kept safe through centuries when Latin Europe had largely lost it, and eventually handed back to European scholars who would make something new of it. The story is not exactly false, but it reduces a vigorous scientific culture to a warehouse and implies that its value lay in what it passed along rather than in what it did.

What it did was considerable, and much of it arose from needs the Greeks never had. Muslim communities had to determine the direction of Mecca from any city, fix the times of five daily prayers by the sun's position, and anticipate the sighting of the new crescent moon that begins each month of a lunar calendar. These were not abstract puzzles but daily obligations, and solving them called for spherical trigonometry, refined tables and instruments such as the astrolabe, made into objects of great precision and beauty. By the thirteenth century many large mosques employed a timekeeper, a salaried astronomer whose expertise was woven into the rhythm of worship.

Astronomy was also institutional in ways that anticipate modern science. Rulers funded observatories, such as the one at Maragha in the thirteenth century and at Samarkand in the fifteenth, staffed by teams who compiled new observations over years. Scholars working in these settings criticized Ptolemy's models for violating Ptolemy's own physical principles and devised geometrical alternatives, some of which bear a striking resemblance to devices later used by Copernicus.

None of this requires denying the debt to Greek sources; the scholars themselves acknowledged it openly. The point is that astronomy in this world was not a borrowed possession awaiting return. It was a practice shaped by religious life, courtly patronage and craft, and it answered to the questions of the people who sustained it. To see it only as a bridge between Athens and Krakow is to look at the bridge and ignore the city built upon it.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the 'storehouse' story is that it:
o: overlooks the original work and cultural setting of this astronomy.
Correct: paragraph 1 says the story values only 'what it passed along rather than... what it did.'
exaggerates the debt Islamic astronomers owed to Greek sources.
Paragraph 4 affirms the debt to Greek sources, which the scholars acknowledged.
wrongly claims that translation happened in Baghdad.
The author does not dispute where translation occurred.
gives too much credit to the observatory at Samarkand.
The storehouse story ignores such institutions; the author highlights them.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the storehouse story values astronomy for 'what it passed along rather than in what it did.' Paragraphs 2 and 3 then describe original work driven by local needs and institutions. The author does not say the story exaggerates the Greek debt; paragraph 4 affirms that debt openly.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, one stimulus for astronomical work that the Greeks lacked was the need to:
o: predict eclipses for royal astrologers.
Eclipse prediction and astrology are not mentioned in the passage.
determine prayer times and the direction of Mecca.
Correct: paragraph 2 lists these religious obligations as 'needs the Greeks never had.'
navigate ships across the open ocean.
Navigation is not among the needs listed in paragraph 2.
translate Arabic texts into Latin.
Translation into Latin concerns transmission, not the needs that drove research.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists religious needs the Greeks never had: finding the direction of Mecca, timing the five daily prayers and anticipating the new crescent moon. Translating Arabic texts into Latin is tempting because it fits the storehouse story, but it is a matter of transmission, not a need that drove new research.

qs.q: The author mentions the resemblance between some Islamic models and devices later used by Copernicus primarily to:
o: show that these scholars produced innovations rather than only preserving texts.
Correct: the resemblance highlights original alternatives to Ptolemy (paragraph 3), countering the storehouse image.
prove that Copernicus copied his entire system from Maragha.
The author says only that 'some' devices bear a resemblance, not that Copernicus copied his system.
suggest that Islamic astronomy mattered only through European influence.
Paragraph 4 warns against seeing it 'only as a bridge' to Europe.
argue that Ptolemy's models were essentially correct.
Paragraph 3 says these scholars criticized Ptolemy's models.
qs.x: The Copernicus comparison shows the Maragha scholars invented new geometrical models instead of only preserving Ptolemy (paragraph 3), which counters the warehouse image. The author says only that 'some' devices resemble Copernicus's, so claiming Copernicus copied his whole system goes far beyond the text.

qs.q: The closing image of looking 'at the bridge' while ignoring 'the city built upon it' suggests that:
o: Islamic astronomy had little influence on later European science.
The author grants influence; the objection is to seeing it 'only' as a bridge.
focusing on transmission hides the culture that produced and used the astronomy.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the practice was shaped by religion, patronage and craft, the 'city' the bridge view misses.
observatories were usually built in large cities.
The 'city' is a metaphor, not a claim about observatory locations.
Greek astronomy deserves more attention than Islamic astronomy.
The author argues the reverse emphasis is the problem.
qs.x: In the metaphor, the bridge is transmission from Greece to Europe and the city is the culture of worship, patronage and craft that paragraph 4 says shaped this astronomy. The author does not deny influence on Europe; the objection is to seeing the astronomy 'only' as a bridge, which hides where and why it was practiced.

qs.q: Which discovery would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Records showing Arabic manuscripts were copied unchanged from Greek originals.
Unchanged copying supports the storehouse image the author criticizes.
Records showing observatories were rarely funded by rulers.
This contradicts paragraph 3's claim about courtly patronage.
Records showing mosque timekeepers made new tables for their own city's latitude.
Correct: this shows original work driven by local religious needs, as paragraph 2 argues.
Records showing astrolabes were mostly imported from Europe.
This undercuts the passage's claim of local craft and precision.
qs.x: The author argues that Islamic astronomy was original work driven by local religious needs (paragraph 2). Timekeepers making new tables for their own city's latitude is original, needs-driven work, so it strengthens that view. Unchanged copying of Greek texts would instead support the storehouse story the author rejects.

qs.q: How would the author most likely judge a museum exhibit that presents medieval astrolabes solely as precursors of later European navigation tools?
o: As accurate, since astrolabes were built mainly for navigation.
Paragraph 2 ties astrolabes to religious timekeeping and calculation, not navigation.
As exemplary, since it stresses the debt to Greek sources.
The exhibit as described stresses later European use, and the author wants local context shown.
As misleading, since astrolabes had no scientific use at all.
Paragraph 2 describes astrolabes as precise scientific instruments.
As incomplete, since it frames them by later European use rather than their own setting.
Correct: paragraph 4 objects to viewing this astronomy 'only' in terms of what it passed on.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 objects to seeing this astronomy 'only as a bridge' to Europe and says it answered the questions of the people who sustained it. Paragraph 2 ties astrolabes to religious timekeeping and calculation. An exhibit framing them solely as precursors to European tools leaves out that setting, so it is incomplete rather than plainly false.

passages.title: The Retreating Mirage
text: Few complaints are as common among travelers as the complaint that a place has been ruined by tourists. The village festival has become a show, the market sells souvenirs made elsewhere, the dancers perform on a schedule printed in the hotel lobby. The traveler who voices this complaint usually exempts himself from the crowd he blames, imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing.

Sociologists have long described the resulting predicament. Hosts, aware that visitors crave authenticity, stage a version of it, arranging back regions that appear private but are designed to be seen. Visitors, sensing the staging, push further in search of something unarranged, and the hosts follow. On this view, authenticity is a mirage that retreats as the tourist approaches, and every encounter is quietly counterfeit.

The analysis is shrewd, but it smuggles in an assumption I find untenable: that a practice performed for outsiders is thereby less genuine than one performed for insiders alone. Cultures have always presented themselves to visitors, and the presentation is itself a cultural act. A dance revived for tourist audiences may be learned by young people who would otherwise have let it lapse, debated by elders over what counts as correct, and altered in ways the community chooses. To call the result fake is to deny the community the right that every culture exercises, the right to change.

The deeper problem lies in the tourist's ideal. The longing for the untouched place casts its residents as inhabitants of the past, people whose value depends on their remaining unlike the visitor. Smartphones in the market, a pop song from a doorway, a guide who studied business administration: these register as intrusions only because the traveler has decided in advance what the place is for. Authenticity, if the word is worth keeping, should describe the relation between a people and their practices, not the match between a destination and a visitor's expectations.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's position?
o: Practices performed for tourists can be authentic; the trouble lies in tourists' expectations.
Correct: paragraphs 3 and 4 defend such performances and locate 'the deeper problem' in the tourist's ideal.
Tourism inevitably makes every cultural encounter counterfeit.
That is the sociological view in paragraph 2, which the author challenges.
Authenticity can be found only in places tourists have not reached.
Paragraph 4 criticizes this longing for the untouched place.
Communities should stop performing traditional dances for visitors.
Paragraph 3 suggests such performances can sustain and renew traditions.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that performing for outsiders does not make a practice less genuine, and paragraph 4 places 'the deeper problem' in the tourist's ideal of an untouched place. The claim that every encounter is counterfeit is tempting because the passage presents it, but it is the sociological view the author challenges.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the sociological analysis in paragraph 2 is best described as:
o: wholly dismissive of its account of staged authenticity.
Calling it 'shrewd' shows the author credits part of it.
fully supportive, since it explains why places are ruined.
The author rejects its conclusion that every encounter is counterfeit.
indifferent, since it concerns hosts rather than tourists.
The author engages it directly and builds the argument against it.
appreciative of its insight but critical of a hidden assumption.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls it 'shrewd' but says it 'smuggles in an assumption I find untenable.'
qs.x: Calling the analysis 'shrewd' credits its insight into staged authenticity, while saying it 'smuggles in an assumption I find untenable' marks the author's disagreement. That mix of credit and criticism rules out both 'wholly dismissive' and 'fully supportive'; attitude questions often hinge on such qualifying words.

qs.q: The example of a dance revived for tourist audiences is used to show that:
o: tourist demand always distorts traditional forms beyond recognition.
The example shows changes 'the community chooses,' not distortion imposed from outside.
elders oppose any change to traditional practices.
Elders debate what is correct; the passage does not say they oppose all change.
performing for outsiders can involve real community choice and continuity.
Correct: paragraph 3 notes young people learn it, elders debate it, and the community chooses how it changes.
dances are the only practices tourists find authentic.
The dance is one example, not a claim about tourists' preferences.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a revived dance may be learned by young people, debated by elders and changed 'in ways the community chooses.' The example shows that performing for visitors can involve real choice and continuity. It does not show distortion beyond recognition, since the changes come from the community itself.

qs.q: In noting that the complaining traveler 'exempts himself from the crowd he blames,' the author implies that:
o: solitary travelers are more respectful than tour groups.
The author treats this self-image as an illusion, not a fact.
the complainer shares the very tourist position he criticizes.
Correct: paragraph 1 suggests he is part of the crowd while imagining he alone seeks 'the real thing.'
complaints about tourism are usually accurate.
The author goes on to question the assumptions behind such complaints.
locals blame individual travelers for overcrowding.
The remark concerns the traveler's self-perception, not locals' views.
qs.x: The traveler blames the crowd while 'imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing' (paragraph 1). The author's irony is that he is part of the crowd he criticizes. Taking his self-image at face value, that solo travelers are more respectful, misses that the author presents it as an illusion.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument in paragraph 3?
o: Young residents often learn revived dances to perform them for visitors.
This matches paragraph 3's own example and supports the argument.
Tourist dances are typically choreographed by outside tour firms, excluding residents.
Correct: paragraph 3 rests on the community choosing how the practice changes; outside control would undercut that.
Some tourists prefer performances they believe are unstaged.
Paragraph 2 already assumes tourists crave the unstaged; this adds nothing against paragraph 3.
Residents of tourist towns frequently own smartphones.
This relates to paragraph 4 and does not bear on community control of performances.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's argument depends on the community choosing how a performance changes; that is why it counts as genuine. If outside tour firms choreographed the dances and excluded residents, that support would collapse. Smartphone ownership relates to paragraph 4, not to who controls the performances, so it does not weaken paragraph 3.

passages.title: The Mirror That Answers Back
text: It is tempting to read the English Romantic poets as the first nature writers, men and women who turned from the drawing room toward mountains, rivers and weather. Their poems are full of landscapes, and admirers have often treated them as early prophets of environmental feeling. The reading is not wrong, but it misses where the poems' attention actually falls.

Consider how often a Romantic landscape poem is about remembering a landscape rather than seeing one. Wordsworth described poetry as emotion recollected in tranquillity, and many of his best-known poems take place years after the scene they evoke, in a room or on a return visit, as the speaker measures how he has changed. The valley is present, but it is present as the occasion for a meditation on memory, loss and the growth of a mind. Nature is less the subject than the mirror.

Critics who notice this sometimes accuse the Romantics of a grand self-absorption, an appropriation of the natural world for the purposes of autobiography. The charge has force, yet it simplifies the poems. The mirror in these works is not passive. The landscape shapes the speaker as much as he interprets it; a childhood spent among particular hills determines what the adult can feel, and the poems repeatedly record moments when the external scene overwhelms or corrects the mind's expectations. The relation runs in both directions.

This mutual shaping, rather than any simple love of scenery, is the Romantics' real legacy for thinking about nature. They did not imagine a wilderness wholly apart from human experience, and they did not reduce the world to a projection of the self. They described a traffic between the two, in which a person is partly made by place. Those who would enlist them as environmentalists should do so on these terms, as witnesses not to nature's otherness but to our dependence on it for the very shape of our inner lives.

qs.q: The author's central thesis is that Romantic nature poetry chiefly depicts:
o: wild nature as wholly separate from human experience.
Paragraph 4 says they 'did not imagine a wilderness wholly apart from human experience.'
the natural world as a mere projection of the poet's self.
Paragraph 4 says they 'did not reduce the world to a projection of the self.'
a two-way relationship in which mind and landscape shape each other.
Correct: paragraph 4 names 'this mutual shaping' as the Romantics' real legacy.
accurate scientific descriptions of particular landscapes.
The passage stresses memory and inner life, not scientific description.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 names 'this mutual shaping' between mind and place as the Romantics' real legacy. The author rejects both extremes: nature wholly apart from human experience, and nature as a mere projection of the self. The projection choice is tempting because paragraph 2 calls nature a mirror, but paragraph 3 says that mirror is not passive.

qs.q: The author cites Wordsworth's phrase 'emotion recollected in tranquillity' to support the claim that Romantic poems often:
o: were composed outdoors in the presence of the landscape.
Paragraph 2 places the poems 'in a room or on a return visit,' years later.
avoid strong feeling in favor of calm description.
The phrase concerns recollected emotion, not the absence of feeling.
reject the idea that the speaker changes over time.
Paragraph 2 says the speaker 'measures how he has changed.'
dwell on remembered rather than directly observed scenes.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the poems are 'about remembering a landscape rather than seeing one.'
qs.x: Paragraph 2 uses the phrase to support the claim that many poems are 'about remembering a landscape rather than seeing one,' set years later in a room or on a return visit. The phrase is about emotion recalled later, not about avoiding feeling, so reading it as a preference for calm description misses its point.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the charge that the Romantics were self-absorbed?
o: By granting it some force but arguing it ignores how landscape shapes the speaker.
Correct: paragraph 3 says 'the charge has force, yet it simplifies the poems' because 'the mirror... is not passive.'
By rejecting it entirely as a misreading of the poems.
The author concedes that the charge 'has force.'
By accepting it fully and treating the poems as autobiography.
The author argues the relation 'runs in both directions,' not just inward.
By arguing that self-absorption is a virtue in poetry.
The author does not defend self-absorption; the reply concerns nature's active role.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the self-absorption charge 'has force, yet it simplifies the poems,' because the landscape shapes the speaker as much as he interprets it. This is a partial concession, not a full rejection. Watch for wording like 'has force, yet' that signals the author grants part of a criticism before qualifying it.

qs.q: A newly found poem from the period describes a mountain storm that forces the speaker to abandon a planned reflection and feel his own smallness. How does this poem bear on the passage?
o: It supports the critics' charge of grand self-absorption.
Here the scene overrides the speaker's self-directed plans, which counters that charge.
It contradicts the author's claim that nature is a mirror.
The author's mirror 'is not passive'; a scene that acts on the speaker fits this.
It fits the claim that external scenes can overwhelm or correct the mind.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the poems record moments when 'the external scene overwhelms or corrects the mind's expectations.'
It shows that Romantic poems never concern memory.
One poem of immediate experience cannot show that; paragraph 2 says only 'how often.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the poems record moments when 'the external scene overwhelms or corrects the mind's expectations.' A storm that overrides a planned reflection is a clear case of this. It does not contradict the mirror idea, because the author's mirror is active, and it counters the self-absorption charge rather than supporting it.

qs.q: The final sentence implies that environmental arguments drawing on the Romantics should stress:
o: that nature has value only because it is wholly other than us.
The author explicitly says they are witnesses 'not to nature's otherness.'
that human inner life depends on the places people inhabit.
Correct: paragraph 4 says they witness 'our dependence on it for the very shape of our inner lives.'
that scenery should be preserved mainly for its beauty.
Paragraph 4 contrasts mutual shaping with 'any simple love of scenery.'
that poets understood ecology better than scientists did.
The passage makes no comparison between poets and scientists.
qs.x: The last sentence says the Romantics are witnesses 'not to nature's otherness but to our dependence on it for the very shape of our inner lives.' So environmental arguments should stress how places shape people. Preserving scenery for beauty is tempting, but paragraph 4 contrasts mutual shaping with 'any simple love of scenery.'

qs.q: Which modern work would the author most likely see as closest to the Romantics' real legacy?
o: A memoir tracing how growing up on one coastline shaped its writer's fears and hopes.
Correct: it shows 'a person is partly made by place,' the mutual shaping of paragraph 4.
A field guide that catalogs coastal species without commentary.
This treats nature apart from inner life, which the author says the Romantics avoided.
A manifesto praising wilderness for being untouched by humans.
Paragraph 4 says the Romantics did not imagine nature 'wholly apart from human experience.'
A novel that uses landscapes only as decorative backdrops.
Passive backdrop is the opposite of the active landscape the author describes.
qs.x: The legacy in paragraph 4 is that 'a person is partly made by place.' A memoir about how a coastline shaped its writer's fears and hopes shows exactly that two-way relation. A manifesto praising untouched wilderness is tempting as environmental writing, but it treats nature as wholly apart from people, which the author says the Romantics did not do.

passages.title: What a Society Thought People Were
text: The census presents itself as the most modest of documents: a count, nothing more. Yet counting people has never been a neutral act. Roman officials registered citizens and their property in order to tax them and to know whom they could call to arms; the great survey that William the Conqueror ordered in 1086 was remembered by the English as a book of judgment from which there was no appeal. Long before statistics became a science, rulers understood that to number a population was to gain a kind of grip on it.

Modern censuses inherited this purpose and added another: they came to define the categories by which a society understands itself. The first American census, in 1790, was required by the Constitution to apportion representation, and its schedule already embodied a politics, distinguishing free persons from enslaved ones, the latter counted under the infamous three-fifths rule. In later decades the racial categories on the form shifted repeatedly, appearing, splitting and vanishing in response to immigration, scientific fashion and political pressure. A category on a census form does not merely record a group; it helps bring into being the group it claims to find.

It would be easy to conclude that the census is simply an instrument of control. That conclusion overlooks how often the counted have turned the count to their own ends. Because funds, representation and recognition follow the numbers, communities have campaigned to be counted accurately, to have their languages and identities listed, and to resist undercounts that would render them invisible. When the American census in 2000 first allowed respondents to mark more than one race, the change followed years of advocacy by people whose lives did not fit the earlier boxes.

The census, then, is best understood as a site of negotiation between a state that wishes to see its population in usable terms and a population that wishes to be seen on its own terms. Neither side fully wins. Each form is a provisional settlement of that contest, and reading old schedules closely tells us less about how many people there were than about what a society thought people were.

qs.q: The author's main argument is that the census is best understood as:
o: a neutral count that simply records how many people exist.
Paragraph 1 says counting 'has never been a neutral act.'
purely an instrument by which states control their subjects.
Paragraph 3 calls this conclusion too easy because the counted use the count too.
a modern invention with no ancient precedents.
Paragraph 1 cites Roman registration and the survey of 1086.
a contested process in which state and population negotiate how people are classified.
Correct: paragraph 4 calls it 'a site of negotiation' between the state and the counted.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 calls the census 'a site of negotiation' between a state that wants usable categories and people who want to be seen on their own terms. The tempting view that it is purely a tool of control is the 'easy' conclusion paragraph 3 rejects, because the counted also use the count for their own ends.

qs.q: The author mentions the 2000 option to mark more than one race primarily as an example of:
o: the state imposing new categories for tax purposes.
The example shows pressure from the population, not state-imposed taxation.
scientific fashion driving changes in racial categories.
Paragraph 3 attributes this change to advocacy, not science.
an undercount that made a community invisible.
The example concerns adding a response option, not an undercount.
counted people reshaping census categories through advocacy.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the change 'followed years of advocacy' by those who did not fit the boxes.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says the 2000 multiple-race option 'followed years of advocacy' by people who did not fit the old boxes. It shows the counted reshaping the form. Paragraph 2 does mention scientific fashion as one cause of changing categories, but the author ties this particular change to advocacy.

qs.q: The claim that a census category 'helps bring into being the group it claims to find' most directly suggests that census categories:
o: are invented with no relation to people's actual lives.
The author says categories 'help' create groups, not that they are wholly fictional.
can shape how groups are recognized, not just reflect groups that already exist.
Correct: paragraph 2 says a category 'does not merely record a group.'
have remained stable since the first census of 1790.
Paragraph 2 says categories 'shifted repeatedly.'
are less important than total population counts.
The author argues categories reveal more than totals do (paragraph 4).
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says a category 'does not merely record a group; it helps bring into being' the group it names. Categories shape recognition rather than only reflect it. The word 'helps' matters: it means categories partly create groups, not that they are pure fictions unrelated to people's lives.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, why have communities campaigned to be counted accurately?
o: Because funds, representation and recognition depend on the numbers.
Correct: paragraph 3 says 'funds, representation and recognition follow the numbers.'
Because inaccurate counts lead to higher taxes on their members.
Taxation is the Roman motive in paragraph 1, not the reason given in paragraph 3.
Because the Constitution requires each person to register.
The Constitution is cited for apportionment, not as a reason communities campaign.
Because accurate counts reduce military conscription.
Conscription appears only in the Roman example of paragraph 1.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 explains that communities campaign for accurate counts because 'funds, representation and recognition follow the numbers.' Taxation and military service are tempting distractors, but they are the Roman motives in paragraph 1, describing why rulers counted, not why the counted cared.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument of paragraph 3?
o: Communities often lobbied to have their languages listed on the form.
This is what paragraph 3 itself describes, so it supports the argument.
Federal funds are distributed partly on the basis of census counts.
This supports paragraph 3's claim that resources follow the numbers.
Category changes were nearly always made by officials with no public input.
Correct: paragraph 3 claims the counted turn the count to their own ends; officials acting alone would undercut that.
Roman censuses were used to identify men for military service.
This concerns paragraph 1's history and does not address the counted's agency.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that the counted shape the census through advocacy. If category changes were nearly always made by officials with no public input, that agency would disappear, weakening the argument. Choices about lobbying for languages or funds following counts restate what paragraph 3 already claims, so they support it.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's account of how the counted influence the count?
o: A hospital tallies its beds to plan next year's budget.
This is a neutral count with no negotiation over categories.
A ruler surveys land holdings to raise taxes on landowners.
This parallels paragraph 1's state control, not the counted's influence.
Patient groups lobby a hospital to add a language field, winning interpreter funding.
Correct: like census advocacy, a group reshapes a form's categories to gain resources and recognition.
A statistician corrects an arithmetic error in a published table.
This involves accuracy, not a contest over how people are classified.
qs.x: The author's model is a group pressing an institution to change a form's categories so that it gains resources and recognition (paragraph 3). Patient groups winning a language field and interpreter funding share that structure. A ruler surveying land to tax it is tempting because it involves counting, but it reflects paragraph 1's state control, not the counted's influence.

passages.title: The Mercy of Fading
text: Moral philosophy has long treated memory as a virtue and forgetting as a lapse. We are told to remember the dead, to remember our promises, to remember the lessons of history, and the person who forgets these things is judged careless or worse. Yet this picture leaves something out. A great deal of ordinary moral life depends not on remembering but on letting memory fade, and the ability to forget may be as much an achievement of character as the ability to recall.

Consider the neighbor who, years ago, said something cruel at a funeral. If everyone who heard the remark kept it vividly in mind, the neighbor would remain forever the person who said it. What actually happens, in most communities, is that the remark softens, loses its details, and eventually becomes at most a vague unease. This decay is not the same as forgiveness, which is a deliberate act, but it makes forgiveness easier and sometimes does its work when no one has the strength to forgive. Forgetting, in this sense, is the background condition that lets people change.

Collective memory is a different matter. When a society forgets a massacre or an injustice, the forgetting rarely happens by itself; it is usually arranged by those who benefit from silence. Here the duty to remember is real, because the victims cannot speak and the perpetrators would prefer that no one else did. The ethics of memory, then, is not uniform. What we owe to the wronged is remembrance; what we owe to the merely flawed is, often, a gradual release.

The difficulty of our moment is that the natural decay of memory has been engineered away. Searchable archives preserve the cruel remark at the funeral with the same fidelity as the record of the massacre. Some respond by demanding a legal right to have old information erased. I am sympathetic, but law is a crude instrument for a delicate task. What was once accomplished by the slow erosion of detail cannot simply be restored by deletion orders, which are themselves remembered, recorded, and argued over. The more promising path may be cultural: learning to treat old records of minor wrongs as we once treated faded memories, as things that are technically present but no longer count.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim?
o: Forgetting minor personal wrongs can be valuable, while collective injustices call for remembrance.
Correct: paragraph 3 contrasts remembrance owed to the wronged with release owed to the merely flawed.
Memory is always a virtue, and forgetting is always a moral failure.
Paragraph 1 presents this as the view the author says leaves something out.
Old digital records of personal wrongs should be erased by law.
Paragraph 4 says the author is sympathetic but calls law a crude instrument for this task.
Forgetting and forgiving are two names for the same moral act.
Paragraph 2 explicitly says decay of memory is not the same as forgiveness.
qs.x: The author's thesis has two halves: paragraph 2 values the fading of minor personal wrongs, and paragraph 3 insists on remembering collective injustices. A main-idea answer must capture both. The tempting extremes each grab one detail, such as legal erasure, which paragraph 4 explicitly calls too crude a tool.

qs.q: According to the passage, forgetting differs from forgiveness in that forgetting:
o: occurs without anyone deciding that it should.
Correct: paragraph 2 calls forgiveness a deliberate act, while the remark simply softens over time.
requires the wrongdoer to first apologize.
The passage never ties forgetting to apology; paragraph 2 describes a passive softening.
is morally worthless unless forgiveness follows.
Paragraph 2 says fading sometimes does forgiveness's work when no one can forgive.
applies only to collective memory, not to individuals.
Paragraph 2's example is an individual neighbor; paragraph 3 treats collective memory separately.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 calls forgiveness a deliberate act, while forgetting is a passive softening that just happens over time. That contrast in agency is the whole difference the question targets. The claim that forgetting is worthless without forgiveness fails because the author says fading sometimes does forgiveness's work.

qs.q: The author notes that deletion orders are 'themselves remembered, recorded, and argued over' most likely to suggest that:
o: courts should refuse all requests to remove old information.
The author is 'sympathetic' to such requests in paragraph 4, only doubtful about law.
deletion orders are usually granted to the wealthy.
Paragraph 4 says nothing about who receives deletion orders.
legal erasure cannot reproduce the quiet, unnoticed character of natural fading.
Correct: paragraph 4 contrasts slow erosion of detail with deletion orders that create new records.
archives are more reliable than human memory.
Reliability is not the point; paragraph 4 objects to preservation itself, not its accuracy.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 contrasts natural fading, which is quiet and unnoticed, with deletion orders, which create new records and new arguments. The point is that law cannot reproduce the self-erasing quality of forgetting. Refusing all removal requests is too strong, since the author is openly sympathetic to the goal.

qs.q: The claim in paragraph 3 that collective forgetting is 'usually arranged' depends on which assumption?
o: Societies naturally forget injustices faster than individuals forget insults.
Paragraph 3 says collective forgetting rarely happens by itself, the opposite of natural decay.
Victims of injustice usually prefer that their suffering be forgotten.
Paragraph 3 says victims cannot speak, not that they want silence.
Searchable archives make collective forgetting impossible.
Archives appear only in paragraph 4 and are not the basis for the 'arranged' claim.
Those who benefit from an injustice often have the motive and means to suppress its memory.
Correct: paragraph 3 says silence is arranged by those who benefit and that perpetrators prefer no one speak.
qs.x: A claim that silence is arranged assumes someone wants it and can produce it. Paragraph 3 names those who benefit from silence and the perpetrators as that party, so the hidden premise is their motive and means. The idea of natural collective forgetting is the opposite of the claim, which says such forgetting rarely happens by itself.

qs.q: Suppose a study found that people who recall others' past offenses in vivid detail remain distrustful even after sincere apologies. This finding would most:
o: weaken the author's distinction between individual and collective memory.
The study concerns individuals only and does not bear on paragraph 3's distinction.
support the author's view that the fading of detail helps people move past wrongs.
Correct: paragraph 2 argues that softened, detail-poor memory makes forgiveness and change easier.
show that the duty to remember applies to minor personal wrongs.
It suggests vivid memory hinders reconciliation, which runs against such a duty.
prove that legal deletion of records is the best remedy.
The study is about memory, and paragraph 4 doubts legal remedies regardless.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that softened, detail-poor memory makes forgiveness easier and lets people change. A finding that vivid recall keeps distrust alive even after apology fits that mechanism exactly, so it supports the author. It says nothing about collective memory, so it cannot weaken the individual versus collective distinction.

qs.q: Which policy would the author most likely favor?
o: A law requiring deletion of every public record older than ten years.
Paragraph 4 calls law crude, and blanket deletion would also erase records of injustice owed remembrance.
A professional norm that employers disregard minor online posts more than a decade old.
Correct: paragraph 4 favors a cultural practice of treating old minor records as present but no longer counting.
An official archive removing references to a past atrocity to promote harmony.
Paragraph 3 says the duty to remember atrocities is real.
A registry ensuring that every personal wrong is permanently publicized.
Paragraph 2 argues such vivid permanence would keep people from changing.
qs.x: The author prefers cultural norms to legal ones and wants old minor wrongs treated as present but no longer counting. An employer norm of ignoring decade-old minor posts matches both features. A blanket deletion law fails twice: it relies on crude legal tools and would also erase records of injustice that paragraph 3 says we must keep.

passages.title: Fixed in Type
text: The familiar story about the printing press is a story of liberation. Before Gutenberg, the argument goes, knowledge was hoarded by monasteries and universities, copied slowly by hand, and interpreted by authorities whose word could not be checked. After him, texts multiplied, prices fell, and readers could judge for themselves. The press, in this telling, was a solvent of authority, dissolving the power of the priest and the master.

There is truth in this, but it captures only half of what happened. Print did weaken certain authorities, yet it also manufactured new ones, and the new ones were in some ways more formidable because they were harder to see. A manuscript was always a particular object made by a particular scribe, and every reader knew that copies varied. A printed edition, by contrast, presented a thousand identical pages, and identity looked like reliability. The authority that once belonged to a person who vouched for a text began to migrate into the text itself.

This migration had concrete consequences. Printers introduced title pages, standardized spellings, numbered pages, and indexes, all of which made it possible to cite a passage precisely and to accuse an opponent of misquoting it. Errata lists, which might seem to confess fallibility, actually reinforced the ideal of a correct text against which deviations could be measured. Censors, too, discovered that print made control easier in one respect: a single forbidden edition could be traced to a single shop, whereas scattered manuscript copies had been nearly impossible to police.

None of this means that the liberation story is false. It means that liberation and new forms of domination arrived together, often through the same mechanisms. The reader freed from the priest's interpretation found herself bound instead to the authority of the standard edition, the authorized translation, and eventually the copyright holder. We tend to celebrate each new medium as an escape from gatekeepers. The history of print suggests a more sober expectation: that every technology which loosens one kind of authority quietly builds the scaffolding for another.

qs.q: The author's main point about the printing press is that it:
o: freed readers from every form of authority over texts.
Paragraph 2 says the liberation story captures only half of what happened.
weakened some authorities while creating new and less visible ones.
Correct: paragraph 2 says print weakened certain authorities yet manufactured new ones that were harder to see.
strengthened the power of priests and university masters.
Paragraph 1 and paragraph 4 agree print loosened the priest's interpretive hold.
had little real effect on how people read and cited texts.
Paragraph 3 describes concrete changes like indexes and precise citation.
qs.x: The author keeps the liberation story but calls it half the truth: print weakened old authorities while building new, harder-to-see ones. The best answer must hold both effects together. The claim that print freed readers from all authority is the one-sided view the author sets out to complicate.

qs.q: According to the passage, a reader of manuscripts, unlike a reader of printed editions, typically:
o: knew that different copies of the same text might vary.
Correct: paragraph 2 says every manuscript reader knew that copies varied.
trusted the text more because it was handmade.
Paragraph 2 says identical printed pages looked more reliable, not handmade ones.
could easily locate passages by page number.
Paragraph 3 credits printers with introducing numbered pages.
faced stricter censorship of individual copies.
Paragraph 3 says scattered manuscripts were nearly impossible to police.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says each manuscript was made by a particular scribe and every reader knew copies varied, whereas identical printed pages looked reliable. The answer is a direct detail retrieval. The censorship option reverses paragraph 3, which says scattered manuscripts were nearly impossible to police.

qs.q: The author's discussion of errata lists primarily serves to show that:
o: even apparent admissions of error strengthened the idea of a single correct text.
Correct: paragraph 3 says errata lists reinforced the ideal of a correct text against which deviations are measured.
printers were more careless than scribes.
Paragraph 3 makes no comparison of carelessness between printers and scribes.
readers learned to distrust printed books.
Paragraph 2 says printed identity looked like reliability, the opposite of distrust.
censors relied on errata to find forbidden editions.
Paragraph 3 links censorship to tracing editions to shops, not to errata.
qs.x: Errata lists look like admissions of fallibility, but paragraph 3 argues they actually reinforced the ideal of one correct text against which errors are measured. That counterintuitive twist is the function of the example. Options about careless printers or distrustful readers read the lists at face value, which the author rejects.

qs.q: Which claim in the passage receives the least direct support?
o: Printed editions made it easier to trace a forbidden text to its source.
Paragraph 3 explains this with the single-shop versus scattered-copies contrast.
Print made precise citation of passages possible.
Paragraph 3 supports this with title pages, page numbers, and indexes.
Manuscript copies of a text often differed from one another.
Paragraph 2 grounds this in each manuscript being made by a particular scribe.
Every technology that loosens one authority builds the scaffolding for another.
Correct: paragraph 4 generalizes to every technology from the single case of print.
qs.x: Least-supported questions reward spotting a sweeping generalization drawn from thin evidence. Paragraph 4 leaps from the single history of print to every technology, while the other claims are each backed by specific examples in paragraphs 2 and 3. A claim being plausible is not the same as being supported in the passage.

qs.q: Which modern development would the author most likely see as parallel to the effects of print?
o: An open online encyclopedia that bypasses expert editors but whose pages readers treat as definitive.
Correct: like print in paragraph 4, it loosens one gatekeeper while a standardized text gains new authority.
A library that restricts rare books to credentialed scholars.
This simply preserves an old gatekeeper rather than trading one authority for another.
A poet who circulates handwritten drafts among friends.
This resembles manuscript culture, which paragraph 2 contrasts with print.
A government that bans a newspaper outright.
This is plain censorship, not the hidden migration of authority the passage describes.
qs.x: The pattern to match is a trade: one gatekeeper is bypassed while a standardized, identical-looking text gains authority of its own. An open encyclopedia that skips expert editors yet is treated as definitive does exactly that. A newspaper ban is control, but it lacks the hidden migration of authority into the text itself.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim about censorship?
o: Some printers produced editions full of errors.
This bears on accuracy, not on whether print eased control by censors.
Manuscript copying continued for decades after print appeared.
Coexistence of media does not contradict the claim that print eased tracing.
Readers used indexes to locate controversial passages.
This fits paragraph 3's account of precise citation and does not touch censorship.
Authorities found printed pamphlets harder to suppress than manuscripts because they spread too fast to trace.
Correct: paragraph 3 claims print made control easier because editions could be traced to a shop.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says print made censorship easier because a forbidden edition could be traced to one shop. To weaken it, you need evidence that print made suppression harder, such as pamphlets spreading too fast to trace. Facts about errors, indexes or continued manuscript copying do not address whether print helped censors.

passages.title: The Cracked Bowl
text: Western admirers of the Japanese tea ceremony often describe its aesthetic as a rejection of luxury. The rough, irregular bowls, the cramped thatched rooms, the single flower in a bamboo vase: all of this is read as a gentle protest against wealth and display, a turn toward simplicity that modern consumers might do well to imitate. The reading is attractive, but it gets the history nearly backward.

The tea masters of the sixteenth century who refined this aesthetic served warlords and wealthy merchants. Their rustic bowls were not cheap; some became so prized that they were given in place of land as rewards for military service. A plain-looking tea caddy could be worth a castle. What the aesthetic rejected was not expense but a particular kind of expense, the obvious splendor of imported Chinese porcelain whose value anyone could recognize. In its place it put objects whose worth could be perceived only by a trained eye.

This is why it would be a mistake to call the tea aesthetic anti-materialist. It was, if anything, intensely materialist, devoted to the texture of glaze, the weight of a bowl in the hand, the way a crack mended with lacquer altered the surface. What it demanded was not indifference to things but an unusually patient attention to them. The irregular bowl rewarded a viewer who looked long enough to see why it had been chosen over a thousand others.

Does this make the tradition hypocritical, a game of status disguised as humility? I do not think so. The charge of hypocrisy assumes that the aesthetic claimed to transcend wealth, and the masters made no such claim. They claimed instead that beauty is found in what is incomplete and impermanent, and that seeing it requires cultivation. That claim survives the discovery that cultivation was costly and that the wealthy pursued it. A truth about perception does not become false because rich people were the first to be taught it.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose is to:
o: correct a common misreading of tea aesthetics and defend the tradition against a charge of hypocrisy.
Correct: paragraph 1 says the usual reading gets history backward, and paragraph 4 rejects the hypocrisy charge.
urge modern consumers to adopt the simplicity of the tea ceremony.
Paragraph 1 attributes this suggestion to admirers whose reading the author disputes.
expose the tea masters as status seekers disguised as humble men.
Paragraph 4 explicitly says the author does not think the tradition hypocritical.
compare the artistic merits of Japanese and Chinese ceramics.
Chinese porcelain appears in paragraph 2 only to show what kind of expense was rejected.
qs.x: The passage first says the anti-luxury reading gets history nearly backward, then answers the charge that the tradition is hypocritical. A purpose answer must cover both moves. Exposing the masters as status seekers is the reverse of the author's conclusion, since paragraph 4 explicitly rejects the hypocrisy charge.

qs.q: According to the passage, what the tea aesthetic rejected was:
o: value that anyone could recognize at a glance, such as imported porcelain.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it rejected obvious splendor whose value anyone could recognize.
costly objects of any kind.
Paragraph 2 says rustic bowls were not cheap and a caddy could be worth a castle.
close attention to material qualities.
Paragraph 3 says it demanded unusually patient attention to things.
the patronage of warlords and merchants.
Paragraph 2 says the tea masters served warlords and wealthy merchants.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 is precise: the aesthetic rejected not expense but obvious splendor whose value anyone could recognize, like imported porcelain. It replaced that with worth only a trained eye could see. Costly objects of any kind is the tempting misreading, but rustic bowls could be worth land or even a castle.

qs.q: The remark that a tea caddy 'could be worth a castle' is used mainly to:
o: show that the tea masters were poorly paid.
The remark concerns object value, not masters' wages, which paragraph 2 never mentions.
suggest that warlords valued tea more than land.
Paragraph 2 shows high value for objects, not a general ranking of tea over land.
undercut the view that the tea aesthetic was a rejection of expensive things.
Correct: paragraph 2 offers it as evidence against the anti-luxury reading set up in paragraph 1.
illustrate the fragility of handmade ceramics.
Fragility is not discussed; paragraph 2 is about price and status.
qs.x: The castle comparison is evidence: an object that looks plain could carry enormous value. It undercuts paragraph 1's view that the aesthetic rejected expensive things. Reading it as a ranking of tea over land misses its role, which is to show expense was present, not to compare two kinds of wealth.

qs.q: The author's reply to the hypocrisy charge depends on distinguishing between:
o: Japanese and Western standards of beauty.
Paragraph 4 never contrasts national standards of beauty.
expensive objects and cheap imitations of them.
Paragraph 4 does not discuss imitations at all.
what the tradition claimed about beauty and who had the means to pursue it.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the claim about beauty survives the fact that the wealthy pursued its costly cultivation.
the views of sixteenth-century masters and later practitioners.
Paragraph 4 treats the masters' own claim and does not appeal to later practitioners.
qs.x: Hypocrisy would require the masters to claim they had transcended wealth. Paragraph 4 says they claimed only that beauty lies in the incomplete and must be learned, and that claim survives the fact that wealthy people pursued it. So the defense separates the content of the claim from who could afford it, not East from West or old from new.

qs.q: Which present-day practice most closely parallels the tea aesthetic as the author describes it?
o: A minimalist who gives away most possessions to escape materialism.
Paragraph 3 says the aesthetic was not anti-materialist, so this matches the misreading.
Collectors paying high prices for unpolished handmade furniture whose merits only experts discern.
Correct: like paragraph 2's bowls, value is high but perceptible only to a trained eye.
A luxury brand that prints its logo in large letters on every item.
This is obvious splendor anyone can recognize, which paragraph 2 says was rejected.
A factory producing thousands of identical bowls in a rustic style.
Paragraph 3 stresses a bowl chosen over a thousand others, not mass sameness.
qs.x: The aesthetic is high value hidden in plain-looking objects, perceptible only to a trained eye. Collectors paying a lot for unpolished furniture that only experts appreciate fits that pattern. The minimalist who gives things away fits the anti-materialist misreading that paragraph 3 explicitly rejects.

passages.title: Blueprints for Eden
text: The nineteenth century was crowded with attempts to build a better world in miniature. In the United States alone, dozens of communities were founded on principles of shared property, equality of labor, or religious perfection. Most dissolved within a generation, and their failure is usually explained by appeal to human nature: people, it is said, are too selfish to share everything, and any society that asks them to will soon fall apart.

The records of these communities tell a more interesting story. Many did not collapse in poverty and quarreling; they collapsed after they had become prosperous. Communities that had survived hungry winters through common effort found, once their farms and workshops turned a profit, that members began to ask why the wealth should not be divided and taken elsewhere. The children raised inside them, who had not chosen the communal life but inherited it, were often the first to leave. Selfishness played a role, but it was a selfishness awakened by success and by the passing of the founding generation, not one that had defeated the project from the start.

Some of the longest-lived communities were also the strictest. Groups that demanded celibacy, distinctive dress, or the surrender of all property on entry tended to outlast those that asked little. This seems paradoxical until one notices that costly requirements screen out the half-committed and give those who remain a reason to value what they have sacrificed for. Generosity of terms, it turns out, was no protection against dissolution.

If this account is right, the usual lesson drawn from utopian failures is the wrong one. These communities do not show that cooperation is impossible; they show that it is fragile in specific, identifiable ways, especially at the moment of prosperity and the moment of inheritance. Treated as failed proofs of an impossible ideal, they teach nothing. Treated as experiments, which is what many of their founders believed them to be, they offer evidence that no amount of armchair speculation about human nature could supply.

qs.q: According to the passage, many utopian communities dissolved:
o: during their first hungry winters, from lack of food.
Paragraph 2 says communities survived hungry winters through common effort.
because outside governments outlawed shared property.
The passage never mentions government action against the communities.
after becoming prosperous, when members questioned keeping the new wealth in common.
Correct: paragraph 2 says many collapsed after prosperity, as members asked why wealth should not be divided.
because their rules were too strict for most members.
Paragraph 3 says the strictest communities tended to last longest.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 reports that many communities collapsed after becoming prosperous, when members asked why the new wealth should not be divided and taken away. This is the passage's key surprise. Rules that were too strict is a trap, since paragraph 3 says the strictest communities tended to last longest.

qs.q: The author indicates that many founders of these communities regarded them as:
o: permanent proofs that cooperation is natural.
Paragraph 4 contrasts the experimental view with treating them as proofs.
temporary refuges from religious persecution.
The passage never describes the communities as refuges from persecution.
experiments.
Correct: paragraph 4 says many founders believed the communities to be experiments.
business ventures meant to generate profit.
Paragraph 2 treats profit as a later development that caused strain, not the founding aim.
qs.x: Paragraph 4's final sentence says many founders believed their communities to be experiments, which is why the author treats them as evidence. Permanent proofs is tempting but reverses the point: the author contrasts treating them as failed proofs, which teaches nothing, with treating them as experiments.

qs.q: The author's explanation for why strict communities lasted longer relies on the idea that:
o: strict leaders could expel members who wanted to leave.
Paragraph 3 says nothing about expulsion; its mechanism is self-selection.
celibacy prevented a second generation from forming.
Paragraph 3 lists celibacy as one cost but does not explain survival through absent children.
generous terms attracted selfish members.
Paragraph 3 says generous terms gave no protection, not that they drew selfish people.
costly requirements filter out the uncommitted and make membership more valued by those who stay.
Correct: paragraph 3 says costly requirements screen out the half-committed and give members reason to value their sacrifice.
