qs.x: Paragraph 3 explains durability through screening: costly demands drive away the half-committed and give those who stay a reason to value what they gave up. Celibacy is tempting because fewer children means no restless heirs, but the author lists celibacy only as one cost and never argues that mechanism.

qs.q: The author would most likely say the 'human nature' explanation is flawed because it:
o: denies that selfishness played any role in the communities' collapse.
The explanation stresses selfishness; paragraph 2 grants that selfishness played a role.
relies on records the author considers unreliable.
The author relies on the records in paragraph 2 rather than doubting them.
treats as fixed and immediate a selfishness that the records show arose under particular conditions.
Correct: paragraph 2 says selfishness was awakened by success and generational change, not present from the start.
overstates how long the communities actually lasted.
The explanation concerns why they failed, not their duration.
qs.x: The author grants that selfishness mattered but says it was awakened by success and generational change, not present from the start. So the human-nature account is wrong in treating selfishness as fixed and immediate. Saying it denies any role for selfishness gets it backward, since that explanation is built entirely on selfishness.

qs.q: A modern cooperative wants to last. Which step would the author most likely see as addressing a vulnerability the passage identifies?
o: Keeping membership requirements as light as possible.
Paragraph 3 says generosity of terms gave no protection against dissolution.
Screening applicants for a naturally generous temperament.
This relies on fixed human nature, the explanation paragraph 4 rejects.
Setting rules, before any profit is earned, for how future surpluses will be handled.
Correct: paragraph 4 names the moment of prosperity as a specific point of fragility.
Postponing discussion of finances until a dispute arises.
Paragraph 2 shows disputes over wealth arose with success, so waiting leaves the weakness untouched.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 names two points of fragility: the moment of prosperity and the moment of inheritance. Agreeing in advance how future surpluses will be handled targets the first directly. Light membership terms is the tempting wrong step, because paragraph 3 says generous terms gave no protection.

qs.q: Which discovery would most challenge the author's argument?
o: Most dissolved communities broke up within their first few years amid shortages and labor disputes.
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that many collapsed after prosperity rather than in poverty.
A few communities survived for more than a century.
Long survival by some fits paragraph 3's account of durable strict groups.
Children raised in the communities often left as adults.
Paragraph 2 already reports that inheritors were often first to leave.
Some founders wrote that they expected their communities to change over time.
This fits paragraph 4's description of founders who saw them as experiments.
qs.x: The argument depends on paragraph 2's claim that many communities failed after they became prosperous, not in early poverty. Evidence that most broke up within a few years amid shortages would restore the human-nature story the author rejects. Children leaving as adults is already part of the author's account, so it cannot weaken it.

passages.title: The Seriousness of Games
text: We tend to define play by contrast with work. Work is what we must do; play is what we do when the musts are finished. On this view play is a leftover, a pleasant waste of time that a sufficiently efficient life could do without. I want to suggest that this gets the relation backward, and that play reveals something about value that work tends to hide.

Consider what a game actually is. A golfer who wanted only to get the ball into the hole would walk over and drop it in. The golfer instead accepts a set of rules that make the goal harder to achieve, and accepts them for no reason other than that they make the activity possible. A game, in this sense, is the voluntary acceptance of unnecessary obstacles. What makes it valuable is not the outcome, which is trivial, but the activity that the obstacles bring into being.

Work, by contrast, is valued for what it produces. We would gladly reach its results by an easier route if one existed, and much of human ingenuity has gone into finding such routes. This is not a criticism of work. But it means that work, by its nature, points beyond itself, while play does not. If we ask what anything is ultimately for, play offers one of the few clear examples of an activity whose point lies wholly within it.

This is why recent efforts to gamify ordinary tasks deserve suspicion. Adding points and badges to exercise or study borrows the outward form of games while reversing their logic. The obstacles are no longer chosen for their own sake; they are devices for producing an external result, whether health, test scores, or engagement with an app. Such schemes can be useful, but they are not play, and to the extent they persuade us that play is merely a technique for motivation, they obscure the very thing that made play worth imitating. A culture that values play only as an instrument has lost track of the reasons anything is worth doing at all.

qs.q: According to the passage, the golfer example illustrates that a game involves:
o: reaching an outcome by the most efficient route available.
Paragraph 2 says the golfer refuses the efficient route of dropping the ball in.
competing against others for a valuable prize.
Paragraph 2 calls the outcome trivial and never mentions prizes or opponents.
relaxing after the necessary work of the day is done.
This is the leftover view of play that paragraph 1 says gets things backward.
accepting rules that make a goal harder to reach than necessary.
Correct: paragraph 2 defines a game as the voluntary acceptance of unnecessary obstacles.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 defines a game as the voluntary acceptance of unnecessary obstacles; the golfer could just drop the ball in but accepts rules that make the goal harder. Outcome and efficiency are beside the point. Relaxing after work is the leftover view of play that paragraph 1 rejects.

qs.q: The author's claim that work 'points beyond itself' means that work is:
o: less morally worthy than play.
Paragraph 3 explicitly says this is not a criticism of work.
valued mainly for its results rather than for the activity itself.
Correct: paragraph 3 says work is valued for what it produces and we would take an easier route.
always directed toward helping other people.
Paragraph 3 speaks of results in general, not service to others.
enjoyable only when it resembles a game.
Paragraph 3 makes no claim about when work is enjoyable.
qs.x: Work points beyond itself because it is valued for its results, and we would take an easier route to them if one existed. Play's point lies within the activity. Calling work less morally worthy is the trap, since paragraph 3 explicitly says this is not a criticism of work.

qs.q: The author says gamification schemes 'can be useful' in order to:
o: recommend them as a replacement for genuine play.
Paragraph 4 warns that such schemes obscure what made play worth imitating.
concede their practical value while denying that they count as play.
Correct: paragraph 4 follows the concession immediately with 'but they are not play.'
argue that study and exercise should never be rewarded.
Paragraph 4 does not oppose rewards, only calling them play.
show that work and play are ultimately identical.
Paragraphs 3 and 4 insist on the difference between work and play.
qs.x: The phrase is a concession: the author grants gamification its practical benefits and then immediately says they are not play. Conceding a point while holding the main claim is a common rhetorical move. Reading it as a recommendation ignores the warning that follows in the same paragraph.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's objection to gamification?
o: It uses the features of games to serve external ends, inverting what gives play its value.
Correct: paragraph 4 says it borrows the outward form while reversing the logic of chosen obstacles.
It makes ordinary tasks too difficult for most people to complete.
Paragraph 4 objects to its logic, not to difficulty.
It fails to improve health or test scores in practice.
Paragraph 4 grants the schemes can be useful for such results.
It replaces trivial outcomes with even more trivial ones.
Paragraph 4 says gamified tasks aim at real external results like health.
qs.x: In real games, obstacles are chosen for the sake of the activity. Gamification keeps points and badges but uses them to produce external results like health or test scores, reversing that logic. The claim that it fails to work is wrong, because the author concedes the schemes can be useful.

qs.q: An online chess player secretly uses a computer program to choose every move in order to win. The author would most likely say this player:
o: is playing well, since winning is the point of any game.
Paragraph 2 calls the outcome trivial; value lies in the activity.
has discarded the obstacles that make up the game and so is not really playing it.
Correct: paragraph 2 says a game exists through freely accepted unnecessary obstacles.
is doing work, since he is pursuing an efficient result.
Cheating seeks an easier route, but the author would stress the abandoned game, not relabel it work.
shows that play is best understood as a motivation technique.
Paragraph 4 rejects reducing play to a technique for motivation.
qs.x: On the author's account the game exists only through voluntarily accepted obstacles. A player who hands every move to a computer has removed those obstacles to get the outcome, so he is no longer really playing. Calling it winning well fails because the author treats the outcome as trivial; the value is in the activity.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's account of what makes play valuable?
o: Many people play games during work breaks.
Timing of play does not bear on where its value lies.
Some games have very elaborate rule systems.
Elaborate rules fit paragraph 2's account of chosen obstacles.
Players' enjoyment depends almost entirely on prizes and vanishes when no prizes are offered.
Correct: paragraph 2 locates play's value in the activity, not in outcomes or rewards.
Gamified study apps raise test scores modestly.
Paragraph 4 already concedes such schemes can be useful.
qs.x: The author locates play's value in the activity itself, not in its outcome or any reward. If enjoyment depended almost entirely on prizes and disappeared without them, play would look instrumental, which directly challenges that account. Gamified apps raising scores does not challenge it, since paragraph 4 already concedes such usefulness.

passages.title: Boxes at the Opera
text: Anyone who attends an opera today learns the rules quickly. The lights go down, conversation stops, latecomers wait outside, and applause is withheld until the end of an aria or an act. Many people assume these customs are as old as the art form and that they express the only fitting response to great music. In fact they are relatively recent, and the audiences for whom much of the standard repertoire was written behaved very differently.

In eighteenth-century Italian houses, the auditorium remained lit throughout the performance. Wealthy families rented boxes for the season, furnished them like drawing rooms, and received guests there. They ate, played cards, and conducted business and courtship, turning toward the stage when a favorite singer began a celebrated aria and turning away again during the recitatives. Composers knew this and wrote accordingly, concentrating their most memorable music in moments designed to recapture a distracted crowd.

The hushed, darkened theater emerged in the nineteenth century, promoted by composers who wanted listeners absorbed in an unbroken musical drama and by a growing middle class eager to show that it approached art with proper seriousness. The new etiquette was presented as a refinement, and in one sense it was: it made possible works of a length and continuity that the old social opera house could not have sustained. But it was also a form of discipline, and it changed who felt welcome. A patron who did not know when to clap could now be marked as an outsider.

I do not wish to romanticize the chattering boxes, which were themselves exclusive and often indifferent to the music. My point is narrower. When we treat silent reverence as the natural and correct way to hear opera, we forget that it is a historical choice with costs as well as benefits. It traded sociability for absorption. Recognizing this does not oblige us to bring back the card tables, but it should make us less certain that newcomers who whisper or clap at the wrong moment are failing to understand the art.

qs.q: According to the passage, audiences in eighteenth-century Italian opera houses:
o: sat in darkness and kept silent throughout.
Paragraph 3 says the darkened, hushed theater emerged in the nineteenth century.
were drawn mostly from the growing middle class.
Paragraph 2 describes wealthy families renting boxes; paragraph 3 links the middle class to later etiquette.
applauded only at the end of each act.
Withheld applause is a modern rule described in paragraph 1.
socialized in lit boxes and attended closely mainly to favored arias.
Correct: paragraph 2 describes eating, cards, and courtship, with attention turning to celebrated arias.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 describes lit auditoriums where wealthy families socialized in rented boxes, eating and playing cards, and turned to the stage mainly for favorite arias. Darkness, silence and withheld applause are the modern customs from paragraphs 1 and 3. Projecting present etiquette backward is exactly the assumption the passage corrects.

qs.q: The author notes that composers 'wrote accordingly' to suggest that:
o: composers disapproved of their audiences' conduct.
Paragraph 2 describes adaptation, not disapproval.
the shape of the music was influenced by how the audience behaved.
Correct: paragraph 2 says composers concentrated memorable music where it could recapture a distracted crowd.
recitatives were the most admired parts of an opera.
Paragraph 2 says audiences turned away during recitatives.
composers demanded darkened theaters from the start.
Paragraph 3 places that demand in the nineteenth century.
qs.x: Composers knew audiences would be distracted, so they placed their most memorable music where it could pull attention back. The claim is that audience behavior shaped the music's structure. Reading it as disapproval adds an attitude the passage never gives; paragraph 2 describes adaptation, not complaint.

qs.q: Which of the following does the author present as a genuine benefit of the newer etiquette?
o: It allowed long, continuous works that a distracted audience could not have sustained.
Correct: paragraph 3 says in one sense it was a refinement that made such works possible.
It made opera houses more welcoming to newcomers.
Paragraph 3 says it could mark unfamiliar patrons as outsiders.
It ended the exclusivity of the private boxes.
The passage never says the etiquette ended exclusivity.
It restored the audience customs of opera's earliest days.
Paragraph 1 says the customs are recent, not a restoration.
qs.x: The author is balanced: paragraph 3 calls the new etiquette a refinement in one sense because it allowed long, continuous works the old social opera house could not sustain. The costs come right after. Being more welcoming to newcomers is the reverse, since the new rules could mark unfamiliar patrons as outsiders.

qs.q: The statement 'I do not wish to romanticize the chattering boxes' mainly serves to:
o: head off the reading that the author prefers the older practice, narrowing the claim.
Correct: paragraph 4 follows it with 'My point is narrower' and declines to bring back the card tables.
concede that the author's history of the boxes is inaccurate.
Paragraph 4 adds criticisms of the boxes but does not retract the history.
argue that eighteenth-century audiences understood music better.
Paragraph 4 calls the boxes often indifferent to the music.
call for a return to lit auditoriums.
Paragraph 4 says recognizing the history does not oblige us to restore old customs.
qs.x: The disclaimer limits the argument. The author does not claim the old boxes were better, only that silent reverence is a historical choice with costs as well as benefits. Calling for a return to lit theaters is ruled out directly, since paragraph 4 says we are not obliged to bring back the card tables.

qs.q: Which change is most analogous to the one the author describes?
o: A stadium adds more seats to sell more tickets.
Capacity changes do not involve the trade of sociability for absorption.
A theater lowers ticket prices to attract students.
This widens access without changing norms of attention.
A museum that once allowed picnics in its galleries adopts strict silence, deterring casual visitors but enabling long viewing.
Correct: like paragraph 3's shift, it trades sociability for absorption and changes who feels welcome.
A concert hall installs better acoustics without changing any rules.
No change in audience etiquette is involved.
qs.x: The change to match trades sociability for absorption, makes longer attention possible, and changes who feels welcome. A museum that drops picnics for strict silence does all three. Cheaper tickets or better acoustics change access or sound, but neither changes the norms of attention, which is the heart of the analogy.

qs.q: Suppose evidence showed that the silent etiquette was adopted by all classes at once and never used to judge newcomers. This would most weaken the claim that the etiquette:
o: permitted longer and more continuous works.
The evidence concerns social exclusion, not musical form.
arose later than the eighteenth century.
The evidence does not touch the timing described in paragraph 3.
was promoted partly by composers.
Who promoted it is a separate claim from how it treated newcomers.
changed who felt welcome at the opera.
Correct: paragraph 3 bases this claim on the etiquette marking unfamiliar patrons as outsiders.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 supports the claim that the etiquette changed who felt welcome by noting it could mark patrons who did not know when to clap as outsiders. Evidence that it was never used to judge newcomers attacks exactly that. It leaves the claims about timing, composers and longer works untouched.

passages.title: The Scarce Resource
text: Economists like to say that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. When books, broadcasts, and feeds multiply without limit, the limiting factor is no longer the supply of things to read or watch but the hours and focus of the people who might read or watch them. From this observation a whole vocabulary has grown up: attention is a currency, a market, a resource to be captured and sold. Advertisers buy it, platforms harvest it, and users, we are told, pay with it.

The metaphor is useful, but it misleads in at least one important way. Money is fungible: a dollar spent on bread is the same as a dollar spent on books, and a dollar saved today can be spent tomorrow. Attention is neither. An hour of distracted scrolling and an hour of absorbed reading are not two equal units allocated to different ends; they are different experiences that shape the person who has them. Nor can attention be stored. The hour not spent attending to something is not banked for later; it is simply spent on something else.

This matters because the industries that measure attention measure it as if it were money. Their metrics count seconds on a screen, clicks, and return visits, and they reward whatever increases those counts. By such measures a feed that keeps a user anxiously refreshing for an hour has captured more attention than a novel that holds a reader for twenty quiet minutes. The quality of attention, the very thing that determines whether time was well used, disappears from the ledger.

The remedy is not to abandon the economic analysis but to complete it. Any serious accounting of attention must ask not only how much was captured but what kind of attention it was and what it left behind. A person whose capacity for sustained focus has been worn down by constant interruption has lost something real, even if every individual transaction appeared voluntary. Until our measures register that loss, the market in attention will continue to reward those who spend our attention most carelessly.

qs.q: The author's main point is that:
o: economic analysis of attention should be abandoned entirely.
Paragraph 4 says the remedy is to complete the analysis, not abandon it.
information is becoming scarcer as attention grows.
Paragraph 1 says information is abundant and attention is the limiting factor.
advertisers pay too little for the attention they buy.
The passage never argues about advertising prices.
treating attention like money ignores differences in its quality that matter for how time is used.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 argue attention is not fungible and that metrics drop its quality.
qs.x: The author accepts the economics of attention but argues that treating attention like money leaves out its quality, which determines whether time was well used. Abandoning the analysis is the tempting extreme, but paragraph 4 says the remedy is to complete it, not discard it.

qs.q: According to the passage, attention differs from money in that attention:
o: can be exchanged freely between different uses.
Paragraph 2 says this fungibility belongs to money, not attention.
is not limited in supply.
Paragraph 1 calls attention the limiting factor.
cannot be saved for use at a later time.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the unspent hour is not banked for later.
is never bought or sold.
Paragraph 1 says advertisers buy it and platforms harvest it.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 gives two differences: attention is not fungible, and it cannot be stored, since an unspent hour is not saved for later. The second matches the answer. Free exchange between uses is a property of money, which is the very contrast the author draws.

qs.q: The comparison between an anxious hour on a feed and twenty minutes with a novel is used to show that:
o: novels hold attention longer than feeds do.
Paragraph 3 says the feed holds the user longer, an hour versus twenty minutes.
readers prefer novels to online feeds.
Paragraph 3 makes no claim about preferences.
time on a screen is always wasted time.
Paragraph 3 faults the measure, not all screen time.
standard metrics can rank a poorer experience above a better one.
Correct: paragraph 3 says by such measures the feed wins while quality disappears from the ledger.
qs.x: By a seconds-on-screen metric, an hour of anxious refreshing beats twenty quiet minutes with a novel, even though the novel was the better use of attention. The comparison shows quantity metrics can rank a worse experience above a better one. Saying novels hold attention longer gets the numbers backward.

qs.q: The author's remark that a loss is real 'even if every individual transaction appeared voluntary' implies that:
o: users are usually forced to use attention-capturing products.
The remark grants that the transactions appeared voluntary.
voluntary choices can never cause harm.
Paragraph 4 says the opposite: a real loss arises despite voluntariness.
only involuntary interruptions reduce sustained focus.
Paragraph 4 attributes the loss to constant interruption regardless of consent.
harm can build up across many choices that each look acceptable on their own.
Correct: paragraph 4 says worn-down focus is a real loss despite each choice seeming voluntary.
qs.x: The phrase means each act of scrolling or clicking looked freely chosen, yet together they wore down the capacity to focus. So harm can build up across many choices that each seem acceptable alone. Forced use is ruled out because the remark assumes the transactions looked voluntary.

qs.q: Which new metric would the author most likely regard as an improvement?
o: One counting total screen minutes more accurately across devices.
Paragraph 3 faults counting quantity alone, however precisely.
One measuring how many times a day users return to an app.
Return visits are among the quantity metrics criticized in paragraph 3.
One rewarding apps that raise clicks per session.
Paragraph 3 says rewarding higher counts is the problem.
One tracking whether users later judge their time worthwhile and can still focus on long tasks.
Correct: paragraph 4 asks what kind of attention was captured and what it left behind.
qs.x: The author wants metrics that ask what kind of attention was captured and what it left behind. Tracking whether users judge their time worthwhile and can still focus on long tasks does that. Counting screen minutes more accurately is a trap, since paragraph 3's objection is to measuring quantity at all, however precisely.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that attention is not fungible?
o: Most people spend more time scrolling than reading.
How time is allocated does not show the hours are interchangeable.
An hour of scrolling and an hour of reading have indistinguishable effects on mood, memory, and later focus.
Correct: paragraph 2 rests on such hours being different experiences that shape the person.
Advertisers pay more for longer viewing sessions.
This describes pricing, not whether attention differs in kind.
Information supply has grown faster than population.
This supports paragraph 1's scarcity point without bearing on fungibility.
qs.x: The non-fungibility claim rests on the idea that different kinds of hours are different experiences that shape the person. If scrolling and reading had the same effects on mood, memory and focus, the hours would be interchangeable in the sense that matters. Facts about how people spend their time or what advertisers pay do not bear on this.

passages.title: The Patron's Shadow
text: The popular image of the Renaissance artist is of a genius struggling against the demands of patrons who cared more for gold leaf than for vision. The image draws on real documents. Contracts of the fifteenth century often specified the subject of a painting, the number of figures, the date of delivery, and even the quantity of costly ultramarine blue to be used in the Virgin's robe. To modern eyes such terms look like the shackles from which art later had to escape.

Read more carefully, the same documents suggest a different relationship. Over the course of the century, contracts increasingly shifted their emphasis from materials to skill. Patrons who once paid for so much gold and so much blue began to specify that the figures be painted by the master's own hand rather than by assistants, and to pay accordingly. What they were buying was no longer chiefly precious substances but the artist's distinctive ability, and that shift gave the most sought-after painters considerable bargaining power.

Competition among patrons sharpened this power. Rival princes, cities, and religious orders wanted the same few celebrated artists, and some artists exploited the rivalry, delaying commissions, negotiating higher fees, or leaving one court for another. A system that looks, in its contracts, like a regime of control often functioned in practice as a market in which talent could command terms.

None of this makes patronage a paradise of artistic freedom. Lesser painters had little leverage, and even great ones worked within subjects and settings chosen by others. But the contrast between the constrained Renaissance artist and the free modern artist is overdrawn. The modern artist who answers to no prince still answers to dealers, collectors, critics, and the demands of a market that can be more impersonal and less forgiving than any duke. Every arrangement for paying artists imposes constraints. The interesting question is not whether art is free of its patrons but which kinds of dependence leave room for invention.

qs.q: According to the passage, over the fifteenth century, painting contracts increasingly emphasized:
o: the exact quantity of ultramarine to be used.
Paragraph 2 presents material quantities as the older emphasis being replaced.
strict penalties for late delivery.
The passage mentions delivery dates but no growing emphasis on penalties.
the master's personal skill over the cost of materials.
Correct: paragraph 2 says contracts shifted emphasis from materials to skill, specifying the master's own hand.
work by assistants to lower costs.
Paragraph 2 says patrons specified the master's hand rather than assistants.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says contracts shifted from paying for materials like gold and blue to paying for the master's own hand, which gave sought-after painters bargaining power. Quantities of ultramarine are the trap, since they are the earlier emphasis the shift moved away from.

qs.q: The author mentions ultramarine in paragraph 1 primarily to:
o: show that Renaissance painters preferred blue to gold.
Paragraph 1 says nothing about painters' color preferences.
argue that patrons understood art better than artists did.
Paragraph 1 makes no comparison of understanding.
prove that artists had full control over their materials.
Paragraph 1 cites ultramarine as a term patrons dictated.
illustrate the detailed terms that lend support to the popular view of constrained artists.
Correct: paragraph 1 says the popular image draws on real documents with such terms.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states the popular view of the constrained artist and admits it draws on real documents. Ultramarine quantities are an example of those detailed terms, so they illustrate the evidence for the view the author goes on to complicate. They are not evidence of artistic control or of color preferences.

qs.q: The author would most likely describe the popular image of the Renaissance artist as:
o: an invention with no basis in historical records.
Paragraph 1 states that the image draws on real documents.
based on real evidence but misleading in the conclusion drawn from it.
Correct: paragraph 1 says it draws on real documents, and paragraph 2 says careful reading suggests a different relationship.
an accurate account that the author fully endorses.
Paragraphs 2 through 4 argue the contrast it implies is overdrawn.
true of famous painters but false of lesser ones.
Paragraph 4 says lesser painters had little leverage, which fits the popular image better.
qs.x: The author treats the popular image as resting on real documents that were read too quickly. A careful reading in paragraph 2 points to a different relationship. So the image is grounded but misleading. Calling it pure invention fails because paragraph 1 says it draws on real records.

qs.q: The author's closing question implies that patronage systems should be judged by:
o: whether they free artists from all constraints.
Paragraph 4 says every arrangement imposes constraints, so this test is pointless.
how much money they pay the average artist.
Paragraph 4 frames the question around invention, not income.
how much room for invention their forms of dependence allow.
Correct: paragraph 4 asks which kinds of dependence leave room for invention.
whether patrons or markets choose the subjects.
Paragraph 4 treats both as constraints and asks a different question.
qs.x: Because paragraph 4 says every way of paying artists imposes constraints, freedom from all constraint cannot be the test. The author instead asks which kinds of dependence leave room for invention. The pay and subject-choice options ignore that reframing.

qs.q: A novelist's publisher sets her genre and deadlines but pays well because several publishers bid for her books. This best illustrates the author's point that:
o: modern artists are entirely free of patrons.
Paragraph 4 says modern artists still answer to markets and buyers.
competition among buyers can give talent leverage even within constraints.
Correct: paragraph 3 says rivalry among patrons let celebrated artists command terms.
contracts that specify details always stifle creativity.
Paragraph 3 says controlling contracts often worked as a market favoring talent.
lesser artists have more freedom than famous ones.
Paragraph 4 says lesser painters had little leverage.
qs.x: The novelist works within limits set by others, much as Renaissance painters did, yet competition among publishers gives her leverage over pay. That matches paragraph 3: rivalry among patrons let celebrated artists command terms. It does not show she is free of patrons, which paragraph 4 denies of modern artists.

qs.q: Which discovery would most undermine the author's claim about artists' bargaining power?
o: Fees paid to famous painters stayed flat across the century despite rising competition among courts.
Correct: paragraph 3 says rivalry let artists negotiate higher fees, which flat fees would contradict.
Some contracts still specified the amount of gold leaf late in the century.
Paragraph 2 describes a trend, which a few holdover contracts do not overturn.
Lesser painters rarely changed patrons.
Paragraph 4 already says lesser painters had little leverage.
Religious orders commissioned many altarpieces.
Paragraph 3 lists religious orders among competing patrons, consistent with the claim.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 ties bargaining power to rivalry among patrons, which let artists negotiate higher fees. If famous painters' fees stayed flat even as courts competed harder, that mechanism would look false. A few late contracts that still listed gold leaf do not overturn a general trend.

passages.title: What a Promise Binds
text: Why is it wrong to break a promise? One popular answer looks to consequences for the promisee. When I promise to help you move, you plan around my help; if I fail to appear, I have disappointed expectations I deliberately created and perhaps cost you a truck rental. On this view the wrong of promise-breaking is the harm of frustrated reliance.

The view has the merit of simplicity, but it struggles with familiar cases. Suppose you never relied on my promise at all, because you had independently arranged for movers and only accepted my offer out of politeness. Most people would still say I ought to show up, or at least ask to be released. Or consider a promise made to a dying friend to look after her garden. She will never learn whether I keep it, and no expectation of hers will be disappointed, yet breaking the promise seems a betrayal rather than a neutral act.

These cases suggest that a promise does something more than create expectations. It transfers a kind of authority. When I promise, I give you a right to my performance, and with it the standing to hold me to it or to release me. That is why the promisee, and only the promisee, can cancel the obligation, and why it would be odd for a stranger to forgive my broken promise on your behalf. Reliance is often present and often increases the stakes, but it is a consequence of the promise, not its foundation.

This account has limits that should be acknowledged. A right can be transferred only by someone free to give it, so promises extracted by threat do not bind, and neither do promises to do what is independently wrong. A promise to commit a crime gives the promisee no genuine authority, whatever expectations it may have created. These exceptions are not embarrassments for the view; they follow directly from it. What a promise binds is the will, and a will that was coerced, or that had no right to bind itself to wrongdoing, transferred nothing.

qs.q: The author's central thesis is that making a promise:
o: is binding only when the promisee relies on it.
Paragraph 2 offers cases where promises bind without reliance.
creates obligations that no one can ever cancel.
Paragraph 3 says the promisee can release the promisor.
transfers to the promisee a right to the promised performance.
Correct: paragraph 3 says a promise transfers authority, giving the promisee a right to performance.
is wrong to break only when harm results.
This is the reliance view the author criticizes in paragraph 2.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 states the thesis: a promise transfers authority, giving the promisee a right to the performance and the power to release the promisor. The reliance options state the view the author argues against. The claim that promises can never be cancelled contradicts the release power the author emphasizes.

qs.q: The example of the promise to a dying friend is meant to show that:
o: promises to the dying are more binding than other promises.
Paragraph 2 uses the case to test the reliance view, not to rank promises.
a promise can bind even when breaking it would disappoint no one's expectations.
Correct: paragraph 2 says she will never learn of a breach, yet breaking it seems a betrayal.
people rarely keep promises once the promisee is gone.
Paragraph 2 makes no claim about how often such promises are kept.
reliance always increases the seriousness of a promise.
The example has no reliance at all, so it cannot show this.
qs.x: In the garden case, the friend will never learn whether the promise was kept, so no expectation can be disappointed, yet breaking it still feels like betrayal. That is a counterexample to the reliance view. It is not a claim that promises to the dying matter more; it is a test case where reliance is absent.

qs.q: The point that only the promisee can release the promisor is offered as evidence that:
o: strangers are usually indifferent to broken promises.
Paragraph 3 says a stranger's forgiveness would be odd, not that strangers are indifferent.
promises are binding only in legal contexts.
Paragraph 3 discusses moral authority, not legal settings.
reliance is the foundation of promissory obligation.
Paragraph 3 says reliance is a consequence, not the foundation.
the obligation is owed to a specific person who holds authority over it.
Correct: paragraph 3 says this follows from the promisee's right and standing to hold or release.
qs.x: If only the promisee can cancel the obligation, and a stranger cannot forgive the breach on her behalf, the duty must be owed to her specifically. That fits the view that she holds a right. Choosing reliance as the foundation is the reverse, since paragraph 3 says reliance is a consequence of promising.

qs.q: Which statement about reliance is most consistent with the author's view?
o: It is irrelevant to how seriously a broken promise should be judged.
Paragraph 3 grants that reliance often increases the stakes.
It is the only reason promises to the living are binding.
Paragraph 2's movers case shows binding force without reliance among the living.
It often raises the stakes of a promise but does not explain why the promise binds.
Correct: paragraph 3 says reliance often increases the stakes but is a consequence, not the foundation.
It can make a coerced promise binding.
Paragraph 4 says coerced promises transfer nothing, whatever expectations exist.
qs.x: The author does not dismiss reliance. Paragraph 3 grants that it is often present and raises the stakes, but says it is a result of the promise, not the reason it binds. Calling it irrelevant goes too far, because the author explicitly allows that it can make a broken promise more serious.

qs.q: A man promises to cover a coworker's shifts after she threatens to report an unrelated mistake of his. On the author's view, this promise:
o: binds, because the coworker now expects him to work.
Paragraph 4 says expectations do not create authority when the will was coerced.
binds only if the coworker relied on it.
Paragraph 3 rejects reliance as the foundation, and paragraph 4 voids coerced promises.
does not bind, because it was extracted by threat.
Correct: paragraph 4 says promises extracted by threat do not bind.
binds, because only she can release him from it.
Release presupposes a right was transferred, which paragraph 4 denies under coercion.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says a right can be transferred only by someone free to give it, so promises extracted by threat do not bind. The coworker's threat makes this such a case. The coworker's expectations do not matter, because coercion means no authority was ever transferred.

qs.q: Which case would pose the greatest difficulty for the author's account?
o: A promise most people judge still binding after the promisee has freely released the promisor.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the promisee's release cancels the obligation, so this would conflict.
A promise to a friend who never relied on it and still ought to be kept.
This mirrors paragraph 2's movers case, which supports the author.
A promise to commit a crime that people judge non-binding.
Paragraph 4 says such promises do not bind, so this fits.
A broken promise that caused a large financial loss.
Paragraph 3 allows that reliance raises the stakes, so this fits.
qs.x: On the author's view the promisee holds the right and can release the promisor, which ends the obligation. A case where a promise still binds after a free release would contradict that core claim. The criminal-promise and no-reliance cases are already explained by the theory, so they support it.

passages.title: Sounding the Dark
text: For most of history the ocean floor was not mapped so much as imagined. Nineteenth-century surveyors lowered weighted lines over the sides of ships and waited, sometimes for hours, until the line went slack. Each sounding yielded a single depth at a single point, and a whole ocean basin might be represented by a few hundred such numbers scattered across thousands of miles. Between them lay guesswork, and the guesses tended to favor a smooth, featureless bottom, because smoothness was the simplest assumption to draw.

Echo sounding, developed in the early twentieth century, replaced the line with a pulse of sound and turned isolated points into continuous profiles along a ship's track. The data grew enormously, but it remained data along lines, not across surfaces. To produce a picture of the seafloor, someone still had to decide how the ridges and valleys seen on one track connected to those seen on another, often a hundred miles away.

The most influential seafloor maps of the mid-century were made by exactly this kind of informed interpretation. Rather than contour charts that showed only measured depths, their makers drew the seafloor as it might look if the water were drained away, with mountain ranges shaded and canyons cut into relief. Critics complained that such pictures showed more than the evidence strictly allowed. They were right, in a sense. Yet it was these pictures, more than the columns of numbers behind them, that made a continuous rift running down the center of the great ridges impossible to ignore, and that helped persuade a skeptical profession that the ocean floor was being pulled apart.

It is tempting to say that the interpretive maps succeeded despite their departure from the data. I would say instead that they succeeded because of it. A map is not merely a container for measurements; it is an argument about how the measurements fit together. The early charts that showed a smooth ocean were also arguments, only weaker ones that did not know they were arguing. Good scientific images do not avoid interpretation. They make it explicit enough to be tested.

qs.q: According to the passage, early charts showed a smooth ocean floor largely because:
o: sparse soundings left wide gaps that were filled with the simplest assumption.
Correct: paragraph 1 says guesses between scattered points favored smoothness as the simplest assumption.
weighted lines gave inaccurate depth readings.
Paragraph 1 faults the sparseness of soundings, not their accuracy.
the ocean floor really is mostly flat.
Paragraph 3 describes mountain ranges, canyons, and a continuous rift.
surveyors deliberately hid features they had found.
Paragraph 4 says the charts did not know they were arguing, implying no deliberate concealment.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 explains that a few hundred soundings were spread across huge basins, and the gaps between them were filled with the simplest assumption, which was smoothness. The problem was too few data points plus a default guess. The weighted-line readings are not described as inaccurate, only as sparse.

qs.q: The passage indicates that echo sounding improved on weighted lines by:
o: measuring entire surfaces of the seafloor at once.
Paragraph 2 says the data remained along lines, not across surfaces.
removing the need to interpret between tracks.
Paragraph 2 says someone still had to connect features across tracks.
proving that the seafloor was being pulled apart.
Paragraph 3 credits the interpretive maps, not echo sounding itself, with persuading geologists.
producing continuous depth profiles along a ship's path.
Correct: paragraph 2 says it turned isolated points into continuous profiles along a track.
qs.x: Echo sounding replaced single depth points with continuous profiles along a ship's track, as paragraph 2 says. But the data still came in lines, not whole surfaces, so people still had to work out how features connected between tracks. Options claiming full surface coverage or no need for interpretation overstate what it did.

qs.q: The author concedes that critics of the mid-century maps were 'right, in a sense' because the maps:
o: relied on outdated weighted-line soundings.
Paragraph 3 says the maps used informed interpretation of newer data.
showed features beyond what the measurements strictly established.
Correct: paragraph 3 says critics complained the pictures showed more than the evidence allowed.
failed to persuade geologists of anything.
Paragraph 3 says the maps helped persuade a skeptical profession.
left out the rift running along the ridges.
Paragraph 3 says the maps made the rift impossible to ignore.
qs.x: The concession is that the shaded maps did show more than the measurements strictly proved, since mapmakers had to infer how features connected between tracks. That is why the critics were right in a sense. The maps did not leave out the rift or fail to persuade; paragraph 3 says the opposite.

qs.q: The claim that the smooth early charts were 'arguments ... that did not know they were arguing' suggests that those charts:
o: contained no interpretation at all.
Paragraph 4 calls them arguments, which means they did interpret.
carried interpretive assumptions without acknowledging them.
Correct: paragraph 4 contrasts them with good images that make interpretation explicit enough to test.
were more honest than the later shaded maps.
Paragraph 4 calls them weaker arguments, not more honest ones.
were drawn to support continental drift.
Paragraph 3 shows the later maps, not smooth charts, supported a spreading seafloor.
qs.x: Calling the smooth charts arguments means they did contain interpretation, the choice of smoothness, but presented it as if it were plain fact. Paragraph 4 contrasts this with good images that make interpretation explicit so it can be tested. Saying they had no interpretation at all takes the charts' self-presentation at face value.

qs.q: Which practice for modern scientific images would the author most likely endorse?
o: Showing only raw measurements and leaving all gaps blank.
Paragraph 4 says good images do not avoid interpretation.
Clearly marking which features were measured and which were inferred, so the inferences can be checked.
Correct: paragraph 4 says good images make interpretation explicit enough to be tested.
Smoothing irregular data to keep images simple.
Paragraph 1 shows smoothing as a weak hidden assumption.
Hiding the methods used to fill gaps to avoid confusion.
Paragraph 4 values making interpretation explicit, not hidden.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says good scientific images do not avoid interpretation; they make it explicit enough to be tested. Clearly marking measured versus inferred features does exactly that. Showing only raw data with blank gaps is tempting as the cautious choice, but the author says avoiding interpretation is not what makes images good.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim about how geologists were persuaded?
o: Most geologists of the time were convinced by tabulated numerical data before seeing any pictorial maps.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the pictures, more than columns of numbers, persuaded the profession.
Critics of the pictorial maps continued to object for years.
Paragraph 3 already acknowledges critics, so lingering objections fit.
Echo sounding data were costly to gather.
Cost of data does not bear on what persuaded geologists.
Later surveys confirmed the rift the maps had shown.
Confirmation supports, rather than weakens, the value of the maps.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 credits the pictorial maps, more than the columns of numbers, with persuading a skeptical profession. If most geologists had already been convinced by numerical tables before seeing the maps, that causal claim fails. Later confirmation of the rift would support the maps, not weaken the claim.

passages.title: Who Holds the Lamp
text: Histories of street lighting usually read as a story of steady progress. Oil lanterns gave way to gas, gas to electricity, and electricity to the cool glare of the light-emitting diode, and with each step the night became safer, the city more open, and the citizen more free to walk where and when she pleased. The story is not wrong, but it leaves out who held the light, and toward whom it was pointed.

When Paris organized its first systematic public lighting in the later seventeenth century, the lanterns were placed under the authority of the newly created lieutenant of police. Householders were charged for their upkeep, and the lanterns hung over the middle of the street, where they marked the reach of royal order as much as they guided pedestrians. Contemporaries understood the point. In the revolutionary crowds of 1789, the lamppost became an improvised gallows, and in later uprisings Parisians smashed lanterns before raising barricades. Darkness, for the insurgent, was a form of cover; light was the eye of the state.

None of this means that lighting was merely repression. Gas lamps in the nineteenth century made possible the evening promenade, the late-opening shop, and the theater crowd spilling into a bright boulevard. Night, once the province of watchmen and thieves, became a time of commerce and sociability for the respectable classes. But the same illumination that welcomed the shopper made the vagrant visible, and the policing of the lit street grew alongside its pleasures. Light expanded freedom for some by sharpening scrutiny of others.

This double character is worth remembering in current debates. Cities replacing old sodium lamps with brighter LEDs present the change as a technical upgrade, justified by energy savings and crime statistics; critics respond with arguments about sleep, wildlife, and the vanished stars. Both sides tend to treat illumination as a neutral quantity, to be measured in lumens and adjusted. The history suggests otherwise. Every decision about where the light falls is also a decision about who is to be seen, and by whom.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Street lighting has steadily made cities safer and freer for everyone.
Paragraph 1 calls this progress story incomplete because it ignores who held the light.
Street lighting has both widened nighttime freedom and extended surveillance, so lighting choices are political.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 show both effects, and paragraph 4 says every lighting decision concerns who is seen.
Street lighting was introduced chiefly as a tool of repression.
Paragraph 3 says lighting was not merely repression and also enabled commerce and sociability.
Modern LED lighting should be rejected because it harms wildlife.
Paragraph 4 reports the critics' wildlife argument but faults both sides for treating light as neutral.
qs.x: A main-point answer must cover the whole argument. Paragraph 1 calls the progress story incomplete, paragraphs 2 and 3 show light both widening freedom and extending surveillance, and paragraph 4 concludes that lighting decisions are about who is seen. The repression choice grabs only paragraph 2 and ignores paragraph 3's explicit statement that lighting was not merely repression.

qs.q: The author mentions the lamppost as gallows and the smashing of lanterns mainly to show that:
o: contemporaries saw public lighting as an instrument of state power
Correct: paragraph 2 says contemporaries understood the point, and light was the eye of the state.
revolutionary crowds wanted to save the cost of lantern upkeep
Paragraph 2 mentions the charge to householders, but not as the crowds' motive.
seventeenth-century lanterns were poorly built and easily broken
The examples concern what lanterns meant, not how well they were made.
street lighting had no effect on crime in Paris
Crime rates are never discussed in paragraph 2.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 piles up details (police authority, lanterns marking royal order, lampposts as gallows, smashed lanterns) to support one claim: contemporaries understood light as the eye of the state. Ask what job an example does in the argument. The upkeep charge is mentioned, but nothing links it to the crowds' motives, so the cost choice reads in a cause the passage never gives.

qs.q: The claim that "light expanded freedom for some by sharpening scrutiny of others" implies that:
o: gas lighting reduced freedom for every group in the city
Paragraph 3 says lighting opened night life to the respectable classes.
only the police benefited from nineteenth-century gas lamps
Shoppers, promenaders and theatergoers also benefited, per paragraph 3.
the benefits and burdens of street lighting fell unequally across social groups
Correct: paragraph 3 says the light that welcomed shoppers made vagrants visible to police.
scrutiny of vagrants fell as the streets grew brighter
Paragraph 3 says policing of the lit street grew, not fell.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's closing line says one group's gain came through another group's exposure: the shopper was welcomed while the vagrant was made visible and policed. That is an unequal distribution of benefits and burdens. The tempting extremes fail because the paragraph names real winners, the respectable classes, so lighting neither reduced freedom for everyone nor benefited only the police.

qs.q: A city defends a switch to brighter LEDs solely by citing energy savings. The author would most likely say this defense:
o: settles the issue, since lighting is a technical matter
Paragraph 4 rejects treating illumination as a neutral quantity to be adjusted.
is flawed only because it ignores harm to sleep and wildlife
The author says the critics who raise sleep and wildlife also treat light as neutral.
proves that modern lighting is no longer linked to policing
Nothing in an energy argument shows the political side of lighting has vanished.
neglects the question of who will be made visible, and to whom
Correct: paragraph 4 says treating light as a neutral, technical quantity misses who is to be seen and by whom.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 faults both sides of the LED debate for treating light as a neutral, measurable quantity, and insists the real issue is who is seen and by whom. An energy-only defense is exactly that neutral framing. The trap is the sleep-and-wildlife option: the author says those critics make the same mistake, so their concerns are not what the city's defense is missing.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's account of early Parisian lighting?
o: Lanterns were often smashed in nineteenth-century Parisian uprisings.
Paragraph 2 already cites this as support for the author's view.
Householders sometimes resented paying for lantern upkeep.
Resentment of the charge fits paragraph 2 and does not challenge it.
Neighborhood groups, not the police, ran the first lanterns purely to guide pedestrians.
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that the lanterns were placed under police authority and marked royal order.
Gas lamps later replaced oil lanterns along the boulevards.
This matches paragraph 1's account of lighting technology and leaves paragraph 2 untouched.
qs.x: To weaken a claim, find evidence that contradicts its core. Paragraph 2 rests on the lanterns being under police authority and marking royal order. If neighborhood groups ran them purely to guide walkers, that political reading collapses. Smashed lanterns and resented upkeep fees are already part of, or fully consistent with, the author's account, so they cannot weaken it.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, nineteenth-century gas lighting:
o: ended the policing of city streets at night
Paragraph 3 says policing of the lit street grew alongside its pleasures.
left night as the province of watchmen and thieves
Paragraph 3 says this was the state of night before gas lighting.
made evening commerce and sociability possible for the respectable classes
Correct: paragraph 3 cites the evening promenade, late-opening shops and theater crowds.
was used mainly to light private homes
Paragraph 3 describes lit boulevards and streets, not homes.
qs.x: This is a detail question: paragraph 3 says gas lamps made possible the evening promenade, late shops and theater crowds, opening night to commerce and sociability for the respectable classes. Watch the timeline trap: night as the province of watchmen and thieves describes the period before gas lighting, not its result. Policing grew rather than ended.

passages.title: Theology in Glass
text: It is a commonplace of guidebooks that the Gothic cathedral was an engine for flooding sacred space with light. The pointed arch, the ribbed vault, and the flying buttress, we are told, freed the walls from their load-bearing duties so that they could dissolve into glass, and medieval builders pursued this structural liberation because they longed for brightness. The story is appealing, and it is half true. The builders did want light. What they did not want, by and large, was brightness.

Anyone who has stood in the nave of Chartres on an overcast afternoon knows that the interior is dim. Its windows, crowded with deep blues and reds, admit only a fraction of the daylight that strikes them. This was not a failure of medieval glassmaking, which could produce paler glass when it chose to. The dimness was the point. Writers such as Abbot Suger, whose rebuilding of Saint-Denis in the 1140s is often called the first Gothic project, praised light that had been changed by passing through precious material. For Suger, the beholder was lifted from the material to the immaterial not by clarity but by transformation: ordinary sunlight entered the church and emerged as something jewel-like and strange.

Later centuries lost this distinction. In the eighteenth century, many cathedral chapters replaced medieval glass with clear panes, valuing legibility and an even, rational illumination. Restorers sometimes scraped painted interiors back to bare stone. The result is the luminous, austere Gothic that modern tourists admire, and that modern taste reads backward into the Middle Ages. We praise these buildings for the virtues of the Enlightenment that partly dismantled them.

Recovering the medieval aim matters because it changes what we think the architecture was for. A building designed to maximize brightness is a building designed for seeing; one designed to transfigure light is a building designed for being changed. The Gothic engineers solved structural problems with extraordinary ingenuity, but they solved them in the service of an experience that clear glass cannot deliver, and that our admiration, however sincere, may be quietly misremembering.

qs.q: The distinction the author draws between "light" and "brightness" is best described as a contrast between:
o: natural sunlight and artificial candlelight
The passage never discusses candles; both terms concern daylight through windows.
light transformed by colored glass and plentiful, even illumination
Correct: paragraph 2 describes light changed by precious material, unlike the clear brightness of paragraph 3.
structural innovation and decorative ornament
Paragraph 1 mentions structure, but the light/brightness contrast concerns the quality of illumination.
the cathedral interior and its exterior facade
The contrast is about how interiors were lit, not about inside versus outside.
qs.x: The author separates light that has been transformed by passing through deep-colored glass, which Suger praised in paragraph 2, from the plentiful, even brightness of clear panes that later centuries preferred in paragraph 3. Both terms describe how daylight enters the building, so the contrast is about the quality of illumination, not structure versus ornament or inside versus outside.

qs.q: According to the passage, the dimness of the Chartres interior was:
o: a result of the limits of medieval glassmaking
Paragraph 2 says medieval glassmakers could produce paler glass when they chose.
a product of alterations made in the eighteenth century
Paragraph 3 says eighteenth-century changes made interiors brighter, not dimmer.
an accident of weather that misleads modern visitors
Overcast weather is just the setting of the example; the author calls the dimness deliberate.
an intended effect consistent with a theology of transformed light
Correct: paragraph 2 says the dimness was the point, tied to Suger's praise of transformed light.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the dimness was the point: glassmakers could make paler glass, and Suger valued sunlight changed into something jewel-like. So the dimness was deliberate and theological. The overcast-afternoon detail is only the setting of the example, and paragraph 3 says eighteenth-century changes brightened interiors, so neither weather nor later alteration explains the dimness.

qs.q: The claim that "we praise these buildings for the virtues of the Enlightenment that partly dismantled them" most strongly suggests that:
o: Enlightenment architects designed most surviving Gothic cathedrals
Paragraph 3 says Enlightenment-era chapters altered existing buildings; they did not design them.
modern tourists generally dislike Gothic architecture
Paragraph 3 says tourists admire these buildings, though for the wrong reasons.
eighteenth-century restorers recovered the original medieval intention
The author says these restorers lost the medieval distinction rather than recovering it.
modern admiration for Gothic clarity reflects later tastes imposed on the buildings
Correct: paragraph 3 says clear glazing and bare stone are later changes that modern taste reads back into the past.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says eighteenth-century chapters installed clear glass and scraped interiors to bare stone, producing the bright, austere look that modern tourists then credit to medieval builders. The irony is that what we admire is a later imposition. The restorers did not recover the original aim; the author says later centuries lost the medieval distinction, which is why we misremember it.

qs.q: Which discovery would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Evidence that medieval glaziers could not make pale glass in large panes
This would weaken paragraph 2's claim that dimness was a choice rather than a technical limit.
A 13th-century contract requiring deep-colored glass so the choir would seem otherworldly
Correct: it shows medieval builders chose colored, transforming light on purpose, as paragraph 2 claims.
Proof that flying buttresses allowed thinner walls than Romanesque designs
The author already accepts the structural story; it does not bear on brightness versus light.
Letters in which 18th-century visitors called clear-glazed naves gloomy
This concerns later taste and would, if anything, cut against paragraph 3's account of it.
qs.x: The argument's key claim is that dimness was a deliberate choice for transformed light, not a technical limit. A medieval contract demanding deep-colored glass to make the choir seem otherworldly directly confirms that intent. Evidence that pale glass could not be made would do the opposite, suggesting dimness was a constraint, and the buttress fact concerns structure the author already accepts.

qs.q: The author would most likely regard a modern project that fills a medieval chapel's windows with clear glass as:
o: a faithful recovery of the builders' original aim
Paragraphs 2 and 3 say the original aim was colored, transformed light, not clarity.
a structural necessity the Gothic engineers would accept
Glazing choices are presented as aesthetic and theological, not structural.
unimportant, since stained glass was purely decorative
The author treats the glass as central to the building's purpose, not mere decoration.
obscuring the experience the building was meant to create
Correct: paragraph 4 says clear glass cannot deliver the transformative experience the builders intended.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the builders designed for being changed by transfigured light, an experience clear glass cannot deliver. Clear-glazing a medieval chapel therefore repeats the Enlightenment alteration the author describes and hides the intended effect. Calling it a faithful recovery gets the original aim backward, since paragraphs 2 and 3 tie that aim to colored glass, not clarity.

passages.title: The Loyal Dissenter
text: Discussions of whistleblowing usually begin with a dilemma. On one side stands loyalty, the employee's duty to the organization that pays her and trusts her with its secrets; on the other stands conscience, her duty to the public that the organization's wrongdoing may harm. The whistleblower, in this picture, is someone who decides that conscience outweighs loyalty, and the ethical debate concerns only how grave the wrong must be before the scale tips.

This framing concedes too much. It assumes that loyalty is owed to an organization's current managers and their wishes, rather than to the purposes for which the organization exists. A hospital exists to heal, an auditing firm to certify the truth of accounts, a newspaper to report. An engineer who reveals that her company has concealed a safety defect is not betraying the firm; she is betraying the executives who betrayed it first. Her disclosure is, in the deepest sense, an act of fidelity.

Reframing whistleblowing this way does not make it easy, nor does it license every disclosure. If the whistleblower acts out of loyalty to the institution's purpose, she has reason to choose the means that damage that purpose least. Ordinarily this means raising concerns internally before going outside, unless internal channels are themselves compromised or the harm is imminent. It also means disclosing what the public needs to know rather than everything she happens to know. The leaker who dumps an archive indiscriminately, exposing innocent colleagues along with guilty superiors, has abandoned the very loyalty that would have justified her.

The older dilemma model has a further cost: it makes whistleblowers look like defectors, and institutions treat them accordingly. Laws that protect whistleblowers are often written as exceptions to a general duty of confidentiality, grudging carve-outs for extraordinary cases. If disclosure is instead understood as a form of loyalty, then protection is not an exception but a recognition that organizations sometimes need members willing to defend them against their own leadership.

qs.q: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to argue that whistleblowing:
o: should be discouraged because it damages institutions
The author defends whistleblowing and wants stronger legal protection for it in paragraph 4.
is justified whenever conscience conflicts with loyalty
The author rejects this dilemma framing as conceding too much (paragraph 2).
should always bypass internal channels and go to the public
Paragraph 3 says concerns should ordinarily be raised internally first.
can be understood as loyalty to an organization's purpose rather than as betrayal
Correct: paragraph 2 calls disclosure an act of fidelity, and the rest of the passage builds on that reframing.
qs.x: The passage's core move is to reject the loyalty-versus-conscience dilemma and recast disclosure as fidelity to what the organization exists to do. Paragraphs 3 and 4 then draw out what that reframing implies for method and for law. The conscience-outweighs-loyalty choice is tempting because it sounds pro-whistleblower, but it is exactly the framing paragraph 2 says concedes too much.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, the leaker who releases an archive indiscriminately:
o: undermines her own justification by harming innocent colleagues and the institution
Correct: paragraph 3 says she has abandoned the very loyalty that would have justified her.
deserves more admiration because she withholds nothing
Paragraph 3 says disclosure should be limited to what the public needs to know.
is justified as long as internal channels were compromised
Compromised channels justify going outside, not disclosing indiscriminately.
displays the institutional loyalty the author endorses
The author says she has abandoned that loyalty.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a whistleblower loyal to the institution's purpose should choose means that damage that purpose least and disclose only what the public needs. The indiscriminate leaker harms innocent colleagues and so abandons the loyalty that justified her. Compromised internal channels can justify going outside, but they never license dumping everything, which is the trap in that option.

qs.q: The claim that the engineer "is betraying the executives who betrayed it first" depends most on which assumption?
o: Executives are legally liable for every product defect.
The argument is about loyalty and purpose, not about legal liability.
Employees owe their employers no duty of confidentiality.
Paragraph 4 acknowledges a general duty of confidentiality; the author does not deny it.
An organization's identity lies in its purposes rather than in its managers' wishes.
Correct: paragraph 2 says loyalty is owed to the purposes the organization exists for, not to managers.
Harm to the public always matters more than harm to the firm.
That is the dilemma model's weighing, which paragraph 2 sets aside.
qs.x: An assumption is an unstated premise the conclusion needs. To say the executives betrayed the firm, the author must treat the firm as its purposes rather than as its managers' wishes; otherwise defying managers would simply be betraying the firm. Weighing public harm over the firm's interest belongs to the dilemma model the author sets aside, so it is not the needed premise.

qs.q: An accountant finds fraud, but the firm's compliance office is run by the executive who planned it. By the passage's reasoning, the best course is to:
o: give the relevant evidence of fraud to outside regulators
Correct: paragraph 3 allows going outside when internal channels are compromised, disclosing what the public needs.
stay silent out of loyalty to the firm's leadership
Paragraph 2 says loyalty is owed to the firm's purpose, not to the managers who betrayed it.
report the fraud first to the compromised compliance office
Paragraph 3 makes an exception to internal reporting when channels are compromised.
release all of the firm's internal files to the press
Paragraph 3 condemns indiscriminate disclosure that exposes innocent colleagues.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says to report internally first unless internal channels are compromised or harm is imminent, and to disclose only what the public needs. Here the compliance office is run by the wrongdoer, so going to outside regulators with the relevant evidence fits both rules. Releasing every file to the press satisfies the exception but violates the limit on indiscriminate disclosure.

qs.q: The author's argument implies that whistleblower protection laws should be:
o: limited to a few extraordinary cases
Paragraph 4 criticizes laws written as grudging carve-outs for extraordinary cases.
written as exceptions to a duty of confidentiality
This is the current framing that paragraph 4 says reflects the flawed dilemma model.
grounded in the recognition that disclosure can serve the institution
Correct: paragraph 4 says protection should recognize that organizations need members who defend them.
repealed, since loyal employees need no legal protection
The author wants protection reframed, not removed.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 criticizes laws written as grudging exceptions to a general duty of confidentiality and says protection should instead recognize that organizations need members who will defend them against their own leadership. So the author wants protection grounded in disclosure as service to the institution. The exception-to-confidentiality choice describes the current framing the author is criticizing.

passages.title: The Authenticity Trap
text: Every folk revival tells the same story about itself. Somewhere, usually in the countryside and usually among the poor, an old music has survived untouched by commerce; the revivalists' task is to find it, record it, and restore it to a public that has forgotten its own inheritance. The American revival of the mid-twentieth century and its British counterpart both drew strength from this narrative, and both were attacked, almost immediately, for betraying it. Critics complained that college students strumming ballads in coffeehouses were playing at a tradition they had no right to.

The charge of inauthenticity depends, however, on a picture of tradition that the revivalists themselves invented. The singers whom collectors visited rarely thought of their repertoire as pure or ancient. They learned songs from relatives, but also from printed broadsides, traveling shows, and, by the 1920s, phonograph records and radio. A ballad sung in an Appalachian kitchen might have come from a Scottish source two centuries old or from a commercial recording made in a city studio the previous year, and the singer was unlikely to care which. Tradition, for them, was not a museum but a practice of borrowing and altering.

Ironically, it was the collectors who introduced fixity. By transcribing a single performance and publishing it as the authentic version of a song, they turned one moment in a living process into a standard against which later performances could be judged deficient. Some collectors went further, quietly omitting songs that showed the influence of popular music because such songs spoiled the image of an untouched culture. The tradition the revival claimed to rescue was partly a product of the rescue.

To say this is not to dismiss the revivals. They preserved recordings that would otherwise have vanished and brought obscure musicians to audiences who paid them, belatedly, some of what they were owed. But their lasting lesson may be the reverse of the one they intended. The coffeehouse singer who changed a verse to suit her own voice was not departing from folk tradition; she was, without knowing it, practicing it more faithfully than the purists who scolded her.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, the singers whom collectors visited generally regarded their songs as:
o: a flexible repertoire drawn from many sources, including commercial ones
Correct: paragraph 2 says they learned from relatives, broadsides, shows, records and radio, and did not care which.
an ancient heritage to be guarded against commercial influence
Paragraph 2 says they rarely thought of their repertoire as pure or ancient.
inferior imitations of the music heard on records
The passage says they mixed sources freely, not that they ranked records above their own songs.
the private property of their own families
Family was one source among many; the passage stresses borrowing, not ownership.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says source singers learned songs from relatives, broadsides, traveling shows, records and radio, and were unlikely to care which source a ballad came from; tradition was a practice of borrowing and altering. The tempting wrong answer, an ancient heritage guarded from commerce, is the revivalists' invented picture, which the paragraph says the singers rarely shared.

qs.q: The author's view of the critics who scolded coffeehouse singers is that they:
o: correctly identified a betrayal of the source singers
Paragraph 4 says the coffeehouse singer practiced the tradition more faithfully than the purists.
were justified because the students lacked rural origins
The author rejects the idea that tradition is tied to an untouched rural source.
were right about the singers but wrong about the collectors
The author faults the critics' view of the singers too, calling the singers faithful to tradition.
relied on a mistaken idea of what folk tradition is
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 4 say their charge depends on an invented picture of pure, fixed tradition.
qs.x: The critics accused coffeehouse students of betraying a pure, untouched tradition. Paragraph 2 says that picture was invented by revivalists, and paragraph 4 says the singer who altered a verse was practicing tradition more faithfully than the purists. So the critics' error lies in their concept of tradition itself, not in a fact about the students' rural or urban origins.

qs.q: The statement that "the tradition the revival claimed to rescue was partly a product of the rescue" most nearly means that:
o: collectors secretly composed most of the songs they published
Paragraph 3 describes selecting and fixing versions, not composing songs.
rural singers stopped performing once they had been recorded
The passage never says that recording ended anyone's performing.
revival audiences paid to keep rural traditions alive
Payment to musicians appears in paragraph 4 but is not what this sentence means.
collectors' choices about what to transcribe and omit shaped the tradition they claimed to find
Correct: paragraph 3 says fixed versions and omitted pop-influenced songs created the image of an untouched culture.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says collectors fixed one performance as the authentic version and quietly dropped pop-influenced songs, creating the image of an untouched culture. The rescued tradition was thus partly shaped by the rescuers' selections. The composing option overreaches: the passage describes choosing and freezing versions, never inventing the songs themselves.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's account in paragraph 2?
o: Many revival recordings would have been lost without collectors.
Paragraph 4 already grants this; it does not challenge paragraph 2.
Some Appalachian ballads have Scottish sources two centuries old.
Paragraph 2 already says some songs came from old Scottish sources.
Coffeehouse audiences often preferred polished performers.
Audience taste in the revival says nothing about how source singers viewed their songs.
Source singers regularly refused to perform songs learned from records, calling them foreign.
Correct: this would show singers did care about sources, contradicting paragraph 2's picture of free borrowing.
qs.x: Paragraph 2's claim is that source singers borrowed freely and did not care where songs came from. Evidence that they refused record-learned songs as foreign would show they cared deeply about sources, contradicting the claim. The Scottish-sources option merely restates something paragraph 2 already grants, and preservation by collectors is conceded in paragraph 4, so neither challenges it.
