qs.q: Which analogy best captures the author's view of the collectors' transcriptions?
o: A translator renders a foreign poem faithfully into English.
Faithful translation lacks the key idea of freezing one moment of a living process.
A single portrait of a growing child comes to be treated as the child's true face.
Correct: like paragraph 3's transcription, one moment of a changing process becomes the fixed standard.
A gardener moves a wild plant indoors to save it from development.
This captures preservation but not how fixing one version distorts a changing practice.
A critic reviews a concert unfavorably in a newspaper.
Judgment by an outsider misses the point about turning one performance into a standard.
qs.x: The author's complaint in paragraph 3 is that one transcribed performance of a living, changing practice was treated as the fixed, authentic standard. A single portrait of a growing child treated as the child's true face has the same structure: one moment frozen and used to judge later change. Moving a plant indoors captures rescue but lacks the idea of freezing one version as the standard.

passages.title: The Garden and the Empire
text: Botanical gardens present themselves as places of quiet contemplation, and the history of botany is often told in the same key: patient naturalists, armed with hand lenses and Latin, gradually bringing order to the world's bewildering flora. That story is not false, but it omits the circumstance that made much of the ordering possible. From the seventeenth century to the twentieth, European botany grew alongside European empires, and the two were rarely separable.

The connection was partly economic. Imperial gardens functioned as clearing houses for plants of commercial value. Seeds of the cinchona tree, source of the antimalarial drug quinine, were carried out of the Andes in the 1860s and established on plantations in British India and Dutch Java; rubber seeds taken from Brazil in the 1870s were germinated at Kew and shipped on to Ceylon and Malaya. Each transfer enriched one colonial economy and often impoverished another. Botany, in these episodes, was less a contemplative science than an instrument of trade policy.

The connection was also intellectual, and here the costs are harder to see. The plants European botanists "discovered" had nearly always been known, named, and used by local people for generations. Yet the system of classification that came to dominate replaced those names with Latin binomials and credited the first European to publish a description. A seventeenth-century Dutch compendium of the plants of the Malabar coast relied heavily on the knowledge of local physicians, one of whom is named in its preface; most such informants went unrecorded. Classification, in other words, was also a process of erasure.

Some critics conclude that the colonial botanical archive should be treated as hopelessly compromised. This seems to me a mistake. The herbarium sheets, field notes, and correspondence that empire produced are often the only surviving traces of the indigenous expertise they suppressed. Read carefully, with attention to the local names jotted in margins and the guides mentioned in passing, they can be made to testify against their own silences. The archive's complicity is precisely what makes it valuable to those trying to undo it.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
o: European botany was a disinterested science that later critics have misjudged.
Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that botany was tied to empire, rejecting the purely contemplative story.
Colonial botanical archives are too compromised to be useful to historians.
Paragraph 4 calls this conclusion a mistake.
Colonial botany served empire economically and intellectually, yet its records can help recover what it erased.
Correct: paragraphs 2 and 3 show both connections, and paragraph 4 argues the archive is still valuable.
Latin binomials are scientifically inferior to local plant names.
The author criticizes who received credit, not the scientific merit of Latin names.
qs.x: The passage makes three moves: botany served empire economically (paragraph 2), it erased local knowledge intellectually (paragraph 3), and yet the colonial archive can be read against its silences (paragraph 4). A good summary includes all three. The compromised-archive choice is tempting because it echoes critics the author mentions, but paragraph 4 calls their conclusion a mistake.

qs.q: The author mentions cinchona and rubber primarily to:
o: illustrate how imperial gardens served commercial interests
Correct: paragraph 2 uses these transfers to show botany acting as an instrument of trade policy.
demonstrate how indigenous plant names were erased
Erasure of names is the intellectual connection of paragraph 3, not the point of these examples.
show that botanical gardens were places of contemplation
These examples are offered against the contemplative image in paragraph 1.
argue that Europeans first discovered quinine's medical uses
The passage says the seeds were carried out of the Andes; it makes no claim of European discovery.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 opens by calling the connection economic and uses cinchona and rubber transfers to show gardens acting as clearing houses for commercially valuable plants, so that botany was an instrument of trade policy. The erasure of indigenous names is a real theme, but it belongs to paragraph 3's intellectual connection, not to these examples.

qs.q: The quotation marks around "discovered" in paragraph 3 suggest that the author believes:
o: European botanists faked many of their specimens
Nothing in the passage suggests specimens were faked.
the plants were already known to local people before Europeans described them
Correct: paragraph 3 says the plants had nearly always been known, named and used by local people.
most of the plants were found only by accident
The issue is prior local knowledge, not whether finds were accidental.
the plants lacked any real commercial value
Paragraph 2 stresses the plants' commercial value.
qs.x: Scare quotes signal that the author doubts a word's usual meaning. Paragraph 3 immediately explains that the plants had nearly always been known, named and used by local people for generations, so European discovery was really first European publication. Nothing suggests faked specimens; the point is about prior knowledge and who received credit.

qs.q: A historian studying a 19th-century colonial herbarium would best follow the author's advice by:
o: examining marginal local names and mentions of guides to reconstruct indigenous knowledge
Correct: paragraph 4 urges attention to local names in margins and guides mentioned in passing.
setting the herbarium aside as hopelessly compromised
Paragraph 4 rejects treating the archive as hopelessly compromised.
treating the published Latin descriptions as the authoritative record
That would repeat the erasure of local knowledge described in paragraph 3.
returning the specimens to their places of origin without study
The author values studying the archive, not abandoning it unread.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the colonial archive, read carefully with attention to local names in margins and guides mentioned in passing, can testify against its own silences. A historian applying this would mine those traces to recover indigenous expertise. Setting the herbarium aside is the critics' view the author rejects, and treating Latin descriptions as authoritative would repeat the erasure.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that classification was a process of erasure?
o: Some plants transferred between colonies failed to thrive.
Failed transfers concern the economic story of paragraph 2, not erasure of knowledge.
Latin served as a shared language among European scientists.
This explains why binomials were used but does not show local knowledge was credited.
Botanists of the period routinely recorded local names and credited informants in print.
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 3's claim that local names were replaced and most informants went unrecorded.
Local physicians on the Malabar coast used many plants as medicine.
This supports paragraph 3's claim that the plants were already known locally.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's erasure claim rests on local names being replaced by Latin binomials and informants going unrecorded. If botanists routinely recorded local names and credited informants in print, that basis disappears. Latin as a shared scientific language is tempting, but it only explains why binomials were used and says nothing about whether local knowledge was credited.

passages.title: The Uses of Empty Time
text: We are, by most accounts, waging a war against boredom, and winning it. The phone in every pocket ensures that no queue, commute, or pause between tasks need ever be endured unaccompanied. If boredom is merely an unpleasant state, like a headache, this is an unambiguous achievement. But there are reasons to doubt that boredom is merely unpleasant. It may also be useful, and a culture that suppresses it efficiently may be suppressing something it needs.

Consider what boredom actually reports. Unlike fatigue, which signals that our capacities are spent, boredom signals that they are underused: we are awake, able, and willing to attend, but nothing before us seems worth attending to. In this sense boredom is an evaluative emotion. It passes a verdict, however crude, on the meaningfulness of our present situation. The bored student in a lecture hall is registering, rightly or wrongly, a mismatch between her mind and what is being offered to it.

Philosophers have distinguished this situational boredom from a deeper kind. Heidegger described a profound boredom in which not one activity but everything seems indifferent, and he thought this state, unbearable as it is, could disclose something about the shape of a life: that its routines had come to stand in for purposes. Whether or not one accepts his metaphysics, the insight is practical. A person who never allows herself to be bored never receives the message that her pursuits have gone hollow. Distraction does not answer the question boredom asks; it ensures the question is never heard.

None of this is a case for cultivating boredom as a virtue. Chronic boredom is associated with depression, risk-taking, and addiction, and those who suffer it need relief rather than philosophical praise. The point is narrower. Boredom, like pain, is valuable as a signal and harmful as a condition. We do not treat pain by severing the nerves that carry it, and we should be wary of a technology whose chief promise is to make sure that the signal of boredom never arrives at all.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, boredom differs from fatigue in that boredom signals that:
o: our capacities are exhausted rather than idle
This reverses paragraph 2: exhaustion is what fatigue signals.
our capacities are underused rather than used up
Correct: paragraph 2 says fatigue signals spent capacities, while boredom signals underused ones.
we are unwilling to attend to anything at all
Paragraph 2 says the bored person is willing to attend but finds nothing worth it.
our physical needs have gone unmet
Paragraph 2 treats boredom as a verdict on meaning, not a signal of bodily need.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 contrasts the two states directly: fatigue signals that our capacities are spent, while boredom signals that they are underused, since we are awake and willing to attend but find nothing worth attending to. The first choice simply swaps the two definitions, a common reversal trap. Being unwilling to attend is also wrong, because the paragraph stresses that the bored person is willing.

qs.q: The comparison to pain in paragraph 4 serves mainly to:
o: show that a state can be useful as a signal yet harmful as a lasting condition
Correct: paragraph 4 says boredom, like pain, is valuable as a signal and harmful as a condition.
argue that boredom is as physically damaging as pain
The analogy concerns the role of a signal, not equal physical harm.
suggest that chronic boredom needs no treatment
Paragraph 4 says those with chronic boredom need relief.
prove that boredom is a type of physical pain
The author draws an analogy between the two, not an identity.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says boredom, like pain, is valuable as a signal and harmful as a condition, and that we do not treat pain by cutting the nerves that carry it. The analogy is about function: a warning signal worth keeping even though a chronic version is damaging. It does not claim boredom hurts physically or is a kind of pain, and the author says chronic sufferers need relief.

qs.q: With which statement would the author most likely agree?
o: Constant phone use may keep people from noticing that their pursuits lack meaning.
Correct: paragraph 3 says distraction keeps the question boredom asks from ever being heard.
People should cultivate boredom as a personal virtue.
Paragraph 4 opens by denying that this is a case for cultivating boredom as a virtue.
Boredom always gives an accurate verdict on one's situation.
Paragraph 2 calls the verdict crude and says the student registers a mismatch rightly or wrongly.
Heidegger's insight is useful only if one accepts his metaphysics.
Paragraph 3 says the insight is practical whether or not one accepts his metaphysics.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 argues that someone who is never bored never hears the message that her pursuits have gone hollow, because distraction keeps the question from being heard; paragraph 1 names the phone as that distraction. The virtue option is tempting since the author defends boredom, but paragraph 4 explicitly says this is not a case for cultivating boredom as a virtue.

qs.q: Volunteers who sat for 15 minutes without devices later reported reconsidering personal goals more often than volunteers allowed phones. This result would:
o: weaken the claim, since the volunteers' boredom was only situational
Paragraph 2 says situational boredom also passes a verdict on meaning, so the result still fits.
strengthen the claim that boredom can prompt reflection on one's purposes
Correct: it fits paragraph 3's claim that allowing boredom lets its message about hollow pursuits arrive.
weaken the claim by showing that boredom is actually pleasant
The result concerns reflection, not whether boredom felt pleasant.
have no bearing, since the passage concerns only chronic boredom
Paragraphs 1 to 3 concern everyday boredom of the very kind phones relieve.
qs.x: The author claims boredom can deliver a message about whether one's pursuits still have purpose, and that devices block it. Volunteers left device-free who then reconsidered their goals more often is exactly what that predicts. Calling it irrelevant because the passage covers only chronic boredom fails, since paragraphs 1 to 3 discuss the everyday boredom of queues and commutes.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's claim that boredom is an evaluative emotion?
o: Boredom-prone people report higher rates of depression.
Paragraph 4 already notes the link between chronic boredom and depression.
Boredom tracks only sleep loss and is unaffected by how meaningful people rate the task.
Correct: if boredom ignores meaning, it cannot be the verdict on meaningfulness described in paragraph 2.
Students are bored more often in lectures than in seminars.
This fits the idea that boredom registers a mismatch with what is offered.
Phone use reliably reduces self-reported boredom while waiting.
This matches paragraph 1's claim that phones are winning the war against boredom.
qs.x: Calling boredom evaluative means it responds to how meaningful the present situation seems. If boredom tracked only sleep loss and ignored how meaningful a task was rated, it would be a bodily state like fatigue, not a verdict. The depression link is tempting but paragraph 4 already concedes it, and it says nothing about whether boredom registers meaning.

passages.title: The Hand and the Self
text: Whenever a school district drops cursive from its curriculum, defenders of handwriting reach for the same argument: a person's script is an extension of the self, as individual as a face, and a generation that only types will lose a means of self-expression. The argument is moving, but it rests on a historical assumption that does not survive scrutiny. For most of its history, handwriting was valued precisely for not expressing the individual.

Medieval scribes trained for years to reproduce a house style so uniform that the work of different copyists in the same manuscript can be hard to tell apart. The commercial hands of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, from English round hand to American Spencerian script, were taught as professional skills; a clerk's value lay in writing a page that any other clerk could read and that looked like every other clerk's page. Penmanship manuals of the period speak of regularity, speed, and legibility, almost never of personality. Deviation was a fault to be corrected.

The idea that handwriting reveals character gained wide currency only in the later nineteenth century, when graphologists began claiming to read temperament from the slant of a letter or the loop of a descender. Their science proved hollow, but their premise outlived it, merging with a Romantic cult of authenticity that prized the unrepeatable trace of the individual hand. The defenders of cursive are heirs to this relatively recent tradition, not to the scribes they imagine as their ancestors.

This does not settle whether children should learn to write by hand. There may be good reasons to teach it: some studies suggest that forming letters manually helps young children learn to recognize them, and that taking notes by hand encourages summarizing rather than transcription. But these are claims about cognition, and they should be tested as such. Defending handwriting as a sanctuary of the self commits its advocates to a myth, and a myth is a poor foundation for a curriculum.

qs.q: The author's central claim is that:
o: cursive should be removed from school curricula
Paragraph 4 says the question of teaching handwriting is not settled and there may be good reasons for it.
the idea that handwriting expresses individuality is recent and a poor basis for curriculum
Correct: paragraphs 1 and 3 date the idea to the late 1800s, and paragraph 4 calls it a poor foundation.
handwriting has always been prized as an expression of personality
Paragraph 1 says handwriting was long valued for not expressing the individual.
graphology reliably reveals a writer's temperament
Paragraph 3 says graphology's science proved hollow.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the self-expression defense rests on a false history, paragraphs 2 and 3 show handwriting was long valued for uniformity and that the character idea arose with late-nineteenth-century graphology, and paragraph 4 calls it a myth unfit to base a curriculum on. The author does not argue for dropping cursive; paragraph 4 leaves that open and even cites possible cognitive benefits.

qs.q: The reference to penmanship manuals in paragraph 2 mainly supports the claim that:
o: clerks were encouraged to develop distinctive styles
Paragraph 2 says a clerk's page was supposed to look like every other clerk's.
earlier handwriting instruction valued uniformity over individuality
Correct: paragraph 2 says the manuals stress regularity and legibility and treat deviation as a fault.
Spencerian script was harder to read than round hand
The passage does not compare how legible the two scripts were.
medieval scribes wrote faster than later clerks
The manuals concern later commercial hands, and no speed comparison is made.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 builds a case that earlier instruction prized sameness: scribes copied a house style, clerks wrote pages like every other clerk's, and the manuals stress regularity, speed and legibility, treating deviation as a fault. The manuals are cited for what they value, not to compare scripts' legibility, so the Spencerian-versus-round-hand choice invents a comparison.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward graphology is best described as:
o: admiring of its insight into character
Paragraph 3 calls graphology's science hollow.
uncertain whether its methods are valid
The author states flatly that its science proved hollow.
dismissive of its science but aware of its lasting influence
Correct: paragraph 3 says the science proved hollow but its premise outlived it.
indifferent, since it has had no lasting effect
Paragraph 3 says graphology's premise shapes today's defenders of cursive.
qs.x: Attitude questions need both halves of the author's tone. Paragraph 3 says graphology's science proved hollow, a firm dismissal, but also that its premise outlived it and shaped today's defenders of cursive. The indifferent option misses that second half, and the uncertain option misses how flatly the author rejects the science.

qs.q: Which evidence would the author consider the best support for keeping handwriting in schools?
o: Surveys showing parents value their children's distinctive signatures
This appeals to handwriting as self-expression, the myth the author rejects.
Graphologists' reports linking a neat hand to a disciplined personality
Paragraph 3 says graphology's science proved hollow.
A controlled study showing children who form letters by hand recognize them faster
Correct: paragraph 4 says the case for handwriting rests on cognitive claims tested as such.
Essays praising the unrepeatable trace of each person's hand
This echoes the Romantic cult of authenticity criticized in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the good reasons to teach handwriting are claims about cognition and should be tested as such. A controlled study showing that forming letters by hand speeds letter recognition is exactly that kind of evidence. Parental pride in distinctive signatures is tempting but appeals to the self-expression myth the author says is a poor foundation.

qs.q: Which discovery would most undermine the author's claims about medieval scribes?
o: Records showing scribes were praised and paid more for distinctive personal hands
Correct: this contradicts paragraph 2's claim that scribes worked toward uniform, indistinguishable styles.
Manuscripts in which several scribes' hands are nearly identical
This supports paragraph 2's claim about uniform house styles.
Evidence that scribes trained for many years
Paragraph 2 already says scribes trained for years.
Proof that graphology arose in the nineteenth century
This supports paragraph 3 and says nothing against the claim about scribes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 claims medieval scribes trained to reproduce a house style so uniform that different hands are hard to tell apart. Records showing scribes were rewarded for distinctive personal hands would directly contradict that. Nearly identical hands and long training are details the paragraph itself asserts, so they support rather than undermine the claim.

passages.title: The Commons of the Lawn
text: Frederick Law Olmsted, the principal designer of New York's Central Park, believed that a great public park could be a school of democracy. In its meadows, he argued, the banker and the laborer would walk side by side, and the shared enjoyment of scenery would soften the antagonisms of class. It is an attractive vision, and much of the modern case for public space still rests on it.

Historians have been less charitable. The land for Central Park was cleared in part by removing Seneca Village, a community whose residents were largely Black property owners. The park's early regulations forbade many of the activities working people might actually have wanted to pursue there: ball games were restricted, lawns were often closed to walkers, and organized gatherings required permission. Olmsted's democracy, on this reading, was a pedagogy of manners, in which the poor were invited to share the park on condition that they behave like the genteel.

Both accounts treat the park as its designers' creation, whether benevolent or controlling. What they miss is how much of the park's democratic character was won by its users against its design. Over the following decades, immigrant families pressed for picnic grounds, children for playgrounds, and athletic clubs for fields; the restrictions on lawns loosened; and the park eventually became a site of political rallies, concerts, and protests that its founders would hardly have sanctioned. The park did not teach democracy to the public. The public practiced democracy on the park.

This history suggests a test for contemporary public spaces that is different from the one planners usually apply. The question is not whether a plaza or park is beautiful, or even whether everyone is formally permitted to enter. It is whether the space can be claimed: whether its rules can be contested, its uses expanded, and its purposes renegotiated by the people who use it. A park that admits all but permits nothing is a showroom, not a commons.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, historians have criticized Olmsted's vision because the park:
o: displaced residents and imposed genteel rules on working-class visitors
Correct: paragraph 2 cites the removal of Seneca Village and rules that required the poor to act like the genteel.
was too small to serve the city's growing population
Paragraph 2 says nothing about the park's size.
charged admission fees that excluded the poor
No fees are mentioned; the critique concerns rules of behavior and displacement.
ignored scenery in favor of athletic fields
Paragraph 2 says ball games were restricted, the opposite of favoring fields.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 gives the historians' two charges: the park displaced Seneca Village, a largely Black property-owning community, and its early rules restricted the activities of working people so that the poor had to behave like the genteel. Admission fees and size never appear. The athletic-fields option reverses the passage, which says ball games were restricted.

qs.q: The author's position relative to Olmsted and his critics is that both:
o: correctly describe the park as a school of democracy
Only Olmsted held that view, and paragraph 3 rejects it: the park did not teach democracy.
overlook how the park's users created its democratic character
Correct: paragraph 3 says both treat the park as its designers' creation and miss the role of its users.
exaggerate the harm done to Seneca Village
The author does not dispute the historians' account of Seneca Village.
agree that the park's rules were never loosened
Paragraph 3 says the lawn restrictions did loosen over time.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says both Olmsted and his critics treat the park as its designers' creation, benevolent or controlling, and both miss how its democratic character was won by users against the design. The author accepts the historians' facts about Seneca Village, so the exaggeration choice is wrong; the disagreement is over who made the park democratic.

qs.q: The statement "A park that admits all but permits nothing is a showroom, not a commons" implies that:
o: formal open access is not enough to make a space democratic
Correct: paragraph 4 says the test is whether users can contest rules and expand uses, not mere entry.
parks should charge admission to fund their upkeep
The sentence concerns how uses are governed, not how parks are funded.
beauty is the most important quality of public space
Paragraph 4 says beauty is not the relevant question.
public spaces should have no rules at all
The author wants rules that can be contested and renegotiated, not the absence of rules.
qs.x: Paragraph 4's test asks not whether everyone may enter but whether users can contest rules, expand uses and renegotiate purposes. A showroom lets you in to look; a commons lets you shape it. So open admission alone does not make a space democratic. The no-rules option overreads: the author wants rules that can be challenged, not the absence of rules.

qs.q: By the test in paragraph 4, which public space would the author consider most democratic?
o: An elegant plaza that is open to all and bans gatherings
This is the showroom paragraph 4 describes: everyone admitted, nothing permitted.
A park built by a famous designer to promote mixing between classes
Design intentions are what paragraph 3 says both earlier accounts overrate.
A garden whose fixed rules are posted clearly at every entrance
Clear rules that cannot be contested fail the test of being claimable.
A plaza where residents petitioned and won permission for markets and demonstrations
Correct: users contested the rules and expanded the uses, which is exactly paragraph 4's test.
qs.x: By paragraph 4's test, a space is democratic when its users can claim it by contesting rules and expanding uses. Residents who petitioned for and won markets and demonstrations did exactly that. A park designed to mix classes is tempting, but paragraph 3 says that focus on designers' intentions is what both earlier accounts got wrong.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3?
o: Immigrant families used the park heavily on weekends.
Heavy use is consistent with the author's account of users claiming the park.
Central Park hosted many political rallies in the twentieth century.
Paragraph 3 already cites rallies as evidence for the author's view.
Commissioners had planned the playgrounds and looser lawn rules from the start, with no public pressure.
Correct: this would credit the designers, not users, with these changes, undercutting paragraph 3.
Olmsted wrote often about the refining effects of scenery.
This confirms paragraph 1's account of Olmsted's vision and does not challenge paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 credits users, through public pressure, with winning playgrounds, fields and looser lawn rules. If commissioners had planned those changes from the start without any pressure, the credit would shift back to the designers and the argument would fail. Rallies and heavy use by immigrant families fit the author's story, so they cannot weaken it.

passages.title: The Licensed Fool
text: Satire enjoys a peculiar legal and cultural status. Courts in many democracies have held that statements no reasonable reader would take as literal fact cannot be defamatory, and the satirist thereby gains a license denied to the pamphleteer. Satirists themselves often describe their work as truth-telling: the jester, alone at court, could say what the courtiers dared not. The comparison is flattering, but it obscures how satire actually works and what it can and cannot accomplish.

Satire's power derives from the fact that it does not assert. The satirist who proposes that the poor relieve their hunger by selling their children as food has not claimed anything false, because he has not claimed anything at all; he has staged an absurdity and left the audience to infer the accusation. This indirection is what protects him. It is also what limits him. Because the meaning must be supplied by the audience, satire tends to tell people what they already think. Studies of audiences for political comedy have found that viewers frequently read the same sketch as endorsing their own side, whichever side that is.

Satire is therefore a poor instrument of persuasion. It is also vulnerable to absorption: the politician who laughs at his own caricature on a late-night program converts the joke into evidence of his good humor. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that satire is politically idle. Its characteristic effects lie elsewhere. It punctures the solemnity on which authority partly depends, making the powerful look ordinary and therefore answerable. And it builds solidarity among those who already share a grievance, assuring them that they are not alone in seeing the absurdity.

This second function explains why satire matters most where speech is least free. Under regimes that punish open criticism, a joke whispered among friends or a cartoon whose target is never named can circulate where an argument could not. Its ambiguity offers deniability, and the laughter it provokes becomes a small, shared act of recognition. In such conditions satire does not change the minds of rulers. It reminds the ruled that their minds are their own.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, courts in many democracies protect satire because:
o: satirists have historically served as advisers at court
The jester comparison is the satirists' self-description, not the courts' reasoning.
statements no reasonable reader would take as literal fact cannot be defamatory
Correct: paragraph 1 states this legal principle as the source of the satirist's license.
satire has been shown to persuade audiences effectively
Paragraph 3 calls satire a poor instrument of persuasion.
political speech of every kind is immune from defamation claims
Paragraph 1 says the satirist gains a license denied to the pamphleteer.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states the legal principle: courts in many democracies hold that statements no reasonable reader would take as literal fact cannot be defamatory, giving the satirist a license. The jester image is tempting but it is how satirists describe themselves, not the courts' reasoning, and the license is explicitly denied to pamphleteers, so not all political speech is immune.

qs.q: According to the passage, the indirection that protects the satirist also:
o: exposes the satirist to charges of false assertion
Paragraph 2 says the satirist has claimed nothing false, since he asserts nothing.
makes satire too obscure for most audiences to enjoy
The passage says audiences enjoy and interpret satire, often in their own favor.
forces the satirist to state accusations plainly
Indirection means the accusation is left for the audience to infer.
leaves the meaning to the audience, who tend to find their own views confirmed
Correct: paragraph 2 says because the audience supplies the meaning, satire tells people what they already think.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the same indirection that protects the satirist also limits him: because he asserts nothing, the audience must supply the meaning, and audiences tend to read satire as confirming what they already believe, as political comedy studies show. Saying the satirist is exposed to false-assertion charges reverses the point, since asserting nothing is what protects him.

qs.q: The example of the politician who laughs at his own caricature illustrates that satire:
o: can be neutralized when its targets embrace it
Correct: paragraph 3 calls this absorption, turning the joke into evidence of the politician's good humor.
reliably changes the minds of the powerful
Paragraph 4 says satire does not change the minds of rulers.
works best when aimed at unnamed targets
Unnamed targets come up in paragraph 4, in a different context.
succeeds only when it offends its target
The example shows a target who is amused rather than offended, not a rule about offense.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls this absorption: by laughing at his own caricature, the politician turns the joke into evidence of his good humor, defusing its sting. The lesson is that satire can be neutralized when its target embraces it. Unnamed targets are discussed only in paragraph 4's context of repression, and nothing here claims satire must offend to work.

qs.q: The author finds the comparison of satirists to the court jester misleading mainly because:
o: jesters were never allowed to criticize their rulers
The author does not dispute the jester's license; the issue is how satire works.
satire is politically idle and changes nothing
Paragraph 3 says it would be a mistake to call satire politically idle.
satire works by staging absurdities, not by directly stating truths
Correct: paragraph 2 says satire's power comes from not asserting, unlike the truth-telling the jester image implies.
modern satirists face harsher legal penalties than jesters did
Paragraph 1 says satirists enjoy legal protection.
qs.x: The jester image casts satirists as truth-tellers who say plainly what others dare not. Paragraph 2 says satire's power comes from not asserting at all: it stages an absurdity and leaves the audience to infer the accusation. The idle option is tempting because the author doubts satire's persuasive power, but paragraph 3 says calling satire politically idle would be a mistake.

qs.q: Which scenario best exemplifies the function of satire described in paragraph 4?
o: A senator reads a satirical column aloud on television and laughs.
This is absorption, as in paragraph 3, not solidarity under repression.
A newspaper in a free country publishes a signed editorial against a policy.
An open, direct argument is what paragraph 4 contrasts with satire.
A comedian persuades rival voters to switch parties with one sketch.
Paragraph 3 says satire is a poor tool of persuasion.
Citizens of a repressive state pass around an unsigned cartoon mocking an unnamed leader.
Correct: an anonymous, unnamed target gives deniability and builds shared recognition, as paragraph 4 describes.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says satire matters most where speech is unfree: a joke or cartoon with an unnamed target can circulate with deniability, and the shared laughter reminds the ruled that their minds are their own. An unsigned cartoon passed among citizens of a repressive state fits. The senator laughing on television is absorption from paragraph 3, a different effect.

qs.q: A study finds that viewers of satirical segments on a policy changed their positions far more than controls did, across party lines. This finding would:
o: strengthen the claim that satire tells people what they already think
Changed positions across parties are the opposite of confirming prior views.
strengthen the claim that satire matters most under repression
The study says nothing about repressive regimes.
have no bearing on any claim made in the passage
It bears directly on paragraph 3's claim about persuasion.
weaken the claim that satire is a poor instrument of persuasion
Correct: it contradicts paragraphs 2 and 3, which say satire mostly confirms what audiences already think.
qs.x: Paragraphs 2 and 3 argue that because audiences supply satire's meaning, it mostly confirms existing views, making it a poor instrument of persuasion. Viewers changing positions across party lines would directly contradict that. Choosing no bearing misses the link, and the first option gets the direction backward: changed minds are the opposite of confirmed prior views.

passages.title: The Birthday Card Economy
text: In his classic essay on the gift, the anthropologist Marcel Mauss argued that no gift is truly free. To give is to create an obligation: the recipient must accept, and must eventually reciprocate, and the cycle of giving binds people into relationships that a simple exchange of goods for payment never could. Mauss drew his examples from Polynesia, Melanesia, and the Pacific Northwest. He might have found equally good ones in the break room of any modern office.

Consider the envelope that circulates for a colleague's birthday, the tray of pastries left by the coffee machine, the card signed by thirty people who barely know the recipient. These rituals are easy to mock as trivial, but they follow Mauss's rules with striking fidelity. Contributions are nominally voluntary yet socially compulsory; refusing to sign the card is noticed. Reciprocity is expected but deferred and never precisely calculated; the person who brought doughnuts last month does not invoice the person who brings them this month. Indeed, precise accounting would destroy the gesture, converting a gift into a trade.

This is why management efforts to systematize office generosity so often fall flat. When a firm replaces the passed envelope with a company-funded monthly cake, it means to relieve employees of a burden. But a gift from the employer is not received as a gift. It belongs to the world of wages and benefits, where it is measured, compared, and found wanting; employees who would never criticize a colleague's homemade brownies feel free to complain about the catering. The firm has not joined the gift economy so much as abolished it.

None of this implies that office gift economies are benign. Their obligations fall unevenly. Those who organize collections and remember birthdays are disproportionately women and junior staff, and their labor, precisely because it belongs to the realm of gifts, is rarely counted as work. The moral economy of the break room creates real bonds, but it also reproduces the hierarchies it seems to soften. Understanding it as an economy, rather than as mere niceness, is the first step toward asking who pays.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, Mauss argued that gifts:
o: create obligations to accept and eventually reciprocate
Correct: paragraph 1 says to give is to create an obligation to accept and reciprocate.
are freely given and carry no expectation of return
Paragraph 1 says Mauss held that no gift is truly free.
are simply exchanges of goods for payment
Paragraph 1 contrasts gift cycles with simple exchange of goods for payment.
occur only in small-scale, non-industrial societies
The author says modern offices supply equally good examples.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says that for Mauss no gift is truly free: giving creates an obligation for the recipient to accept and eventually reciprocate, and these cycles bind people in ways payment cannot. The tempting option limiting gifts to non-industrial societies confuses where Mauss found his examples with the scope of his theory; the author says offices supply equally good cases.

qs.q: The claim that "precise accounting would destroy the gesture" supports the view that office gift exchange:
o: is wholly voluntary and carries no social pressure
Paragraph 2 says contributions are socially compulsory and refusals are noticed.
works best when reimbursed by management
Paragraph 3 says employer funding abolishes the gift economy.
depends on deferred, uncalculated reciprocity unlike that of trade
Correct: paragraph 2 says reciprocity is deferred and never precisely calculated, or the gift becomes a trade.
is a trivial ritual with no real social effects
The author says these rituals create real bonds and hierarchies.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says office reciprocity is expected but deferred and never precisely calculated, and that exact accounting would turn a gift into a trade. The line therefore marks the boundary between gift exchange and commerce. Calling the exchange wholly voluntary ignores the same paragraph's point that contributions are socially compulsory and refusals get noticed.

qs.q: According to the author, employees complain about company-funded cake but not a colleague's brownies because:
o: homemade food is generally of better quality than catering
The author explains the difference by the type of relationship, not by food quality.
colleagues expect the brownies to be repaid at once
Paragraph 2 says reciprocity among colleagues is deferred, not immediate.
the employer's provision is judged as compensation within the wage relationship
Correct: paragraph 3 says a gift from the employer belongs to wages and benefits, where it is measured and found wanting.
the monthly cake is served too rarely to satisfy staff
Frequency is never mentioned; the issue is gift versus compensation.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says a gift from the employer is not received as a gift: it belongs to wages and benefits, where it is measured, compared and found wanting. Colleagues' brownies belong to the peer gift economy, where such judging feels out of place. The food-quality option is tempting but the author explains the difference by relationship type, not taste.

qs.q: Which act would the author predict is most likely to be received as a true gift?
o: The firm adds a holiday bonus to every employee's paycheck.
Paragraph 3 says employer provisions are received as wages and benefits, not gifts.
A coworker, unprompted, brings soup to a colleague recovering from illness.
Correct: a peer's voluntary act with no tally fits paragraph 2's description of gift exchange.
Human resources requires each team to hold a monthly party.
Mandated, systematized generosity is what paragraph 3 says falls flat.
A colleague leaves pastries with a note listing what each person owes.
Precise accounting turns a gift into a trade, per paragraph 2.
qs.x: Gift exchange in paragraph 2 involves peers, nominal voluntariness and no precise tally. A coworker bringing soup to a recovering colleague unprompted fits all three. A holiday bonus is employer provision, which paragraph 3 says is received as compensation, and a note listing what each person owes adds the exact accounting that turns a gift into a trade.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the argument in paragraph 4?
o: Women log more unpaid hours planning office events, and such tasks are absent from job reviews.
Correct: it supports paragraph 4's claims that this labor falls unevenly and is rarely counted as work.
Most employees say they enjoy office birthday celebrations.
Enjoyment says nothing about who bears the burden of organizing.
Senior managers contribute more money to collections than junior staff do.
This suggests burdens fall on seniors, cutting against paragraph 4.
Firms that fund parties report higher employee satisfaction.
This would cut against paragraph 3 and does not address paragraph 4's claim about unequal labor.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 claims the labor of office gift economies falls disproportionately on women and junior staff and is rarely counted as work. Data showing women log more unpaid hours planning events and that these tasks are absent from job reviews supports both halves. Employees' enjoyment of celebrations is tempting but says nothing about who carries the burden.

qs.q: Replacing the passed envelope with company-funded cake is most analogous to:
o: a friend who returns a borrowed book a month later
Returning a borrowed book repays a loan; no gift is being replaced by payment.
a neighbor who brings a dish to a potluck
Peer giving at a potluck is a gift exchange, not its replacement by payment.
a guest who brings wine to a dinner party
This is a peer gift, not an employer turning gifts into benefits.
a parent who starts paying a child for favors the child used to do freely
Correct: as in paragraph 3, payment moves the act from gift to compensation and changes how it is received.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says that when the employer funds the cake, an act that once lived in the gift economy moves into the world of wages, where it is measured and found wanting. A parent who starts paying for favors a child once did freely shows the same shift from gift to compensation. The potluck and dinner-wine options are just more peer gifts, with no conversion into payment.

passages.title: The Master's Measure
text: Historians of industrial labor have long treated the factory clock as an instrument of domination. Before the mill, the argument runs, work followed the task: the harvest was brought in when it ripened, the cloth finished when the weaver finished it. The mill owner replaced this rhythm with the hour, and the clock above the gate announced that a worker's day no longer belonged to her. There is much truth in this account. Early mill records describe owners who set the clocks forward in the morning and back in the evening, stretching the working day while workers, forbidden to carry their own watches, had no means of proving the theft.

Yet the story of pure imposition leaves out what happened next. Once time had become the unit in which labor was bought, it also became the unit in which labor could be argued over. The campaigns for a ten-hour day, and later an eight-hour one, would have been unintelligible to a workforce that still measured its effort by the task. Workers did not reject clock time; they seized it. A demand for shorter hours presupposes that hours are the right thing to count.

This is why I find the language of 'internalized discipline' only half useful. It is true that factory workers came to feel time as something spent rather than lived, and that this habit followed them home. But internalization cut in both directions. A worker who knew precisely when her shift ought to end could also know precisely when she was being cheated, and the cheap pocket watch, once a forbidden object, became a modest tool of resistance.

None of this redeems the factory clock. A standard that can be contested is still a standard someone else set, and the fact that workers bargained in hours did not give them control over what an hour of work would demand; owners answered shorter days by speeding up the machines. My point is narrower. To describe the clock only as a weapon is to imagine workers as its passive targets, when the record shows them learning, with remarkable speed, to turn the master's measure into a measure of the master.

qs.q: The author mentions that early mill workers were forbidden to carry their own watches mainly to show that:
o: workers preferred to measure their labor by the task
Paragraph 1 ties task-based work to the pre-mill era, not to the watch ban.
owners could alter the working day without workers being able to prove it
Correct: Paragraph 1 says workers 'had no means of proving the theft' when clocks were reset.
pocket watches were too expensive for most workers to own
The passage never cites cost as the reason; Paragraph 1 says watches were forbidden.
owners wanted workers to rely on the bell rather than the clock
No bell is mentioned; Paragraph 1 describes owners manipulating the clock itself.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 pairs the watch ban with owners setting clocks forward and back: without their own watches, workers 'had no means of proving the theft.' The detail illustrates the clock as an instrument of domination. Cost and task-based work are never linked to the ban, so those choices import ideas the passage does not connect to it.

qs.q: The statement that 'a demand for shorter hours presupposes that hours are the right thing to count' primarily serves to:
o: show that workers rejected the factory's system of timekeeping
Paragraph 2 says the opposite: workers 'did not reject clock time; they seized it.'
suggest that the ten-hour movement was organized by mill owners
Nothing in Paragraph 2 credits owners with the campaigns for shorter days.
show that labor's demands accepted clock time as the measure of work
Correct: Paragraph 2 argues the hours campaigns depended on treating time as labor's unit.
argue that task-based work was more humane than clock-based work
Paragraph 2 compares the two only to show hours campaigns needed clock time, not to rank them.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues that the ten- and eight-hour campaigns only make sense if time is already the unit of labor; demanding fewer hours accepts hours as the thing to count. So the sentence shows workers adopted clock time rather than resisting it. The tempting choice that workers rejected timekeeping reverses the author's explicit claim that they 'seized' it.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the idea of 'internalized discipline' is best described as:
o: partial acceptance, since internalized time-awareness also aided resistance
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the idea 'only half useful' because internalization 'cut in both directions.'
complete rejection, since workers never came to feel time as spent
Paragraph 3 grants that workers did come to feel time 'as something spent rather than lived.'
enthusiastic endorsement, since it explains the clock's oppressive power
Paragraph 3 calls the concept only half useful, which is not an endorsement.
indifference, since the author considers the concept irrelevant
The author engages the concept directly in Paragraph 3 and qualifies it.
qs.x: In Paragraph 3 the author grants that workers did internalize clock time but calls the concept 'only half useful' because internalization also let workers detect cheating. That is qualified, partial acceptance. Complete rejection fails because the author concedes workers felt time as 'spent rather than lived'; endorsement fails because the author limits the idea.

qs.q: Which detail in the passage most limits the claim that bargaining over hours gave workers real power?
o: Workers learned to feel time as something spent rather than lived.
Paragraph 3 presents this as a habit of mind, not as a check on workers' bargaining power.
Campaigns sought first a ten-hour and then an eight-hour day.
Paragraph 2 offers these campaigns as evidence for the workers' use of clock time.
Cheap pocket watches became modest tools of resistance.
Paragraph 3 offers this as support for workers' agency, not a limit on it.
Owners responded to shorter days by speeding up the machines.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says hours bargaining gave no control over what an hour of work would demand.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 concedes that bargaining in hours did not give workers control over what an hour demanded, since owners answered shorter days by speeding up machines. That detail directly caps workers' power. The pocket watch and the hours campaigns are offered as evidence of worker agency, so they support the claim rather than limit it.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the workers' use of clock time as the author describes it?
o: Students who dislike standardized tests refuse to take them at all.
This is rejection of the standard, which Paragraph 2 says workers did not do.
Tenants use a rent index set by landlords to dispute their own rent increases.
Correct: like workers in Paragraph 4, they turn a measure imposed on them against those who set it.
A manager adopts a new scheduling system that employees never notice.
This lacks the contest over the measure that Paragraphs 2 and 3 emphasize.
Farmers return to planting by season after a failed experiment with quotas.
This is a retreat to task rhythms, not seizing the imposed measure as in Paragraph 2.
qs.x: The author's thesis is that workers turned 'the master's measure into a measure of the master': they accepted an imposed standard and used it against those who set it. Tenants using a landlord-set index to dispute rent do exactly that. Refusing a test or returning to seasonal planting rejects the imposed measure, which Paragraph 2 says workers did not do.

qs.q: Suppose historians found that most nineteenth-century mill strikes concerned pay per piece of cloth rather than hours. This would most challenge the author's claim that:
o: owners manipulated clocks to lengthen the working day
Strike demands about piece rates say nothing about clock tampering in Paragraph 1.
factory workers carried habits of clock time into their homes
Paragraph 3's claim about home life is not tested by what strikes demanded.
workers made the hour the main terms on which they bargained
Correct: Paragraph 2 says workers 'seized' clock time; output-based demands would undercut that.
a standard that can be contested is still set by someone else
Paragraph 4's point about who sets the standard is unaffected by the content of strikes.
qs.x: Paragraph 2's claim is that workers bargained in hours, making clock time the terms of labor disputes. If most strikes concerned pay per piece of cloth, workers would have bargained by output, the task-based logic the author says they left behind. The other claims, about clock tampering, home habits, or who sets standards, do not depend on what strikes demanded.

passages.title: Legible Hands
text: Every restoration of an old painting rests on an answer, usually unspoken, to a deceptively simple question: what is the painting? For much of the nineteenth century the answer was the image the artist intended, and restorers acted accordingly, repainting lost passages, scrubbing away darkened varnish, and occasionally 'improving' a composition they judged clumsy. The results were often handsome and nearly always irreversible. A restorer confident that he knew what the master meant had no reason to leave a trace of himself.

The reaction against this confidence produced its own orthodoxy. Critics began to celebrate patina, the yellowed varnish and fine cracking that time lays over a canvas, as an integral part of the work. To clean a painting, on this view, was to erase its biography. But the cult of patina is no more modest than the cult of intention; it merely transfers authority from the artist to the centuries, and it can license neglect as easily as the older view licensed overpainting. A varnish so dark that the figures beneath it are illegible does not preserve a history. It conceals one.

I would propose a different answer. A painting is both an image and a document, and restoration ought to respect the second role without abandoning the first. This is the logic behind the Italian practice of tratteggio, in which losses are filled with fine vertical hatching that blends into the surrounding paint at a normal viewing distance but reveals itself on close inspection. The viewer sees a coherent picture; the scholar sees exactly where the original stops.

The principle can be stated simply: an intervention should be legible and, wherever possible, reversible. Legibility admits that the restorer is a later hand, working with later knowledge and later taste. Reversibility admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded. Neither principle tells us how far to clean a particular picture, and honest conservators will continue to disagree about that. What the principles rule out is the pretense that any restoration can be invisible, as though the painting had simply been returned to a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen.

qs.q: According to the passage, tratteggio is valuable because it:
o: restores a painting exactly to the artist's original intention
Paragraph 4 denies any restoration can return a work to its original moment.
preserves the darkened varnish that records a painting's age
Tratteggio fills losses; Paragraph 3 says nothing about keeping varnish.
allows restorers to correct compositional flaws in the original
'Improving' compositions is the nineteenth-century practice Paragraph 1 criticizes.
blends in at viewing distance yet shows its boundaries up close
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the hatching blends at normal distance but reveals itself on close inspection.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 describes tratteggio as hatching that blends into the picture at normal distance but shows itself up close, so viewers get a coherent image and scholars see where the original ends. This serves the author's view that a painting is both image and document. It does not restore original intention, which Paragraph 4 says no restoration can do.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the 'cult of patina' is that it:
o: shifts authority to the passage of time and can excuse neglect
Correct: Paragraph 2 says it 'transfers authority from the artist to the centuries' and can 'license neglect.'
encourages restorers to repaint lost passages of the original
Repainting belongs to the cult of intention in Paragraph 1, not the cult of patina.
relies on chemical methods that damage the canvas
Paragraph 2 raises no technical or chemical objection.
treats the painting as a document rather than an image
The author endorses the document view in Paragraph 3; the objection to patina is different.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says the cult of patina is 'no more modest' than the cult of intention: it simply moves authority from the artist to the centuries and can excuse leaving a painting illegible. Repainting lost passages belongs to the nineteenth-century intention view in Paragraph 1, so attributing it to patina confuses the two orthodoxies the author criticizes.

qs.q: The final phrase, 'a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen,' suggests that:
o: old paintings were rarely displayed when they were first made
Paragraph 4 makes no claim about original display practices.
restorers should consult eyewitness accounts of original works
The point of Paragraph 4 is that no such witnesses exist, not that they should be consulted.
a painting's original appearance is not directly known to anyone today
Correct: Paragraph 4 says claims to restore the original moment are a pretense, since no one has seen it.
modern viewers lack the taste to appreciate old paintings
Paragraph 4 concerns knowledge of appearance, not the quality of modern taste.
qs.x: The closing phrase says the 'original moment' a restorer claims to return to has never been seen by anyone alive, so the painting's first appearance is not directly known. That is why invisible restoration is a pretense. The eyewitness choice misreads the point: the author stresses that no such witnesses exist, not that they should be consulted.

qs.q: The author's call for reversible restoration depends most on which assumption?
o: Original paint is always more valuable than restorers' additions.
Paragraph 4 bases reversibility on future knowledge, not a ranking of paint.
Later conservators may know things that make present choices look wrong.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says reversibility 'admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded.'
Most viewers can tell restored passages from original ones.
Paragraph 3 says tratteggio blends in at normal distance, so viewers often cannot tell.
Patina is the most important record of a painting's history.
Paragraph 2 criticizes the cult of patina, so this is not the author's premise.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 justifies reversibility by saying it 'admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded': later conservators may know better and need to undo present work. The assumption is about the fallibility of current knowledge. The choice that viewers can spot restorations contradicts Paragraph 3, where tratteggio blends in at normal distance.

qs.q: A museum repaints a damaged face so seamlessly that experts cannot find the repair even under magnification, but uses a paint that can be fully removed. The author would most likely:
o: praise the repair because it restores the artist's intended image
Paragraph 1 rejects the confidence that restorers know the intended image.
reject the repair because any filling of losses is improper
Paragraph 3 endorses filling losses through tratteggio, so filling is not itself improper.
accept the repair fully, since it can be undone later
Paragraph 4 requires legibility as well as reversibility; this repair is not legible.
approve its reversibility but object that it is not legible
Correct: Paragraph 4 requires interventions to be legible and reversible; this meets only one test.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 sets two tests: an intervention should be legible and, where possible, reversible. A repair no expert can find even under magnification passes the reversibility test but fails legibility, since it pretends to be invisible. Full acceptance is the tempting trap; it ignores that reversibility alone does not satisfy the author's principle.

qs.q: Which discovery would most strengthen the author's criticism of nineteenth-century restoration?
o: A famous 'improvement' rested on a misreading, but cannot be removed without harm.
Correct: it shows the danger Paragraph 1 notes, confident changes that are irreversible.
Some nineteenth-century restorers kept detailed records of their work.
Good records would soften, not strengthen, the critique of leaving no trace in Paragraph 1.
Darkened varnish slowly damages the paint layer beneath it.
This bears on the patina debate in Paragraph 2, not on nineteenth-century overpainting.
Modern viewers prefer cleaned paintings to uncleaned ones.
Viewer preference does not address the irreversibility the author criticizes in Paragraph 1.
qs.x: The author faults nineteenth-century restorers for confident changes that were 'nearly always irreversible' and left no trace. Finding that a celebrated 'improvement' rested on a misreading and cannot be safely removed shows both flaws causing real harm. Detailed records would soften the critique, and varnish damage concerns the separate patina debate.

passages.title: The Wealth That Walks
text: To the officials of agrarian states, the herders who moved across their margins have usually looked like a problem awaiting solution. Nomads paid taxes irregularly, ignored borders, and could not easily be counted or conscripted. From this administrative vantage point it was natural to describe pastoralism as an earlier stage of human development, a way of life that settled agriculture had outgrown and that the herders themselves would abandon once offered schools, clinics, and permanent houses.

The archaeological record does not support this sequence. In many regions mobile herding emerged after farming, not before it, as communities learned to exploit grasslands too dry or too unpredictable to cultivate. Pastoralism was not a remnant but an innovation, and its central technique was movement itself. Rain in arid rangelands falls patchily; a pasture lush one year may be bare the next. A herd that stays in place depends on the luck of a single location. A herd that moves can follow the grass.

Seen this way, much of what outsiders read as disorder is better understood as insurance. The kin networks that bind distant camps, the customary rights that allow one group to graze another's land in a drought year, and the habit of dividing animals among relatives all spread risk across space. Wealth held in livestock is wealth that can walk away from a failing pasture, and wealth that is loaned is wealth that will be returned when one's own herds are thinned by disease.

The twentieth-century campaigns to settle nomads, undertaken by colonial and independent governments alike, often foundered on precisely this misunderstanding. Herders resettled around a borehole or a ration point concentrated their animals on a single patch of ground, which was overgrazed within a few seasons. Officials then cited the degraded land as evidence of pastoral mismanagement. The lesson is not that every pastoral society is wise or that mobility solves every problem; herders have overgrazed land, too, and fought bitterly over water. It is that a way of life should be judged by the conditions it was built to meet, not by how legible it is to a census taker.

qs.q: According to the passage, the main function of mobility in pastoral societies is to:
o: avoid paying taxes to agrarian states
Paragraph 1 notes irregular taxes as officials' complaint, not as mobility's purpose.
allow herders to trade with settled farmers
Trade is not discussed; Paragraph 2 ties movement to patchy rainfall.
reduce dependence on rainfall at any single location
Correct: Paragraph 2 says a moving herd 'can follow the grass' rather than rely on one place's luck.
keep kin groups from competing over the same pasture
Paragraph 3 says kin networks share pasture rights; it does not say movement prevents competition.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 explains that rain in arid rangelands falls patchily, so a herd that stays put depends on one location's luck while a herd that moves 'can follow the grass.' Mobility spreads ecological risk. Tax avoidance is how officials saw herders in Paragraph 1, not the purpose the author assigns to movement.

qs.q: The author notes that mobile herding often emerged after farming in order to:
o: show that farmers taught herders how to manage animals
Paragraph 2 says nothing about farmers teaching herding techniques.
undercut the view that pastoralism is an earlier stage of development
Correct: Paragraph 2 says the record 'does not support this sequence' described in Paragraph 1.
explain why pastoralists ignored state borders
Border-crossing is an official complaint in Paragraph 1, not explained by this chronology.
suggest that farming is a more advanced way of life
The author argues the reverse of a ranking, calling pastoralism 'an innovation' in Paragraph 2.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 describes the official view of pastoralism as an earlier stage that farming outgrew. Paragraph 2 counters that in many regions herding arose after farming, as an innovation for dry grasslands, so the chronology refutes the stage model. Reading it as proof that farming is more advanced reverses the author's point.

qs.q: The author's remark that officials 'cited the degraded land as evidence of pastoral mismanagement' implies that the officials:
o: blamed herders for damage that the settlement policy itself caused
Correct: Paragraph 4 says overgrazing followed from concentrating herds at resettlement sites.
correctly identified overgrazing as a long-standing pastoral problem
Paragraph 4 links this overgrazing to resettlement, so the officials' reasoning is faulted.
deliberately falsified reports on the condition of the land
The passage suggests a misunderstanding, not deliberate falsification.
recognized that mobility had protected the land in the past
If they recognized this, they would not have blamed pastoral practice, as Paragraph 4 says they did.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says resettled herders crowded animals onto one patch, which was overgrazed within seasons, and officials then blamed pastoral mismanagement. The damage came from the settlement policy, so the officials misattributed its cause. The passage frames this as misunderstanding, not deliberate falsification, so the fabrication choice goes too far.

qs.q: Which practice best fits what the passage calls 'insurance'?
o: A farmer stores a full year's grain in a single locked granary.
Concentrating reserves in one place is the opposite of spreading risk across space in Paragraph 3.
A town builds a permanent wall to keep out raiders.
This is fixed defense, not the shared, spatially spread risk Paragraph 3 describes.
A government counts households to plan tax collection.
This reflects the administrative view in Paragraph 1, not pastoral insurance.
Fishing households share surplus catches, expecting the favor returned.
Correct: like loaned livestock in Paragraph 3, reciprocal sharing spreads risk among households.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls kin networks, shared grazing rights, and loaned animals 'insurance' because they spread risk across space and people, with loans returned when one's herd suffers. Fishing households sharing surplus and expecting the favor back is the same reciprocal pooling. A single granary concentrates risk in one place, the opposite of the passage's idea.

qs.q: The author's concession that 'herders have overgrazed land, too' primarily serves to:
o: concede that officials were right to resettle nomads
Paragraph 4 still says resettlement 'foundered' on a misunderstanding.
avoid romanticizing pastoralism while keeping the main argument
Correct: Paragraph 4 says the lesson is not that every pastoral society is wise, only that it be judged fairly.
show that mobility is the cause of land degradation
Paragraph 4 ties the cited degradation to settlement, not to mobility.
introduce a new argument against pastoral land rights
The concession limits the claim; it does not argue against grazing rights in Paragraph 3.
qs.x: After defending pastoralism, Paragraph 4 admits herders have also overgrazed land and fought over water, then says the lesson is not that every pastoral society is wise. The concession heads off a charge of romanticism while keeping the main claim that ways of life be judged by their conditions. It does not endorse resettlement, which the author says 'foundered.'

passages.title: The Third Thing
text: Modern talk about friendship borrows heavily from the vocabulary of romance. We speak of friends who 'really know' each other, of opening up, of emotional closeness, as though the measure of a friendship were how completely two people disclose themselves. On this picture friends face each other, and the friendship is deepest when nothing is left hidden.

I want to suggest that this picture, however appealing, gets the structure of friendship backward. Most friendships do not begin with two people looking at each other. They begin with two people looking at the same thing: a problem in mathematics, a neighborhood garden, a band no one else has heard of. The friendship forms around this third thing, and the intimacy that follows is less its foundation than its byproduct. Friends learn each other's characters by watching how each responds to what both care about.

Aristotle distinguished friendships of utility, of pleasure, and of virtue, and ranked the last highest because each friend loves the other for who he is rather than for what he provides. The distinction is useful, but it can mislead if we take 'who he is' to mean an inner self detached from any activity. Even Aristotle's virtuous friends spend their time together doing things, deliberating, and arguing about how to live. Their regard for each other is formed in, not apart from, a shared pursuit.

This view has an unsentimental consequence. If friendship lives in a shared object, then friendships may legitimately fade when the object does: when the team disbands, the project ends, or one friend's interests move elsewhere. We tend to treat such fading as a small moral failure, evidence that the bond was never real. I think it is more often the natural completion of something that was entirely real while it lasted. A friendship need not be permanent to have been genuine, any more than a conversation must go on forever to have been worth having.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the passage's main idea?
o: Friendship is structured mainly around a shared interest or activity.
Correct: Paragraph 2 says friendship 'forms around this third thing' that both care about.
Friendship is deepest when friends disclose everything to each other.
This is the modern picture the author says 'gets the structure of friendship backward' in Paragraph 2.
Friendships of utility are superior to friendships of virtue.
Paragraph 3 reports Aristotle ranking virtue highest and the author does not reverse this.
Friendships that fade were never genuine to begin with.
Paragraph 4 rejects this, calling faded friendships 'entirely real while it lasted.'
qs.x: The author argues in Paragraph 2 that friendships form around a 'third thing' both people care about, and that intimacy follows from this shared focus. Paragraphs 3 and 4 extend the idea. The disclosure model is the modern view the author says gets friendship 'backward,' so it is the passage's target rather than its thesis.

qs.q: The author's discussion of Aristotle mainly functions to:
o: refute Aristotle's ranking of the three kinds of friendship
Paragraph 3 calls the distinction 'useful' and does not overturn the ranking.
show that ancient thinkers favored the romantic model
Paragraph 3 says Aristotle's friends spend time doing things together, unlike the romantic model.
argue that friendships of pleasure are really friendships of virtue
Paragraph 3 does not merge the categories.
reinterpret a classic account so that it supports the author's view
Correct: Paragraph 3 reads virtuous friendship as 'formed in, not apart from, a shared pursuit.'
qs.x: Paragraph 3 accepts Aristotle's distinction as 'useful' but warns against reading 'who he is' as a self detached from activity, noting that his virtuous friends deliberate and argue together. The author reinterprets Aristotle to support the shared-pursuit view. The passage never overturns his ranking, so the refutation choice overstates the critique.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author regards intimacy between friends as:
o: an illusion created by the language of romance
The author does not deny intimacy exists; Paragraph 2 says it 'follows.'
the necessary foundation on which friendship is built
Paragraph 2 says intimacy is 'less its foundation than its byproduct.'
a real result of friendship rather than its basis
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls intimacy the byproduct of attention to a shared object.
a danger that tends to end friendships prematurely
Nothing in the passage describes intimacy as a threat to friendship.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says intimacy is 'less its foundation than its byproduct': it really develops as friends watch each other respond to what both care about. So intimacy is genuine but not the basis. Calling it an illusion goes too far, since the author affirms that intimacy follows; calling it the foundation repeats the view the author rejects.

qs.q: The comparison to a conversation in the final sentence suggests that the author believes:
o: friends should spend most of their time in conversation
Paragraph 4 uses conversation as an analogy, not as a recommendation for activity.
the worth of a friendship does not depend on how long it lasts
Correct: Paragraph 4 says a friendship need not be permanent to have been genuine.
friendships end because people run out of things to say
Paragraph 4 ties fading to the end of a shared object, not exhausted topics.
short friendships are more valuable than long ones
The author defends short friendships as genuine, not as superior.
qs.x: The final sentence says a friendship need not be permanent to be genuine, just as a conversation need not last forever to be worthwhile. The analogy separates value from duration. It does not rank short friendships above long ones; the author only defends them as real, so the 'more valuable' choice overreads the comparison.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's account of friendship?
o: People often form friendships through shared hobbies and clubs.
This supports Paragraph 2's claim that friendships form around a third thing.
Some friendships fade after a joint project ends.
Paragraph 4 predicts exactly this, so it does not challenge the view.
Closest friendships usually begin with mutual disclosure between people sharing no activity.
Correct: this reverses Paragraph 2's claim that intimacy follows shared interest rather than founding it.
Aristotle's friends often argued about how to live.
Paragraph 3 cites this as support for the author's view.
qs.x: The author's account holds that friendship forms around a shared object and intimacy follows. Evidence that the closest friendships usually start with mutual disclosure between people who share no activity would reverse that order. Friendships forming through clubs, or fading when projects end, are what the author predicts, so they support rather than challenge the view.

qs.q: A man feels guilty for losing touch with a friend after their chess club closed. The author would most likely tell him that:
o: he should revive the friendship by sharing more personal feelings
This applies the disclosure model the author rejects in Paragraph 2.
the friendship was probably one of mere utility from the start
Nothing suggests utility; Paragraph 4 says such bonds can be 'entirely real while it lasted.'
his guilt shows the friendship was based on virtue
The passage does not link guilt to friendship of virtue.
the fading need not mean the friendship was false
Correct: Paragraph 4 calls such fading 'the natural completion' of something genuine.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 argues that when a shared object ends, a friendship may fade as 'the natural completion' of something real, and that we wrongly treat such fading as a moral failure. The author would reassure the man that the friendship was still genuine. Advising more personal disclosure applies the romantic model the author rejects.

passages.title: Noise in the Nickelodeon
text: Few stories about the cinema are repeated as often as the one about its first audiences fleeing in terror from a filmed train pulling into a station. The anecdote flatters us. It casts early viewers as innocents who could not yet tell an image from a thing, and it casts us, by contrast, as sophisticated spectators who know better.
