Contemporary accounts of the earliest screenings, however, record astonishment far more often than panic, and the astonishment was frequently directed at the machine rather than the picture: people marveled that a projector could do such a thing, not that a train had entered the room.

Early film audiences were not naive; they were noisy. In the nickelodeons of the first decade of the twentieth century, viewers came and went in the middle of programs, ate, shouted at the screen, translated intertitles aloud for neighbors who could not read English, and sang along with the illustrated songs that filled the gaps between reels. A film was one item in a variable evening that might include a lecturer, a pianist, and a vaudeville act. The audience was less a crowd of isolated watchers than a gathering that happened to have a screen.

This sociability was gradually suppressed, and not by accident. Exhibitors who wanted to attract middle-class patrons, and reformers who worried about what immigrant and working-class crowds were doing in the dark, both favored a new etiquette: arrive on time, sit still, stay quiet, attend to the story. The grand picture palaces of the 1910s and 1920s, with their uniformed ushers, were built partly to teach this discipline.

It is in this context that the myth of the terrified spectator becomes interesting. A story about viewers who could not distinguish film from reality suggests that cinema's natural mode is absorption, and that audiences needed only time to grow into it. The history suggests the reverse. Absorbed, silent viewing was not the discovery of cinema's true nature but a learned behavior, promoted by people with reasons to promote it. The rowdy nickelodeon was not a primitive stage of moviegoing. It was another way of doing it.

qs.q: According to the passage, contemporary accounts of the earliest film screenings mostly record:
o: panic as viewers fled from images of trains
Paragraph 1 says accounts record astonishment 'far more often than panic.'
boredom with the short length of early films
Boredom is never mentioned in the passage.
anger at the high price of admission
Ticket prices are not discussed in Paragraph 1.
wonder, often directed at the projector itself
Correct: Paragraph 1 says astonishment was often aimed 'at the machine rather than the picture.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says contemporary accounts record astonishment far more often than panic, and that wonder was often aimed at the projector rather than the image. This undercuts the famous story of fleeing audiences. The panic choice repeats the myth the author sets out to correct.

qs.q: The author suggests that the story of the terrified train audience persists partly because it:
o: flatters present-day viewers as more sophisticated
Correct: Paragraph 1 says 'the anecdote flatters us' by casting modern viewers as knowing better.
is well documented in early newspaper reports
Paragraph 1 says contemporary accounts mostly do not record panic.
was promoted by vaudeville performers
Nothing links vaudeville performers to the anecdote.
accurately reflects how immigrants experienced film
The author disputes the anecdote's accuracy and does not tie it to immigrants.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the anecdote 'flatters us' by casting early viewers as innocents and modern viewers as sophisticated, which helps explain its appeal. The author also says contemporary accounts rarely record panic, so the story does not survive because it is well documented; that choice contradicts the passage.

qs.q: The main point of the third paragraph is that the shift toward quiet viewing:
o: happened naturally as audiences grew used to films
Paragraph 3 says the shift happened 'not by accident,' so it was not merely natural.
was caused mainly by the arrival of synchronized sound
Sound technology is never mentioned in the passage.
was deliberately encouraged by exhibitors and reformers
Correct: Paragraph 3 says both groups 'favored a new etiquette' that palaces were built to teach.
was resisted successfully by working-class audiences
Paragraph 3 says sociability was 'gradually suppressed,' not that resistance succeeded.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says sociability was suppressed 'not by accident': exhibitors seeking middle-class patrons and reformers worried about working-class crowds promoted a new etiquette, and picture palaces with ushers were built to teach it. The natural-adjustment choice is exactly the view Paragraph 4 rejects when it calls silent viewing a learned behavior.

qs.q: Suppose trade journals from the 1910s urged theaters to silence talkers in order to attract 'a better class of patron.' This would:
o: weaken the claim that early audiences were noisy
The journals imply audiences were noisy enough to need silencing, consistent with Paragraph 2.
strengthen the claim that silent viewing was promoted for social reasons
Correct: it matches Paragraph 3's claim that exhibitors seeking middle-class patrons pushed the new etiquette.
strengthen the claim that audiences once fled from trains
The journals concern etiquette, not the panic story in Paragraph 1.
weaken the claim that picture palaces taught discipline
Such advice fits the role Paragraph 3 assigns to picture palaces.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims exhibitors pushed quiet viewing to attract middle-class patrons. Journals urging theaters to silence talkers to win 'a better class of patron' directly confirm that social motive. They do not weaken the claim that audiences were noisy; the need to silence talkers implies audiences were in fact noisy.

qs.q: Which argument most closely parallels the author's reasoning in the final paragraph?
o: Silent reading, long seen as natural, was a norm institutions enforced after group reading aloud.
Correct: like Paragraph 4, it recasts a supposedly natural mode as a learned, promoted behavior.
Early automobiles were unreliable, so drivers preferred horses.
This concerns technical reliability, not a learned norm presented as natural.
Theater audiences have always been quieter than sports crowds.
This asserts a constant difference rather than a historical shift in norms.
Modern viewers prefer longer films than early audiences did.
A change in preference is not the same as a promoted norm disguised as nature.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 argues that absorbed, silent viewing seems natural but was a learned norm promoted by interested groups, with the rowdy nickelodeon an alternative rather than a primitive stage. Silent reading recast as an institutionally enforced norm has the same structure. A constant difference between theater and sports crowds lacks the historical shift the argument depends on.

passages.title: Correctness in Disguise
text: Every standard language has a birthplace, and it is rarely the countryside. Standard French grew from the speech of Paris and the royal court; standard Italian was built largely on the literary Tuscan of a few celebrated writers; the national languages of nineteenth-century Europe were assembled by grammarians, schoolteachers, and ministries who chose one variety among many and declared it the language. Once chosen, the standard was codified in dictionaries and grammars, taught in schools, and used in courts and newspapers, until it came to seem not one dialect among others but the language itself, from which the others were deviations.

There were good reasons for this work. A shared written norm allowed laws to be read the same way across a territory, made mass literacy easier to organize, and let a peasant from one province understand an official from another. It would be glib to treat standardization as nothing more than the imposition of elite taste.

But the benefits arrived together with a hierarchy. When one variety is labeled correct, the others are not merely different; they are wrong, and so are their speakers. A rural child who said things her grandparents had always said learned at school that she spoke badly. Linguists have shown repeatedly that nonstandard varieties are as rule-governed as the standard, often preserving older forms the standard has lost. The judgment of error, in other words, is a social judgment presented as a grammatical one.

The political interest of standardization lies in this disguise. A state that announced it would reward speakers from the capital and penalize speakers from the provinces would provoke resistance. A school that teaches correct grammar provokes very little, because correctness appears to belong to the language rather than to anyone in particular. I do not conclude that standards should be abolished; a shared norm remains a public good. I conclude that it should be taught as what it is, a convention adopted for useful purposes, so that learning it need not require learning contempt for the speech one brought from home.

qs.q: According to the passage, standard languages typically began as:
o: blends of all the regional dialects in a territory
Paragraph 1 says officials 'chose one variety among many,' not a blend.
the speech of a political or cultural center chosen over others
Correct: Paragraph 1 cites Paris and literary Tuscan as varieties elevated to the standard.
the oldest forms of a language preserved in rural areas
Paragraph 3 says rural varieties often preserve older forms, but they were not the standard.
artificial languages invented by grammarians from scratch
Paragraph 1 says grammarians chose and codified an existing variety, not invented one.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says standards came from centers like Paris and the court or the literary Tuscan of famous writers, and that officials 'chose one variety among many.' A standard is a selected existing dialect, not a blend or an invention. The rural-forms choice is tempting because Paragraph 3 says rural speech preserves older forms, but those varieties were the ones ranked as wrong.

qs.q: The second paragraph primarily serves to:
o: argue that standardization was purely a matter of elite taste
Paragraph 2 calls that view 'glib,' so it rejects this reading.
show that nonstandard dialects are rule-governed
That point appears in Paragraph 3, not Paragraph 2.
propose abolishing standard languages
The author rejects abolition in Paragraph 4.
acknowledge real benefits of standardization before criticizing it
Correct: Paragraph 2 lists legal, literacy and communication gains before Paragraph 3 turns to costs.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists real gains of a shared norm, such as uniform reading of laws, easier mass literacy, and communication across provinces, and calls it 'glib' to see standardization as mere elite taste. This concession comes before Paragraph 3's critique of hierarchy. The elite-taste choice reverses the paragraph, which explicitly rejects that reading.

qs.q: According to the author, linguists' research shows that nonstandard varieties:
o: follow grammatical rules as consistently as the standard does
Correct: Paragraph 3 says they are 'as rule-governed as the standard.'
are simplified versions of the standard language
Paragraph 3 says they often preserve older forms the standard has lost, so not simplified.
are disappearing because of mass schooling
The passage never reports on the survival rate of dialects.
are harder for children to learn than the standard
Paragraph 3 makes no claim about relative ease of learning.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 reports that linguists find nonstandard varieties 'as rule-governed as the standard,' often keeping older forms the standard lost. That supports the author's claim that calling them errors is a social judgment. The 'simplified versions' choice is the common misconception the research refutes, since preserving older forms is the opposite of simplification.

qs.q: The 'disguise' referred to in the final paragraph is best understood as:
o: the state's open policy of rewarding speakers from the capital
Paragraph 4 says such an open policy would provoke resistance, so it is not disguised.
the habit of rural speakers hiding their dialect at school
The disguise in Paragraph 4 belongs to the standard, not to speakers' behavior.
a social preference presented as a property of the language itself
Correct: Paragraph 4 says correctness 'appears to belong to the language rather than to anyone.'
the use of dictionaries to conceal how words are pronounced
Paragraph 1 mentions dictionaries only as tools of codification.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says an open policy favoring capital speakers would provoke resistance, while teaching 'correct grammar' provokes little because correctness seems to belong to the language itself. The disguise is a social ranking passed off as a linguistic fact. The open-policy choice is the undisguised alternative the author contrasts with the disguise.

qs.q: Which school policy is most consistent with the author's recommendation?
o: Banning the standard so pupils speak only their home dialects
Paragraph 4 says a shared norm 'remains a public good' and should not be abolished.
Correcting dialect forms in speech as errors to be eliminated
This is the hierarchy Paragraph 3 criticizes.
Teaching each region's dialect as a separate official standard
Paragraph 4 recommends teaching the shared standard as a convention, not multiplying standards.
Teaching the standard as a useful convention while treating home dialects as systematic
Correct: Paragraph 4 urges teaching the standard 'as what it is' without contempt for home speech.
qs.x: The author keeps the standard as a public good but wants it taught as 'a convention adopted for useful purposes,' without teaching contempt for home speech. Teaching the standard while treating dialects as systematic does both. Banning the standard is the tempting overcorrection; Paragraph 4 explicitly says standards should not be abolished.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that judgments of error are social judgments presented as grammatical ones?
o: Rural dialects preserve some forms the standard has lost.
Paragraph 3 cites this as support for the author's claim.
Correctness ratings track only features that impair understanding, not the speaker's class.
Correct: this would make error judgments functional rather than social, against Paragraph 3.
Schools in many countries teach the standard language.
This is consistent with the account of codification in Paragraph 1.
Standard languages helped spread mass literacy.
Paragraph 2 already grants this benefit; it does not address the social nature of judgments.
qs.x: The author claims error judgments rank speakers socially while posing as grammar. If correctness ratings tracked only features that actually impair understanding and ignored class, the judgments would be functional, not social. Evidence that dialects preserve older forms supports the author, and literacy gains are a benefit Paragraph 2 already grants, so neither weakens the claim.

passages.title: Music as Address
text: German music theorists of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries borrowed freely from the classical art of rhetoric. Treatises described a composition as an oration, with an opening that captures attention, a body that develops an argument, and a close that drives the point home. Writers catalogued musical 'figures' on the model of rhetorical ones: a descending chromatic line for grief, a sudden silence for breathlessness or death, a melody that climbs on a word like 'heaven.' The goal of music, like the goal of the orator, was to move the passions of the hearer.

In the twentieth century, some scholars seized on these catalogues as a key to Baroque music. If composers wrote in figures, then a piece could be decoded, figure by figure, the way one parses the tropes of a speech. The approach produced elaborate analyses in which nearly every gesture of a cantata was assigned a name and a meaning. It also produced a problem. The treatises disagree with one another, name figures inconsistently, and were often written after the music they describe. The catalogues look less like a code composers followed than like attempts, after the fact, to find words for what composers did.

The more lasting value of the rhetorical analogy lies elsewhere. Rhetoric is not, at bottom, a list of devices; it is a theory of how speech acts on an audience. To call music rhetorical was to insist that it was addressed to someone, that it aimed at an effect, and that its success could be judged by whether the effect occurred. This is a claim about purpose, not a dictionary.

That claim remains useful precisely because it cuts against a later habit of mind. The nineteenth century taught listeners to regard great music as autonomous, an object to be contemplated for its internal structure, indifferent to whether anyone was moved. Baroque theorists would have found this odd. A sermon that persuaded no one had failed, however elegant its periods, and so had a cantata. We need not adopt their catalogues to recover their conviction that music is a form of address.

qs.q: According to the passage, Baroque theorists held that the goal of music was to:
o: display the composer's mastery of counterpoint
Paragraph 1 names no technical display as music's goal.
preserve the forms of classical oratory
Paragraph 1 says theorists borrowed rhetoric's model, not that music aimed to preserve it.
move the passions of those who heard it
Correct: Paragraph 1 says music's goal, like the orator's, 'was to move the passions of the hearer.'
be contemplated for its internal structure
Paragraph 4 attributes this view to the nineteenth century, not the Baroque.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says Baroque theorists modeled music on oratory and that its goal, like the orator's, 'was to move the passions of the hearer.' Contemplating internal structure is the tempting wrong answer, but Paragraph 4 assigns that autonomous view to the nineteenth century, the very habit the Baroque conviction cuts against.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT cited in the passage as a problem with decoding Baroque music figure by figure?
o: Composers openly rejected the rhetorical theory of music.
Correct: Paragraph 2 never says composers rejected the theory; the other three problems are listed there.
The treatises disagree with one another.
Paragraph 2 lists this as a problem, so it is cited.
The treatises name figures inconsistently.
Paragraph 2 lists inconsistent naming, so it is cited.
Many treatises were written after the music they describe.
Paragraph 2 lists this timing problem, so it is cited.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 names three problems with decoding: treatises disagree, they name figures inconsistently, and many postdate the music. Nowhere does the passage say composers rejected rhetorical theory; Paragraph 1 implies theorists embraced it. For NOT questions, verify each listed option against the text and pick the one never mentioned.

qs.q: The statement 'This is a claim about purpose, not a dictionary' most directly implies that:
o: Baroque composers did not use any recurring musical gestures
Paragraph 1 describes recurring figures; the author doubts only that they formed a fixed code.
the analogy matters for its view of music's aim, not for fixed meanings of gestures
Correct: Paragraph 3 says rhetoric is 'a theory of how speech acts on an audience,' not a list of devices.
modern scholars should write new dictionaries of musical figures
The author questions dictionaries of figures in Paragraph 2 rather than calling for new ones.
Baroque music cannot be understood by modern listeners
Paragraph 4 says we can recover the Baroque conviction, so it is not lost to us.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says rhetoric is not a list of devices but a theory of how speech acts on an audience, so calling music rhetorical claims it is addressed to someone and aims at an effect. The analogy's value lies in purpose, not in a dictionary of gestures. The author does not deny recurring figures existed; Paragraph 1 describes them, only doubting they formed a fixed code.

qs.q: Which view would the Baroque theorists described in the passage most likely reject?
o: A cantata should stir the feelings of its congregation.
This matches the goal Paragraph 1 attributes to the theorists.
A composition can be organized like a persuasive speech.
Paragraph 1 says treatises described compositions as orations.
A failed sermon and a failed cantata fail in similar ways.
Paragraph 4 draws this very comparison on the theorists' behalf.
A symphony's worth lies wholly in its form, whatever listeners feel.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says theorists would find music 'indifferent to whether anyone was moved' odd.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says Baroque theorists would find it odd to treat music as autonomous and 'indifferent to whether anyone was moved,' since a cantata that moved no one had failed like an unpersuasive sermon. A view locating a symphony's worth wholly in form, regardless of listeners, is what they would reject. The other choices restate views the passage attributes to them.

qs.q: Suppose a newly found letter shows one Baroque composer planning a cantata figure by figure from a treatise. This would most likely:
o: refute the claim that rhetoric shaped Baroque music theory
Such a letter would show rhetoric's influence, which Paragraph 1 already affirms.
prove that all Baroque music can be decoded figure by figure
One composer's practice cannot establish a rule for all composers.
modestly weaken the view that catalogues were mostly after-the-fact descriptions
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls catalogues attempts 'after the fact'; one counterexample weakens this somewhat.
support the nineteenth-century view of music as autonomous
Planning figures to move hearers fits Paragraph 1's aims, not the autonomy view in Paragraph 4.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 argues the catalogues look more like after-the-fact descriptions than a code composers followed. A letter showing one composer planning figure by figure from a treatise is a counterexample that weakens this somewhat. It cannot prove all Baroque music is decodable, because a single case does not establish a general rule.

passages.title: The Half-Kept Bargain
text: We tend to speak of patents as rewards that inventors earn, as though an inventor had a natural right to his idea and the state merely recorded it. The history of the institution suggests a more transactional origin. The early patents of Renaissance Venice and Tudor England were grants of privilege, issued by governments eager to attract foreign craftsmen and new industries. A glassmaker who brought a technique into the kingdom might receive the exclusive right to practice it for a term of years. The privilege was a lure, not an acknowledgment of desert.

Such grants were easily abused. English monarchs sold monopolies over salt, playing cards, and other ordinary goods to favored courtiers, and the resulting prices provoked enough anger that Parliament, in 1624, restricted monopolies largely to genuinely new inventions and limited their duration. From this reform emerged the logic that still underwrites patent law: the public grants a temporary exclusive right, and in exchange the inventor discloses how the invention works, so that when the term expires anyone may use it.

This is a bargain, and like any bargain it can be judged by whether both sides receive what they were promised. The inventor's side is easy to verify; exclusivity is enforced in court. The public's side is harder to see. Disclosure is supposed to teach, to put into the common store of knowledge something that might otherwise have stayed a trade secret. A patent that discloses nothing useful has collected its price without delivering its goods.

There is reason to think the public's side of the bargain has weakened. Patent documents are now drafted by specialists whose aim is to claim as much territory as possible while revealing as little as necessary, and many engineers report that they never read patents to learn anything at all, only to avoid infringing them. If that is so, the system is drifting back toward its origins: a grant of privilege justified by the language of reward. Reform need not mean abolition. It might mean simply holding inventors to the half of the bargain that has been allowed to lapse.

qs.q: According to the passage, the early patents of Venice and Tudor England were chiefly:
o: inducements to bring skilled craftsmen and new industries
Correct: Paragraph 1 says they were issued by governments 'eager to attract foreign craftsmen.'
recognitions of an inventor's natural right to an idea
Paragraph 1 says the privilege 'was a lure, not an acknowledgment of desert.'
requirements that inventors publish their methods
Disclosure emerged from the later reform described in Paragraph 2.
taxes imposed on the sale of imported goods
Paragraph 1 describes exclusive rights to practice a technique, not taxes.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says early patents were privileges granted by governments eager to attract foreign craftsmen and industries, 'a lure, not an acknowledgment of desert.' The natural-right choice is the modern view the author opens by questioning. Disclosure requirements came later, from the logic Paragraph 2 traces to the 1624 reform.

qs.q: According to the passage, the 1624 reform by Parliament:
o: abolished all exclusive rights to manufacture goods
Paragraph 2 says it restricted monopolies, not that it abolished all of them.
gave courtiers monopolies over salt and playing cards
Paragraph 2 says monarchs did this before the reform, which was a response to it.
required engineers to read existing patents
Engineers' reading habits are discussed in Paragraph 4 as a modern issue.
largely limited monopolies to new inventions and capped their length
Correct: Paragraph 2 says it restricted monopolies to new inventions and 'limited their duration.'
qs.x: Paragraph 2 says Parliament, angered by monopolies sold over salt and playing cards, restricted monopolies largely to genuinely new inventions and limited their duration. It did not abolish all exclusive rights, which is the tempting overstatement. The courtier monopolies were the abuse the reform answered, not its result.

qs.q: The phrase 'collected its price without delivering its goods' is used to argue that a patent with useless disclosure:
o: should be enforced more strictly in court
Paragraph 3 says enforcement is already the easy side to verify; the issue is disclosure.
fails to give the public its side of the bargain
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the public's side is disclosure that teaches, which such a patent lacks.
is more valuable to the inventor than a trade secret
Paragraph 3 does not compare the value of patents and secrets to inventors.
should last longer to compensate the inventor
Nothing in Paragraph 3 supports lengthening the term.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 frames patents as a bargain: the inventor gets enforced exclusivity, and the public gets disclosure that teaches. A patent whose disclosure is useless has taken its exclusivity, the price, without giving the public its goods. Stricter enforcement misses the point, since the author says the inventor's side is already easy to verify.

qs.q: The claim that the patent system is 'drifting back toward its origins' depends most on the assumption that:
o: modern patents are granted only to foreign craftsmen
Paragraph 4 says nothing about the nationality of modern inventors.
Parliament never intended patents to involve disclosure
Paragraph 2 says disclosure logic emerged from the 1624 reform.
like early privileges, modern patents confer exclusivity with little real return to the public
Correct: Paragraph 4 links weakened disclosure to privilege 'justified by the language of reward.'
engineers infringe patents more often than they once did
Paragraph 4 says engineers read patents to avoid infringing, not that infringement rose.
qs.x: Early patents were privileges justified by attracting industry rather than by any public return. Saying the system is drifting back assumes modern patents, like those privileges, give exclusivity while the public gets little useful disclosure. The foreign-craftsman choice reads 'origins' too literally; the parallel concerns the one-sided bargain, not who receives patents.

qs.q: Which reform would the author most likely support?
o: Voiding patents that are not described clearly enough for a skilled worker to reproduce
Correct: this enforces the disclosure half that Paragraph 4 says 'has been allowed to lapse.'
Abolishing patents in favor of trade secrecy
Paragraph 4 says 'reform need not mean abolition.'
Extending patent terms to reward inventors more fully
The author faults the reward framing in Paragraph 4, not the shortness of terms.
Letting patent specialists draft broader claims
Paragraph 4 criticizes drafting that claims much while revealing little.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says reform could mean holding inventors to the disclosure half of the bargain that has lapsed. Voiding patents too vague for a skilled worker to reproduce enforces exactly that. Abolition is ruled out by 'reform need not mean abolition,' and broader claims or longer terms would worsen the imbalance the author criticizes.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's argument in the final paragraph?
o: Patent lawyers often draft claims as broadly as possible.
Paragraph 4 already asserts this, so it supports rather than weakens the argument.
Courts reliably enforce inventors' exclusive rights.
Paragraph 3 grants this; it does not bear on whether disclosure teaches.
Some monopolies in Tudor England covered ordinary goods.
This concerns history in Paragraph 2, not the modern disclosure claim.
Most engineers regularly consult patents to learn solutions they build on later.
Correct: this contradicts Paragraph 4's report that engineers never read patents to learn.
qs.x: Paragraph 4's argument rests on evidence that disclosure no longer teaches, notably engineers who read patents only to avoid infringing. If most engineers regularly consult patents to learn solutions, the public's side of the bargain is being delivered. Broad drafting by patent lawyers is already part of the author's case, so it strengthens rather than weakens it.

passages.title: The Shadow of Suspension
text: Ancient skepticism is often caricatured as the doctrine that nothing can be known. The Pyrrhonists, whose views survive chiefly in the writings of Sextus Empiricus, would have rejected that description, because it is itself a doctrine, and doctrines were exactly what they declined to hold. Their method was to set arguments against arguments, appearance against appearance, until the two sides balanced. Faced with this equipollence, the skeptic suspended judgment, neither affirming nor denying. Tranquility, Sextus reports, followed upon suspension 'as a shadow follows a body.'

Critics, ancient and modern, have answered with a practical objection. A person who believes nothing, they say, cannot act. If I do not judge that the bread before me is nourishing, why would I eat it rather than the stone beside it? The skeptic, on this view, must either starve or quietly hold the beliefs he claims to suspend.

The Pyrrhonist reply deserves more credit than it usually receives. Sextus distinguishes between assenting to how things appear and assenting to claims about how things really are. The bread appears nourishing; hunger moves me; custom teaches me to eat at midday. I can follow all of this without asserting, as a philosopher might, that bread possesses a nature that truly nourishes. The skeptic lives as others live. What he gives up is not action but the theoretical commitments that ordinary action never required.

Where the Pyrrhonist is more vulnerable is in his promise. The claim that suspension brings tranquility looks suspiciously like a belief about how things really are, namely, about the causes of human peace of mind. Sextus can answer that he reports only what has happened to him, as a patient might describe a remedy that worked. But a remedy offered to others implies some confidence that it will work for them, too. The skeptic's therapy, in other words, seems to rest on just the kind of generalization his method was meant to dissolve. That this tension can be stated so precisely is perhaps a tribute to how carefully the skeptics drew their own boundaries.

qs.q: According to the passage, the Pyrrhonist suspended judgment when:
o: a claim was supported by the senses
Paragraph 1 says suspension followed balance between sides, not sensory support.
opposing arguments seemed equally strong
Correct: Paragraph 1 says skeptics set arguments against arguments 'until the two sides balanced.'
custom forbade taking a position
Custom appears in Paragraph 3 as a guide to action, not a trigger for suspension.
a philosopher proved that nothing can be known
Paragraph 1 says Pyrrhonists rejected that claim as itself a doctrine.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the Pyrrhonists set arguments against arguments until the sides balanced, and that this equipollence led them to suspend judgment. The choice about proving nothing can be known is the caricature the passage rejects: such a claim is itself a doctrine, which skeptics declined to hold.

qs.q: The example of the bread and the stone in the second paragraph is used to:
o: show that skeptics could tell food from non-food by appearance
That is the skeptic's reply in Paragraph 3, not the point of Paragraph 2.
prove that tranquility follows suspension of judgment
Tranquility is discussed in Paragraphs 1 and 4, not in the bread example.
illustrate the objection that a skeptic cannot act without beliefs
Correct: Paragraph 2 uses it to ask why a skeptic without beliefs would eat bread rather than stone.
show that Sextus himself doubted his own method
Paragraph 2 presents critics' objection, not Sextus's doubts.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 presents the critics' practical objection: someone who believes nothing has no reason to eat bread rather than stone, so the skeptic must starve or secretly hold beliefs. The example illustrates that objection. The idea that skeptics act on appearances is Sextus's reply in Paragraph 3, so it is not the example's purpose in Paragraph 2.

qs.q: As the passage describes him, Sextus answers the practical objection by claiming that the skeptic:
o: acts on appearances, impulses and custom without claims about real natures
Correct: Paragraph 3 says the skeptic follows appearance, hunger and custom without asserting bread's true nature.
secretly holds the beliefs he claims to suspend
Paragraph 2 offers this as the critics' charge, which Paragraph 3 rejects.
refrains from action until arguments are settled
Paragraph 3 says the skeptic 'lives as others live,' so he does not refrain from acting.
relies on philosophers to tell him what is nourishing
Paragraph 3 contrasts the skeptic with the philosopher who asserts real natures.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says Sextus separates assent to how things appear from assent to how things really are. The skeptic eats because bread appears nourishing, hunger moves him, and custom guides him, without claiming bread has a nourishing nature. Secretly holding beliefs is the critics' charge in Paragraph 2, which this reply is meant to answer.

qs.q: The author's main criticism of Pyrrhonism is that:
o: it cannot explain how skeptics manage to eat and act
The author defends the skeptic on this point in Paragraph 3.
Sextus misreported his own experience of tranquility
Paragraph 4 does not question the truth of Sextus's report.
its method of balancing arguments is logically invalid
The author never attacks equipollence as invalid.
its promise of tranquility rests on a general claim about how things are
Correct: Paragraph 4 says the therapy 'seems to rest on just the kind of generalization' the method dissolves.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says the promise that suspension brings tranquility looks like a belief about the real causes of peace of mind, and offering it to others implies a generalization the method should dissolve. The practical objection about eating is tempting, but the author defends the skeptic on that point in Paragraph 3 and places the vulnerability elsewhere.

qs.q: Which person's conduct best fits the Pyrrhonist as the author describes him?
o: A scientist who refuses to eat any food whose chemistry she cannot verify
Paragraph 3 says the skeptic acts without requiring theoretical verification.
A thinker who argues that no knowledge is possible
Paragraph 1 calls this a caricature, since it is itself a doctrine.
A traveler who follows local customs but takes no position on whether they are morally true
Correct: like Paragraph 3's skeptic, he acts by custom while suspending claims about how things really are.
A judge who decides cases only when the evidence is unbalanced
Deciding when evidence favors one side affirms a claim, which the skeptic declines to do.
qs.x: Paragraph 3's skeptic lives as others do, following appearances and custom, while withholding claims about how things really are. A traveler who follows local customs without judging their moral truth fits that pattern. The thinker who argues no knowledge is possible matches the caricature from Paragraph 1, since that position is itself a doctrine.

passages.title: Bread and Salt
text: Salt has carried an unusual load of meaning for so humble a substance. In many cultures to share bread and salt with a guest was to bind host and guest to mutual protection; ancient texts speak of covenants 'of salt' meant to be unbreakable; folk custom throws it over the shoulder, sprinkles it on thresholds, and spills it only at one's peril. It is tempting to treat this symbolism as a collection of curiosities, the arbitrary inventions of superstition. I think the meanings are less arbitrary than they look, and that they follow closely from what salt actually does.

Before refrigeration, salt was the chief means of keeping food from rotting. Salted fish, meat, and vegetables could be stored through winter and carried across oceans. A substance that arrests decay is a natural emblem of permanence, and it is not surprising that it should seal agreements meant to last. The hospitality of salt follows a similar logic: to offer it was to offer a share of what kept a household alive through the lean months.

Salt was also universally needed and unevenly available, a combination that made it irresistible to governments. Few commodities could be taxed so reliably, because no one could do without it. The French gabelle, a salt tax levied at sharply different rates across provinces, became one of the most hated institutions of the old regime, and it was abolished in the early years of the Revolution. The popular tale that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is doubtful, but the Latin salarium does appear to derive from the word for salt, a reminder of how closely the substance was tied to value and payment.

This history explains why salt could become, in 1930, the center of one of the century's most effective protests. When Gandhi marched to the sea to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly, he chose an object every Indian used and none could be persuaded to regard as a luxury. A tax on salt fell on the poorest household as surely as on the richest, and an act of defiance involving salt could be repeated by anyone with access to seawater. The march succeeded symbolically because salt already meant what it meant: not a rare treasure, but the shared ground of ordinary life.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the passage's central claim?
o: Salt symbolism is a collection of arbitrary superstitions.
Paragraph 1 names this view as tempting, then rejects it.
Salt was valued mainly because it was rare and luxurious.
Paragraph 4 says salt was 'not a rare treasure' and no one saw it as a luxury.
Salt taxes were the chief cause of the French Revolution.
Paragraph 3 calls the gabelle hated but does not make it the Revolution's chief cause.
Salt's meanings follow largely from its practical and economic role.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the meanings 'follow closely from what salt actually does.'
qs.x: Paragraph 1 rejects the view that salt symbolism is arbitrary superstition and says its meanings 'follow closely from what salt actually does,' a claim the later paragraphs support with preservation, taxation, and the Salt March. The arbitrary-superstition choice is the tempting view the author raises only to dismiss. The gabelle detail is supporting evidence, not the thesis.

qs.q: According to the second paragraph, salt became an emblem of permanence because it:
o: was too costly for most households to waste
Paragraph 2 ties permanence to preservation, not expense.
kept food from decaying for long periods
Correct: Paragraph 2 says 'a substance that arrests decay is a natural emblem of permanence.'
was mined from ancient underground deposits
Mining is never mentioned in the passage.
was required by law in sealing contracts
Paragraph 2 offers no legal requirement; the link is symbolic.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 explains that before refrigeration salt preserved food for winter and long voyages, and that 'a substance that arrests decay is a natural emblem of permanence.' Its symbolic link to lasting covenants comes from this practical function. Cost is not the reason given; Paragraph 4 stresses salt was an everyday necessity, not a luxury.

qs.q: The author mentions the tale of Roman soldiers being paid in salt in order to:
o: doubt the tale while keeping the link between salt and payment
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls the tale 'doubtful' but notes salarium derives from the word for salt.
prove that salt was once used as currency throughout Europe
Paragraph 3 calls the tale doubtful, so it is not offered as proof.
show that Roman taxes on salt resembled the gabelle
No Roman salt tax is described in Paragraph 3.
argue that most claims about salt's history are false
The author doubts one tale while affirming the other claims in Paragraph 3.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 calls the story of soldiers paid in salt 'doubtful' but notes that salarium does seem to come from the word for salt, still showing salt's tie to payment. The author sets aside the weak anecdote while keeping the stronger etymology. Using a doubted tale as proof of salt currency misreads its role.

qs.q: Based on the final paragraph, the author suggests the Salt March was effective chiefly because:
o: salt's universality let everyone share both the grievance and the act of defiance
Correct: Paragraph 4 says the tax hit every household and the protest 'could be repeated by anyone.'
salt was a luxury good that symbolized British wealth
Paragraph 4 says no Indian could be persuaded to regard salt as a luxury.
the British monopoly on salt was new and unfamiliar
Paragraph 4 says nothing about the monopoly being new.
seawater was available only to a few coastal communities
Paragraph 4 stresses that anyone with access to seawater could repeat the act.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 argues the march worked because salt was universal: the tax fell on rich and poor alike, and anyone with seawater could repeat the act. A universal necessity made both the grievance and the protest shared. The luxury choice inverts the passage, which says no Indian could be persuaded to see salt as a luxury.

qs.q: Which case most closely parallels the reasoning the author applies to the gabelle?
o: A tax on yachts that few citizens notice
A luxury tax lacks the necessity that Paragraph 3 says made salt taxes reliable.
A tax on drinking water, which no household can forgo, that breeds wide resentment
Correct: like salt in Paragraph 3, a universal necessity can be taxed reliably but is resented.
A voluntary donation collected for public festivals
Voluntary giving is not a tax on a necessity as described in Paragraph 3.
A tariff on rare spices bought by wealthy merchants
Rare goods bought by few differ from the universal need Paragraph 3 emphasizes.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says salt taxes were reliable because everyone needed salt, and that the gabelle was hated for the same reason. A tax on drinking water, which no household can forgo, has both features: dependable revenue and broad resentment. A yacht tax or spice tariff targets goods few people buy, lacking the universal necessity the reasoning depends on.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's argument about the origin of salt's meanings?
o: Salt was heavily taxed in several ancient empires.
Taxation of a necessity fits Paragraph 3 and supports the argument.
Salted fish was a key food on long sea voyages.
This matches Paragraph 2's account of salt as a preservative.
Salt covenant rituals in a culture predate its use of salt to preserve food.
Correct: Paragraph 2 derives covenant meaning from preservation; earlier rituals would undercut that.
Many people still toss spilled salt over the shoulder.
Persistence of the custom says nothing about its origin as argued in Paragraph 1.
qs.x: The author derives salt's meanings from its uses; Paragraph 2 says covenant symbolism of permanence follows from salt's power to arrest decay. If a culture held salt covenants before it used salt as a preservative, the meaning could not have come from preservation. Salted fish on voyages and salt taxation fit the author's account, so they strengthen it.

passages.title: The Unfair Persuader
text: Defenders of advertising aimed at children usually make two arguments. Advertising, they say, is a form of speech that informs consumers about products, and parents, who control the household budget, stand between the child and any purchase. Both arguments assume a listener who can recognize persuasion as persuasion. Developmental research suggests that this assumption fails for young children: many children under about eight treat commercials as a kind of entertainment or as neutral information, not as messages designed by someone who wants their money.

The case against child-directed advertising is often made on grounds of harm, by linking advertisements to sugary diets or to materialism. Those links are real but contested, and I think they are not the heart of the matter. The deeper wrong lies in an asymmetry. A persuasive message aimed at a person who cannot identify its purpose is closer to manipulation than to argument, because the listener cannot weigh the message against the motive behind it. Even if a child's newfound craving for a cereal led to no harm at all, the exchange would be defective in the way a swindle is defective even when the victim happens to lose nothing.

The parental-gatekeeper defense fares no better. The industry's own term for one of its strategies, “pester power,” reveals the plan: rather than persuading the parent, the advertiser recruits the child as an advocate inside the home. A defense that names parents as the filter cannot easily survive a marketing practice designed to go around them.

I concede that the line is blurry. Older children and teenagers recognize the intent of advertising and yet remain susceptible to it. Recognition, then, is necessary for fair persuasion but not sufficient. For adolescents, the case for restriction must lean on harm-based arguments, which I regard as relevant but less decisive. Yet newer formats complicate even this concession. Sponsored unboxing videos and branded games erase the boundary between content and commercial on which older children depend to recognize a sales pitch. Such formats, I suggest, return older children to the protected class from which their maturity had seemed to remove them.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central thesis?
o: Advertising to children is wrong mainly because it reliably causes unhealthy eating.
Paragraph 2 calls harm links real but contested and says they are not the heart of the matter.
Advertising to young children is wrong chiefly because it targets people who cannot recognize its persuasive intent.
Correct: paragraph 2 locates the deeper wrong in this asymmetry, which makes the message closer to manipulation.
Parents should be held fully responsible for what advertisements their children watch.
Paragraph 3 argues the parental-gatekeeper defense fails, so the author does not place full responsibility on parents.
All advertising directed at people under eighteen should be banned on equal grounds.
Paragraph 4 says the case for adolescents rests on weaker, harm-based grounds, so the grounds are not equal.
qs.x: The thesis sits in paragraph 2: the deeper wrong is an asymmetry, since a child who cannot recognize persuasive intent cannot weigh the message against the motive. The harm-based option is tempting, but the author explicitly calls harm links real but contested and not the heart of the matter.

qs.q: The author mentions the industry term “pester power” primarily in order to:
o: show that children are more persuasive than adults realize.
Paragraph 3 uses the term to expose a strategy, not to praise children's persuasive skill.
argue that advertisers have become more honest about their methods.
The author treats the term as revealing, not as evidence of growing honesty or reform.
suggest that parents are to blame for giving in to their children.
Paragraph 3 faults the advertiser's strategy for routing around parents, not the parents themselves.
undermine the claim that parents serve as an effective filter between child and advertiser.
Correct: paragraph 3 says a defense naming parents as the filter cannot survive a practice designed to bypass them.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 quotes the industry's own phrase to turn it against the industry: a strategy built to recruit children as advocates is designed to bypass parents. That undercuts the gatekeeper defense. Blaming parents is the trap; the author faults the advertiser's plan, not the parents who are routed around.

qs.q: The comparison to a swindle in paragraph 2 serves to illustrate that:
o: a persuasive exchange can be wrong even if it produces no measurable harm.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the exchange would be defective even if the craving led to no harm, as with a harmless swindle.
children who see advertisements typically lose money as a result.
The analogy stresses the victim losing nothing, so it does not claim children lose money.
advertisers knowingly commit crimes that should be prosecuted.
The author draws a moral parallel, not a legal claim about prosecution.
harm-based arguments are the strongest case against advertising.
Paragraph 2 sets harm aside as not the heart of the matter, the opposite of this claim.
qs.x: A swindle is wrong because of how it treats the victim, even if the victim happens to lose nothing. Paragraph 2 uses this to show the author's objection does not depend on harm. Reading it as a claim that children lose money reverses the analogy's point.

qs.q: Which new finding would most weaken the author's argument regarding young children?
o: Children exposed to more food advertising consume slightly more sugar.
This supports a harm argument, which the author already treats as secondary, and does not touch the main premise.
Teenagers who recognize advertising intent still buy advertised products.
Paragraph 4 already concedes that recognition does not end susceptibility in older children.
Most children as young as four can reliably explain that commercials try to make people buy things.
Correct: the argument rests on young children failing to recognize persuasive intent, and this finding removes that premise.
Parents report frequent arguments with children over advertised toys.
This fits the pester-power point in paragraph 3 rather than weakening the argument.
qs.x: To weaken an argument, attack its key premise. Paragraph 1's premise is that young children do not recognize persuasive intent, and the whole manipulation argument rests on it. Evidence about teenagers or sugar intake touches only claims the author already concedes or treats as secondary.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely regard an undisclosed video in which a popular host plays with toys supplied by their maker as:
o: acceptable for older children, since they understand advertising intent.
Paragraph 4 says such formats return older children to the protected class, so they are not exempt.
harmless as long as no purchase follows from viewing it.
Paragraph 2 says an unfair persuasive exchange is defective even without harm or loss.
less troubling than a standard commercial, because it does not ask for a sale.
The author sees blurred formats as worse, because hiding the pitch defeats recognition.
especially objectionable, because it hides the persuasive intent that even older children rely on detecting.
Correct: paragraph 4 says such formats erase the content-commercial boundary older children need.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says hidden formats such as sponsored videos erase the content-commercial boundary that older children use to spot a pitch, putting them back in the protected class. So concealment makes the case worse, not better. The older-children option ignores this; the harmless option ignores paragraph 2's point that harmlessness does not cure unfairness.

qs.q: Which best describes the author's attitude toward harm-based arguments against child-directed advertising?
o: They are irrelevant and should be abandoned by critics of advertising.
Paragraph 4 calls them relevant, so the author does not dismiss them as irrelevant.
They are relevant but less decisive than the argument from unrecognized intent.
Correct: paragraph 2 calls the harm links real but contested, and paragraph 4 calls them relevant but less decisive.
They are conclusive for young children but irrelevant for adolescents.
The author relies on harm arguments mainly for adolescents, the reverse of this description.
They are stronger than the manipulation argument once data are complete.
The author never ranks harm above the asymmetry argument, which paragraph 2 calls the deeper wrong.
qs.x: The author keeps harm arguments in play, calling them relevant (paragraph 4), but ranks them below the unrecognized-intent argument, which paragraph 2 calls the deeper wrong. Calling them irrelevant overstates the author's dismissal; the author leans on them for adolescents.

passages.title: Reading the Swell
text: For much of the twentieth century, many Western scholars explained the settlement of the remote Pacific as a series of accidents: canoes blown off course, drifting until they struck land. The revival of traditional voyaging in the 1970s, when a double-hulled canoe sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti guided by a navigator using no instruments, made the drift theory hard to sustain. But the more interesting question raised by such voyages is not historical. It is about what kind of knowledge the navigator held.

Wayfinding integrates many sources at once: the rising and setting points of stars arranged into a mental compass, the patterns of ocean swells felt through the hull, the flight of birds that fish by day and return to land at dusk, the faint green tint that a lagoon casts on the underside of clouds. In the Carolinian system called etak, the navigator imagines the canoe as fixed while a reference island moves past the stars on the horizon. Outsiders once called this a mental trick. It is better understood as a coordinate system, as legitimate as latitude and longitude, designed for a mind that must keep track of position without writing anything down.

There is a temptation to honor wayfinding by translating it into Western terms, showing that it “really” amounts to dead reckoning. The gesture is well meant, but it concedes that only what maps onto laboratory science counts as knowledge. A better test asks whether a practice yields reliable success in its domain and whether it can be taught, checked, and corrected. Wayfinding meets every part of that test. Its knowledge lives in bodies, memory, and apprenticeship rather than in texts, but that is a difference of medium, not of standing.

The tradition's near disappearance is sometimes cited as proof of its weakness. Under colonial rule and missionary disdain, apprenticeship lapsed, and by the mid-twentieth century only a handful of master navigators remained. Yet this history shows something general rather than something peculiar to oral learning: every body of knowledge depends on institutions that sustain it. Libraries burn too.

qs.q: According to the passage, the voyages of the 1970s were significant historically because they:
o: proved that every Pacific island was settled deliberately.
Paragraph 1 says only that the drift theory became hard to sustain, a weaker claim than proof for every island.
showed that instruments were secretly used by early navigators.
Paragraph 1 stresses that the navigator used no instruments at all.
made the theory of accidental drift settlement difficult to maintain.
Correct: paragraph 1 says the revival made the drift theory hard to sustain.
revealed that Western navigation had borrowed from Pacific methods.
The passage never claims any borrowing by Western navigation.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the instrument-free voyage made the drift theory hard to sustain. The tempting answer claims proof that every island was settled deliberately, which is far stronger than the passage's cautious wording. In CARS, prefer the answer that matches the passage's strength of claim.

qs.q: The author regards efforts to show that wayfinding is “really” dead reckoning as:
o: well intentioned but implicitly accepting a standard of knowledge the author rejects.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls the gesture well meant but says it concedes that only what maps onto science counts.
hostile attempts to diminish Pacific achievements.
Paragraph 3 explicitly calls the gesture well meant, not hostile.
the most persuasive defense of wayfinding available.
The author proposes a better test instead, so this is not the preferred defense.
factually mistaken, because wayfinding shares nothing with dead reckoning.
The author objects to the premise of translation, not to any factual overlap.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 grants the translation is well meant but says it concedes that only what maps onto laboratory science counts as knowledge, a standard the author replaces with a test of reliability and teachability. Calling the effort hostile ignores the explicit words well meant.

qs.q: As described in the passage, a navigator using etak:
o: records star positions in a notebook during the voyage.
Paragraph 2 says the system works without writing anything down.
steers solely by the color of clouds over lagoons.
Cloud color is one of several cues listed, and etak is described separately.
converts observations into latitude and longitude.
The author compares etak to latitude and longitude but does not say it converts into them.
treats the canoe as stationary while a reference island moves relative to the stars.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the navigator imagines the canoe as fixed while the island moves past the stars.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 describes etak as imagining the canoe fixed while a reference island moves past horizon stars, a coordinate system for a mind that writes nothing down. The latitude-longitude option is tempting because the author compares the two, but a comparison of legitimacy is not a conversion.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's interpretation of the near loss of wayfinding?
o: A medical theory abandoned after controlled trials showed it was wrong.
This implies the knowledge failed on its merits, which the author denies happened to wayfinding.
A guild's building techniques that nearly vanished after its apprenticeships were banned.
Correct: paragraph 4 attributes the loss to suppressed institutions of transmission, not to weak knowledge.
A folk remedy that faded because a cheaper drug replaced it.
This is replacement by a better option, not loss through destroyed institutions.
A language that changed gradually as speakers adopted new words.
Gradual change is not the near loss of a body of knowledge.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 blames colonial rule and lapsed apprenticeship, not any failure of the knowledge itself. The best analogy is knowledge lost because its institutions of transmission were suppressed. A theory disproved by trials is the trap: it lost on the merits, the opposite of the author's reading.

qs.q: The final sentence, “Libraries burn too,” functions mainly to:
o: warn that written records are less reliable than oral memory.
The author argues for parity between media, not the superiority of oral memory.
describe a historical event in which navigation texts were lost.
The sentence is a general point, and no such event is described in the passage.
argue that vulnerability to loss is not a distinctive weakness of orally transmitted knowledge.
Correct: paragraph 4 says every body of knowledge depends on sustaining institutions, written ones included.
concede that wayfinding was weaker than written science.
The author rejects the claim that near disappearance proves weakness.
qs.x: The sentence generalizes paragraph 4's point that every body of knowledge depends on sustaining institutions: written knowledge is also fragile. It establishes parity between oral and written media. It does not claim oral memory is superior; that would overshoot the author's argument.

passages.title: The Circle of Learning
text: The word encyclopedia descends from a Greek phrase meaning, roughly, a circle of education. Ancient compilers such as Pliny aimed to gather everything worth knowing about the natural world. Medieval compendia, like Isidore of Seville's Etymologies, went further and arranged their material in a hierarchy meant to mirror the order of creation, with sacred subjects placed before worldly ones.

Alphabetical order, which came to dominate eighteenth-century works such as Chambers's Cyclopaedia and the great French Encyclopédie edited by Diderot and d'Alembert, looks like a neutral convenience. It was a quiet revolution. Under the alphabet, the entry on God sits beside entries on trivial matters, placed there by the accident of spelling rather than by rank. Diderot sharpened a further weapon, the cross-reference. An entry might say nothing objectionable on its face, yet direct the reader to another entry whose juxtaposition invited an irreverent conclusion; the article on cannibals, for instance, pointed readers toward the article on the Eucharist.

The lesson is that an encyclopedia has never been a mere container. Its form makes claims about the shape of knowledge. Alphabetization implies that knowledge consists of discrete units of equal standing; the cross-reference implies that meaning lies in connections the reader must trace for herself.

Online collaborative encyclopedias are often praised as a democratic break with the past. I would say they extend the Encyclopédie's logic rather than abandoning it: the hyperlink is the cross-reference made universal. Something has been lost, however. The Encyclopédie had an editorial voice; it was a polemic as much as a reference. The ideal of a neutral point of view, which governs much collaborative writing, makes the modern form resemble Chambers more than Diderot. Neutrality is itself a choice about what an encyclopedia is for. The real question is never whether a reference work is neutral, but which kind of non-neutrality it has chosen.

qs.q: According to the passage, medieval encyclopedias such as Isidore's arranged their entries:
o: in a hierarchy intended to reflect the order of creation, with sacred subjects first.
Correct: paragraph 1 says medieval compendia mirrored the order of creation and placed sacred subjects first.
alphabetically, as later French works would also do.
Paragraph 2 associates alphabetical order with eighteenth-century works, not medieval ones.
by cross-references that linked unrelated topics.
Paragraph 2 credits Diderot with using cross-references as a weapon.
according to the etymology of each word.
The title Etymologies may tempt this, but paragraph 1 describes a hierarchy, not word origins.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says medieval compendia like Isidore's arranged material in a hierarchy mirroring the order of creation, sacred subjects first. The title Etymologies tempts a word-origin answer, and alphabetization is tempting too, but paragraph 2 dates that to the eighteenth century.

qs.q: The author calls alphabetical order “a quiet revolution” because it:
o: allowed readers to locate entries far more quickly.
Speed is the neutral convenience the author looks past, not the revolutionary effect.
was introduced by revolutionaries seeking to overthrow the monarchy.
The passage makes no claim about who introduced alphabetization or why.
placed sacred and trivial subjects side by side by the arbitrary accident of spelling.
Correct: paragraph 2 says God sits beside trivial entries by spelling rather than rank, dethroning hierarchy.
eliminated the need for any editorial judgment.
The author later argues that every form, including neutrality, reflects a choice.
qs.x: The revolution was quiet because alphabetization looked neutral while silently abolishing rank: God's entry sits beside trivia by the accident of spelling (paragraph 2). Faster lookup is precisely the surface convenience the author says hides the deeper change.

qs.q: In the passage, Diderot's use of cross-references is presented as:
o: a navigational aid with no ideological purpose.
Paragraph 2 calls the cross-reference a weapon, not a neutral aid.
a way of hinting at critical conclusions that individual entries did not openly state.
Correct: paragraph 2 says an inoffensive entry could point to another whose juxtaposition invited irreverence.
a device meant chiefly to save printing space.
Paragraph 2 presents the cross-reference as an ideological weapon, not a space-saving measure.
an attempt to defend religious doctrine against critics.
The cannibals-Eucharist example suggests irreverence, not a defense of doctrine.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 calls the cross-reference a weapon: an innocent entry pointed to another, and the juxtaposition, such as cannibals beside the Eucharist, invited an irreverent conclusion left unstated. The neutral navigational aid reading ignores the word weapon.

qs.q: The author's claim that modern collaborative encyclopedias resemble Chambers more than Diderot rests mainly on their:
o: reliance on hyperlinks to connect entries.
Paragraph 4 says hyperlinks extend Diderot's logic, so they point toward Diderot, not Chambers.
preference for alphabetical rather than topical arrangement.
The comparison in paragraph 4 turns on editorial voice, not on ordering.
large numbers of anonymous contributors.
Collaboration is noted, but the Chambers comparison is tied to the neutrality ideal.
commitment to a neutral point of view, which suppresses a polemical editorial voice.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the neutrality ideal makes the form resemble Chambers, losing Diderot's polemic.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says hyperlinks extend Diderot's logic, but the neutrality ideal removes the polemical editorial voice, making modern works resemble Chambers. The hyperlink option is the trap, since the author ties hyperlinks to Diderot, not to Chambers.

qs.q: Which example would best support the author's claim that an encyclopedia's form makes claims about knowledge?
o: A reference work arranged in a tree of topics whose editors said it reflected the natural ranking of the sciences.
Correct: the arrangement itself asserts a structure of knowledge, as paragraph 3 argues forms do.
An encyclopedia that sold more copies after adding illustrations.
Sales figures say nothing about what the form claims about knowledge.
A dictionary that corrected spelling errors in a later edition.
Error correction concerns accuracy, not the structural claims of form.
An encyclopedia printed in a smaller format to lower its price.
Physical size and price are not claims about the shape of knowledge.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 claims that form itself asserts something about knowledge, as alphabetization implies equal units. A topic tree presented as the natural ranking of the sciences is an arrangement making exactly such a claim. Sales, price and error correction concern the product, not its claims about knowledge.

qs.q: Given the final sentence, how would the author most likely respond to an editor who says her encyclopedia has no point of view?
o: By praising her for achieving the ideal of perfect neutrality.
Paragraph 4 treats neutrality as itself a choice, so the author would not accept the claim at face value.
By urging her to adopt Diderot's political views.
The author asks which non-neutrality is chosen, not that one specific politics be adopted.
By arguing that encyclopedias should be abolished.
Nothing in the passage suggests the author wants to abolish the form.
By asking what assumptions about knowledge her organizing choices already embed.
Correct: the author says the real question is which kind of non-neutrality a work has chosen.
qs.x: The last sentence says the real question is never whether a work is neutral but which kind of non-neutrality it has chosen. So the author would probe the assumptions embedded in her organizing choices. Urging Diderot's politics is tempting but goes beyond the author, who asks for awareness, not a specific stance.

passages.title: Against the Machine for Living
text: When Le Corbusier declared that a house is a machine for living in, he gave modernism a slogan and its critics a target. Jane Jacobs, in her 1961 attack on postwar planning, condemned the replacement of busy streets with towers standing in empty parkland. When the Pruitt-Igoe housing project in St. Louis was demolished in the 1970s, the critic Charles Jencks pronounced it the moment modern architecture died.

The critics often blamed the wrong culprit. Pruitt-Igoe failed for many reasons that had little to do with its flat roofs and long corridors: maintenance budgets were starved, the project was shaped by segregation, and the city's population was shrinking, leaving units empty. To read the collapse of a single project as a verdict on a style is to confuse an aesthetic with the social program that housed it.

Yet the critics grasped something real. Modernism claimed universality: the same rational solution was supposed to suit any site, climate, or people. It ignored the slow accretion of habits through which streets become neighborhoods. Jacobs's deepest insight concerned knowledge rather than style. Planners believed they could design social life from above, whereas the life of a sidewalk emerges from countless small uses that no one plans, the shopkeeper who watches the street, the stoop where neighbors linger.

The postmodern reply, with its ornament, color, and playful quotations of historical styles, answered the aesthetic complaint but not the deeper one. A pastiche tower dropped onto a neighborhood by a distant authority shares the modernist's presumption, however charming its facade. The lasting lesson of modernism's critics is about the humility of the planner, not the decoration of the building.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
o: Modernist buildings failed chiefly because their style was unattractive to residents.
Paragraph 2 says the critics blamed the wrong culprit when they faulted the style.
The most enduring criticism of modernism concerns planners' presumption to design social life from above.
Correct: paragraphs 3 and 4 say the lasting lesson concerns the planner's humility, not decoration.
Postmodern architecture successfully corrected the failures of modernism.
Paragraph 4 says postmodernism answered only the aesthetic complaint.
Pruitt-Igoe proves that public housing cannot succeed.
The author attributes Pruitt-Igoe's failure to specific conditions, not to public housing as such.
qs.x: The author first clears away a false culprit, style (paragraph 2), then names the real lesson: planners cannot design social life from above, so the lasting lesson is humility, not decoration (paragraphs 3 and 4). The postmodern option fails because paragraph 4 says it answered only the aesthetic complaint.

qs.q: The author's discussion of Pruitt-Igoe suggests that its failure:
o: was caused mainly by its flat roofs and long corridors.
Paragraph 2 says the failure had little to do with those design features.
was exaggerated by critics, since the project was largely successful.
The author accepts that it failed and disputes only the cause.
owed much to social and economic conditions, making it weak evidence against modernist form.
Correct: paragraph 2 cites starved budgets, segregation and population loss, and warns against confusing style with program.
confirms Jencks's claim that modern architecture died at that moment.
The author cites Jencks as an example of blaming the wrong culprit.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 lists starved maintenance, segregation and population loss, then warns against confusing an aesthetic with the social program that housed it. So the failure is weak evidence against modernist form. The author accepts that the project failed, ruling out the claim that it was a success.

qs.q: The author's view of postmodern architecture is best described as:
o: it addressed critics' aesthetic objections while repeating modernism's deeper error.
Correct: paragraph 4 says a pastiche tower imposed from above shares the modernist's presumption.
it was a complete rejection of modernism's assumptions.
Paragraph 4 says it kept the presumption that critics found most serious.
it was a frivolous movement with no merit at all.
The author grants that it answered the aesthetic complaint, so it had some merit.
it was more humble than modernism in its approach to planning.
The author says it shares the modernist's presumption, not that it was more humble.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says ornament answered the aesthetic complaint, but a pastiche tower imposed by a distant authority repeats the modernist presumption. That is partial credit, not total rejection or total dismissal. The trap is assuming that a stylistic reversal also reversed the underlying assumptions.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's account of Pruitt-Igoe?
o: Residents of Pruitt-Igoe reported complaints about broken elevators.
Broken elevators fit the starved maintenance budgets the author already cites.
Other American cities also lost population in the same decades.
This is consistent with the author's emphasis on social and economic conditions.
Jane Jacobs never wrote specifically about Pruitt-Igoe.
Whether Jacobs discussed it does not bear on what caused the failure.
Nearly identical towers failed in the same way in well-funded, integrated cities with growing populations.
Correct: if the same form failed without those conditions, the form itself becomes a likelier cause.
qs.x: The author's account attributes failure to conditions, not form. The strongest challenge holds those conditions absent and still finds failure: identical towers failing in well-funded, integrated, growing cities would point back to design. Broken elevators and shrinking cities fit the author's account rather than challenge it.

qs.q: Which urban plan would the author most likely favor?
o: A complete district designed in detail by an expert team and built at once.
Paragraph 3 criticizes the belief that planners can design social life from above.
A tower complex decorated with historical ornament to please residents.
Paragraph 4 says ornament does not cure the presumption of top-down design.
A framework of minimal rules that lets residents adapt ground-floor uses over time.
Correct: paragraph 3 says sidewalk life emerges from countless small unplanned uses.
A plan that replaces narrow streets with open parkland between towers.
This is the very approach paragraph 1 says Jacobs condemned.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 praises the unplanned accumulation of small uses, the shopkeeper and the stoop, over top-down design. A light framework letting residents adapt uses over time fits that humility. A detailed expert master plan is the trap: however well made, it repeats the presumption the author criticizes.

passages.title: The Poet Among the Stones
text: An Old English poet, standing among the broken Roman walls of what was probably Bath, marveled at the stonework, calling it the work of giants and lamenting the fate that had shattered it. Centuries later, Renaissance poets visiting Rome drew from its fallen arches a familiar moral: worldly glory passes, and even the mightiest city is subject to time.

Shelley's “Ozymandias” seems at first to repeat that moral. A colossal statue lies broken in the desert, its pedestal still boasting, “Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!” to an audience of empty sand. But the poem is less a sermon on vanity than a meditation on what survives. What endures is not the king's power but the sculptor's skill, the hand that mocked the tyrant's passions by recording them. And the scene reaches us thrice removed, from statue to traveller to speaker to reader, so that the stone is known to us only through layers of telling. Representation, not power, has the last word.

I would argue that poets rarely visit ruins to learn about the past. The ruin is a mirror in which the present rehearses its own ending. This is a claim about when cultures write, not about how a lone visitor feels among the stones. Ruins crowd into poetry at moments when a culture fears its own decline: Renaissance writers who saw their states rise and fall, and English poets of the imperial age who could not look at Rome without thinking of London.

Hence the genre's central paradox. Ruin poetry monumentalizes transience; the poem becomes a structure that hopes to outlast the very stones it describes. Some readers call this hypocrisy, a boast about permanence disguised as humility. I think it is the genre's honest wager, that words endure where marble does not, a wager that poets make knowing that they, too, may lose it.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim about ruin poetry?
o: It is primarily a source of accurate information about ancient builders.
Paragraph 3 says poets rarely visit ruins to learn about the past.
It always teaches that worldly glory is vain.
Paragraph 2 says Ozymandias is less a sermon on vanity than it first appears.
It reveals that poets value marble above language.
Paragraph 4 says poets wager that words endure where marble does not.
It uses ruins mainly to reflect on the poet's own era and its fears about lasting.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls the ruin a mirror in which the present rehearses its own ending.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 gives the author's thesis: poets rarely visit ruins to learn about the past; the ruin is a mirror for the present's fears about its own ending, which is why the genre clusters in anxious times. The vanity-of-glory option describes the older moral that paragraph 2 says Ozymandias goes beyond.

qs.q: The author's observation that the scene in “Ozymandias” reaches us “thrice removed” primarily supports which claim?
o: Shelley never saw the statue himself and so wrote inaccurately.
The author makes no claim about Shelley's accuracy or travels.
The poem's real survivor is representation rather than power.
Correct: paragraph 2 says the stone is known only through layers of telling, so representation has the last word.
The traveller in the poem is an unreliable narrator.
Nothing in paragraph 2 questions the traveller's reliability.
Old English poetry used the same framing technique.
The passage draws no such link to the Old English poem's technique.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes the scene reaches us through a chain from statue to traveller to speaker to reader, so the stone is known only through layers of telling. That supports the closing line that representation, not power, has the last word. Nothing questions Shelley's accuracy or the traveller's honesty.

qs.q: According to the author, ruins appear most often in poetry when:
