o: a culture is anxious about its own decline.
Correct: paragraph 3 says ruins crowd into poetry when a culture fears its own decline.
new archaeological discoveries are made.
The author ties ruin poetry to cultural anxiety, not archaeology.
poets travel abroad for the first time.
Travel appears in examples, but paragraph 3 names fear of decline as the cause.
religious authorities discourage secular verse.
The passage says nothing about religious authorities shaping the genre.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says ruins crowd into poetry when a culture fears its own decline, citing Renaissance writers and imperial-age English poets. Travel is tempting because the examples involve visits, but the author names cultural anxiety, not travel, as the trigger.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the charge that ruin poetry is hypocritical?
o: By admitting the charge and calling the genre a failure.
Paragraph 4 rejects the hypocrisy reading rather than admitting it.
By denying that poets hope their poems will last.
The author affirms that the poem hopes to outlast the stones.
By calling it a deliberate wager that language outlasts stone, made with awareness it could fail.
Correct: paragraph 4 calls it an honest wager that poets make knowing they may lose it.
By arguing that marble is in fact more durable than language.
The author describes the poets' wager as words enduring where marble does not.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 reports the hypocrisy charge but reframes the paradox as an honest wager that words endure where marble does not, made knowing the poets may lose. The author neither concedes failure nor denies that poems hope to last; the hope is affirmed and called honest.

qs.q: Which modern work most resembles what the author says poets do with ruins?
o: A documentary that carefully reconstructs daily life in an ancient city.
This aims to learn about the past, which the author says poets rarely do.
A film showing a flooded future city to dramatize present fears about climate.
Correct: like the ruin in paragraph 3, the imagined ruin mirrors the present's fear of its own ending.
A museum label listing the dates and materials of a temple.
Factual description of the past is not the mirroring the author describes.
A travel guide recommending the best time to visit ancient sites.
Practical tourism advice has nothing to do with the present rehearsing its end.
qs.x: The author says poets use ruins to stage the present's fear of its own end, not to learn history. A film imagining a drowned future city to dramatize present climate fears does exactly this. The documentary reconstruction is the trap: it seeks knowledge of the past, which paragraph 3 says poets rarely seek.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's historical claim in paragraph 3?
o: Ruin poems clustered in periods of confident expansion, when writers widely expected their nations to flourish.
Correct: paragraph 3 ties ruin poetry to fear of decline, so a link to confident eras would undercut it.
Some ruin poems describe buildings that the poet never visited.
Whether poets visited the ruins is irrelevant to the link with cultural anxiety.
Renaissance poets wrote about Rome more than about Greece.
Which ruins were favored does not test the claim about fear of decline.
Imperial-age English poets also wrote many poems about nature.
Writing on other subjects does not bear on when ruin poems appear.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 makes a historical claim: ruin poems cluster when cultures fear decline. Finding that they cluster in confident, expansive eras would directly contradict that correlation. The other options concern which ruins or subjects poets chose, which leaves the link to cultural anxiety untouched.

passages.title: The Jurisdiction of Experts
text: Mid-century sociology offered a flattering portrait of the professions. Medicine, law, and engineering existed, on this functionalist view, because complex knowledge required trustworthy specialists, and society rewarded those specialists with autonomy and prestige in exchange for their ethic of service. The professional was a kind of secular guardian.

In the 1970s, critics recast this story. Professionalization, they argued, was a project pursued by occupational groups seeking market control and social status. By monopolizing credentials and persuading the state to license them, a profession restricts the supply of practitioners and raises its own price. The critique was a valuable corrective to complacency, but it overcorrects. If expertise were nothing more than a cartel, it would be hard to explain why so many people, given a free choice among healers, still seek out licensed physicians for serious illness.

A more useful account treats professions as rivals competing for jurisdiction, that is, for the right to control a set of tasks. Boundaries between occupations are never fixed. Psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, and clergy have all claimed authority over personal troubles, and the line between them has moved repeatedly. On this view, expertise is partly real, since a profession's abstract knowledge lets it redefine problems and invent new treatments, and partly a claim that must be won before the public, the courts, and the workplace.

The familiar question, whether expertise is genuine knowledge or a disguised grab for power, therefore presents a false choice. Expertise is real knowledge whose authority must be socially secured. This has a sobering implication for the present. Widespread distrust of experts is not simply a symptom of public ignorance; it is a jurisdictional contest. Experts who defend their standing by pointing to credentials alone, rather than by demonstrating what their knowledge can accomplish, should expect to lose ground.

qs.q: Which statement best reflects the author's own view of expertise?
o: Expertise is purely a strategy for controlling markets.
Paragraph 2 says this critique overcorrects, so it is not the author's view.
Expertise deserves autonomy as a reward for an ethic of service.
This is the functionalist portrait of paragraph 1, which the author does not adopt.
Expertise involves genuine knowledge whose authority must still be socially won.
Correct: paragraph 4 says expertise is real knowledge whose authority must be socially secured.
Expertise is an illusion created by public ignorance.
Paragraph 4 says distrust is not simply ignorance and that expertise is real.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 states the author's view: the choice between genuine knowledge and power grab is false, because expertise is real knowledge whose authority must be socially secured. The pure-market-control option is the 1970s critique that paragraph 2 says overcorrects.

qs.q: The author's point about people freely choosing licensed physicians is meant to:
o: show that licensing laws are too strict.
The example concerns why people choose physicians, not whether licensing is too strict.
prove that the functionalist view was entirely correct.
The author also rejects the functionalist portrait in favor of a jurisdictional account.
suggest that alternative healers are more effective than physicians.
The example implies the opposite preference and makes no claim about effectiveness.
challenge the view that professional authority is nothing but market control.
Correct: paragraph 2 says pure cartel theory cannot explain why people choose physicians when free to choose.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 asks why, if expertise were only a cartel, people free to choose any healer still pick licensed physicians for serious illness. The example tests the pure-cartel view against behavior. It does not vindicate functionalism, which the author also moves past in paragraph 3.

qs.q: In the jurisdictional account described in paragraph 3, professions primarily:
o: share authority cooperatively according to fixed rules.
Paragraph 3 says boundaries are never fixed and describes rivalry, not cooperation.
compete with one another for control over sets of tasks.
Correct: paragraph 3 defines jurisdiction as the right to control a set of tasks, contested among rivals.
rely solely on state licensing to define their boundaries.
The account names the public, courts and workplace as arenas, not licensing alone.
abandon abstract knowledge in favor of practical skill.
Paragraph 3 says abstract knowledge lets a profession redefine problems.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 defines jurisdiction as the right to control a set of tasks and says boundaries are never fixed, with psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and clergy all competing. Licensing alone is tempting, but the author names the public, courts and workplace as arenas.

qs.q: Nurse practitioners winning authority to prescribe medication in some states, over physicians' objections, best illustrates:
o: a shift in jurisdictional boundaries between competing occupations.
Correct: paragraph 3 describes tasks moving between rival occupations as boundaries shift.
the functionalist claim that autonomy rewards service.
The case involves contest between occupations, not a reward granted for service.
proof that physicians' expertise is not real.
The author holds expertise to be real even when its authority is contested.
the public's ignorance about medical knowledge.
The author rejects reading such contests as mere ignorance.
qs.x: In the jurisdictional account, tasks move between rival occupations through contests before the public, courts and workplace. Nurse practitioners gaining prescribing authority over physician objections is exactly such a boundary shift. It does not show physicians' expertise is unreal, since the author says expertise is real but contested.

qs.q: The author would most likely advise a scientific body facing public skepticism to:
o: emphasize the advanced degrees held by its members.
Paragraph 4 warns that relying on credentials alone will cost experts ground.
dismiss skeptics as uninformed and avoid engaging them.
The author says distrust is not simply ignorance but a contest to be won.
seek laws that forbid others from discussing its subject.
This leans on monopoly rather than demonstrated results, which the author warns against.
demonstrate the practical results its methods can achieve.
Correct: paragraph 4 says experts should show what their knowledge can accomplish.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 warns that experts who defend their standing by credentials alone, rather than demonstrating what their knowledge accomplishes, will lose ground. So the advice is to show results. Emphasizing degrees is the trap: it is the credential-only strategy the author predicts will fail.

passages.title: Founders and Fables
text: Every state tells a story about its birth. Rome had its twins suckled by a wolf and, under Augustus, Virgil's epic of Aeneas carrying his gods from burning Troy. Japan's early chronicles, compiled in the eighth century, traced the imperial line to the sun goddess. A familiar rationalist assumption holds that such myths belong to the childhood of political life and fade as states become bureaucratic and literate.

The assumption mistakes a change of content for a disappearance. Revolutionary France, having dethroned both king and church, staged a festival to a Supreme Being. Nineteenth-century schools taught national histories in which peoples awakened to their destinies, and modern republics still speak of their founders with reverence. By myth I do not mean a false story. I mean a narrative that presents a contingent political order as necessary, natural, or destined.

States need such narratives because coercion is costly and legitimacy is cheap. A story in which citizens are the heirs of a shared origin converts obedience into loyalty. But myths do not serve rulers alone; they also bind them. Augustus presented himself as the restorer of the Republic, and that story limited what he could openly do. A myth of founding by the people can be turned against any government that betrays it.

It follows that debunking a founding myth is not enough. Stripping a polity of its story without offering another leaves a vacuum, and vacuums in political imagination are seldom left empty; they tend to be filled by cruder and more exclusive tales. The task of the critic is to contest which story a people tells about itself, not to imagine a people that tells none.

qs.q: As the author uses the term, a “myth” is:
o: a narrative presenting a contingent political order as necessary or destined.
Correct: paragraph 2 defines myth this way and explicitly denies it means a false story.
any story about the past that has been shown to be false.
Paragraph 2 says, by myth I do not mean a false story.
a religious account of the origins of the world.
Religious content appears in examples, but the definition is political, not cosmological.
a tale told only in states that lack bureaucracies.
The author rejects the view that myth fades with bureaucracy.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 defines myth as a narrative presenting a contingent political order as necessary, natural or destined, and explicitly says it does not mean a false story. The everyday sense of myth as falsehood is the trap; CARS often tests an author's stipulated definition over common usage.

qs.q: The author uses the example of Augustus primarily to show that:
o: Roman emperors relied on force more than legitimacy.
Paragraph 3 uses Augustus to show myth's constraints, not reliance on force.
founding stories can limit the very rulers who promote them.
Correct: paragraph 3 says Augustus's restorer story limited what he could openly do.
Virgil's epic was written to criticize the emperor.
The passage says nothing about Virgil criticizing Augustus.
the Roman Republic was successfully restored.
The author describes a self-presentation, not a factual restoration.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says myths bind rulers too: Augustus styled himself restorer of the Republic, and that story limited what he could openly do. The point is constraint on the promoter. Reading it as proof that the Republic was restored confuses a self-presentation with a historical fact.

qs.q: According to the passage, states rely on founding narratives partly because:
o: literate citizens demand entertaining stories.
Paragraph 3 explains the need in terms of cost and loyalty, not entertainment.
myths are required by law in most modern republics.
No legal requirement is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
securing loyalty through a shared story costs less than ruling by force.
Correct: paragraph 3 says coercion is costly and legitimacy is cheap.
religious authorities insist on them.
Paragraph 3 grounds the need in the cost of coercion; religious pressure is never given as the reason.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 says coercion is costly and legitimacy cheap, and a shared-origin story converts obedience into loyalty. So myth economizes on force. Religion is tempting given the examples, but the author's own definition of myth is political, and Revolutionary France made myth after dethroning the church.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the rationalist assumption described in paragraph 1 is that it:
o: is correct for ancient states but not for medieval ones.
The author rejects it for modern states, not by distinguishing ancient from medieval.
is basically sound but overstated.
The author says it mistakes a change of content for a disappearance, a basic error.
is supported by the example of Revolutionary France.
Paragraph 2 uses France as a counterexample to the assumption.
mistakes a change in myth's content for its disappearance.
Correct: paragraph 2 opens by saying exactly this.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 opens by saying the rationalist assumption mistakes a change of content for a disappearance, then gives modern counterexamples. That is a basic error, not mere overstatement. Revolutionary France is offered against the assumption, so it cannot support it.

qs.q: Which policy would the author most likely support?
o: Removing all national history from schools to avoid indoctrination.
Paragraph 4 warns that leaving a vacuum invites cruder myths.
Teaching a revised national story that includes previously excluded groups.
Correct: the author says the critic's task is to contest which story is told, not to tell none.
Preserving the oldest founding myth unchanged regardless of its content.
The author urges contesting stories, not freezing the oldest one.
Replacing civic education with instruction in debunking techniques.
Paragraph 4 says debunking alone is not enough.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says debunking without a replacement leaves a vacuum that cruder tales fill, and the critic's task is to contest which story is told. A revised, more inclusive national story does that. Removing national history entirely is the trap: it creates the very vacuum the author warns against.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument in paragraph 4?
o: Several states revised their founding stories during the twentieth century.
Revision is consistent with the author's call to contest which story is told.
Founding myths are often taught in primary schools.
This fits the author's account of myth's role and does not weaken it.
States that deliberately abandoned founding narratives kept a stable civic life without new myths arising.
Correct: paragraph 4 predicts a vacuum filled by cruder tales, which this finding contradicts.
Some citizens can name few details of their nation's founding.
Weak recall of details does not test whether removing myths creates a vacuum.
qs.x: Paragraph 4's claim is predictive: abandoning a founding story produces a vacuum soon filled by cruder, more exclusive tales. States that dropped their narratives yet kept a stable civic life with no new myths would directly falsify that prediction. Revising stories is consistent with the author's advice.

passages.title: Yours Faithfully
text: For most of its history the letter was not a private document. Medieval manuals of letter writing taught a fixed sequence: a salutation, a passage designed to win the reader's goodwill, a narration of the facts, a petition, and a conclusion. Letters were read aloud, copied, and passed along. Cicero's correspondence was gathered and published, and the apostle Paul addressed his epistles to whole communities.

The eighteenth century, with its expanding postal systems, prized a new ideal, the familiar letter, in which a person was supposed to pour out a sincere and private self. Novels told entirely in letters became a sensation. Yet the spontaneous style was itself learned. Samuel Richardson, whose epistolary novels made readers weep, conceived his first one while preparing a book of model letters for ordinary people to copy.

The history of the letter, then, is not a journey from artifice to authenticity. It is a passage from one set of conventions to another. Sincerity on paper has always been a performance, which is not to say that it was false. A convention is a shared form that makes a certain kind of feeling legible to others.

This is why the common lament that email and text messages have killed the art of the letter misreads what has changed. Those who mourn usually imagine a lost authenticity, but letters were never free of convention, and messages have conventions of their own. The decisive change is delay. Because a letter took days to arrive, its writer had to compose a self that would still be true when the page was opened; one wrote for the reader's future. Instant messages are written for the moment. What we have lost is not sincerity but a particular discipline of considered self-presentation, and that loss is real.

qs.q: According to the passage, letters before the eighteenth century were often:
o: intended to be read by audiences beyond the named recipient.
Correct: paragraph 1 says letters were read aloud, copied, passed along and sent to communities.
written without any fixed structure.
Paragraph 1 describes manuals that taught a fixed sequence of parts.
kept secret from everyone but the recipient.
Paragraph 1 opens by saying the letter was not a private document.
valued mainly as expressions of a sincere private self.
Paragraph 2 says that ideal arose in the eighteenth century.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says the letter was not a private document: letters were read aloud, copied, passed along, published (Cicero) and addressed to communities (Paul). The sincere-private-self option is the eighteenth-century ideal described in paragraph 2, so it is the wrong period.

qs.q: In the medieval structure described in paragraph 1, the section following the salutation was meant to:
o: state the writer's request directly.
The petition comes later in the sequence described in paragraph 1.
win the reader's favor.
Correct: paragraph 1 lists a passage designed to win the reader's goodwill right after the salutation.
narrate the relevant facts.
Narration is the third element, after the goodwill passage.
close the letter politely.
The conclusion is the final element, not the second.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 lists the medieval sequence in order: salutation, a passage to win the reader's goodwill, narration, petition, conclusion. The second part is the goodwill passage. The petition is tempting because it is the letter's purpose, but it comes fourth.

qs.q: The detail about Samuel Richardson's book of model letters supports the claim that:
o: epistolary novels were more popular than letter manuals.
Paragraph 2 makes no comparison of popularity between the two.
Richardson's novels were insincere and manipulative.
Paragraph 3 says performed sincerity is not therefore false.
the sincere familiar style was itself learned from conventions.
Correct: paragraph 2 offers it as evidence that the spontaneous style was learned.
medieval manuals were still used unchanged in the eighteenth century.
The detail concerns new model letters, not unchanged medieval manuals.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 notes that Richardson, whose letters seemed spontaneous, conceived his first novel while writing model letters for others to copy. That supports the claim that the sincere familiar style was itself learned. Reading it as proof of insincerity ignores paragraph 3: a performed sincerity is not therefore false.

qs.q: The author's position on laments that digital messaging has killed the art of the letter is that they:
o: are fully justified, since letters were more authentic than messages.
Paragraph 4 denies that letters were free of convention or more authentic.
are baseless, since nothing of value has been lost.
Paragraph 4 ends by calling the loss real.
are correct that sincerity has disappeared from writing.
The author says what was lost is not sincerity.
misidentify what was lost, even though something real was lost.
Correct: paragraph 4 says the change is delay and the loss is considered self-presentation, not sincerity.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says mourners imagine a lost authenticity, which letters never had, so they misidentify the loss; yet it ends by calling the real loss, a discipline of considered self-presentation forced by delay, genuine. Saying nothing was lost ignores the closing words that the loss is real.

qs.q: Which finding would best support the author's claim about the role of delay?
o: People revise messages more when they know these will be read only after a long delay.
Correct: paragraph 4 says delay forced writers to compose a self that would still hold when read.
Email users write longer messages to coworkers than to friends.
This concerns audience, not the effect of delay on composition.
Letters written by famous authors sell well at auction.
Market value says nothing about how delay shapes writing.
Text messages contain more abbreviations than letters do.
Abbreviation is a convention difference, not evidence about delay.
qs.x: The author's claim is causal: delay forced writers to compose a self that would still hold when read. Evidence that people revise more when they expect delayed reading isolates delay and shows the predicted effect. The audience and abbreviation options compare writing without varying delay.

passages.title: Grace Under Rules
text: Kant described beauty as purposiveness without purpose, the appearance of design in something not made to serve an end. Sport seems disqualified at once, since nearly every sport has an obvious purpose: winning. The philosopher David Best accordingly distinguished purposive sports, such as soccer or basketball, in which only results count, from aesthetic sports, such as diving or figure skating, in which the manner of performance is itself what is judged. In the first kind, Best held, beauty is a by-product; a clumsy goal counts as much as an elegant one.

Best's distinction is useful, but his conclusion does not match how sport is actually lived. Players and spectators care intensely about how a goal is scored, and fans of soccer call it the beautiful game without irony. Often, elegance is efficiency made visible: the most economical movement, free of wasted effort, is frequently the one we find graceful.

We should not, however, collapse beauty into efficiency. A bicycle kick is less reliable than a simple header, yet crowds rise for it. We admire the risk, the improbable, the thing that might easily have failed. The philosopher Bernard Suits defined playing a game as the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles. Rules create artificial difficulties, forbidding hands in soccer or limiting steps in basketball, and grace consists in mastering those difficulties with apparent ease.

Paradoxically, it is the aesthetic sports that have the most trouble with beauty. Once grace is translated into points, with difficulty values attached to each element, athletes are pushed to stack difficulty rather than pursue elegance, and critics complain that gymnastics now rewards acrobatics over artistry. Beauty in sport flourishes when it is not the score. When it becomes the score, it turns into one more thing to be calculated and maximized.

qs.q: As presented in the passage, Best's distinction holds that:
o: all sports are equally aesthetic in nature.
Paragraph 1 says Best separated sports into two different kinds.
in some sports the manner of performance is judged, while in others only results count.
Correct: paragraph 1 defines aesthetic sports by judged manner and purposive sports by results.
only team sports can be beautiful.
Best's examples of aesthetic sports, such as diving, are individual sports.
beauty in sport depends on the size of the crowd.
The passage never ties beauty to audience size.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 says Best split sports into purposive ones, where only results count, and aesthetic ones, like diving, where the manner of performance is judged. The team-sports option misreads the line he draws; it concerns what is scored, not how many compete.

qs.q: The author's main objection to Best is that:
o: Kant's definition of beauty does not apply to any human activity.
The author uses Kant as a starting point and does not reject him.
aesthetic sports should be scored only on results.
The author never proposes scoring diving or skating by results.
Best was wrong to distinguish kinds of sport at all.
Paragraph 2 calls the distinction useful while disputing its conclusion.
in purposive sports the manner of achievement is in fact widely valued.
Correct: paragraph 2 says players and spectators care intensely about how a goal is scored.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 accepts Best's distinction as useful but rejects his conclusion that beauty is a mere by-product in purposive sports, noting that players and fans care intensely how goals are scored. Rejecting the distinction outright is the trap, since the author calls it useful.

qs.q: The example of the bicycle kick serves mainly to show that:
o: admiration for athletic beauty cannot be reduced to efficiency.
Correct: paragraph 3 says the kick is less reliable than a header yet crowds rise for it.
headers are the most beautiful move in soccer.
Paragraph 3 uses the header as the efficient but less admired option.
risky moves should be banned for player safety.
Paragraph 3 praises risk as part of what we admire, not as a safety problem.
soccer is really an aesthetic sport in Best's sense.
The author does not reclassify soccer; goals still count regardless of manner.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 notes the bicycle kick is less reliable than a header, yet crowds rise for it, because we admire risk and improbability. That blocks equating beauty with efficiency, which paragraph 2 had partly endorsed. The author does not reclassify soccer as an aesthetic sport.

qs.q: According to the author, beauty in sport lies chiefly in:
o: the size of the victory margin.
The author separates beauty from results, so margin of victory is not the source.
the absence of any rules limiting movement.
Paragraph 3 says grace consists in mastering the difficulties that rules impose.
the graceful mastery of difficulties that the rules deliberately impose.
Correct: paragraph 3 links grace to overcoming unnecessary obstacles created by rules.
the judges' scores awarded for artistry.
Paragraph 4 argues that scoring beauty tends to undermine it.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 draws on Suits: games are voluntary attempts to overcome unnecessary obstacles, and grace means mastering rule-made difficulties with apparent ease. Judges' scores for artistry are the trap; paragraph 4 argues that scoring beauty tends to corrupt it.

qs.q: If a soccer league began awarding bonus points for goals that judges rated as elegant, the author would most likely predict that:
o: the beauty of soccer would increase because it is now rewarded.
Paragraph 4 argues that scoring beauty undermines rather than increases it.
players would ignore the bonus because goals already count fully.
The author expects athletes to respond to scoring incentives, as gymnasts did.
the rule would turn soccer into a purely purposive sport.
Judging manner would move soccer toward the aesthetic kind, not away from it.
players would chase whatever moves judges reward, making elegance a calculated target.
Correct: paragraph 4 says beauty becomes one more thing to calculate and maximize once it is the score.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 says that once grace becomes points, athletes pursue whatever earns them, as gymnasts stacked difficulty, so beauty becomes something calculated and maximized. A bonus for judged elegance would do the same in soccer. Predicting that beauty would rise ignores the author's warning.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's claim in paragraph 4?
o: Gymnasts added more difficult elements after difficulty values rose.
This supports the author's claim that points push athletes to stack difficulty.
Routines widely praised as graceful became more common after a judged sport gave artistry more weight in scoring.
Correct: the author says beauty withers when it becomes the score, which this outcome contradicts.
Soccer fans prefer close games to lopsided ones.
Fan taste for close games does not bear on scoring beauty in aesthetic sports.
Divers practice their entries more often than their takeoffs.
Training habits do not test whether scoring beauty undermines it.
qs.x: The author claims beauty flourishes when it is not the score and withers when it is. A judged sport that gave artistry more weight and saw more widely praised graceful routines would contradict that. The gymnasts stacking difficulty fits the author's claim, so it supports rather than challenges it.

passages.title: The Unlucky Driver
text: Two drivers, equally tired and equally careless, take the same curve too fast. For one, the road is empty. For the other, a child runs into the street. We blame the second driver far more, and the law punishes her far more harshly. Yet most of us also accept a principle of control: people may be morally judged only for what lies within their control. Since nothing distinguishes the two drivers except what happened to be in the road, the principle and our practice collide.

The philosopher Thomas Nagel showed how far the problem reaches. Beyond luck in outcomes, there is luck in circumstances: an ordinary citizen of Nazi Germany who collaborated may have been no worse than someone who emigrated before being tested, and who would have collaborated too. There is also luck in constitution, in the temperament and dispositions a person never chose. Applied consistently, the control principle leaves almost nothing to judge, since even the will is shaped by temperament and circumstance.

One response is to say that only the will deserves blame, and that our harsher feelings toward the unlucky driver are an illusion. This rescues consistency at the price of making morality unrecognizable. It would make irrational what Bernard Williams called agent-regret, the distinctive anguish of a truck driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over a child. He feels something a bystander does not, and we would think less of him if he felt nothing.

Moral luck, I think, is not a paradox to be dissolved but a fact about agents who act in a world they do not control. The practical lesson is to separate blame from responsibility. Blame should track the will and be tempered by mercy. Responsibility is something we take on for what our actions actually bring about. The unlucky driver need not be judged more wicked than the lucky one, but she owes the repair that the lucky one does not.

qs.q: As described in the passage, the principle of control states that:
o: people should be judged by the outcomes of their actions.
This describes our practice of blaming outcomes, which collides with the principle.
the law should punish all careless drivers equally.
Paragraph 1 states a moral principle, not a rule about legal punishment.
people may be morally judged only for what lies within their control.
Correct: paragraph 1 states the principle in exactly these terms.
temperament determines all moral choices.
Constitutive luck is a separate idea in paragraph 2, not the principle itself.
qs.x: Paragraph 1 states the control principle: people may be judged only for what lies within their control. Judging by outcomes is the trap; it is our actual practice, which paragraph 1 says collides with the principle, since the two drivers differ only in what was in the road.

qs.q: The example of citizens in Nazi Germany is used to illustrate:
o: luck in the circumstances a person happens to face.
Correct: paragraph 2 introduces it as luck in circumstances, beyond luck in outcomes.
luck in the outcomes of a single action.
Outcome luck is the drivers' case; the Nazi example is offered as something beyond it.
luck in inborn temperament.
Paragraph 2 presents constitutive luck separately, after the Nazi example.
the success of the control principle in history.
The example shows the principle's trouble, not its success.
qs.x: Paragraph 2 offers Nagel's Nazi-era example as luck in circumstances: whether one faced the test at all. It is introduced as something beyond outcome luck, the drivers' case, and before luck in constitution, which concerns temperament. Keep the three kinds distinct.

qs.q: The author objects to the view that only the will deserves blame because that view:
o: fails to explain why careless drivers are careless.
The author's objection concerns moral responses, not the causes of carelessness.
would require harsher punishment for lucky drivers.
The view would equalize blame, not raise blame for the lucky driver.
is inconsistent with the principle of control.
Paragraph 3 says the view rescues consistency with that principle.
preserves consistency but makes ordinary responses such as agent-regret seem irrational.
Correct: paragraph 3 says it makes morality unrecognizable and agent-regret irrational.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 grants that the will-only view rescues consistency with the control principle, but says it makes morality unrecognizable by rendering agent-regret irrational. So inconsistency with the control principle is exactly wrong: consistency is that view's strength, not its flaw.

qs.q: A hiker carefully douses her campfire, but a freak gust revives an ember that burns a cabin. Applying the author's final distinction, the author would say she:
o: is more blameworthy than a hiker whose fire stayed out.
Paragraph 4 says blame tracks the will, which was the same in both hikers.
is no more blameworthy than a lucky hiker but should help repair the loss.
Correct: paragraph 4 separates blame, tracking the will, from responsibility for outcomes.
bears no connection to the fire and owes nothing.
Paragraph 4 says agents take on responsibility for what their actions bring about.
should be punished as harshly as an arsonist.
Blame should track the will and mercy; she had no ill will.
qs.x: Paragraph 4 separates blame, which tracks the will and is tempered by mercy, from responsibility, which we take on for what our actions bring about. The careful hiker's will matched a lucky hiker's, so blame is no greater, but she owes repair. Saying she owes nothing ignores the responsibility half.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's use of agent-regret?
o: Drivers in faultless accidents often report lasting distress.
This supports the author's description of agent-regret.
Bystanders to accidents also feel some sorrow.
The author already allows that bystanders feel something, only less.
People who felt no special distress after faultless accidents were generally judged admirable rather than deficient.
Correct: paragraph 3 relies on the claim that we would think less of someone who felt nothing.
Courts rarely punish drivers in faultless accidents.
Legal practice does not bear on whether agent-regret is a fitting moral response.
qs.x: Paragraph 3 rests the argument on our intuition that we would think less of an agent who felt nothing after harming someone faultlessly. If people who felt no such distress were judged admirable, that intuition, and so the use of agent-regret, would collapse. Lasting distress in drivers supports rather than weakens it.
